children.title: Schedule-Class Inclusion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Containment relations, dominance distinctions, and instances separating the schedule classes.

assumptions_latex: Schedules are feasible and nonpreemptive under the standard local-shift, global-shift, and avoidable-idleness definitions.
The instance class permits examples with genuine sequencing choices and release or precedence restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In general, \(\mathcal{N}\subsetneq\mathcal{A}\subsetneq\mathcal{S}\); equality may hold for special instance classes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the non-delay, active, and semi-active classes have the standard nested hierarchy
source_required: strictness hypotheses and witness instances require an authoritative scheduling source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the general hierarchy; special environments can collapse one or both inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every non-delay schedule is active, because a global left shift would expose avoidable idle capacity before some operation; every active schedule is semi-active, because a feasible local left shift is a particular global left shift. Consequently \(\mathcal{N}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\). Across general nonpreemptive scheduling instances, both inclusions are strict: active schedules with avoidable idleness and semi-active schedules admitting an improving resequencing exist. For restricted instance families, either inclusion may become equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-delay schedules form a subclass of active schedules, which form a subclass of semi-active schedules; both inclusions are strict in general.
knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Class Inclusion Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A property is appropriate for the inclusion-boundary leaf, but the generality and strictness of both inclusions require an authoritative scheduling source and a precise ambient instance class. The statement also contains proof-style justification ('because'), which must be removed from a knowledge statement after the mathematical claim is sourced.

children.title: Preemptive Processing
children.top_down_role: Scheduling regimes permitting interruption and later continuation of work.

assumptions_latex: Each operation \(o\) has required processing amount \(p_o>0\).
Processing rates and feasibility constraints determine which execution intervals contribute to completed work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The processing regime is preemptive exactly when feasible schedules may use \(k_o>1\) for some operation \(o\).

notation.meaning: required processing amount of operation o
disjoint execution intervals of operation o
number of processing pieces of operation o

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: preemption conventionally permits interrupted execution whose pieces complete one processing requirement
source_required: supplied splitting-off locator is unrelated to scheduling preemption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines interruption permission without implicitly permitting migration or parallel execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operation \(o\) is processed preemptively when its execution may occupy finitely many pairwise disjoint intervals \([a_{oq},b_{oq})\), \(q=1,\ldots,k_o\), whose credited processing sums to \(p_o\), with execution suspended between consecutive intervals. Unless migration is separately allowed, all intervals use the same machine; unless parallel execution is separately allowed, the intervals do not overlap. A preemptive regime permits \(k_o>1\), whereas a nonpreemptive regime requires \(k_o=1\) for every operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preemption permits an operation to be interrupted and resumed in multiple intervals, without by itself permitting machine migration or simultaneous pieces.
knowledge_statements.title: Preemptive Processing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the preemptive-processing leaf and correctly distinguishes preemption from migration and parallel execution, but the only inventory locator concerning splitting-off is unrelated. A scheduling source is required, and 'credited processing sums to p_o' must be made precise for the assumed processing-rate model.

children.title: Migratory Processing
children.top_down_role: Scheduling regimes permitting resumed work to use a different eligible resource.

assumptions_latex: There is a finite job set \(J\) and machine set \(M\).
Each job \(j\in J\) requires total processing volume \(p_j>0\).
A machine processes at most one job at each time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible schedule is migratory precisely when some job may be processed on different machines at disjoint times while never executing simultaneously on two machines.

notation.meaning: Set of times at which job j executes on machine m
Lebesgue measure of a measurable time set
Processing volume required by job j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preemptive migration without simultaneous execution of one job on multiple machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Migratory processing allows a preempted job to resume on another machine, but the job cannot execute on multiple machines simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.title: Migratory Processing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is plausible, but no scheduling source supports the unit-rate processing model, measure-zero convention, or distinction between permitting migration and a schedule actually using migration.

children.title: Job-Splitting Regimes
children.top_down_role: Models permitting a job or lot to be divided into separately scheduled portions.

assumptions_latex: There is a finite job set \(J\) and machine set \(M\).
Each job \(j\in J\) has processing requirement \(p_j>0\) and split limit \(q_j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
Each piece is assigned nonnegative processing volume.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is unsplittable when \(q_j=1\), finitely splittable when \(1<q_j<\infty\), and arbitrarily divisible when no finite split limit is imposed.

notation.meaning: Number of pieces created from job j
Processing volume of piece ell of job j
Maximum permitted number of pieces of job j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Volume partitioning; concurrency and machine eligibility remain separate modeling coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A job-splitting regime specifies, for each \(j\in J\), whether its processing requirement may be replaced by pieces \((j,1),\ldots,(j,k_j)\) satisfying \(1\le k_j\le q_j\), \(p_{j\ell}>0\), and \(\sum_{\ell=1}^{k_j}p_{j\ell}=p_j\). Each piece receives its own feasible machine and time assignment, while any precedence, setup, and simultaneous-execution restrictions are imposed separately. The unsplittable regime fixes \(q_j=1\); a finitely splittable regime has finite \(q_j>1\); and a continuously divisible regime permits arbitrary finite partitions, equivalently imposing no finite upper bound on \(k_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job-splitting regime determines whether a job's processing volume may be partitioned into one, boundedly many, or arbitrarily many schedulable pieces.
knowledge_statements.title: Job-Splitting Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The volume-partition model is coherent, but the bounded, arbitrary-finite, and continuously divisible terminology and the separation from simultaneous execution require an inspectable scheduling source.

children.title: Interruption Cost Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Setup loss, migration cost, indivisibility, and continuity restrictions limiting processing flexibility.

assumptions_latex: Each job \(j\) has a schedule containing \(n_j\ge 1\) maximal execution intervals.
Each additional interval after the first incurs cost \(c_j\in[0,+\infty]\).
The base schedule objective is \(F(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundaries \(c_j=0\), \(0<c_j<+\infty\), and \(c_j=+\infty\) distinguish free, penalized, and forbidden interruption, respectively.

notation.meaning: Number of maximal execution intervals of job j
Cost per interruption of job j
Base objective value of schedule S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear per-interruption costs, including zero-cost and prohibition limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a schedule \(S\), define the number of interruptions of job \(j\) by \(r_j(S)=n_j(S)-1\), where \(n_j(S)\) counts its maximal positive-length execution intervals. Under a linear interruption penalty, evaluate \(S\) by \(F_c(S)=F(S)+\sum_j c_jr_j(S)\). The boundary \(c_j=0\) makes interruptions cost-free; \(0<c_j<+\infty\) permits but penalizes them; and \(c_j=+\infty\) enforces \(r_j(S)=0\) for every finite-valued feasible schedule. A fixed charge may equivalently be constrained by a budget \(\sum_j c_jr_j(S)\le B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero, finite positive, and infinite interruption costs respectively model free preemption, penalized preemption, and nonpreemptive processing.
knowledge_statements.title: Interruption Cost Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear per-interruption model is mathematically coherent and the content kind fits the boundary container, but no source establishes this particular cost model or the claimed budget equivalence as the intended taxonomy.

children.title: Static Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies formed from a fixed instance before schedule execution.

assumptions_latex: The instance data \(I\) are available before execution begins.
No realized execution history is an argument of the decision rule.
The output belongs to the feasible schedule set \(\mathcal{S}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A policy is static exactly when its complete schedule is a function of the initial instance alone.

notation.meaning: Set of feasible schedules for instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-loop policies fixed before schedule execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) contain all data declared available at planning time, and let \(\mathcal{S}(I)\) be the feasible schedules. A static scheduling policy is a map \(\pi:I\mapsto S\in\mathcal{S}(I)\) whose entire assignment and timing decisions are fixed before execution. Thus, for any two execution histories \(h_t\) and \(h'_t\) compatible with the same initial instance, the prescribed future decisions coincide whenever both prescriptions remain executable. If deviations make the original schedule infeasible, the static policy itself supplies no history-dependent replacement decision; invoking such a rule changes the policy class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static policy fixes the complete schedule from initially available instance data and does not adapt decisions to execution history.
knowledge_statements.title: Static Scheduling Policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The open-loop definition is plausible, but the treatment of infeasible prescribed actions and the exact static-policy convention need an authoritative scheduling-policy source.

children.title: Dynamic Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies making decisions as jobs, resources, or state information evolve.

assumptions_latex: At each decision epoch \(t\), the scheduler observes a state \(x_t\).
The admissible action set is \(A(x_t)\).
State evolution may depend on realized disturbances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A policy is dynamic when its action at each decision epoch is a nonanticipative function of the currently observed history or state.

notation.meaning: Information history available at time t
Observed scheduling state at time t
Admissible scheduling actions in state x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-loop, nonanticipative scheduling at successive decision epochs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At decision epochs \(t=0,1,\ldots\), let \(H_t\) be the observed history and \(x_t\) its scheduling state, including released unfinished jobs and available resources. A dynamic scheduling policy is a sequence \(\pi=(\pi_t)_t\) with actions \(a_t=\pi_t(H_t)\in A(x_t)\). Nonanticipativity requires that histories identical through \(t\) receive the same action at \(t\), regardless of later data or disturbances. The policy is genuinely state-adaptive when there exist feasible histories \(H_t\neq H'_t\) for which \(\pi_t(H_t)\neq\pi_t(H'_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic policy chooses each scheduling action from the information observed so far and may choose differently in different realized states.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Scheduling Policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonanticipative closed-loop formulation is coherent, but no cited source supports the asserted requirement that a dynamic policy be genuinely state-adaptive rather than merely permitted to depend on state.

children.title: Reactive Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies revising an incumbent schedule after disruptions or deviations.

assumptions_latex: A baseline schedule \(S^0\) is available.
A disruption event \(e_t\) is observed at time \(t\).
Decisions completed before \(t\) are immutable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A policy is reactive when a disruption triggers a feasible revised continuation schedule, optionally balancing operating quality against deviation from the baseline.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-triggered revision of a baseline schedule after disruption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^0\) be a baseline schedule and let \(e_t\) denote a disruption observed at time \(t\), such as a breakdown, delay, or urgent arrival. A reactive scheduling policy applies a nonanticipative repair map \(R(S^0,H_t,e_t)=S^t\), where \(S^t\) preserves completed decisions and supplies a feasible continuation under the updated data. A common reactive criterion selects \(S^t\) to minimize \(F(S^t)+\lambda D(S^t,S^0)\) over feasible continuations, with \(D\) measuring schedule disruption and \(\lambda\ge0\). Without a triggering event, the baseline remains prescribed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reactive policy repairs a baseline schedule after an observed disruption, often trading operating performance against deviation from the original plan.
knowledge_statements.title: Reactive Scheduling Policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event-triggered repair interpretation fits the leaf, but reactive scheduling conventions vary; the mandatory baseline, preservation rule, and stability objective require a specific source.

children.title: Policy Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundaries between fixed planning, state-dependent dispatch, and disruption-driven revision.

assumptions_latex: There is an indexed family of admissible policies \((\Pi_r)_{r\in R}\).
The active regime at epoch \(t\) is \(r_t\in R\).
Switching from \(r	o r'\) may incur cost \(K(r,r')\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A transition regime is specified by the allowed regime graph, switching rule, and any transition costs, delays, or frequency constraints.

notation.meaning: Cost of switching from regime r to regime r prime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Switching among policy classes during a scheduling horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) index scheduling-policy classes and let \(G=(R,E)\) be a directed transition graph. A policy transition regime consists of an active-class process \((r_t)_t\), a switching rule \(r_{t+1}=g(H_t,r_t)\), and policies \(\pi_t\in\Pi_{r_t}\), subject to \((r_t,r_{t+1})\in E\). A transition may add cost \(K(r_t,r_{t+1})\), consume delay \(d(r_t,r_{t+1})\), or be limited by \(\sum_t\mathbf{1}\{r_{t+1}\neq r_t\}\le L\). Static, event-triggered, and unrestricted transition regimes arise by restricting \(g\) and \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A policy transition regime specifies when scheduling may switch between policy classes and which switching costs, delays, or frequency limits apply.
knowledge_statements.title: Policy Transition Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed switching-system model is internally coherent, but “policy transition regime” is broad and no authoritative source establishes this graph-and-cost formalization as its intended scheduling meaning.

children.title: Offline Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling with complete instance information available before decisions begin.

assumptions_latex: The complete finite instance \(I\) is revealed before any scheduling decision.
The algorithm has no computational restriction unless separately stated.
The objective \(F_I(S)\) is defined on feasible schedules \(\mathcal{S}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Offline scheduling minimizes the objective over schedules selected with knowledge of the entire instance.

notation.meaning: Objective value of schedule S on I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-instance information is available before the first decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An offline scheduling regime reveals the complete instance \(I\), including all jobs and all deterministic parameters designated by the model, before any irrevocable scheduling decision. An offline algorithm is therefore a map \(A:I\mapsto A(I)\in\mathcal{S}(I)\). For a minimization objective, the offline benchmark is \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}(I)}F_I(S)\). Offline information does not imply polynomial-time solvability, clairvoyance about random quantities excluded from \(I\), or permission to violate the schedule-feasibility rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In offline scheduling, the entire modeled instance is known before decisions begin; the offline optimum is the best feasible full-information schedule.
knowledge_statements.title: Offline Scheduling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The full-information offline formulation is standard and precise, but the candidate supplies no scheduling or online-algorithms citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Online Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling with arrivals or attributes revealed during decision making.

assumptions_latex: Instance information is revealed over time as a history \(H_t\).
Decisions prescribed at time \(t\) may be irrevocable.
Future unrevealed data cannot influence the current action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An online scheduling policy is feasible and nonanticipative, and its quality may be measured by a competitive ratio against the offline optimum.

notation.meaning: Cost incurred by online algorithm A on instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipative decisions under sequential revelation of instance data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an online scheduling regime, information arrives sequentially. At every decision time \(t\), an algorithm \(A\) chooses a feasible action \(a_t=A_t(H_t)\) using only the revealed history \(H_t\); identical histories through \(t\) must induce identical actions. For a minimization objective, \(A\) is \(\rho\)-competitive with additive constant \(\beta\ge0\) if \(F_A(I)\leho\operatorname{OPT}(I)+\beta\) for every admissible instance \(I\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) knows the full instance. Randomized policies require an explicitly stated expectation or adversary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online scheduling makes feasible decisions from information revealed so far; competitive analysis compares its cost with a full-information offline optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Scheduling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonanticipative online definition and competitive-ratio formula are plausible, but no source supports the conventions for additive constants, randomization, and adversaries.

children.title: Lookahead Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling with bounded advance information about future arrivals or states.

assumptions_latex: At time \(t\), the ordinary online history \(H_t\) is known.
A lookahead operator reveals prescribed future data \(L_w(t)\).
Actions remain nonanticipative beyond the revealed window.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A width-\(w\) lookahead policy may depend on \((H_t,L_w(t))\) but not on information outside that view.

notation.meaning: Future information exposed by width-w lookahead at t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite future information supplements, but does not replace, online revelation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a lookahead specification \(L_w(t)\), such as jobs released during \((t,t+w]\) or the next \(w\) arrivals. A width-\(w\) lookahead scheduling policy chooses \(a_t=\pi_t(H_t,L_w(t))\) from the currently feasible actions. If two instances agree on \(H_t\) and on all data exposed by \(L_w(t)\), they must induce the same action at \(t\), even if they differ later. The case \(w=0\) recovers the corresponding online-information regime; full-horizon lookahead recovers offline information when it reveals the complete remaining instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lookahead policy sees a specified finite portion of future input while remaining unable to use information beyond that revealed view.
knowledge_statements.title: Lookahead Scheduling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly makes the lookahead specification explicit, but time-window and next-arrival lookahead are distinct models whose endpoint cases require a cited convention.

children.title: Information-Advantage Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Performance effects associated with additional foresight, predictions, or delayed commitment.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Advantage Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic value of information and additive or multiplicative advantage boundaries for a fixed minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an information model \(\mathcal{I}\), let \(\Pi(\mathcal{I})\) be its admissible nonanticipative policies and define \(V(\mathcal{I})=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal{I})}\mathbb{E}[F(\pi)]\), where the expectation is taken under a fixed specified probability and randomization convention. If \(\mathcal{I}_1\preceq\mathcal{I}_2\) means that every observation available under \(\mathcal{I}_1\) is available under \(\mathcal{I}_2\), then \(\Pi(\mathcal{I}_1)\subseteq\Pi(\mathcal{I}_2)\) and therefore \(V(\mathcal{I}_2)\le V(\mathcal{I}_1)\). The additive information advantage is \(V(\mathcal{I}_1)-V(\mathcal{I}_2)\ge 0\). When \(V(\mathcal{I}_2)>0\), the multiplicative advantage is \(V(\mathcal{I}_1)/V(\mathcal{I}_2)\ge 1\); a zero denominator requires a separately stated convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed minimization and probability model, richer information cannot increase the best achievable expected cost; additive and, when defined, multiplicative gaps quantify the advantage.
assumptions_latex: The problem has a nonnegative minimization objective \(F\).
A fixed probability law and policy-randomization convention define \(\mathbb{E}[F(\pi)]\).
Information models \(\mathcal{I}_1\) and \(\mathcal{I}_2\) satisfy \(\mathcal{I}_1\preceq\mathcal{I}_2\), so every \(\mathcal{I}_1\)-policy can be simulated under \(\mathcal{I}_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(\mathcal{I}_2)\le V(\mathcal{I}_1)\), with additive advantage \(V(\mathcal{I}_1)-V(\mathcal{I}_2)\ge0\) and multiplicative advantage defined when \(V(\mathcal{I}_2)>0\).

notation.meaning: Policies admissible under information model I
Best attainable expected cost under information model I
Information model I2 reveals at least every observation revealed by I1

children.title: Makespan Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on the terminal completion horizon of a schedule.

knowledge_statements.title: Makespan Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite scheduling with completion time measured from a common time origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible schedule \(S\in\mathcal{S}\), let \(C_j(S)\) be the completion time of job \(j\), meaning the time at which all processing required by that job has finished. The makespan is \(C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}C_j(S)\). A makespan objective selects a schedule satisfying \(S^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{S\in\mathcal{S}}C_{\max}(S)\), with optimal value \(C_{\max}^\star=\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}}C_{\max}(S)\). When the common time origin is zero, this is the elapsed time until all jobs are complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Makespan is the completion time of the last finished job; makespan minimization seeks a feasible schedule that finishes all jobs earliest.
assumptions_latex: There is a finite job set \(J\).
Every feasible schedule \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) gives each job \(j\in J\) a finite completion time \(C_j(S)\).
The objective is minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The makespan objective is \(\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}}C_{\max}(S)\), where \(C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}C_j(S)\).

notation.meaning: Completion time of job j in schedule S
Maximum job completion time in schedule S

children.title: Machine-Load Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on total or extremal work assigned to individual machines.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Load Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Load objectives evaluate how processing work is distributed among machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For machines \(M\) and jobs \(J\), let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that job \(j\) is assigned to machine \(i\), with processing time \(p_{ij}\ge 0\). The load of machine \(i\) is \(B_i=\sum_{j\in J}p_{ij}x_{ij}\). A machine-load objective minimizes a specified function \(g(B_1,\ldots,B_{|M|})\), such as the peak load \(\max_{i\in M}B_i\), a weighted total \(\sum_{i\in M}a_iB_i\), or an imbalance measure \(\sum_{i\in M}(B_i-\bar B)^2\), where \(\bar B=|M|^{-1}\sum_{i\in M}B_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machine-load objectives minimize peak, weighted total, or imbalance functions of the processing work assigned to each machine.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) and \(J\) are finite.
\(p_{ij}\ge 0\) whenever assignment \(x_{ij}=1\) is permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x g(B_1(x),\ldots,B_{|M|}(x))\) over feasible schedules or assignments.

notation.meaning: processing load assigned to machine i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard deterministic scheduling objective definitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Machine-Load Objectives container and is mathematically coherent, but no scheduling source or inspectable locator is supplied for the proposed objective family and examples. Standard-field rationale alone does not satisfy the statement-review evidence requirement.

children.title: Resource-Utilization Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on productive resource use, idle capacity, or occupancy.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Utilization Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Utilization normalizes occupied resource time by available capacity over a specified horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let resource \(i\) provide capacity \(c_i(t)\ge 0\) over a horizon \([0,H]\), and let \(b_i(t)\) be the capacity occupied by a feasible schedule, with \(0\le b_i(t)\le c_i(t)\). Its utilization is \(U_i=\frac{\int_0^H b_i(t)\,dt}{\int_0^H c_i(t)\,dt}\) whenever the denominator is positive. Resource-utilization objectives maximize an aggregate such as \(\sum_i w_iU_i\), maximize \(\min_i U_i\), or minimize deviations \(\sum_i w_i(U_i-u_i^*)^2\) from prescribed targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resource-utilization objectives optimize occupied capacity relative to available capacity, using aggregate, minimum, or target-deviation criteria.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\int_0^H c_i(t)\,dt<\infty\) for every evaluated resource \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each evaluated schedule induces \(U_i\in[0,1]\) and an objective value determined by the chosen utilization aggregator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and capacity-time ratio fit Resource-Utilization Objectives, but utilization conventions depend on the scheduling model and no authoritative scheduling source with a specific locator supports this formulation or its listed aggregators.

children.title: Load–Utilization Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions among horizon reduction, load distribution, and capacity usage.

knowledge_statements.title: Load–Utilization Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bicriteria representation separates absolute congestion from normalized productive use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each feasible schedule \(s\in\mathcal S\), let \(L(s)=\max_{i\in M}B_i(s)\) be peak machine load and let \(U(s)=\sum_{i\in M}w_iU_i(s)\) be aggregate utilization, where \(w_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_iw_i=1\). The load–utilization tradeoff is the bicriteria problem \(\min_{s\in\mathcal S}(L(s),-U(s))\). Equivalent scalarized models include \(\min_{s\in\mathcal S}\{L(s)-\lambda U(s)\}\) for \(\lambda\ge0\), or \(\min L(s)\) subject to \(U(s)\ge u\). A schedule is Pareto efficient if no feasible schedule weakly improves both criteria and strictly improves at least one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff jointly reduces peak load and increases utilization; Pareto, weighted-sum, or utilization-threshold formulations select compromises.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is the nonempty feasible schedule set.
\(L(s)\) and \(U(s)\) are finite for every \(s\in\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The attainable objective set is \(\{(L(s),U(s)):s\in\mathcal S\}\), with compromises represented by its Pareto frontier.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard bicriteria and Pareto representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A bicriteria representation fits the terminal container, but the assertion that the weighted-sum and threshold models are equivalent scalarizations requires qualification: weighted sums need not recover every Pareto-efficient point in a nonconvex attainable set. No source is supplied to establish the intended scheduling setting or supported equivalence.

children.title: Completion-Time Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on individual or aggregate job completion epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Completion-Time Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completion-time criteria evaluate the absolute finishing times of scheduled jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible schedule of jobs \(J\), let \(C_j\) be the time at which all processing required by job \(j\) is finished. A completion-time objective minimizes a nondecreasing function of \((C_j)_{j\in J}\). Standard forms are total completion time \(\sum_{j\in J}C_j\), weighted total completion time \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j\) with \(w_j\ge0\), and maximum completion time \(\max_{j\in J}C_j\). Unlike flow time, completion time is measured from the common time origin rather than from each job's release time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Completion-time objectives minimize a nondecreasing aggregate of job finishing times, such as their sum, weighted sum, or maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(C_j\) is finite for each job in every evaluated feasible schedule.
\(w_j\ge0\) in weighted criteria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{s\in\mathcal S}G((C_j(s))_{j\in J})\) for a specified coordinatewise nondecreasing function \(G\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes absolute completion time from release-relative flow time and fits the container, but it has no cited scheduling source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Flow-Time Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on time spent in the scheduling system after release.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Time Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow time measures each job's elapsed residence after release and before completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For job \(j\) with release time \(r_j\) and completion time \(C_j\), its flow time is \(F_j=C_j-r_j\). A flow-time objective minimizes a nondecreasing aggregate of \((F_j)_{j\in J}\), commonly \(\sum_{j\in J}F_j\), \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jF_j\), or \(\max_{j\in J}F_j\). When every release time equals the same constant \(r\), minimizing total or weighted total flow time is equivalent to minimizing the corresponding completion-time criterion because the objectives differ by a schedule-independent constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flow-time objectives minimize elapsed time from each job's release until its completion, using total, weighted, or maximum aggregation.
assumptions_latex: \(C_j\ge r_j\) for every job \(j\).
\(J\) is finite.
\(w_j\ge0\) in weighted criteria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{s\in\mathcal S}G((C_j(s)-r_j)_{j\in J})\) for a specified coordinatewise nondecreasing function \(G\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The flow-time definition and common-release-time equivalence are mathematically precise and fit the container, but no authoritative source with a specific section or page is provided.

children.title: Waiting-Time Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria focused on queued or nonprocessing portions of job residence.

knowledge_statements.title: Waiting-Time Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Waiting time excludes intervals during which a released job is actually processed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For job \(j\), let \(r_j\) and \(C_j\) be its release and completion times, and let \(P_j\) be its total processing time within \([r_j,C_j]\). Its waiting time is \(W_j=C_j-r_j-P_j\), including all released but nonprocessing intervals under the chosen scheduling convention. A waiting-time objective minimizes a nondecreasing aggregate such as \(\sum_{j\in J}W_j\), \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jW_j\), or \(\max_{j\in J}W_j\). If \(P_j\) is schedule-independent, total flow-time and waiting-time objectives differ only by a constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Waiting-time objectives minimize released time spent without processing, aggregated by a sum, weighted sum, or maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(C_j-r_j\ge P_j\ge0\) for every job \(j\).
\(J\) is finite.
\(w_j\ge0\) in weighted criteria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{s\in\mathcal S}G((W_j(s))_{j\in J})\), where \(W_j(s)=C_j(s)-r_j-P_j(s)\).

notation.meaning: total time job j is processed

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard flow-time minus processing-time convention
waiting convention may require model-specific refinement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed identity fits Waiting-Time Objectives under the stated convention, but that convention is model-sensitive and lacks a source. In addition, the notation table introduces F_j even though the statement and conclusion do not use or define it explicitly.

children.title: Residence-Time Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Structural links among release epochs, processing durations, waiting periods, and completion epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Residence-Time Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The decomposition partitions release-to-completion residence into processing and nonprocessing time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each job \(j\), partition its residence interval \([r_j,C_j]\) into measurable processing periods of total length \(P_j\) and nonprocessing periods of total length \(W_j\). Then \(F_j=C_j-r_j=P_j+W_j\). Consequently, \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jF_j=\sum_{j\in J}w_jP_j+\sum_{j\in J}w_jW_j\). If each \(P_j\) is fixed independently of the schedule, minimizing weighted total residence time is equivalent to minimizing weighted total waiting time; if processing duration is schedule-dependent, that equivalence need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job's residence time equals processing time plus waiting time; weighted flow and waiting objectives are equivalent when processing times are fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(C_j\ge r_j\) and \([r_j,C_j]\) is partitioned into processing and nonprocessing periods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_j=P_j+W_j\) and \(\sum_jw_jF_j=\sum_jw_jP_j+\sum_jw_jW_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind is appropriate, and the residence-time decomposition is internally coherent under the stated measurable partition. It nevertheless lacks an authoritative scheduling source and inspectable locator.

children.title: Lateness Objectives
children.top_down_role: Signed due-date deviation criteria at job or schedule level.

knowledge_statements.title: Lateness Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lateness records signed deviation from a job's due date.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each job \(j\) with completion time \(C_j\) and due date \(d_j\), define lateness by \(L_j=C_j-d_j\). Thus \(L_j<0\) denotes early completion and \(L_j>0\) denotes late completion. Lateness objectives include minimizing maximum lateness \(L_{\max}=\max_{j\in J}L_j\) and, when a signed aggregate is intended, minimizing \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jL_j\). Because signed total lateness rewards earliness, it is distinct from total tardiness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lateness is signed completion-time deviation from a due date; objectives commonly minimize maximum lateness or a specified signed aggregate.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(C_j\) and \(d_j\) are finite real numbers.
\(w_j\ge0\) in weighted criteria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{s\in\mathcal S}\max_{j\in J}(C_j(s)-d_j)\), or another explicitly selected aggregate of signed lateness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed lateness definition and distinction from tardiness fit the container, but no scheduling reference with a specific locator supports the terminology and objective examples.

children.title: Tardiness Objectives
children.top_down_role: Positive due-date violation criteria, including weighted and aggregate variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Tardiness Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tardiness is the nonnegative portion of completion beyond the due date.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each job \(j\), tardiness is \(T_j=(C_j-d_j)^+=\max\{C_j-d_j,0\}\). It is zero for on-time or early completion and equals lateness for late completion. Standard tardiness objectives minimize \(\sum_{j\in J}T_j\), \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jT_j\), or \(T_{\max}=\max_{j\in J}T_j\). These criteria do not reward completion earlier than the due date unless an additional earliness term is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tardiness is positive delay beyond a due date; objectives minimize its total, weighted total, or maximum without rewarding earliness.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(C_j\) and \(d_j\) are finite real numbers.
\(w_j\ge0\) in weighted criteria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{s\in\mathcal S}G((\max\{C_j(s)-d_j,0\})_{j\in J})\) for the selected nondecreasing aggregate \(G\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-part definition and listed tardiness objectives are precise and appropriate for the container, but the record supplies no authoritative source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Service-Level Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on deadline compliance, response targets, or guaranteed service thresholds.

knowledge_statements.title: Service-Level Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Service level measures the fraction or weight of jobs meeting a specified timing promise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given completion times \(C_j\), promised deadlines \(d_j\), and weights \(w_j\ge0\) with \(\sum_jw_j>0\), define the weighted on-time service level by \(S=\frac{\sum_{j\in J}w_j\mathbf 1\{C_j\le d_j\}}{\sum_{j\in J}w_j}\). A service-level objective maximizes \(S\), equivalently minimizing weighted late-job count \(\sum_jw_j\mathbf 1\{C_j>d_j\}\), or imposes the requirement \(S\ge\alpha\) for a prescribed \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). Alternative promised-response thresholds must be specified explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A service-level objective maximizes the weighted proportion of jobs completed by their deadlines or requires that proportion to exceed a target.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and nonempty.
\(w_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jw_j>0\).
\(\alpha\in[0,1]\) when a target is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximize \(S\), or require \(S\ge\alpha\), over feasible schedules.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted on-time fraction is a coherent service-level definition, but service-level semantics are application-dependent. No cited source establishes that this is the intended convention for the terminal container.

children.title: Due-Date Compliance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relationships among signed deviation, late completion, and threshold-based service performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Due-Date Compliance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compliance regimes distinguish hard feasibility, soft penalties, and bounded violation counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For due dates \(d_j\), a hard-compliance regime restricts feasible schedules to those satisfying \(C_j\le d_j\) for every \(j\in J\). A soft-compliance regime permits violations and minimizes a penalty \(\sum_{j\in J}\phi_j((C_j-d_j)^+)\), where each \(\phi_j:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R_+\) is nondecreasing and satisfies \(\phi_j(0)=0\). A quota regime permits limited noncompliance through \(\sum_{j\in J}w_j\mathbf 1\{C_j>d_j\}\le K\). Thus due-date compliance may enter respectively as feasibility, objective cost, or a violation-budget constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Due dates may be enforced as hard deadlines, penalized softly, or controlled through a bounded weighted number of violations.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(w_j\ge0\) and \(K\ge0\) in the quota regime.
Each soft penalty \(\phi_j\) is nondecreasing with \(\phi_j(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compliance is represented by \(C_j\le d_j\), by a tardiness penalty, or by \(\sum_jw_j\mathbf 1\{C_j>d_j\}\le K\), according to the selected regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content kind fits a container about compliance regimes, and the three formulations are coherent. The hard-soft-quota classification is not supported by a scheduling source with a specific locator, so its claimed status as a standard regime taxonomy remains uncertain.

children.title: Earliness–Tardiness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Asymmetric or symmetric penalties for completion before or after target dates.

knowledge_statements.title: Earliness–Tardiness Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymmetric piecewise-linear criteria penalize completion on either side of a due date.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For job \(j\) with completion time \(C_j\) and due date \(d_j\), define earliness \(E_j=(d_j-C_j)^+\) and tardiness \(T_j=(C_j-d_j)^+\). Given penalties \(a_j,b_j\ge0\), the separable earliness–tardiness criterion is \(\sum_{j\in J}(a_jE_j+b_jT_j)\). Equivalently, job \(j\)'s contribution is \(a_j(d_j-C_j)\) when \(C_j<d_j\), zero when \(C_j=d_j\), and \(b_j(C_j-d_j)\) when \(C_j>d_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Earliness–tardiness criteria apply possibly unequal linear penalties to completion before and after each job's due date.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(C_j,d_j\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimize \(\sum_{j\in J}\left(a_j(d_j-C_j)^+ + b_j(C_j-d_j)^+\right)\) over feasible schedules and any permitted due-date decisions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymmetric piecewise-linear earliness-tardiness criterion is mathematically consistent and fits the terminal container, but no authoritative scheduling source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Due-Date Assignment
children.top_down_role: Models where due dates are selected, negotiated, or priced as scheduling decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Due-Date Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint selection of a feasible schedule and endogenous job due dates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be jobs, let \(X\) be the set of feasible schedules, and let \(C_j(x)\) denote job \(j\)'s completion time under \(x\in X\). A due-date-assignment problem chooses \((x,d)\in X\times D\), where \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the admissible set of due-date vectors, to minimize
\[\sum_{j\in J}\bigl(\alpha_j(d_j-C_j(x))^+ +\beta_j(C_j(x)-d_j)^+ +g_j(d_j)\bigr),\]
with \(\alpha_j,\beta_j\ge 0\), assignment-cost functions \(g_j\), and \(z^+=\max\{z,0\}\). Thus due dates are decision variables rather than fixed job data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A due-date-assignment model jointly chooses a feasible schedule and admissible due dates, balancing earliness, tardiness, and the cost of promising particular dates.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is specified.
\(\alpha_j,\beta_j\ge 0\) for every \(j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimization variables are \((x,d)\in X\times D\), and their objective is the displayed timing-and-assignment cost.

notation.meaning: completion time of job j in schedule x
assigned due date of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the specific separable earliness–tardiness-plus-assignment-cost formulation has no cited scheduling source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Common Due-Date Regimes
children.top_down_role: Shared-target, restricted-target, and unrestricted-target due-date structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Due-Date Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard exogenous and endogenous variants of a due date shared by all jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For jobs \(J=\{1,…,n\}\), a common-due-date model imposes \(d_j=d\) for every \(j\in J\). Three principal regimes are represented by
\[d=\bar d,\qquad d\in D,\qquad d\in D\text{ with cost }g(d),\]
respectively: a fixed common date \(\bar d\), a freely optimized common date in an admissible set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), and an optimized common date penalized or priced by \(g\). A restricted regime additionally bounds \(d\), for example \(D=[0,D_{\max}]\); an unrestricted endogenous regime takes \(D=\mathbb{R}\) or \(D=\mathbb{R}_+\), according to the time convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All jobs share one due date, which may be fixed, optimized within a restricted set, or optimized while incurring an assignment cost.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is a finite job set.
All jobs obey \(d_j=d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common due date is exogenous when \(d=\bar d\) and endogenous when \(d\) is optimized over \(D\).

notation.meaning: due date common to every job
admissible set of common due dates
cost of assigning common due date d

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf, but the asserted three-regime taxonomy and restricted/unrestricted terminology require an authoritative scheduling citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Timing–Assignment Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between selected due dates and the resulting early or late completion costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Timing–Assignment Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto and scalarized formulations for schedule timing versus due-date assignment quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y\subseteq X\times D\) be the feasible schedule–assignment pairs, with timing loss \(T:Y\to\mathbb{R}\) and assignment loss \(A:Y\to\mathbb{R}\). A pair \(y^*\in Y\) exhibits an efficient timing–assignment tradeoff precisely when no \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(T(y)\le T(y^*)\) and \(A(y)\le A(y^*)\), with at least one strict inequality. For every \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), any minimizer of
\[\lambda T(y)+(1-\lambda)A(y)\quad\text{over }y\in Y\]
is efficient. Conversely, every supported efficient point minimizes such a weighted sum for some nonnegative weights not both zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Timing and due-date-assignment losses define a Pareto frontier; positive weighted sums recover its supported efficient solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\neq\varnothing\).
Both \(T\) and \(A\) are real-valued losses to be minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive weighted-sum minimizers are Pareto efficient, and every supported efficient outcome has a nonnegative supporting weight vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto and weighted-sum claims are mathematically standard and the principle kind fits, but no multiobjective or scheduling source supports the formulation.

children.title: Throughput Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on completed, accepted, or on-time work volume.

knowledge_statements.title: Throughput Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality- and weight-based completion of admitted jobs by their deadlines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be a finite job set, \(X\) the feasible schedules, \(C_j(x)\) the completion time of job \(j\), and \(d_j\) its deadline. With values \(w_j\ge 0\), the weighted-throughput objective is
\[\max_{x\in X}\ \sum_{j\in J}w_j\mathbf{1}\{C_j(x)\le d_j\}.\]
Equivalently, if \(U_j(x)=\mathbf{1}\{C_j(x)>d_j\}\), it minimizes \(\sum_j w_jU_j(x)\) up to the constant \(\sum_jw_j\). Unweighted throughput is the special case \(w_j=1\), which maximizes the number of jobs completed no later than their deadlines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A throughput objective maximizes the number or total weight of jobs completed by their deadlines; equivalently, it minimizes weighted late jobs.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(w_j\ge 0\) and \(d_j\in\mathbb{R}\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weighted throughput equals \(\sum_jw_j\mathbf{1}\{C_j(x)\le d_j\}\), and maximizing it is equivalent to minimizing \(\sum_jw_jU_j(x)\).

notation.meaning: indicator that job j is late

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly relates weighted throughput to weighted late-job minimization, but no relevant scheduling source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Job-Rejection Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria combining selective admission with penalties for omitted work.

knowledge_statements.title: Job-Rejection Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling with an explicit accepted set and penalties for rejected jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be a finite job set and let \(X(A)\) denote the feasible schedules of an accepted subset \(A\subseteq J\). Given rejection penalties \(r_j\ge 0\) and a scheduling cost \(F(x,A)\), a job-rejection model solves
\[\min_{A\subseteq J,\ x\in X(A)}\ F(x,A)+\sum_{j\in J\setminus A}r_j.\]
Jobs in \(A\) must satisfy all scheduling constraints, whereas rejected jobs incur penalties but consume no processing capacity. A rejection-budget variant instead minimizes \(F(x,A)\) subject to \(\sum_{j\notin A}r_j\le B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model chooses which jobs to accept and schedules them feasibly, charging penalties or enforcing a budget for rejected jobs.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(r_j\ge 0\) for all \(j\in J\).
At least one pair \((A,x)\) with \(x\in X(A)\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective combines the accepted jobs' scheduling cost with \(\sum_{j\notin A}r_j\), the total rejection penalty.

notation.meaning: feasible schedules for accepted set A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits job-rejection objectives, but the penalty and rejection-budget formulations lack a supporting scheduling citation.

children.title: Scheduling Profit Objectives
children.top_down_role: Criteria balancing job rewards, operating costs, penalties, and resource use.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Profit Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Net value of accepted jobs after scheduling and rejection costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be finite, let \(A\subseteq J\) be the accepted jobs, and let \(x\in X(A)\) schedule them feasibly. If accepted job \(j\) yields value \(v_j(x)\), scheduling incurs cost \(K(x,A)\), and rejected job \(j\) incurs cost \(r_j\ge 0\), then scheduling profit is
\[P(x,A)=\sum_{j\in A}v_j(x)-K(x,A)-\sum_{j\in J\setminus A}r_j.\]
A scheduling-profit objective maximizes \(P(x,A)\) over all feasible \((A,x)\). Constant values \(v_j(x)=v_j\) give the basic admission-profit model; time-dependent values permit rewards that decay with completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scheduling profit is accepted-job value minus scheduling costs and rejection penalties, maximized jointly over admission and scheduling decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(X(A)\) specifies feasible schedules for each accepted set.
All displayed values and costs are finite on feasible pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal profit schedule belongs to \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{A\subseteq J,\ x\in X(A)}P(x,A)\).

notation.meaning: value earned from accepted job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits, but the proposed profit convention, including simultaneous rejection penalties and accepted-job values, is model-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Admission–Value Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural interactions among acceptance decisions, capacity scarcity, and economic value.

knowledge_statements.title: Admission–Value Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto relation between admission quantity and value or scheduling cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be the nonempty set of feasible accepted-set schedules \(y=(A,x)\). Let \(Q:Y\to\mathbb{R}\) measure admission quantity, such as \(|A|\), and let \(V:Y\to\mathbb{R}\) measure net value, with both criteria maximized. A feasible pair \(y^*\in Y\) is admission–value efficient if no \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(Q(y)\ge Q(y^*)\) and \(V(y)\ge V(y^*)\), with at least one strict inequality. For \(\lambda,\mu>0\), every maximizer of \[\lambda Q(y)+\mu V(y)\quad\text{over }y\in Y\] is efficient. A threshold formulation may maximize \(V(y)\) subject to \(Q(y)\ge q\); selecting, among its value-maximizers, one that maximizes \(Q\) yields an efficient solution whenever these maxima are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admission quantity and net value can conflict. Positive weighted sums produce nondominated schedules, while an admission-threshold model requires an efficiency-preserving tie-break among equal-value optima.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\neq\varnothing\).
\(Q,V:Y\to\mathbb{R}\) are finite quantities to be maximized.
Any stated maximizer is assumed to exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every maximizer with \(\lambda,\mu>0\) is admission–value efficient; a value-maximizing threshold solution is efficient when ties are resolved by maximizing \(Q\).

notation.meaning: net scheduling value of solution y

children.title: Multiobjective Scheduling Criteria
children.top_down_role: Criteria combining competing scheduling measures through scalar, lexicographic, or Pareto structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiobjective Scheduling Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto comparison of schedules under several explicitly oriented criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the nonempty feasible schedule set and let \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k):X\to\mathbb{R}^k\), where \(k\ge 2\) and every component is oriented for minimization. A schedule \(x^*\in X\) is Pareto efficient if there is no \(x\in X\) such that \(f_i(x)\le f_i(x^*)\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and \(f_\ell(x)<f_\ell(x^*)\) for at least one \(\ell\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). The nondominated criterion image is \[\{f(x):x\in X,\ x\text{ is Pareto efficient}\}.\] Maximization criteria can be included by negating their values before applying this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiobjective scheduling model compares feasible schedules componentwise and retains those whose criterion vector cannot be improved in at least one component without worsening another.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(k\ge 2\) and each \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is real-valued.
All criteria are oriented for minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set consists of schedules not dominated under the componentwise order on \(\mathbb{R}^k\).

children.title: Scheduling Fairness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Criteria governing balance across jobs, customers, workers, machines, or time periods.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Fairness Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dispersion, worst-off, and max–min representations of equity among stakeholders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u_i(x)\in\mathbb{R}\) be the utility delivered by feasible schedule \(x\in X\) to stakeholder \(i\in I\). Common fairness criteria include
\[\max_{x\in X}\min_{i\in I}u_i(x),\qquad \min_{x\in X}\max_{i\in I}\ell_i(x),\qquad \min_{x\in X}\sum_{i\in I}|u_i(x)-\bar u(x)|,\]
where \(\ell_i\) is a burden and \(\bar u(x)=|I|^{-1}\sum_i u_i(x)\). The first protects the least utility, the second limits the greatest burden, and the third controls absolute dispersion. Their fairness meanings require stakeholder-comparable, consistently oriented measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fairness can maximize the least stakeholder utility, minimize the greatest burden, or minimize dispersion, provided stakeholder outcomes are comparable and consistently oriented.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and nonempty.
\(X\neq\varnothing\).
Utilities or burdens are comparable across stakeholders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed max–min, min–max, and dispersion objectives define distinct mathematically checkable fairness criteria.

notation.meaning: utility of stakeholder i under schedule x
burden of stakeholder i under schedule x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits and the formulas are internally coherent, but their interpretation as scheduling-fairness criteria depends on comparability assumptions and requires a fair-scheduling source.

children.title: Schedule-Stability Criteria
children.top_down_role: Criteria measuring deviation from a baseline schedule after revision.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Stability Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deviation of a revised schedule from a designated baseline schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^0\) be a baseline schedule and \(X'\) the feasible schedules after an update or disruption. A schedule-stability criterion minimizes a prescribed distance \(D(x,x^0)\) over \(x\in X'\). For jobs present in both schedules, common choices are
\[D_{\mathrm{time}}(x,x^0)=\sum_j w_j|S_j(x)-S_j(x^0)|,\qquad D_{\mathrm{pos}}(x,x^0)=\sum_j w_j|\pi_j(x)-\pi_j(x^0)|,\]
where \(S_j\) and \(\pi_j\) are start time and sequence position. A directed instability measure may replace the absolute difference by \((S_j(x^0)-S_j(x))^+\) when earlier-than-announced execution alone is disruptive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule stability measures how far a revised feasible schedule moves from a baseline in start times, positions, assignments, or another prescribed feature.
assumptions_latex: A baseline schedule \(x^0\) is designated.
\(X'\neq\varnothing\).
Weights satisfy \(w_j\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stability-optimal revision lies in \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X'}D(x,x^0)\) for the selected deviation metric.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The baseline-deviation definition fits the leaf, but the proposed time, position, and directed-instability metrics require a schedule-stability source with a specific locator.

children.title: Efficiency–Equity–Stability Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Conflicts among aggregate performance, balanced treatment, and limited schedule disruption.

knowledge_statements.title: Efficiency–Equity–Stability Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-criterion Pareto formulation for performance, fairness, and disruption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the feasible schedules, and let \(E(x)\), \(Q(x)\), and \(S(x)\) be efficiency loss, inequity, and instability, respectively, all oriented for minimization. A schedule \(x^*\in X\) is efficiency–equity–stability efficient when no \(x\in X\) satisfies
\[(E(x),Q(x),S(x))\le(E(x^*),Q(x^*),S(x^*))\]
componentwise with at least one strict inequality. For weights \(\lambda_E,\lambda_Q,\lambda_S>0\), every minimizer of \(\lambda_EE+\lambda_QQ+\lambda_SS\) is Pareto efficient. Such scalarizations recover supported efficient points; nonsupported points may require constraint, reference-point, or direct Pareto methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Efficiency loss, inequity, and schedule instability define a three-way Pareto frontier; positive weighted sums find supported nondominated schedules.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(E,Q,S:X\to\mathbb{R}\) are finite losses.
\(\lambda_E,\lambda_Q,\lambda_S>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer of \(\lambda_EE(x)+\lambda_QQ(x)+\lambda_SS(x)\) is nondominated in \((E,Q,S)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-criterion Pareto principle is mathematically coherent and correctly distinguishes supported from nonsupported points, but it has no cited multiobjective scheduling source.

children.title: Scheduling Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Classical machine and project environments, preserving the legacy problem-family branch while separating environment-specific theory.

children.title: Machine Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Single-machine, parallel-machine, and shop environments together with machine-side extensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: EDD is a 2-approximation with negative due dates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-machine maximum-lateness minimization with release dates and a negative due date for every job.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem \(1\mid r_j,\ d_j<0\mid L_{\max}\), the earliest-due-date rule is a \(2\)-approximation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimizing maximum lateness on one machine with release dates and negative due dates, the earliest-due-date rule is a 2-approximation algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \text{There is one machine.}
\text{Each job }j\text{ has release date }r_j.
d_j<0\quad\text{for every job }j.
\text{The objective is to minimize }L_{\max}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{\max}(\mathrm{EDD})\le 2L_{\max}^{*}

source_evidence.locator: Greedy algorithms and local search / 2.1. Scheduling jobs with deadlines on a single machine / Theorem 2.2

source_refs.locator: Greedy algorithms and local search / 2.1. Scheduling jobs with deadlines on a single machine / Theorem 2.2

children.title: Single-Machine Completion-Time Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models organized by individual, weighted, aggregate, or extremal completion criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Machine Completion-Time Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpreemptive single-machine completion times induced by a job permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be jobs processed nonpreemptively on one continuously available machine, with processing times \(p_j>0\) and all jobs available at time zero. A feasible schedule is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(J\), and its completion times satisfy
\[C_{\pi(k)}=\sum_{h=1}^{k}p_{\pi(h)},\qquad k=1,\ldots,n.\]
A single-machine completion-time model optimizes a function \(F(C_1,\ldots,C_n)\) over permutations; standard instances include \(F=\sum_jw_jC_j\), \(F=\max_jC_j\), and \(F=\max_j(C_j-d_j)\). With release dates or inserted idle time, the recurrence must be modified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpreemptive single-machine schedule is a job permutation whose completion times are cumulative processing times; the model optimizes a function of those times.
assumptions_latex: All jobs are available at time zero.
Processing is nonpreemptive on one continuously available machine.
Each \(p_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every permutation \(\pi\) induces completion times \(C_{\pi(k)}=\sum_{h=1}^{k}p_{\pi(h)}\), over which \(F\) is optimized.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is correct for nonpreemptive, no-idle single-machine permutation schedules with all jobs released at zero, but no single-machine scheduling source supports the model and examples.

children.title: Single-Machine Flow-Time Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models organized by job residence after release.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Machine Flow-Time Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines deterministic single-machine flow time and its standard aggregate objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be jobs with processing times \(p_j>0\) and release dates \(r_j\). In a feasible nonpreemptive single-machine schedule, job \(j\) starts at \(S_j\ge r_j\), completes at \(C_j=S_j+p_j\), and its flow time is \(F_j=C_j-r_j\). A single-machine flow-time model minimizes an aggregate such as \(\sum_{j\in J}F_j\), \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jF_j\) for \(w_j\ge0\), or \(\max_{j\in J}F_j\), subject to nonoverlap of processing intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flow time is elapsed time from a job's release until completion. The model minimizes total, weighted total, or maximum flow time on one machine.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(p_j>0\) for every job.
Processing is nonpreemptive on one machine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_j=C_j-r_j\), with the chosen aggregate of \((F_j)_{j\in J}\) serving as the objective.

notation.meaning: start and completion times of job j
release date and processing time of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the flow-time leaf, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator. The listed local inventory concerns network flows and does not support this scheduling claim.

children.title: Release-Date Effects
children.top_down_role: How nonzero release epochs separate completion-time criteria from flow-time criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Release-Date Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates completion-time and flow-time objectives when release dates are fixed instance data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every feasible schedule of a fixed job set, \(F_j=C_j-r_j\), and therefore \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jF_j=\sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j-\sum_{j\in J}w_jr_j\). Because the final term is independent of the schedule, minimizing weighted total flow time and weighted total completion time yields the same optimal schedules under identical feasibility constraints. Nevertheless, release dates can change those constraints through \(S_j\ge r_j\), forcing idle time and excluding otherwise admissible job orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed release dates, weighted total flow and completion time differ by a constant, but release dates still alter feasibility and may force idle time.
assumptions_latex: \(r_j\) and \(w_j\ge0\) are fixed instance data.
The compared objectives use the same feasible schedules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}\sum_j w_jF_j=\operatorname*{argmin}\sum_j w_jC_j\), although feasibility may depend on \((r_j)_j\).

children.title: Single-Machine Lateness Models

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Machine Lateness Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines signed due-date deviation and the standard maximum-lateness objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each job \(j\in J\) have processing time \(p_j>0\), due date \(d_j\), and completion time \(C_j\) in a feasible single-machine schedule. Its lateness is the signed deviation \(L_j=C_j-d_j\), which may be negative. The canonical single-machine lateness model minimizes maximum lateness, \[L_{\max}=\max_{j\in J}L_j,\] subject to the selected release-date, precedence, setup, and nonoverlap constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Job lateness is completion time minus due date and may be negative. The canonical model minimizes the largest job lateness.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and every job has a specified due date.
Each job receives a completion time in a feasible single-machine schedule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_j=C_j-d_j\) and \(L_{\max}=\max_{j\in J}(C_j-d_j)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed-lateness and maximum-lateness definitions are precise and fit the lateness-model leaf. The candidate has no source reference, and the local network-optimization inventory is not relevant evidence.

children.title: Single-Machine Tardiness Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models using positive due-date violations and weighted variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Machine Tardiness Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines nonnegative due-date deviation and common single-machine tardiness objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a job \(j\) with completion time \(C_j\) and due date \(d_j\), its tardiness is \(T_j=(C_j-d_j)^+=\max\{C_j-d_j,0\}\). A single-machine tardiness model minimizes an aggregate such as \(\sum_{j\in J}T_j\), \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jT_j\) with \(w_j\ge0\), or \(T_{\max}=\max_{j\in J}T_j\), over feasible schedules. Completing early incurs zero tardiness rather than a negative contribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tardiness is the positive part of completion time minus due date. Early jobs contribute zero to total, weighted, or maximum tardiness.
assumptions_latex: Every job has a completion time \(C_j\) and due date \(d_j\).
Weights, when present, satisfy \(w_j\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_j=\max\{C_j-d_j,0\}\), and the chosen aggregate of \((T_j)_{j\in J}\) is minimized.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes tardiness from signed lateness and gives standard aggregate objectives. Definition fits the terminal container, but no authoritative scheduling citation or specific locator is supplied.
