children.title: Single-Machine Tardy-Job Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models using the number or weight of late jobs.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Machine Tardy-Job Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines binary due-date violation and the number or weight of tardy jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each job \(j\in J\) with completion time \(C_j\) and due date \(d_j\), define \(U_j=\mathbf{1}\{C_j>d_j\}\). Thus \(U_j=1\) exactly when job \(j\) is tardy and \(U_j=0\) otherwise, including \(C_j=d_j\). A single-machine tardy-job model minimizes \(\sum_{j\in J}U_j\) or, for penalties \(w_j\ge0\), \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jU_j\), over feasible single-machine schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary variable records whether each job finishes after its due date. The objective minimizes the number or total weight of tardy jobs.
assumptions_latex: Every job has a completion time \(C_j\) and due date \(d_j\).
Penalties, when present, satisfy \(w_j\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_j=\mathbf{1}\{C_j>d_j\}\), with objective \(\sum_jU_j\) or \(\sum_jw_jU_j\).

notation.meaning: indicator that job j is tardy
penalty for job j being tardy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict due-date violation indicator and its unweighted and weighted objectives are standard and appropriate for this leaf. The record lacks any supporting source reference and inspectable locator.

children.title: Due-Date Metric Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among signed, magnitude-based, and indicator-based due-date penalties.

knowledge_statements.title: Due-Date Metric Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates lateness, tardiness, and tardy-job metrics at and around the due date.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For deviation \(x_j=C_j-d_j\), lateness, tardiness, and tardy-job status are respectively \(L_j=x_j\), \(T_j=x_j^+\), and \(U_j=\mathbf{1}\{x_j>0\}\). Hence early completion gives \(L_j<0\) but \(T_j=U_j=0\); on-time completion gives all three values zero; and late completion gives \(L_j=T_j>0\) while \(U_j=1\), discarding the violation magnitude. Consequently, these metrics are not interchangeable except under additional restrictions on attainable deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lateness preserves signed deviation, tardiness truncates early completion to zero, and the tardy-job indicator discards every positive violation's magnitude.
assumptions_latex: \(C_j\) and \(d_j\) are measured on the same time scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_j=x_j\), \(T_j=x_j^+\), and \(U_j=\mathbf{1}\{x_j>0\}\) encode distinct information.

notation.meaning: completion deviation from the due date

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison correctly identifies the information boundaries among lateness, tardiness, and tardy-job status. Failure_boundary is suitable for the exact leaf, but no cited scheduling source supports the definitions or the non-interchangeability statement.

children.title: Release-Date Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models with job-specific earliest processing times.

knowledge_statements.title: Release-Date Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the temporal feasibility restriction imposed by job-specific release dates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let job \(j\) have release date \(r_j\), start time \(S_j\), processing time \(p_j>0\), and completion time \(C_j\). In a release-date model, job \(j\) is temporally feasible only if \[S_j\ge r_j.\] Under nonpreemptive processing, \(C_j=S_j+p_j\). Under preemptive processing with processing set \(P_j\), the corresponding condition is \(P_j\subseteq[r_j,\infty)\) and the total measure of \(P_j\) equals \(p_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job cannot start or receive processing before its release date; its full processing requirement must be met afterward.
assumptions_latex: Each job has a specified release date and positive processing requirement.
The processing convention is explicitly nonpreemptive or preemptive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No portion of job \(j\)'s processing occurs before \(r_j\).

notation.meaning: times at which a preemptive job is processed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The release-date feasibility condition is standard and condition fits the leaf. The measurable processing-set formulation implicitly uses unit-rate processing and requires an authoritative source or an explicitly stated convention; no source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Machine-Availability Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models with operating intervals, shutdowns, or unavailable periods.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Availability Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility when the single machine is usable only during prescribed time intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the machine-availability calendar be a measurable set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). A nonpreemptive execution of job \(j\), occupying \([S_j,S_j+p_j)\), is feasible only if \([S_j,S_j+p_j)\subseteq A\). If resumable preemption is allowed, job \(j\) may instead use a measurable set \(P_j\subseteq A\) of total measure \(p_j\). In either case, processing sets of distinct jobs must be disjoint because the machine has unit capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processing may occur only while the machine is available. Nonpreemptive jobs require one available interval; preemptive jobs may use several available pieces.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is the prescribed set of available times.
The machine has unit processing capacity.
The preemption convention is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every job-processing set lies in \(A\), has measure \(p_j\), and is disjoint from every other job-processing set.

notation.meaning: processing-time set assigned to job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The availability-set conditions are coherent for unit-rate, resumable processing, and condition fits this feasibility leaf. The candidate provides no citation, and the preemptive measurable-set convention requires scheduling-specific support.

children.title: Calendar Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interactions between job release calendars and machine operating calendars.

knowledge_statements.title: Calendar Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines job release dates with machine calendars under nonpreemptive processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For machine-availability set \(A\), release date \(r_j\), and nonpreemptive processing time \(p_j>0\), define the compatible-start set \[K_j=\{t\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}:t\ge r_j\text{ and }[t,t+p_j)\subseteq A\}.\] A schedule is calendar-compatible precisely when \(S_j\in K_j\) for every job and the intervals \([S_j,S_j+p_j)\) are pairwise disjoint. If \(K_j=\varnothing\) for some job, the instance is infeasible under the nonpreemptive calendar regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible start must follow the job's release and fit its entire processing interval inside machine availability. An empty compatible-start set proves infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Processing is nonpreemptive on one machine.
Each job has \(p_j>0\) and release date \(r_j\).
\(A\) is fixed instance data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires pairwise nonoverlap and \(S_j\in K_j\) for all \(j\); \(K_j=\varnothing\) implies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: calendar-compatible start times for job j
chosen start time of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatible-start set precisely combines release dates, nonpreemptive processing, availability, and machine nonoverlap. Condition is the correct role, but the record has no authoritative scheduling source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-Constrained Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States finish-before-start precedence constraints for single-machine scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(J,E)\) be a directed acyclic graph on the jobs. An arc \((i,j)\in E\) requires job \(i\) to precede job \(j\). For nonpreemptive jobs with start and completion times \(S_j\) and \(C_j=S_j+p_j\), precedence feasibility is \[S_j\ge C_i\qquad\text{for every }(i,j)\in E.\] These inequalities are imposed together with single-machine nonoverlap and any release-date or availability constraints. A directed cycle with strictly positive processing times makes the model infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each precedence arc requires its predecessor to finish before its successor starts. Positive-duration jobs cannot satisfy a cyclic precedence relation.
assumptions_latex: Every processing time satisfies \(p_j>0\).
Processing is nonpreemptive.
Precedence means finish-before-start without lag.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_j\ge C_i\) for all \((i,j)\in E\); feasibility requires an acyclic precedence relation.

notation.meaning: job i must finish before job j starts
start and completion times of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finish-before-start inequalities are correct for positive-duration nonpreemptive jobs without lags, and condition is suitable for the topic. Although the statement initially assumes a DAG, its later cycle observation is merely redundant rather than contradictory. No supporting scheduling citation is supplied.

children.title: Setup-Time Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models with sequence-independent or sequence-dependent preparation times.

knowledge_statements.title: Setup-Time Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents sequence-dependent setup times through immediate-successor constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_{ij}\ge0\) be the setup time required when job \(j\) is processed immediately after job \(i\), and let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that immediate-successor relation. With a valid upper bound \(M\), the temporal implication is represented by \[S_j\ge C_i+s_{ij}-M(1-x_{ij})\qquad(i\ne j).\] Together with path constraints making the selected arcs a single job sequence, this enforces the applicable setup between consecutive jobs. Initial setups may be represented by a dummy source job \(0\) with values \(s_{0j}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequence-dependent setup time separates consecutive jobs. Binary successor variables and timing constraints apply the setup associated with each chosen transition.
assumptions_latex: Setups are nonnegative and depend on the ordered pair of consecutive jobs.
\(M\) is large enough to deactivate an unselected implication.
Successor variables form one valid machine sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x_{ij}=1\), then \(S_j\ge C_i+s_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: setup time before j when i is its predecessor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct kind for this immediate-successor mixed-integer formulation. Its validity depends on explicit finite time bounds and a quantitatively valid value of M, while the referenced path constraints are not specified. A formulation source with a precise locator is required before the mathematical version can be relied upon.

children.title: Job-Family Models
children.top_down_role: Single-machine models grouping jobs by shared tooling, processing, or preparation characteristics.

knowledge_statements.title: Job-Family Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a partition of jobs into families sharing setup or processing attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A job-family model consists of a finite job set \(J\), a finite family set \(F\), and an assignment \(f:J\to F\). Jobs \(i\) and \(j\) belong to the same family exactly when \(f(i)=f(j)\). Family membership may parameterize common processing characteristics or setup rules; for example, a setup \(s_{f(i),f(j)}\) may depend only on the families of consecutive jobs. The assignment itself does not require jobs of one family to be contiguous unless an additional batching or grouping constraint is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job is assigned to one family. Families may determine shared parameters or transition setups, but membership alone does not force contiguous processing.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(F\) are finite.
Every job is assigned to exactly one family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fibers \(J_g=\{j\in J:f(j)=g\}\), for \(g\in F\), partition \(J\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite assignment map correctly induces a partition and does not by itself impose contiguity. Definition fits the job-family leaf, but no authoritative scheduling citation or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Family-Based Setup Regimes
children.top_down_role: Setup structures induced by transitions within or between job families.

knowledge_statements.title: Family-Based Setup Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-dependent family setups on one nonpreemptive machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the jobs be partitioned into families by a map \(f:J\to F\). Job \(j\) has processing time \(p_j\ge 0\), and \(s_{gh}\ge 0\) is the setup time incurred when a job of family \(h\) immediately follows one of family \(g\); an initial setup \(s_{0h}\) may also be specified. For a permutation \(\pi\) of \(J\), feasibility requires \(S_{\pi_1}\ge s_{0,f(\pi_1)}\) and \(S_{\pi_k}\ge C_{\pi_{k-1}}+s_{f(\pi_{k-1}),f(\pi_k)}\) for \(k\ge2\), with \(C_j=S_j+p_j\). A family-setup regime is sequence independent when \(s_{gh}\) depends only on \(h\), and family-sequence dependent otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs belong to families, and changing from one family to another may require a family-pair-dependent setup before the next job starts.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(F\) are finite.
Jobs are processed nonpreemptively on one machine.
Setups occupy the machine and cannot overlap processing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\pi_k}\ge C_{\pi_{k-1}}+s_{f(\pi_{k-1}),f(\pi_k)}\) for every \(k\ge2\).

notation.meaning: setup time from family g to family h
start and completion times of job j

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports family-setup scheduling definitions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No scheduling source or locator supports the setup convention. The formula charges a setup between every adjacent pair, including equal-family pairs, whereas the plain statement describes only family changes; a source is needed to determine whether s_{gg}=0 is intended.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Family-Based Setup-Time Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Setup conventions for single-machine jobs partitioned into families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $n$ jobs belong to $F$ families. Consecutive jobs from the same family require no intervening setup. A transition from family $g$ to family $h$ requires setup time $s_{gh}$ when setups are sequence dependent, $s_h$ when the setup depends only on the entering family, and $s$ when it is independent of both families. For the sequence-dependent setups considered here, $s_{fg}+s_{gh}\ge s_{fh}$ for all families $f,g,h$. If the first processed job belongs to family $h$, its initial setup time is $s_{0h}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs are partitioned into families. Consecutive jobs of one family need no setup, whereas a change of family can incur a sequence-dependent, entering-family-dependent, or constant setup. The sequence-dependent setup times considered satisfy the triangle inequality, and the first family may require an initial setup.
assumptions_latex: n\text{ jobs belong to }F\text{ families}
s_{fg}+s_{gh}\ge s_{fh}\quad\forall f,g,h\quad\text{for the sequence-dependent setup times considered}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Within-family transitions require no setup; interfamily and initial setups follow the specified regime.}

children.title: Serial Batch Models
children.top_down_role: Models grouping jobs into lots while retaining serial processing within each batch.

knowledge_statements.title: Serial Batch Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-machine batches whose members are processed sequentially after a common setup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be partitioned into an ordered sequence of nonempty batches \((B_1,\ldots,B_q)\). Each batch \(B_r\) incurs one setup time \(s(B_r)\ge0\), after which its jobs are processed one at a time in an internal order, without overlap. If batch \(B_r\) starts at \(T_r\), its processing interval has length \(s(B_r)+\sum_{j\in B_r}p_j\), and every job in the batch completes when its own serial processing finishes. Consecutive batches satisfy \(T_{r+1}\ge T_r+s(B_r)+\sum_{j\in B_r}p_j\). Thus batching couples jobs through a shared setup but does not make their processing simultaneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A serial batch pays one common setup, then processes its member jobs consecutively; its duration is the setup plus their total processing time.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(p_j\ge0\) for every job.
Batches are nonempty, disjoint, and cover \(J\).
The single machine processes at most one setup or job at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{r+1}\ge T_r+s(B_r)+\sum_{j\in B_r}p_j\) for \(r=1,\ldots,q-1\).
review_flags: Serial-batch conventions vary concerning completion times and setup dependence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is plausible, but serial-batch conventions vary in setup dependence and job completion semantics. No cited source with a specific locator establishes this version.

children.title: Batch-Processing Machine Models
children.top_down_role: Models where compatible jobs occupy a machine simultaneously as a processing batch.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Processing Machine Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous nonpreemptive processing of compatible jobs in capacity-limited batches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A batch-processing machine handles a nonempty compatible set \(B\subseteq J\) simultaneously, subject to a capacity constraint \(\sum_{j\in B}a_j\le K\). A feasible schedule partitions \(J\) into batches and assigns each batch a nonoverlapping machine interval. In the standard parallel-batch model, the duration is \(P(B)=\max_{j\in B}p_j\); all jobs in \(B\) start at the batch start \(S_B\) and complete together at \(C_B=S_B+P(B)\). No job may belong to more than one batch, and a batch cannot be interrupted once processing begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible jobs may run simultaneously as one capacity-feasible batch, whose standard duration is the longest processing time among its members.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite, with \(p_j\ge0\) and sizes \(a_j\ge0\).
The machine capacity is \(K>0\).
Batch processing is nonpreemptive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_j=C_B=S_B+\max_{k\in B}p_k\) for every \(j\in B\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the standard parallel-batch convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parallel-batch max-duration convention is standard in one important model but is not universal. No cited source or locator supports this exact simultaneous, capacity-limited formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dynamic program for maximum lateness with unlimited batch size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward dynamic programming for \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(\infty)\mid L_{\max}\) over SPT-batch schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Index jobs so that \(p_1\le\cdots\le p_n\). Let \(V(j)\) be the minimum maximum lateness of an SPT-batch schedule for jobs \(j,\ldots,n\) starting at time zero, and set \(V(n+1)=-\infty\). For \(j=n,\ldots,1\), compute
\[
V(j)=\min_{k=j+1,\ldots,n+1}\max\left\{V(k)+p_{k-1},\ \max_{h=j,\ldots,k-1}(p_{k-1}-d_h)\right\}.
\]
Here \(\{j,\ldots,k-1\}\) is inserted as the first batch. The optimal maximum lateness is \(V(1)\), and the algorithm runs in \(O(n^2)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After sorting jobs by processing time, a backward dynamic program chooses each first batch. Its transition compares the shifted lateness of the remaining schedule with the largest lateness inside the new first batch. V(1) is optimal and the running time is quadratic.
assumptions_latex: p_1\le p_2\le\cdots\le p_n
b=\infty\ \text{(equivalently, }b\ge n\text{)}
d_j\in\mathbb{R}\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
V(n+1)=-\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}\left(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(\infty)\mid L_{\max}\right)=V(1),\qquad T(n)=O(n^2).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Batch Is Deferred Relative to a Non-Full Batch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary structural condition for optimal schedules in single-machine capacity-b batch processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid\sum_j C_j\), a batch is full if it contains exactly \(b\) jobs and non-full otherwise. Batch \(\mathcal B_k\) is deferred with respect to \(\mathcal B_\ell\) if \(p(\mathcal B_k)<p(\mathcal B_\ell)\) and \(\mathcal B_k\) is sequenced after \(\mathcal B_\ell\). In any optimal schedule, no batch is deferred with respect to a non-full batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an optimal schedule, a batch with lower processing time cannot occur after a higher-processing-time batch that contains fewer than b jobs.
assumptions_latex: The problem is \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid\sum_j C_j\).
\(p(\mathcal B)=\max_{j\in\mathcal B}p_j\).
A batch is non-full exactly when \(\lvert\mathcal B\rvert<b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,k,\ell:\ \operatorname{pos}(\mathcal B_k)>\operatorname{pos}(\mathcal B_\ell),\quad p(\mathcal B_k)<p(\mathcal B_\ell),\quad \lvert\mathcal B_\ell\rvert<b\quad\text{in an optimal schedule.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of an Optimal Schedule with Nonintertwined Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural existence result for single-machine capacity-b batch processing with a total-completion-time objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid\sum_j C_j\), with the jobs indexed in nondecreasing processing-time order, \(p_1\leq\cdots\leq p_n\). Two batches are nonintertwined if their sets of job indices do not interleave: either every index in the first batch is smaller than every index in the second, or conversely. There exists an optimal schedule having no two intertwined batches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When jobs are indexed in nondecreasing processing-time order, an optimal schedule can be chosen so that the job-index ranges of any two batches are disjoint and ordered rather than interleaved.
assumptions_latex: \(p_1\leq p_2\leq\cdots\leq p_n\)
The problem is \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid\sum_j C_j\).
Each feasible batch contains at most \(b\) jobs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\) an optimal schedule such that, for every pair of distinct batches \(\mathcal B_k,\mathcal B_\ell\), either \(\max_{j\in\mathcal B_k}j<\min_{j\in\mathcal B_\ell}j\) or \(\max_{j\in\mathcal B_\ell}j<\min_{j\in\mathcal B_k}j\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward dynamic program for minimizing tardy jobs with unlimited batch size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward dynamic programming for \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(\infty)\mid\sum_jU_j\) over SPT-batch schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V(j,u,k)\) be the minimum makespan of an SPT-batch schedule for jobs \(1,\ldots,j\) having exactly \(u\) late jobs and a last batch of duration \(p_k\), with that batch intended to contain jobs through \(k\). Initialize \(V(0,0,0)=0\) and \(V(0,0,k)=\infty\) for \(k\ne0\). For \(j=1,\ldots,n\), \(u=0,\ldots,j\), and \(k=j,\ldots,n\), set \(V(j,u,k)\) to the minimum feasible member of
\[
\begin{aligned}
&V(j-1,u,k) &&\text{if }V(j-1,u,k)\le d_j,\\
&V(j-1,u-1,k) &&\text{if }V(j-1,u-1,k)>d_j,\\
&V(j-1,u,j-1)+p_k &&\text{if }V(j-1,u,j-1)+p_k\le d_j,\\
&V(j-1,u-1,j-1)+p_k &&\text{if }V(j-1,u-1,j-1)+p_k>d_j,
\end{aligned}
\]
using \(\infty\) when no transition is feasible. The first two transitions place job \(j\) in the current batch; the last two start a new batch. The optimum is
\[
\min\{u:V(n,u,n)<\infty\},
\]
and the running time is \(O(n^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward dynamic program records the number of late jobs, the current makespan, and the processing time of the last batch. Each job either joins the current batch or starts a new one, and each case is split according to whether the job meets its due date. The smallest reachable number of late jobs is optimal, with cubic running time.
assumptions_latex: p_1\le p_2\le\cdots\le p_n
b=\infty\ \text{(equivalently, }b\ge n\text{)}
d_j\in\mathbb{R}\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
V(0,0,k)=\infty\quad(k\ne0)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}\left(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(\infty)\mid\sum_jU_j\right)=\min\{u:V(n,u,n)<\infty\},\qquad T(n)=O(n^3).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Batch-processing single-machine model and SPT-batch schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines simultaneous batch processing, capacity regimes, and SPT-compatible batching on one machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A batch-processing machine processes every job in a batch simultaneously, with batch processing time \(p(B)=\max_{j\in B}p_j\), so all jobs in \(B\) complete when its longest job completes. Feasible batches satisfy \(|B|\le b\). The case \(b=1\) is ordinary single-job processing, while \(b=\infty\), equivalently \(b\ge n\), is unlimited-capacity batching. If \(p_1\le\cdots\le p_n\), an SPT-batch schedule partitions the ordered sequence \(1,\ldots,n\) into contiguous batches. Under unlimited capacity, processing all jobs together yields \(C_{\max}=\max_{1\le j\le n}p_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs in one batch are processed simultaneously and complete after the longest processing time in that batch. Batch capacity is b; b=1 gives ordinary processing and b at least n gives unlimited capacity. With jobs indexed by nondecreasing processing time, an SPT-batch schedule groups contiguous jobs in that order. Under unlimited capacity, one batch minimizes makespan, which equals the largest processing time.
assumptions_latex: n\ge 1
b\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\cup\{\infty\}
p_j\ge 0\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
p_1\le p_2\le\cdots\le p_n\quad\text{for the SPT-batch definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(B)=\max_{j\in B}p_j,\quad |B|\le b;\qquad b\ge n\implies C_{\max}^{*}=\max_{1\le j\le n}p_j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal Sequencing of a Fixed Collection of Batches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary-and-sufficient ordering rule for sequencing fixed feasible batches in the single-machine capacity-b batch-processing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed collection of feasible batches in \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid\sum_j C_j\), let \(p(\mathcal B_k)=\max_{j\in\mathcal B_k}p_j\). A sequence of these batches minimizes total job completion time if and only if the batches are arranged in nonincreasing order of \(\lvert\mathcal B_k\rvert/p(\mathcal B_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the batches have been fixed, their optimal order is nonincreasing batch cardinality divided by batch processing time, where the processing time of a batch is the largest processing time among its jobs.
assumptions_latex: The problem is \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid\sum_j C_j\).
A fixed collection of feasible batches is being sequenced.
\(p(\mathcal B_k)=\max_{j\in\mathcal B_k}p_j\), and \(\lvert\mathcal B_k\rvert\) is the number of jobs in \(\mathcal B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is an optimal sequence of the fixed batches}\iff \frac{\lvert\mathcal B_1\rvert}{p(\mathcal B_1)}\geq\frac{\lvert\mathcal B_2\rvert}{p(\mathcal B_2)}\geq\cdots\geq\frac{\lvert\mathcal B_m\rvert}{p(\mathcal B_m)},\text{ with indices in schedule order.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dynamic program for weighted completion time with unlimited batch size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward dynamic programming for \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(\infty)\mid\sum_j w_jC_j\) over SPT-batch schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Index jobs so that \(p_1\le\cdots\le p_n\). Let \(V(j)\) be the minimum total weighted completion time of an SPT-batch schedule for jobs \(j,\ldots,n\) starting at time zero, and set \(V(n+1)=0\). For \(j=n,\ldots,1\), compute
\[
V(j)=\min_{k=j+1,\ldots,n+1}\left\{V(k)+p_{k-1}\sum_{h=j}^{n}w_h\right\}.
\]
The minimizing \(k\) makes \(\{j,\ldots,k-1\}\) the first batch, whose duration is \(p_{k-1}\). The optimal objective value is \(V(1)\), and the algorithm runs in \(O(n^2)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort jobs by nondecreasing processing time. A backward dynamic program chooses the endpoint of the first batch and adds its duration times the total weight of all jobs delayed by that batch. The value V(1) is optimal, and evaluating all transitions takes quadratic time.
assumptions_latex: p_1\le p_2\le\cdots\le p_n
b=\infty\ \text{(equivalently, }b\ge n\text{)}
w_j\ge 0\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}\left(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(\infty)\mid\sum_jw_jC_j\right)=V(1),\qquad T(n)=O(n^2).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal finite-capacity batching for makespan
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy batch assembly and full-batch structure for \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid C_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(1\mid\operatorname{batch}(b)\mid C_{\max}\), let \(N=\lceil n/b\rceil\). Repeatedly remove the \(b\) longest-processing jobs remaining and place them together in a batch until fewer than \(b\) jobs remain; place all remaining jobs, which are the shortest ones, in the final batch. The resulting \(N\) batches minimize makespan. Their processing order does not affect \(C_{\max}\), and there exists an optimal schedule in which every batch except possibly one is full. This full-batch property is asserted only for the makespan objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finite batch capacity b, minimize makespan by grouping the longest remaining jobs b at a time and placing the shortest leftover jobs in the only possibly nonfull batch. Exactly ceiling(n/b) batches are used, their order is irrelevant to makespan, and the full-batch property need not extend to other objectives.
assumptions_latex: n\ge1
b\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}
1\le b\le n
p_j\ge0\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)
p(B)=\max_{j\in B}p_j
\text{the objective is }C_{\max}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N=\left\lceil\frac nb\right\rceil,\qquad \text{the greedy grouping is optimal, and at most one batch has size }<b.

children.title: Coupled-Task Models
children.top_down_role: Models with separated task segments linked by prescribed or bounded internal delays.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Task Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-operation coupled tasks with an exact prescribed internal delay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each task \(j\in J\) consists of two nonpreemptive operations of lengths \(a_j\ge0\) and \(b_j\ge0\), separated by an exact idle delay \(L_j\ge0\). If the first operation starts at \(S_j\), its occupied interval is \([S_j,S_j+a_j)\), and the second occupies \([S_j+a_j+L_j,S_j+a_j+L_j+b_j)\). A coupled-task schedule on one machine is feasible exactly when all occupied operation intervals are pairwise disjoint; operations of other tasks may be placed inside a task's delay. The task completion time is \(C_j=S_j+a_j+L_j+b_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each task has two operations separated by an exact idle delay; other tasks may use that delay, but all operation intervals must remain disjoint.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
All operation lengths and prescribed delays are nonnegative.
A single machine executes at most one operation at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_j=S_j+a_j+L_j+b_j\), with all occupied intervals pairwise disjoint.

notation.meaning: lengths of the two operations of task j
exact delay between the two operations

review_flags: Coupled-task literature also contains minimum-delay and multiprocessor variants.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-delay, single-machine coupled-task definition is coherent, but the literature also uses minimum-delay and multiprocessor variants. A specific source is required to substantiate the selected variant.

children.title: Batch Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Capacity, compatibility, family, and timing restrictions governing feasible grouping.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise compatibility represented by a graph; feasible batches are cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(J,E)\) be an undirected compatibility graph, where \(\{i,j\}\in E\) means that distinct jobs \(i\) and \(j\) may share a batch. Under a pairwise compatibility regime, a nonempty set \(B\subseteq J\) is batch-compatible exactly when \(G[B]\) is complete, equivalently \(\{i,j\}\in E\) for every distinct \(i,j\in B\). If jobs also have sizes \(a_j\) and batch capacity \(K\), feasibility additionally requires \(\sum_{j\in B}a_j\le K\). Consequently, a feasible batching is a partition of \(J\) into capacity-feasible cliques of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise-compatible batches are precisely cliques of the compatibility graph, optionally restricted by a batch-capacity inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
Compatibility is symmetric and determined pairwise.
When present, \(a_j\ge0\) and \(K>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is feasible}\iff G[B]\text{ is complete and }\sum_{j\in B}a_j\le K\), with the capacity clause omitted when absent.
review_flags: Pairwise compatibility does not cover general higher-order batch constraints.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique representation is valid only when compatibility is symmetric and completely pairwise. No cited source with a locator supports that regime or the optional capacity extension.

knowledge_statements.title: Identical Parallel Machines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical \(P\)-environment with machine-independent processing times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An identical-parallel-machine instance has a finite job set \(J\), machines \(M=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and a processing requirement \(p_j\ge0\) for each job \(j\). Assigning job \(j\) to any machine gives the same processing time \(p_j\). In a nonpreemptive schedule, each job is assigned to exactly one machine and one interval \([S_j,S_j+p_j)\), and intervals assigned to the same machine are pairwise disjoint. With no release dates, the load of machine \(i\) is \(L_i=\sum_{j:x_{ij}=1}p_j\), and the makespan is \(C_{\max}=\max_{i\in M}L_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical machines process every job at the same job-dependent duration; feasibility requires a single assignment and nonoverlapping work on each machine.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
Jobs are nonpreemptive and cannot migrate.
All machines are continuously available from time zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{ij}=p_j\) for all \(i\in M\) and \(j\in J\).

notation.meaning: one when job j is assigned to machine i

review_flags: No supplied source locator concerns parallel-machine scheduling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited scheduling source supports the definition. Moreover, for an arbitrary feasible schedule, no release dates alone does not imply C_max=max_i L_i when idle time is allowed; that equality requires a compact, non-idling realization or an assignment-based optimum interpretation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: List Scheduling Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy construction of a schedule on identical parallel machines from an arbitrary job ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an arbitrary ordering \((j_1,\ldots,j_n)\) of the jobs. Process the jobs in this order, assigning each \(j_k\) to a machine of minimum current load; equivalently, start the next job in the list whenever a machine becomes idle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose any ordering of the jobs and assign each successive job to a currently least-loaded machine; equivalently, start the next listed job whenever a machine becomes idle.
assumptions_latex: \text{The machines are identical.}
(j_1,\ldots,j_n)\text{ is an ordering of all jobs.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure constructs the list schedule induced by }(j_1,\ldots,j_n).

children.title: Uniform Parallel Machines
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine environments with machine-specific speed scaling shared across jobs.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Parallel Machines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical uniform-machine environment with machine-dependent speeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A uniform-parallel-machine instance has machines \(M=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with speeds \(s_i>0\) and jobs \(J\) with processing requirements \(p_j\ge0\). If job \(j\) is assigned nonpreemptively to machine \(i\), its processing time is \(p_{ij}=p_j/s_i\). A feasible schedule assigns every job to exactly one machine and places its interval so that intervals on each machine are pairwise disjoint. Without release dates, the completion load of machine \(i\) is \(L_i=s_i^{-1}\sum_{j:x_{ij}=1}p_j\), giving \(C_{\max}=\max_{i\in M}L_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each machine has a fixed speed, and every job's duration equals its machine-independent work requirement divided by that speed.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
Every speed is strictly positive.
Jobs are nonpreemptive and assigned to one machine each.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{ij}=p_j/s_i\) for every machine-job pair \((i,j)\).

notation.meaning: total processing duration assigned to machine i

review_flags: Terminology overlaps with related-machine scheduling and requires a scheduling source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source with a scheduling-specific locator supports the uniform-machine convention. Also, C_max=max_i L_i is not true for every schedule if avoidable idle time is permitted; it describes a compact realization or the assignment-induced optimum.

children.title: Related-Machine Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Scheduling families built on speed-related parallel-machine environments.

knowledge_statements.title: Related-Machine Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling optimization in the uniformly related \(Q\)-machine environment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In related-machine scheduling, machine \(i\in M\) has speed \(s_i>0\), job \(j\in J\) has work requirement \(p_j\ge0\), and processing \(j\) nonpreemptively on \(i\) takes \(p_j/s_i\) time. For makespan minimization, an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^{M\times J}\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in M}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\), and has objective \(C_{\max}(x)=\max_{i\in M}s_i^{-1}\sum_{j\in J}p_jx_{ij}\). The problem is to select an assignment minimizing this quantity; ordering on each machine is immaterial when all jobs are available at time zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Related-machine makespan scheduling assigns jobs to fixed-speed machines to minimize the largest assigned workload divided by machine speed.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
All jobs are available at time zero.
Jobs are nonpreemptive and machines have positive speeds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x C_{\max}(x)=\min_x\max_{i\in M}s_i^{-1}\sum_{j\in J}p_jx_{ij}\) subject to \(\sum_i x_{ij}=1\).

notation.meaning: binary assignment of job j to machine i

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports the related-machine formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assignment formulation is mathematically coherent for nonpreemptive makespan scheduling with all jobs available at time zero, but no cited source or locator supports the terminology or exact formulation.

children.title: Speed-Class Variants
children.top_down_role: Discrete, bounded, hierarchical, or heterogeneous machine-speed regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Speed-Class Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Related machines restricted to finitely many distinct speed values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A speed-class related-machine instance partitions the machine set as \(M=M_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}M_k\), where every machine in class \(M_h\) has the same speed \(v_h>0\), and the values \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) are distinct. A job with work requirement \(p_j\) takes \(p_j/v_h\) time on any machine in \(M_h\). Thus machines are interchangeable within each class, while processing durations may differ between classes. When \(k\) is bounded independently of the input size, the model is a constant-number-of-speed-classes variant; when \(k=1\), it reduces to identical parallel machines after rescaling time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machines are grouped into equal-speed classes; jobs have equal duration within a class and speed-scaled durations across classes.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
The classes form a disjoint partition of \(M\).
Every class speed is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i\in M_h\implies p_{ij}=p_j/v_h\), and \(k=1\) yields the identical-machine case.

notation.meaning: speed shared by machines in class h

review_flags: The bounded-speed-class convention needs a directly relevant scheduling source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The speed-class definition is coherent, but the bounded-number-of-classes convention and its role as a named scheduling variant require a directly relevant source with a specific locator.

children.title: Identical-Machine Specialization
children.top_down_role: The boundary where speed distinctions disappear and the environment reduces to identical machines.

knowledge_statements.title: Identical-Machine Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal-speed specialization of the uniform related-machine model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a uniform related-machine instance with work requirements \(p_j\) and speeds \(s_i\). If all speeds equal a common value \(s>0\), then every job has machine-independent duration \(p_j/s\). After replacing each requirement by \(p'_j=p_j/s\), every feasible assignment and within-machine ordering is exactly a feasible schedule on identical parallel machines with processing times \(p'_j\), with unchanged start times, completion times, and objective values measured in the rescaled time unit. Consequently, the identical-machine environment is the equal-speed specialization of the uniform-machine environment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When all uniform machines have equal speed, rescaling each job's work by that speed produces an equivalent identical-machine instance.
assumptions_latex: \(s_i=s>0\) for every machine \(i\).
Processing time on machine \(i\) is \(p_j/s_i\).
The same scheduling constraints and objective are used before and after rescaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{ij}=p_j/s=p'_j\) for all \(i,j\), so the instance is identical-machine scheduling after time rescaling.

notation.meaning: rescaled processing time of job j

review_flags: The property is standard but the supplied sources do not document scheduling environments.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-speed specialization is standard, but no scheduling citation is supplied. The assertion that objective values remain unchanged also depends on restricting attention to time-based objectives compatible with the stated rescaling; the present assumption refers only generically to the same objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Unrelated Parallel Machines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical \(R\)-environment with arbitrary machine-job processing times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unrelated-parallel-machine instance specifies a finite machine set \(M\), a finite job set \(J\), and a processing-time matrix \((p_{ij})_{i\in M,j\in J}\), where \(p_{ij}\in[0,\infty]\) is the duration of job \(j\) on machine \(i\); \(p_{ij}=\infty\) may encode ineligibility. No factorization into a job requirement and machine speed is required. A nonpreemptive feasible schedule assigns each job to exactly one machine with finite processing time and places its interval so that intervals on each machine are pairwise disjoint. Without release dates, its makespan is \(C_{\max}=\max_{i\in M}\sum_{j\in J}p_{ij}x_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every machine-job pair may have an arbitrary processing time, and each job must be assigned to one machine on which it is processable.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
Jobs are nonpreemptive and assigned once.
At least one \(p_{ij}\) is finite for every job \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in M}x_{ij}=1\) and \(x_{ij}=1\implies p_{ij}<\infty\) for every job \(j\).

notation.meaning: processing time of job j on machine i

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports unrelated-machine scheduling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the use of infinite processing times to encode ineligibility. For an arbitrary feasible schedule, C_max need not equal the maximum assigned load when idle time is allowed; the formula requires a compact schedule or an assignment-based optimum interpretation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrally and fractionally set jobs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for jobs in an extreme solution of the unrelated-machines relaxation LP(T).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be an extreme point solution of \(\operatorname{LP}(T)\). A job \(j\) is integrally set in \(x\) if it is entirely assigned to one machine; otherwise it is fractionally set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an extreme solution of LP(T), a job is integrally set if it is entirely assigned to one machine and fractionally set otherwise.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is an extreme point solution of \(\operatorname{LP}(T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(j\text{ is integrally set}\iff j\text{ is entirely assigned to one machine};\quad j\text{ is fractionally set otherwise}.\)

children.title: Machine-Eligibility Sets
children.top_down_role: Job-specific or operation-specific sets of machines permitted to process the work.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Eligibility Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment feasibility specified by an allowed-machine set for each job.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite machine set and associate with each job \(j\in J\) a set \(E_j\subseteq M\) of eligible machines. An assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^{M\times J}\) satisfies the machine-eligibility condition exactly when \(\sum_{i\in E_j}x_{ij}=1\) and \(x_{ij}=0\) for every \(i\notin E_j\), for each \(j\in J\). Equivalently, the selected assignment edge for job \(j\) must lie in the bipartite graph \(G=(J\mathbin{\dot\cup}M,E)\), where \(E=\{(j,i):i\in E_j\}\). If some \(E_j\) is empty, no complete assignment—and hence no feasible schedule—exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job must be assigned exactly once to a machine in its eligibility set; an empty eligibility set immediately makes the instance infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
Each job must be assigned to exactly one machine.
Eligibility is fixed independently of scheduling time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in E_j}x_{ij}=1\) for all \(j\), while \(E_j=\varnothing\) for some \(j\) implies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: binary assignment of job j to machine i

review_flags: The supplied set-theory locator does not substantiate the scheduling-specific condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The eligibility condition is coherent and the content kind fits the leaf, but the inventory contains no scheduling-specific source or locator supporting eligibility sets and their bipartite representation.

children.title: Restricted-Assignment Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine models with explicit limits on feasible job-to-machine assignments.

assumptions_latex: There are finite job and machine sets \(J\) and \(M\).
Each job \(j\in J\) has processing requirement \(p_j>0\) and eligibility set \(E_j\subseteq M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible restricted assignment satisfies \(x_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i\notin E_j\), and its machine load is \(L_i=\sum_{j\in J}p_jx_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: Binary indicator that job j is assigned to machine i
Machines eligible to process job j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpreemptive identical-machine restricted assignment with job-dependent eligibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite sets \(J\) and \(M\), a restricted-assignment schedule is a binary matrix \(x\in\{0,1\}^{M\times J}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in E_j}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\in J\) and \(x_{ij}=0\) for \(i\notin E_j\). Job \(j\) has the same processing requirement \(p_j>0\) on every eligible machine. The induced load is \(L_i=\sum_{j\in J}p_jx_{ij}\); a makespan bound \(T\) is feasible exactly when \(L_i\le T\) for all \(i\in M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job must be assigned to one eligible machine, has equal processing time on all eligible machines, and contributes that time to the selected machine's load.
knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Assignment Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the restricted-assignment leaf and is mathematically coherent, but it has no citation or inspectable locator supporting the terminology and model conventions.

children.title: Eligibility Graph Structure
children.top_down_role: Graph-based organization of feasible assignment relations and their sparsity patterns.

assumptions_latex: The job set \(J\), machine set \(M\), and eligibility sets \(E_j\subseteq M\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eligible assignments are precisely the edges of the bipartite graph \(G=(J\mathbin{\dot\cup}M,E)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite representation of job-machine eligibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The eligibility structure is represented by the bipartite graph \(G=(J\mathbin{\dot\cup}M,E)\), where \((j,i)\in E\) if and only if \(i\in E_j\). For \(S\subseteq J\), its machine neighborhood is \(N(S)=\bigcup_{j\in S}E_j\). Thus every assignment selects one incident edge for each job, while machine-capacity or load restrictions constrain how many or which weighted selected edges may meet each machine vertex. Connected components of \(G\) form independent assignment subinstances whenever the objective and constraints are separable across machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite graph joins each job to its eligible machines; assignments select incident edges, and disconnected components can be handled independently under separable constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Eligibility Graph Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bipartite representation and separable-component claim fit the leaf, but neither is supported by a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Assignment-Infeasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Capacity and compatibility patterns that obstruct complete feasible assignment.

assumptions_latex: Each job requires one unit of assignment capacity.
Machine \(i\in M\) has an integer capacity \(b_i\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible eligible assignment exists if and only if \(|S|\le\sum_{i\in N(S)}b_i\) for every \(S\subseteq J\).

notation.meaning: Neighborhood of job subset S in the eligibility graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall-type boundary for unit-demand assignments with integral machine capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the capacitated eligibility graph, a complete assignment of all jobs exists exactly when \(|S|\le\sum_{i\in N(S)}b_i\) for every subset \(S\subseteq J\). Consequently, any \(S\subseteq J\) satisfying \(|S|>\sum_{i\in N(S)}b_i\) is a finite, directly checkable certificate of assignment infeasibility: the jobs in \(S\) collectively demand more units than all their eligible machines can supply. This boundary concerns unit demands; weighted processing-time feasibility under a makespan bound requires stronger load conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit-demand assignment is feasible exactly when every job subset has enough total capacity among its eligible neighboring machines; a violating subset certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-Infeasibility Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The capacitated Hall condition is a suitable feasibility boundary and certificate for unit-demand assignments, but this nontrivial equivalence requires an authoritative citation and locator.

children.title: Preemptive Parallel-Machine Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine regimes permitting interrupted processing on an assigned machine.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) parallel machines and finitely many jobs with processing requirements \(p_j>0\).
A machine processes at most one job at a time, and a job uses at most one machine at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A schedule is preemptive when each job may occupy several disjoint processing intervals whose total length equals \(p_j\).

notation.meaning: Set of times at which job j is processed

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General preemptive regime; migration is left as a separate modeling choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A preemptive parallel-machine schedule assigns to each job \(j\) a measurable set of processing times \(S_j\subseteq[0,\infty)\) with measure \(|S_j|=p_j\). The set \(S_j\) may be a union of disjoint intervals, so processing may stop and later resume. At almost every time, each machine processes at most one job and each job is processed by at most one machine. The completion time is \(C_j=\sup S_j\). Whether distinct intervals of one job may use different machines must be specified separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job may be interrupted and resumed until its accumulated processing equals its requirement; permission to resume on another machine is a separate convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Preemptive Parallel-Machine Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preemption concept fits the leaf, but the formal statement specifies processing-time sets without explicitly defining the associated machine-assignment map. A source is also needed to establish the intended migration convention and formulation.

children.title: Migratory Parallel-Machine Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine regimes permitting resumed processing on a different machine.

assumptions_latex: Jobs may be preempted.
Each job is processed by at most one machine at any instant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A schedule is migratory when some job may resume on a machine different from one used earlier.

notation.meaning: Machine processing job j at time t, when defined

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preemptive scheduling with inter-machine migration but no simultaneous execution of one job.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A migratory parallel-machine schedule permits the machine assignment \(\mu_j(t)\in M\) of a job \(j\) to change between its processing intervals. Feasibility requires that the total duration for which \(\mu_j(t)\) is defined equal \(p_j\), that no job occupy two machines simultaneously, and that no machine process two jobs simultaneously. Hence migration changes location but does not create parallel execution of a single job. Eligibility restrictions additionally require \(\mu_j(t)\in E_j\) whenever job \(j\) is processed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preempted job may continue on another eligible machine, but it never runs on two machines simultaneously and still receives exactly its required processing.
knowledge_statements.title: Migratory Parallel-Machine Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes migration from simultaneous parallel execution and fits the leaf, but no cited source or locator supports the convention.

children.title: Nonmigratory Preemption
children.top_down_role: Interrupted processing constrained to resume on its original machine.

assumptions_latex: Jobs may be preempted and resumed.
Each job has a positive processing requirement \(p_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonmigratory preemption requires one machine \(a(j)\) to execute every processing interval of job \(j\).

notation.meaning: Unique machine assigned to job j
Machine processing job j at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preemption is allowed, but every fragment of a job remains on one machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A preemptive schedule is nonmigratory if there exists an assignment map \(a:J\to M\) such that \(\mu_j(t)=a(j)\) for almost every \(t\in S_j\) and every \(j\in J\). The processing set \(S_j\) may contain multiple disjoint intervals, but all those intervals occur on the same machine. Eligibility is enforced by \(a(j)\in E_j\). Thus interruption and resumption are permitted, whereas changing the executing machine is forbidden.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job may be interrupted repeatedly, but every one of its processing fragments must execute on the same eligible machine.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmigratory Preemption

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition accurately expresses nonmigratory preemption and its content kind fits the leaf, but the record lacks source evidence with a specific locator.

children.title: Migration-Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Models incorporating relocation overhead, state transfer, or machine-dependent restart effects.

assumptions_latex: A preemptive schedule specifies the ordered machine sequence used by every job.
Each transition from machine \(i\) to machine \(k\) for job \(j\) has cost \(c_{jik}\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule's migration cost is the sum of the costs of all consecutive inter-machine transitions.

notation.meaning: Ordered machine sequence used by job j
Cost of moving job j from machine i to machine k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive transition-cost model; delay, setup, and migration-count variants require separate parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the successive processing intervals of job \(j\) use machines \((i_{j,1},\ldots,i_{j,q_j})\), its migration transitions are indices \(r\) with \(i_{j,r}\ne i_{j,r+1}\). Under additive transition costs, the total migration cost is \(C_{\mathrm{mig}}=\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{r=1}^{q_j-1}c_{j,i_{j,r},i_{j,r+1}}\mathbf{1}\{i_{j,r}\ne i_{j,r+1}\}\). A hard budget imposes \(C_{\mathrm{mig}}\le B\); a penalized objective adds \(\lambda C_{\mathrm{mig}}\) with \(\lambda\ge0\). Zero costs recover free migration, while infinite forbidden-transition costs encode nonmigration or topology restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Migration may be free, budgeted, or penalized by summing job-specific costs whenever consecutive processing fragments use different machines.
knowledge_statements.title: Migration-Cost Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive transition-cost regime is plausible, but multiple conventions exist and no source is cited. The statement also invokes infinite forbidden-transition costs although the assumptions declare finite real costs c_{jik}>=0; an extended-real domain or a separate prohibition must be specified.

children.title: Parallel-Task Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Jobs containing components that may execute concurrently on multiple processors.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) identical processors.
Each job \(j\) has processing time \(p_j>0\) and resource width \(q_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: While active, job \(j\) simultaneously occupies exactly \(q_j\) distinct processors for \(p_j\) time units.

notation.meaning: Processor width required by job j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rigid simultaneous-width interpretation of parallel tasks on identical processors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the rigid parallel-task model, job \(j\) requires a set of exactly \(q_j\) distinct processors simultaneously throughout an uninterrupted interval of length \(p_j\). A schedule chooses a start time \(s_j\ge0\) and processor set \(P_j\subseteq\{1,ldots,m\}\) with \(|P_j|=q_j\). Feasibility requires \(P_j\cap P_k=\varnothing\) whenever the intervals \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) and \([s_k,s_k+p_k)\) overlap. The completion time is \(C_j=s_j+p_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each parallel task occupies a fixed number of processors simultaneously for its entire processing interval, and overlapping jobs must use disjoint processor sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Task Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rigid simultaneous-width model is relevant, but terminology varies and no source is supplied. In statement_latex, the processor set contains the typo \{1,ldots,m\} rather than \{1,\ldots,m\}.

children.title: Multiprocessor-Job Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Jobs requiring several processors simultaneously during execution.

assumptions_latex: There is a finite processor set \(M\).
Each job \(j\) requires simultaneous service from a prescribed nonempty processor subset \(R_j\subseteq M\) for duration \(p_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two jobs may overlap only when their required processor subsets are disjoint.

notation.meaning: Prescribed processor subset required by job j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-subset multiprocessor-job model; some literature instead specifies only a processor count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiprocessor-job schedule assigns each job \(j\) an interval \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) during which all processors in its prescribed set \(R_j\) are occupied simultaneously. For distinct jobs \(j\) and \(k\), overlapping execution intervals are feasible only if \(R_j\cap R_k=\varnothing\). Equivalently, each processor \(i\in M\) has a unary-capacity constraint over the intervals of jobs satisfying \(i\in R_j\). If only the cardinality \(|R_j|\) is fixed and the processor identities are selectable, the model reduces to a rigid width-assignment variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job reserves its prescribed processor subset simultaneously; jobs can overlap exactly when their required subsets do not conflict.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiprocessor-Job Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-subset model is internally coherent, but “multiprocessor-job scheduling” is used for differing models in the literature. A specific source is required to support this local interpretation.

children.title: Rigid Resource-Width Regimes
children.top_down_role: Multiprocessor jobs with fixed processor requirements.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) processors.
Each job \(j\) has a fixed width \(q_j\in\{1,ldots,m\}\) and duration \(p_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The allocated processor count of job \(j\) must equal \(q_j\) throughout its execution.

notation.meaning: Fixed resource width of job j
Processors allocated to job j at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-width regime, independent of whether processor identities may change after preemption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A resource-width schedule is rigid when each job \(j\) has a width \(q_j\) fixed before scheduling and satisfies \(|P_j(t)|=q_j\) for almost every \(t\in S_j\). At every time, allocated processor sets of simultaneously active jobs are pairwise disjoint. The width cannot be increased to shorten the job or decreased to conserve capacity. If preemption is allowed, rigidity fixes the cardinality after resumption; whether the processor identities may change is an additional migration convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rigid job always uses its predetermined number of processors; preemption may interrupt it but cannot change that width.
knowledge_statements.title: Rigid Resource-Width Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-width condition fits the rigid-regime leaf, but no source is cited. The assumptions contain the malformed set \{1,ldots,m\}, which must be corrected to \{1,\ldots,m\}.

children.title: Malleable Resource-Width Regimes
children.top_down_role: Jobs whose assigned processor width may vary within an admissible range.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\) processors.
For each job \(j\), processing at width \(q\) has speed \(v_j(q)>0\) for allowed \(q\in Q_j\subseteq\{1,ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Job \(j\) completes when its accumulated normalized work reaches one: \(\int v_j(q_j(t))\,dt\ge1\).

notation.meaning: Processor width allocated to job j at time t
Processing speed of job j at width q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time malleable jobs with discrete processor widths and job-specific speed functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A job is malleable when its allocated width \(q_j(t)\in Q_j\) may vary during execution. At every time \(t\), capacity requires \(\sum_{j}q_j(t)\le m\), where inactive jobs have \(q_j(t)=0\). Normalizing each job's work to one, job \(j\) completes at the least \(C_j\) satisfying \(\int_0^{C_j}v_j(q_j(t))\,dt\ge1\). Thus both the chosen width and its duration determine progress. Common structural assumptions such as nondecreasing speed or nonincreasing efficiency \(v_j(q)/q\) are additional model hypotheses, not consequences of malleability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A malleable job's processor allocation may change over time, and completion occurs when the integrated speed supplied by those changing allocations reaches its workload.
knowledge_statements.title: Malleable Resource-Width Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuous-time speed-function formulation is a plausible malleable model, but malleability and speedup conventions vary. The completion integral and capacity model require a supporting source with a precise locator.

children.title: Parallel-Machine Makespan Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine families centered on the final schedule completion horizon.

assumptions_latex: There are finite job and machine sets \(J\) and \(M\).
Each job is assigned nonpreemptively to one machine and has processing time \(p_{ij}>0\) when assigned to machine \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The makespan objective is \(C_{\max}=\max_{i\in M}\sum_{j
div x_{ij}=1}p_{ij}=\max_{j\in J}C_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment-based makespan model for parallel machines without release dates or sequence-dependent effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parallel-machine makespan model chooses \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\sum_{i\in M}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\in J\). Machine \(i\) receives load \(L_i=\sum_{j\in J}p_{ij}x_{ij}\), and the objective is \(\min C_{\max}\) subject to \(L_i\le C_{\max}\) for all \(i\in M\). With all jobs available at time zero and no sequence-dependent constraints, jobs assigned to each machine can be processed consecutively, yielding \(C_{\max}=\max_{i\in M}L_i=\max_{j\in J}C_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign every job to one machine and minimize the largest resulting machine load, which equals the latest job completion time under consecutive processing.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Machine Makespan Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assignment-based makespan formulation fits the leaf under the stated restrictions, but it lacks citation support. The conclusion_latex expression contains the malformed fragment \sum_{j\ndiv x_{ij}=1}p_{ij} and must be repaired.
