children.title: Parallel-Machine Load-Balancing Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine families centered on balanced assignment of processing load.

assumptions_latex: There are finitely many jobs \(J\) and parallel machines \(M\).
Processing job \(j\) on eligible machine \(i\) requires \(p_{ij}\ge 0\) units of capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The load-balancing objective is \(\min \max_{i\in M} L_i\).

notation.meaning: Binary assignment indicator for job j on machine i
Total assigned processing load of machine i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment-based load balancing on finite parallel machines, including unrelated-machine processing times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parallel-machine load-balancing model chooses binary assignments \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in M}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\in J\), with \(x_{ij}=0\) whenever machine \(i\) is ineligible for job \(j\). The induced machine load is \(L_i=\sum_{j\in J}p_{ij}x_{ij}\), and the maximum load is \(L_{\max}=\max_{i\in M}L_i\). The canonical optimization problem is \(\min_x L_{\max}\), equivalently minimizing \(T\) subject to \(L_i\le T\) for every \(i\in M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign every job to one eligible machine so that the largest total processing load assigned to any machine is minimized.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Machine Load-Balancing Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assignment formulation is mathematically standard and fits the definition container, but the record has no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Maximum-Load Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which assignment load and schedule horizon represent the same criterion.

assumptions_latex: All jobs are available at time \(0\), are processed nonpreemptively, and must be completed.
Machines incur no setup times, and an assigned job can start whenever its machine becomes free.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing makespan is equivalent to minimizing maximum assigned load.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence for assignment-induced processing times without releases, setups, or machine idle-time requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any fixed feasible assignment, process the jobs assigned to each machine consecutively from time \(0\), in any order. Machine \(i\) then finishes at time \(L_i=\sum_{j\text{ assigned to }i}p_{ij}\), so \(C_{\max}=\max_{j\in J}C_j=\max_{i\in M}L_i\). Conversely, every feasible schedule has \(C_{\max}\ge L_i\) for each machine \(i\). Hence the minimum makespan over feasible schedules equals the minimum maximum load over feasible assignments. This equivalence may fail when release dates, sequence-dependent setups, or other timing constraints create unavoidable idle time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without release dates, setups, or other timing restrictions, a schedule's optimal makespan equals the smallest achievable maximum assigned machine load.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Load Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalence claim and stated boundaries fit this property container, but no source supports the precise hypotheses or failure regimes.

children.title: Load-Imbalance Penalties
children.top_down_role: Criteria based on dispersion, deviation, or inequity across machine loads.

assumptions_latex: A feasible assignment induces a nonnegative load vector \(L\in\mathbb{R}_+^{|M|}\).
A reference load \(\bar L\) or penalty functions are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Load imbalance is optimized by minimizing a stated deviation or dispersion functional of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common scalar penalties measuring dispersion of parallel-machine loads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given machine loads \(L_i\), let \(\bar L=|M|^{-1}\sum_{i\in M}L_i\). A load-imbalance penalty is a functional \(\Phi(L)\) that is minimized when loads are more equal, with the chosen functional explicitly defining the model. Standard examples include absolute deviation \(\Phi_1(L)=\sum_{i\in M}|L_i-\bar L|\), squared deviation \(\Phi_2(L)=\sum_{i\in M}(L_i-\bar L)^2\), load range \(\Phi_R(L)=\max_iL_i-\min_iL_i\), and threshold excess \(\Phi_T(L)=\sum_{i\in M}(L_i-T)_+\). These penalties are distinct from merely minimizing \(\max_iL_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Load-imbalance models penalize dispersion, such as absolute deviation, variance, load range, or excess above a target, rather than only the largest load.
knowledge_statements.title: Load-Imbalance Penalties

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the selected penalty family. In particular, threshold excess need not measure load equality when total load is assignment-dependent, so its inclusion requires a precise sourced regime.

children.title: Parallel-Machine Completion-Time Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine models using individual, aggregate, weighted, or extremal completion epochs.

assumptions_latex: Jobs \(J\) are scheduled feasibly on parallel machines \(M\).
Each job \(j\) has completion time \(C_j\) and nonnegative weight \(w_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical objective is \(\min \sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative priority weight of job j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total and weighted completion-time objectives for feasible parallel-machine schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parallel-machine completion-time model associates each feasible schedule with job completion times \(C_j\). Its canonical additive objective is total weighted completion time \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j\), where \(w_j\ge 0\); the unweighted model is obtained by setting \(w_j=1\) for all \(j\). The optimization problem is to find a feasible assignment and machinewise processing order minimizing this sum. Unlike makespan, this objective depends on every job's position in its machine sequence, so two schedules with the same final machine loads can have different objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose assignments and machine orders minimizing the sum of job completion times, optionally weighted by job priorities.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Machine Completion-Time Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-completion-time definition is standard and matches the container, but it has no citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Parallel-Machine Flow-Time Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine models using job residence after release.

assumptions_latex: Each job \(j\) has release time \(r_j\) and completion time \(C_j\ge r_j\).
Weights satisfy \(w_j\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical objective is \(\min \sum_{j\in J}w_j(C_j-r_j)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted sojourn-time objectives with exogenous release times and mandatory jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The flow time, or sojourn time, of job \(j\) is \(F_j=C_j-r_j\), the elapsed time from its release until completion. A parallel-machine flow-time model minimizes \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jF_j=\sum_{j\in J}w_j(C_j-r_j)\) over feasible assignments and machinewise schedules, subject to no job starting before its release. The unweighted objective sets \(w_j=1\). Flow time includes both waiting and processing after release; it excludes calendar time before \(r_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the weighted time each job spends in the system, measured from its release until its completion.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Machine Flow-Time Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The flow-time definition and objective are internally consistent and correctly scoped to release times, but no supporting source is cited.

children.title: Release-Sensitive Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where release dates separate completion-time performance from flow-time performance.

assumptions_latex: Every job is mandatory and has fixed release time \(r_j\) and fixed weight \(w_j\ge 0\).
The feasible schedule set is identical under both compared objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weighted flow-time and weighted completion-time minimizers coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective equivalence for mandatory jobs, with a boundary at endogenous admission or schedule-dependent releases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every feasible schedule, \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jF_j=\sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j-\sum_{j\in J}w_jr_j\). Because the final term is constant when releases, weights, and the mandatory job set are fixed, minimizing weighted flow time and minimizing weighted completion time yield the same optimal schedules. Release dates still affect feasibility and therefore may change the optimizer. The equivalence does not extend automatically to admission models in which the completed set varies, because then \(\sum_j w_jr_j\) over admitted jobs is decision-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed mandatory job set, weighted flow time differs from weighted completion time by a constant; admission decisions can destroy this equivalence.
knowledge_statements.title: Release-Sensitive Objective Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-shift equivalence is precise for a fixed mandatory job set and fits the property container, but the claim and its admission boundary lack cited support.

children.title: Parallel-Machine Due-Date Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine families using lateness, tardiness, deadline, or late-job criteria.

assumptions_latex: Each job \(j\) has a due date \(d_j\), completion time \(C_j\), and weight \(w_j\ge 0\).
A feasible parallel-machine schedule determines all completion times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Due-date performance is measured by a specified lateness, tardiness, or on-time indicator objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel-machine objectives defined relative to job due dates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For job \(j\), lateness is \(L_j=C_j-d_j\), tardiness is \(T_j=\max\{C_j-d_j,0\}\), and the late-job indicator is \(U_j=\mathbf{1}\{C_j>d_j\}\). A parallel-machine due-date model minimizes a specified aggregate such as \(L_{\max}=\max_j L_j\), \(\sum_j w_jT_j\), or \(\sum_j w_jU_j\), subject to the scheduling constraints. These objectives are not interchangeable: lateness may be negative, tardiness measures delay magnitude, and \(U_j\) records only whether the due date is missed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Due-date models evaluate schedules using maximum lateness, total weighted tardiness, or the weighted number of jobs completed late.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Machine Due-Date Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lateness, tardiness, and late-job objectives are correctly distinguished and fit the definition container, but no scheduling source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Parallel-Machine Throughput Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel-machine families maximizing accepted, completed, or on-time work.

assumptions_latex: Each job \(j\) has deadline \(d_j\), reward \(w_j\ge 0\), and completion time \(C_j\) if processed.
Jobs may be rejected or may count as unsuccessful when late.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximum weighted on-time throughput is \(\max \sum_{j\in J}w_jy_j\).

notation.meaning: Indicator that job j is admitted and completed by its deadline

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted on-time throughput under parallel-machine capacity and deadline constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parallel-machine throughput model uses \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\), where \(y_j=1\) only if job \(j\) is processed feasibly and completes by \(d_j\). Its weighted throughput is \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jy_j\), and the canonical objective maximizes this quantity over the admitted set, assignments, and machinewise schedules. With mandatory processing of all jobs, setting \(y_j=\mathbf{1}\{C_j\le d_j\}\) makes maximizing throughput equivalent to minimizing total weight of late jobs because \(\sum_jw_j(1-y_j)=\sum_jw_j-\sum_jw_jy_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select and schedule jobs to maximize the total reward of jobs completed by their deadlines.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Machine Throughput Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The on-time-throughput formulation is mathematically coherent and matches the container, but the formulation and equivalence to late-job weight have no cited source.

children.title: Deadline-Admission Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interactions between admission decisions, deadlines, and limited parallel capacity.

assumptions_latex: Jobs have processing requirements, eligibility restrictions, deadlines \(d_j\), and rewards \(w_j\ge 0\).
Rejected jobs consume no machine capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admission and scheduling are jointly feasible exactly when every selected job is assigned and completed by its deadline.

notation.meaning: Assignment indicator for job j on machine i
Completion time of an admitted job j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard-deadline admission with rejection and joint assignment-scheduling decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deadline-admission solution consists of \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\), assignments \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), and a feasible machinewise schedule such that \(\sum_{i\in M}x_{ij}=y_j\) for every job \(j\), ineligible assignments are zero, and \(C_j\le d_j\) whenever \(y_j=1\). Jobs with \(y_j=0\) are rejected and need not receive completion times. The maximum-reward admission regime optimizes \(\max\sum_{j\in J}w_jy_j\); a budgeted variant instead requires \(\sum_jw_jy_j\ge B\) and tests feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected job must be assigned once and completed by its deadline; the model jointly chooses admissions, assignments, and processing orders.
knowledge_statements.title: Deadline-Admission Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hard-deadline admission condition fits the container, but neither the maximum-reward regime nor the budgeted variant has source support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shop-scheduling models and makespan objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the common operation model, open-, job-, and flow-shop regimes, workload notation, and the makespan objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shop-scheduling instance has jobs $J_1,\ldots,J_n$, machines $M_1,\ldots,M_m$, and operations $O_1,\ldots,O_K$. Each operation $O_k$ belongs to a job, requires a specified machine, and has processing time $p_k$; operations belonging to the same job cannot overlap. In an open shop, a job's operations may be processed in any order. In a job shop, each job has a specified operation order. A flow shop is a job shop in which every job has exactly one operation on each machine and all jobs have the same required machine order. The objective is to minimize the makespan $C_{\max}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shop scheduling consists of jobs whose nonoverlapping operations require specified machines. Open shops allow any within-job order, job shops prescribe a job-dependent order, and flow shops require one operation per machine in a common order. The objective is minimum makespan.
assumptions_latex: O_k\text{ belongs to a job and requires a specified machine}
\text{operations belonging to the same job cannot overlap in time}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min C_{\max},\qquad P_j=\sum_{O_k\in J_j}p_k,\quad P_{\max}=\max_jP_j,\quad \Pi_i=\sum_{O_k\text{ requiring }M_i}p_k,\quad \Pi_{\max}=\max_i\Pi_i

children.title: Permutation Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow-shop regimes using a common job order across machines.

assumptions_latex: Every job visits machines \(1,\ldots,m\) in that order and has processing time \(p_{jk}\ge 0\) on machine \(k\).
Each machine handles at most one job at a time, and each job occupies at most one machine at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One common permutation \(\pi\) determines the job order on every machine.

notation.meaning: Completion time of the job in position q on machine k
Processing time of job j on machine k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical permutation flow shop without preemption or machinewise resequencing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A permutation flow-shop schedule selects one permutation \(\pi=(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n))\) and processes jobs in this order on every machine. For the earliest-start schedule induced by \(\pi\), define boundary values \(C_{0k}=C_{q0}=0\) and recursively set \(C_{qk}=\max\{C_{q-1,k},C_{q,k-1}\}+p_{\pi(q),k}\) for \(q=1,\ldots,n\) and \(k=1,\ldots,m\). Thus each operation waits for both its job's preceding operation and the preceding job on the same machine. A chosen objective, commonly \(C_{nm}\), is then optimized over \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All machines process the jobs in one common order, with each operation waiting for both its job and its machine to become available.
knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Flow Shops

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-permutation definition is standard, but the recurrence additionally presumes the ordinary nonblocking, non-no-wait flow shop and an earliest-start realization; these assumptions need a specific source.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the two-machine sum-finishing-time problem, there exists an optimal schedule in which both machines process the jobs in the same order and there is no unnecessary idle time between jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two-machine sum-finishing-time problem has an optimal permutation schedule: both machines process the jobs in the same order, without unnecessary idle time between jobs.

\text{The objective is to minimize }\sum_{j=1}^{n}F_{2j}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Permutation flow shops and fixed-sequence makespan evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and makespan representation for permutation flow shops with unlimited intermediate storage, including the boundary of permutation optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A permutation flow shop processes the jobs in one common order \(j_1,\ldots,j_n\) on every machine. For a fixed permutation, \(C_{i,j_1}=\sum_{l=1}^{i}p_{l,j_1}\), \(C_{1,j_k}=\sum_{l=1}^{k}p_{1,j_l}\), and \(C_{i,j_k}=\max\{C_{i-1,j_k},C_{i,j_{k-1}}\}+p_{i,j_k}\) for \(i=2,\ldots,m\) and \(k=2,\ldots,n\). The resulting makespan is the maximum-weight path from \((1,j_1)\) to \((m,j_n)\) in the associated operation DAG. For \(F2\|C_{\max}\) and \(F3\|C_{\max}\), an optimal permutation schedule exists; for some four-machine instances, every optimal schedule requires a sequence change between machines 2 and 3.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation flow shop maintains the same job order on every machine. For a fixed order, completion times satisfy the standard machine-and-job predecessor recurrence, and the makespan equals a longest-path weight in the operation DAG. Some optimal permutation schedule always exists for two or three machines, but this fails for certain four-machine instances.
assumptions_latex: m,n\in\mathbb{N}
\text{Jobs traverse the }m\text{ machines in the same technological order}
\text{Intermediate storage is unlimited}
(j_1,\ldots,j_n)\text{ is a fixed job permutation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{m,j_n}=\max_{P:(1,j_1)\leadsto(m,j_n)}\sum_{(i,j_k)\in P}p_{i,j_k},\qquad \exists\text{ an optimal permutation schedule for }m\in\{2,3\},\text{ but not for every }m=4\text{ instance}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Machine-reversal and job-reversal symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Makespan invariance for paired permutation flow shops with reversed machine orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two \(m\)-machine permutation flow shops with \(n\) jobs such that \(p_{ij}^{(1)}=p_{m+1-i,j}^{(2)}\) for every \(i=1,ldots,m\) and \(j=1,ldots,n\). For every permutation \((j_1,\ldots,j_n)\), sequencing the jobs as \((j_1,\ldots,j_n)\) in the first shop and as \((j_n,\ldots,j_1)\) in the second shop gives the same makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the machine order is reversed and the job permutation is also reversed, the makespan of a permutation flow-shop schedule is unchanged.

children.title: Nonpermutation Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow-shop regimes permitting job orders to differ across machines.

assumptions_latex: Every job visits machines \(1,\ldots,m\) in that order.
Processing is nonpreemptive and machine capacity is one job at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Different machines may use different job orders while preserving every job's technological route.

notation.meaning: Start time of job j on machine k
Completion time of job j on machine k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow shops permitting machine-dependent job sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonpermutation flow-shop schedule may choose a distinct job permutation \(\pi_k\) for each machine \(k\). Its operation times satisfy technological precedence \(S_{j,k+1}\ge C_{jk}\) for every job \(j\) and \(k<m\), and machine capacity requires nonoverlap in the order \(\pi_k\): if job \(j\) immediately precedes job \(h\) on machine \(k\), then \(S_{hk}\ge C_{jk}\). The schedule is genuinely nonpermutation when \(\pi_k\ne\pi_\ell\) for some machines \(k\) and \(\ell\). Optimization ranges over these machine-specific sequences and feasible operation times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machines may process jobs in different orders, provided each job still visits the machines in the prescribed route and operations do not overlap.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpermutation Flow Shops

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The machine-specific sequencing definition fits the nonpermutation-flow-shop container, but no authoritative citation or locator supports it.

children.title: Permutation-Dominance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance and objective classes where common-order schedules retain structural relevance.

assumptions_latex: Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be all feasible schedules for a specified flow-shop instance class and objective \(f\).
Let \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\) be its feasible permutation schedules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Permutation dominance holds exactly when \(\min_{S\in\mathcal{P}}f(S)=\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}}f(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact predicate defining when permutation schedules suffice for a flow-shop objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flow-shop instance class is permutation-dominant for objective \(f\) if, for every instance in the class, at least one globally optimal schedule uses the same job order on every machine. Equivalently, with \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\), dominance means \(\min_{S\in\mathcal{P}}f(S)=\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}}f(S)\) for every instance. If the equality fails for one instance, restricting the search to common permutations can exclude every optimum. Permutation dominance is therefore relative to the stated machine count, processing assumptions, and objective; it is not implied solely by the common flow-shop route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permutation dominance means that restricting every machine to one common job order preserves an optimal solution for every instance in the stated regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Dominance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance predicate is precise, properly relative to an instance class and objective, and fits the condition container, but it lacks any cited source or locator.

children.title: Machinewise Resequencing Effects
children.top_down_role: Capacity, waiting, and objective effects arising from order changes between machines.

knowledge_statements.title: Machinewise Resequencing Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares permutation and machine-dependent job orders under a minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_{\mathrm{perm}}\) be the feasible schedules using one common job permutation on every machine, and let \(F_{\mathrm{np}}\) allow a separate permutation on each machine. Then \(F_{\mathrm{perm}}\subseteq F_{\mathrm{np}}\). For any objective \(f\) minimized over schedules, define \(z_{\mathrm{perm}}=\inf_{S\in F_{\mathrm{perm}}}f(S)\) and \(z_{\mathrm{np}}=\inf_{S\in F_{\mathrm{np}}}f(S)\). Consequently, \(z_{\mathrm{np}}\le z_{\mathrm{perm}}\), and the resequencing effect \(\Delta_f=z_{\mathrm{perm}}-z_{\mathrm{np}}\) is nonnegative whenever both values are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing each machine its own job order enlarges the feasible set, so it cannot worsen a minimized objective; the improvement is the nonnegative resequencing gap.
assumptions_latex: The same jobs visit the machines in flow-shop order.
The objective \(f\) is minimized over feasible schedules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{perm}}\subseteq F_{\mathrm{np}}\) and \(\Delta_f=z_{\mathrm{perm}}-z_{\mathrm{np}}\ge 0\).

notation.meaning: Permutation and nonpermutation feasible schedule sets
Objective improvement attributable to machinewise resequencing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-set inclusion and minimization-gap claim are mathematically coherent and the property kind fits the leaf, but no scheduling source is cited for the permutation/nonpermutation model conventions.

children.title: Limited-Storage Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow shops with bounded intermediate buffer capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Limited-Storage Flow Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity buffers between consecutive machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A limited-storage flow shop has machines \(1,\ldots,m\), jobs \(1,\ldots,n\), and buffer capacities \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) between machines \(i\) and \(i+1\). If \(C_{ij}\) is the processing-completion time of job \(j\) on machine \(i\), and \(S_{i+1,j}\) its start time on the next machine, then the buffer occupancy at time \(t\) is \(Q_i(t)=|\{j:C_{ij}\le t<S_{i+1,j}\}|\). Feasibility requires \(Q_i(t)\le b_i\) for every \(i<m\) and every \(t\), with completed jobs retained upstream whenever immediate storage is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each intermediate buffer has finite capacity, and at every time the number of completed jobs waiting there may not exceed that capacity.
assumptions_latex: Each job visits machines \(1,\ldots,m\) in that order.
Processing is nonpreemptive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_i(t)\le b_i\) for all \(i<m\) and all times \(t\).

notation.meaning: Capacity of the buffer after machine i
Occupancy of that buffer at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but the occupancy formula counts every completed operation not yet started downstream, including a job retained on the upstream machine; a source is required to distinguish buffer occupancy from upstream blocking and confirm the transfer convention.

children.title: Blocking Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow shops where a completed job may retain its machine until downstream transfer is possible.

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking Flow Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero intermediate storage with upstream-machine blocking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A blocking flow shop is a flow shop with no intermediate buffer. Let \(C_{ij}=S_{ij}+p_{ij}\) be the processing-completion time of job \(j\) on machine \(i<m\), and let \(D_{ij}\) be its departure time from that machine. The job cannot depart until machine \(i+1\) can accept it, so \(D_{ij}=\max\{C_{ij},S_{i+1,j}\}=S_{i+1,j}\). Machine \(i\) remains occupied by job \(j\) throughout \([S_{ij},D_{ij})\); hence no other job may start there before \(D_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With no intermediate buffers, a completed job holds its current machine until the next machine accepts it, potentially blocking following jobs.
assumptions_latex: Jobs follow the common machine order.
Operations are nonpreemptive and machines process at most one job at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{ij}=S_{i+1,j}\ge C_{ij}\) for every \(i<m\) and job \(j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly describes zero-buffer blocking under the stated timing convention and fits the leaf, but it has no supporting source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Departure-time and critical-path representation of blocking flow shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-intermediate-storage blocking flow shops under a fixed permutation schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In an $m$-machine flow shop with zero intermediate storage, a job that completes processing on machine $i$ while machine $i+1$ is busy remains on machine $i$ and blocks it. For a fixed permutation $(j_1,\ldots,j_n)$, let $D_{i,j_k}$ denote the departure time of job $j_k$ from machine $i$, and let $D_{0,j_k}$ denote its start time on machine 1. Then
\[
D_{i,j_1}=\sum_{l=1}^{i}p_{l,j_1},\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,
\]
\[
D_{i,j_k}=\max\{D_{i-1,j_k}+p_{i,j_k},D_{i+1,j_{k-1}}\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,m-1,\ k=2,\ldots,n,
\]
and
\[
D_{m,j_k}=D_{m-1,j_k}+p_{m,j_k},\qquad k=2,\ldots,n.
\]
The makespan equals the maximum-weight path length from $(0,j_1)$ to $(m,j_n)$ in the associated departure-time digraph. A finite buffer can be represented by zero-processing-time machines, one for each job-sized storage space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With zero intermediate storage, a completed job whose next machine is busy remains on its current machine and blocks it. For a fixed permutation, the departure-time recurrences determine the schedule, and the makespan is the maximum-weight path length in the associated digraph. Finite job-sized buffer spaces can be represented by zero-processing-time machines.
assumptions_latex: m\ge 2
(j_1,\ldots,j_n)\text{ is a fixed permutation schedule}
p_{ij}\ge 0
\text{intermediate storage capacity is zero}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{\max}=D_{m,j_n}=\operatorname{dist}_{\max}\bigl((0,j_1),(m,j_n)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Profile Fitting heuristic for blocking flow shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive permutation heuristic for $Fm\mid\mathrm{block}\mid C_{\max}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Select an initial job $j_1$, optionally one minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^m p_{ij}$, and set
\[
D_{i,j_1}=\sum_{h=1}^{i}p_{h,j_1}.
\]
Given a partial permutation ending in $j_{k-1}$, evaluate each unscheduled candidate $j$ by computing its appended departure profile:
\[
D_{1,j}=\max\{D_{1,j_{k-1}}+p_{1j},D_{2,j_{k-1}}\},
\]
\[
D_{i,j}=\max\{D_{i-1,j}+p_{ij},D_{i+1,j_{k-1}}\},\qquad i=2,\ldots,m-1,
\]
\[
D_{m,j}=\max\{D_{m-1,j},D_{m,j_{k-1}}\}+p_{mj}.
\]
Define
\[
W(j)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(D_{i,j}-D_{i,j_{k-1}}-p_{ij}\right).
\]
Append a candidate minimizing $W(j)$ and repeat until every job is scheduled. A weighted variant replaces $W(j)$ by $\sum_i w_i(D_{i,j}-D_{i,j_{k-1}}-p_{ij})$, with larger weights for more congested machines, for example weights proportional to their total processing loads.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Profile Fitting builds a permutation incrementally. For every unscheduled candidate it computes the resulting blocking-flow-shop departure profile and the total machine time lost to idleness or blocking, then appends a candidate with minimum loss. A weighted variant penalizes lost time more heavily on congested machines.
assumptions_latex: m\ge 2
\text{the instance is }Fm\mid\mathrm{block}\mid C_{\max}
\text{a partial permutation ending in }j_{k-1}\text{ has been constructed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: j_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{j\text{ unscheduled}}W(j),\qquad\text{repeated until a complete permutation is obtained}

children.title: No-Wait Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow shops requiring uninterrupted progression between successive operations.

knowledge_statements.title: No-Wait Flow Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow shops forbidding waiting between consecutive operations of a job.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A no-wait flow shop has start times \(S_{ij}\) and processing times \(p_{ij}>0\) satisfying \(S_{i+1,j}=S_{ij}+p_{ij}\) for every job \(j\) and each \(i<m\). Thus, once job \(j\) begins on machine \(1\), all its later starts are fixed by \(S_{ij}=S_{1j}+\sum_{h=1}^{i-1}p_{hj}\). A schedule is feasible only if these induced operation intervals are pairwise disjoint on every machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job must move immediately to each next machine; choosing its first start fixes all later starts, which must still avoid machine conflicts.
assumptions_latex: Every job visits machines \(1,\ldots,m\) in order.
Processing is nonpreemptive and each machine has unit capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{i+1,j}=S_{ij}+p_{ij}\) for all \(i<m\) and \(j\).

notation.meaning: Start time of job j on machine i
Processing time of job j on machine i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The no-wait equalities, induced starts, and machine-conflict requirement are precise, and definition is the correct kind, but no authoritative flow-shop source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No-wait flow-shop TSP representation and complexity boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Makespan minimization in flow shops where jobs cannot wait between consecutive operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In $Fm\mid\mathrm{nwt}\mid C_{\max}$, each job must begin processing on the next machine immediately after completing processing on its current machine. Define, for the indexed jobs used in the traveling-salesman formulation,
\[
d_{jk}=\max_{1\le i\le m}\left\{\sum_{h=1}^{i}p_{hj}-\sum_{h=1}^{i-1}p_{hk}\right\},\qquad j,k=0,\ldots,n.
\]
Makespan minimization admits a traveling-salesman formulation with these interjob distances. For two machines,
\[
F2\mid\mathrm{block}\mid C_{\max}\equiv F2\mid\mathrm{nwt}\mid C_{\max}.
\]
For more than two machines, the blocking and no-wait problems are different, and the no-wait traveling-salesman formulation is strongly NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a no-wait flow shop, a job must move immediately to each successive machine. Makespan minimization has a traveling-salesman formulation using the stated interjob distances. The blocking and no-wait makespan problems are equivalent with two machines, but differ with more than two machines; in that regime the no-wait formulation is strongly NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: m\ge 2
\text{jobs may not wait between consecutive operations}
d_{jk}=\max_{1\le i\le m}\left(\sum_{h=1}^{i}p_{hj}-\sum_{h=1}^{i-1}p_{hk}\right)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fm\mid\mathrm{nwt}\mid C_{\max}\text{ admits the stated TSP formulation};\quad m=2\Rightarrow F2\mid\mathrm{block}\mid C_{\max}\equiv F2\mid\mathrm{nwt}\mid C_{\max};\quad m>2\Rightarrow\text{the two problems differ and the no-wait formulation is strongly NP-hard}

children.title: Intermediate-Buffer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relations among unlimited storage, finite storage, zero-buffer blocking, and immediate transfer.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Buffer Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-vector classification between zero and effectively unlimited storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) jobs and \(m\) machines, let \(b=(b_1,\ldots,b_{m-1})\), where \(b_i\) is the capacity between machines \(i\) and \(i+1\). An intermediate-buffer regime satisfies \(0\le b_i<n\) for every \(i<m\) and \(0<b_k<n\) for at least one \(k\). Its feasible schedules obey \(|\{j:C_{ij}\le t<S_{i+1,j}\}|\le b_i\) for every \(i<m\) and time \(t\). Thus it excludes both the all-zero blocking regime and the effectively unlimited regime \(b_i\ge n\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intermediate regime has finite buffer capacities, with at least one strictly between zero and the number of jobs, and enforces every capacity over time.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many jobs \(n\ge1\).
A waiting job occupies one buffer unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le b_i<n\) for all \(i<m\), with \(0<b_k<n\) for some \(k\), and buffer occupancies respect \(b\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is plausible, but excluding every capacity vector having any component at least n is an unsupported boundary convention; mixed finite/effectively-unlimited vectors are not classified. The occupancy formula also needs the transfer convention clarified by a source.

children.title: Proportionate Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow shops with cross-machine processing times linked by proportional structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Proportionate Flow Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard equal-across-machines processing-time convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proportionate flow shop consists of jobs \(1,ldots,n\) processed on machines \(1,\ldots,m\) in the same order, with a positive job parameter \(p_j\) such that \(p_{ij}=p_j\) for every machine \(i\) and job \(j\). Equivalently, every row of the processing-time matrix \(P=(p_{ij})\) is the same vector \((p_1,\ldots,p_n)\). Machine-capacity and job-precedence constraints remain those of the underlying flow-shop model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job takes the same amount of processing time on every machine, although different jobs may have different processing times.
assumptions_latex: \(p_j>0\) for every job \(j\).
All jobs follow the same machine order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{ij}=p_j\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

notation.meaning: Machine-independent processing time of job j

review_flags: terminology may differ from rank-one proportional flow shops

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the appropriate kind, but the literature-dependent meaning of proportionate flow shop must be sourced, especially against rank-one proportional models. The opening job range also contains the malformed text “1,ldots,n” and must be corrected when a sourced replacement is prepared.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: New-max jobs and induced sequence segments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence terminology used in the weighted-completion-time analysis of proportionate permutation flow shops.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a permutation \((1,\ldots,n)\), the first job is a new-max job, and a job at position \(j>1\) is new-max if and only if \(p_j>\max\{p_1,\ldots,p_{j-1}\}\). If the new-max jobs occur at positions \(j_1<\cdots<j_r\), they partition the permutation into \(r\) contiguous segments: segment \(\ell<r\) begins at \(j_\ell\) and ends immediately before \(j_{\ell+1}\), while the last segment begins at \(j_r\) and extends through the final job.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first job is new-max, and each later new-max job has processing time strictly greater than every earlier job. The new-max positions uniquely partition the sequence into contiguous segments, each beginning with a new-max job.
assumptions_latex: A permutation of \(n\) jobs with processing times \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: j>1:\ j\text{ is new-max}\iff p_j>\max_{i<j}p_i,\quad\text{and the new-max positions induce the stated contiguous partition.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the unlimited-storage proportionate permutation flow-shop model and SPT–LPT sequences, with its stated two-machine makespan consequence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unequal-machine-speed generalization of a proportionate permutation flow shop and its bottleneck definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a proportionate permutation flow shop with machine speeds $v_i$, the processing time of job $j$ on machine $i$ is $p_{ij}=p_j/v_i$. A machine with minimum speed is called a bottleneck machine. In this generalized model, the makespan is not generally independent of the job sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If machine i has speed v_i, job j requires p_j divided by v_i time on that machine. A slowest machine is a bottleneck machine. Unlike the equal-speed proportionate model, makespan can depend on the sequence.

p_{ij}=\frac{p_j}{v_i}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: WSPT–Minimum-Cost-Insertion Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion algorithm for total weighted completion time in a proportionate permutation flow shop.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $Fm\mid prmu,\ p_{ij}=p_j\mid\sum_j w_jC_j$, re-index the jobs so that $w_1/p_1\geq\cdots\geq w_n/p_n$. Set $\mathcal S_1=(1)$. For $k=2,\ldots,n$, obtain $\mathcal S_k$ by inserting job $k$ into $\mathcal S_{k-1}$ at a position that minimizes the increase in $\sum_j w_jC_j$, choosing the latest such position when there is a tie. Return $\mathcal S_n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Index jobs by nonincreasing weight-to-processing-time ratio. Beginning with job 1, insert each successive job where it causes the smallest increase in total weighted completion time, breaking ties in favor of the latest insertion position. The final sequence is the WSPT–MCI schedule.

\frac{w_1}{p_1}\geq\frac{w_2}{p_2}\geq\cdots\geq\frac{w_n}{p_n}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm returns the sequence }\mathcal S_n.

children.title: Ordered Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow shops with machinewise or jobwise ordering restrictions on processing times.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Flow Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common job ordering induced by processing times on every machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ordered flow shop has a permutation \(\pi\) of the jobs such that \(p_{i,\pi(1)}\le p_{i,\pi(2)}\le\cdots\le p_{i,\pi(n)}\) for every machine \(i\). Equivalently, the row vectors of the processing-time matrix are comonotone: for all jobs \(j,k\), the sign of \(p_{ij}-p_{ik}\) never reverses between machines. Ties are permitted and may be resolved consistently to obtain \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All machines rank jobs by processing time in one common nondecreasing order; ties may be broken consistently.
assumptions_latex: Processing times \(p_{ij}\) are real and nonnegative.
All jobs visit the machines in common flow-shop order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{i,\pi(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{i,\pi(n)}\) for every machine \(i\).

notation.meaning: Common processing-time order of the jobs
Processing time of job j on machine i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common processing-time ordering is internally coherent and definition fits the leaf, but “ordered flow shop” is source-dependent and no citation establishes that this is the intended convention.

children.title: Processing-Time Order Regimes
children.top_down_role: Monotone, agreeable, and dominance patterns across jobs or machines.

knowledge_statements.title: Processing-Time Order Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents machinewise processing-time rankings by compatible preorders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each machine \(i\), define a preorder on jobs by \(j\preceq_i k\) if and only if \(p_{ij}\le p_{ik}\). A processing-time order regime is specified by the tuple \((\preceq_1,\ldots,\preceq_m)\), or equivalently by inequalities describing the corresponding cone \(\mathcal P=\{P\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}:p_{ij}\le p_{ik}\text{ whenever }j\preceq_i k\}\). The common-order regime is the special case in which all \(\preceq_i\) admit one shared linear extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machinewise rankings of job processing times can be encoded as preorders, whose defining inequalities describe a cone of admissible processing-time matrices.
assumptions_latex: The processing-time matrix belongs to \(\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\in\mathcal P\) exactly when it satisfies every inequality encoded by \((\preceq_1,\ldots,\preceq_m)\).

notation.meaning: Set of matrices realizing the specified order regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is a suitable kind, but the preorder-cone formalization and the name “processing-time order regime” are uncited. A source must also confirm whether preorder equivalence classes are intended to impose exact ties.

children.title: Proportionality Breakdown Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Perturbations and heterogeneous effects that remove proportionate processing structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Proportionality Breakdown Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic boundary for rank-one machine-by-job processing times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive processing-time matrix \(P=(p_{ij})\) has the proportional form \(p_{ij}=a_i b_j\) with \(a_i,b_j>0\) if and only if every \(2\times2\) minor vanishes: \(p_{ij}p_{hk}-p_{ik}p_{hj}=0\) for all machines \(i,h\) and jobs \(j,k\). Hence proportionality breaks precisely when at least one such cross-product difference is nonzero. The equal-across-machines proportionate model is the subcase in which all \(a_i\) are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive processing times are machine-job proportional exactly when all cross-product identities hold; one nonzero two-by-two minor certifies breakdown.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=ab^{\mathsf T}\) if and only if \(p_{ij}p_{hk}=p_{ik}p_{hj}\) for all \(i,h,j,k\).

notation.meaning: Positive machine and job factor vectors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vanishing-minor characterization is mathematically correct for positive rank-one matrices and failure_boundary fits its form, but the sibling proportionate-flow-shop record uses the narrower equal-across-machines convention. A source is needed to establish that this leaf concerns rank-one proportionality rather than breakdown of that narrower model.

children.title: Reentrant Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow shops where jobs revisit machines or stages during a routing.

knowledge_statements.title: Reentrant Flow Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow-shop routes that revisit at least one physical machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reentrant flow shop has a set of physical machines \(M\) and, for each job \(j\), an ordered route \(r_j=(r_{j1},\ldots,r_{jL_j})\in M^{L_j}\). Operations must follow this route, so \(S_{j,\ell+1}\ge S_{j\ell}+p_{j\ell}\). The system is reentrant when some route contains two positions \(\ell<q\) with \(r_{j\ell}=r_{jq}\); operations assigned to the same physical machine, including different visits by one job, must occupy disjoint time intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job follows an ordered route that returns to a previously visited physical machine, while all visits compete for that machine’s capacity.
assumptions_latex: Operations are nonpreemptive.
Each physical machine processes at most one operation at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{j\ell}=r_{jq}\) for some job \(j\) and positions \(\ell<q\), with route precedence and machine capacity enforced.

notation.meaning: Ordered physical-machine route of job j
Number of operations or visits of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The route-and-capacity formulation is coherent and definition fits the leaf, but no source confirms that the intended reentrant flow-shop class is exactly any route revisiting a physical machine rather than a more structured common-stage model.

children.title: Cyclic Flow Shops
children.top_down_role: Flow shops organized around repeating production patterns or periodic schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Flow Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic repetition of a finite flow-shop schedule pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cyclic flow-shop schedule is determined by a period \(T>0\) and a finite set of operation types \(O\). For each \(o\in O\), its occurrence in cycle \(k\in\mathbb Z\) starts at \(S_o(k)=s_o+kT\), where \(0\le s_o<T\). Every translated cycle satisfies the same route-precedence and machine-capacity constraints. The cycle time is \(T\), and the long-run production rate is the number of completed job copies per period divided by \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite feasible operation pattern repeats every period, preserving all precedence and machine-capacity constraints and inducing a constant long-run production rate.
assumptions_latex: Processing times and routes repeat identically between cycles.
The infinite translated schedule is feasible on every machine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_o(k+1)=S_o(k)+T\) for every operation type \(o\) and cycle \(k\).

notation.meaning: Phase of operation type o within one period

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The periodic schedule formulation is coherent and definition fits the leaf, but “cyclic flow shop” has source-dependent meanings. An authoritative citation is required to support this exact periodic-copy model and its production-rate interpretation.

children.title: Repeated-Visit Routing
children.top_down_role: Visit multiplicity, revisit order, and stage recurrence within individual job routes.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Visit Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Route-word representation of multiple visits to shared machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent the route of job \(j\) by a word \(r_j=r_{j1}\cdots r_{jL_j}\) over the alphabet of physical machines \(M\). Position \(\ell\) denotes an operation of duration \(p_{j\ell}>0\) on machine \(r_{j\ell}\), and route feasibility requires \(S_{j,\ell+1}\ge S_{j\ell}+p_{j\ell}\). A repeated visit to machine \(q\in M\) occurs exactly when \(|\{\ell:r_{j\ell}=q\}|\ge2\). All positions bearing the same machine symbol share one unit-capacity resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job route is a word over machine labels; repeated symbols encode repeated visits, and all occurrences compete for the same physical machine.
assumptions_latex: Each route has finite length.
Operations are processed in route order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) is revisited by job \(j\) if and only if \(|\{\ell:r_{j\ell}=q\}|\ge2\).

notation.meaning: Machine-label word representing job j’s route
Physical machine used at route position ℓ

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The route-word representation is precise, agrees with the plain statement, and representation is the correct kind, but it lacks a source supporting this formalization in the repeated-visit flow-shop context.

children.title: Periodic Schedule Regimes
children.top_down_role: Steady-state, finite-cycle, and transient structures in repeated production.

assumptions_latex: There is a finite set of job types processed repeatedly through an ordered set of stages.
Processing times and resource requirements repeat identically from one production cycle to the next.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule is periodic with cycle length \(T\).

notation.meaning: Start time of operation o in repetition k
Integer number of periods separating corresponding operations

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard periodic-scheduling definition using translation invariance of corresponding operation starts.
Authoritative scheduling source and exact locator are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steady-state periodicity for indefinitely repeated flow-shop production, excluding transient initialization and termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible schedule for a repetition-structured flow shop is periodic if there exist a period \(T>0\) and integers \(q_o\ge 1\), one for each operation type \(o\), such that corresponding starts satisfy \(S_{o,k+q_o}=S_{o,k}+T\) for every repetition index \(k\) for which both starts are defined. Machine-capacity, technological-precedence, and any blocking or buffer constraints must remain satisfied under this translation. When every \(q_o=1\), one complete copy of each job type is launched per period; more generally, the repeated block contains \(q_o\) copies of operation type \(o\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A periodic regime repeats a feasible block of flow-shop operations after a fixed time translation while preserving all precedence, machine-capacity, and storage constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Schedule Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied. An authoritative periodic-scheduling source with a specific locator is required to verify the operation-dependent integers q_o, the asserted common period T, and the interpretation of the repeated block; these details are not safely established by the standard-field rationale alone.

assumptions_latex: Each job visits a prescribed ordered subset of stages.
Every required operation has at least one eligible machine at its stage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible assignment chooses exactly one eligible stage machine for every required operation.

notation.meaning: Eligible machines for job j at stage s
Binary assignment of job j at stage s to machine m
Processing time under the indicated assignment

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard assignment predicate for flexible and hybrid flow-shop models.
Authoritative scheduling source and exact locator are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine eligibility and assignment within each visited flow-shop stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stagewise machine choice is the decision structure in which, for every job \(j\) and required stage \(s\), processing is assigned to exactly one eligible machine \(m\in M_{js}\). With binary variables \(x_{jsm}\), feasibility requires \(\sum_{m\in M_{js}}x_{jsm}=1\) and \(x_{jsm}\in\{0,1\}\). The selected machine determines the processing interval and, when machines are nonidentical, its duration \(p_{jsm}\). Intervals assigned to the same machine may not overlap, and the completion of the selected operation at stage \(s\) must precede the start of the job's next required stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each required stage, every job chooses exactly one eligible machine; that choice determines its processing interval and possibly its processing time.
knowledge_statements.title: Stagewise Machine Choice

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The assignment formulation fits Stagewise Machine Choice and is mathematically coherent, but the record has no inspectable citation. A scheduling source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is required to support this exact flexible/hybrid flow-shop interpretation.

children.title: Interstage Buffer Structures
children.top_down_role: Unlimited, finite, dedicated, and shared storage between production stages.

assumptions_latex: Jobs move between consecutive visited stages in a flow-shop system.
Storage occupancy is measured after upstream completion and before downstream processing begins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interstage feasibility is characterized by the specified buffer capacities \(B_s\).

notation.meaning: Number of jobs occupying that buffer at time t
Completion and downstream-start times for job j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard finite-buffer occupancy definition, including unlimited-buffer and zero-buffer boundary cases.
A source distinguishing blocking conventions for zero-capacity buffers is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-based classification of storage located between consecutive visited stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interstage buffer structure specifies a capacity \(B_s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) after each stage \(s\). A job \(j\) occupies that buffer during \([C_{js},S_{j,s+1})\) whenever it has completed stage \(s\) but has not begun its next required stage. Thus \(I_s(t)=\lvert\{j:C_{js}\le t<S_{j,s+1}\}\rvert\), and feasibility requires \(I_s(t)\le B_s\) for every time \(t\). The value \(B_s=\infty\) represents unrestricted intermediate storage. The value \(B_s=0\) requires an explicitly chosen no-wait or blocking convention because ordinary positive-duration buffer occupancy is then forbidden.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A buffer structure assigns each interstage location a capacity and limits how many completed jobs may wait there at any time.
knowledge_statements.title: Interstage Buffer Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited, and the treatment of B_s=0 depends materially on the adopted blocking, no-wait, and transfer conventions. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required before the stated occupancy model and boundary cases can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Stage-Bypass Routing
children.top_down_role: Job classes permitted to omit selected stages or processing resources.

assumptions_latex: The system has an ordered stage set, and every job has a prescribed route through a subset of it.
A bypassed stage performs no operation on the bypassing job.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The route is stage-bypassing exactly when some required-stage set omits an intermediate stage.

notation.meaning: Strictly increasing route of job j
Number of stages visited by job j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard route-subsequence definition of bypassing in multistage production systems.
Authoritative scheduling source and exact locator are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-only routing that may omit stages but never revisits an earlier stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stage-bypass routing assigns each job \(j\) a strictly increasing sequence \(R_j=(r_{j1},\ldots,r_{jk_j})\) with \(1\le r_{j1}<\cdots<r_{jk_j}\le S\). The job is processed only at stages in \(R_j\), and precedence requires completion at \(r_{jh}\) before processing begins at \(r_{j,h+1}\). Job \(j\) bypasses stage \(s\) when there exist consecutive route entries satisfying \(r_{jh}<s<r_{j,h+1}\). No machine assignment, processing time, or storage occupancy is created at a bypassed stage, although transportation between the two visited stages may still consume time or capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job follows an increasing subsequence of stages and bypasses every intermediate stage omitted between two consecutive route entries.
knowledge_statements.title: Stage-Bypass Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement matches the forward-only local sense of Stage-Bypass Routing, but no inspectable citation supports the route-subsequence convention or the claim that bypassed stages create no processing or storage occupancy. A specific authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Recirculating Routing
children.top_down_role: Routes permitting jobs to return to earlier stages or machine groups.

assumptions_latex: Each job has a finite ordered sequence of required operations.
Operations are labeled by the stage visited, and stage labels need not increase along the route.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route recirculates exactly when it revisits a stage or returns to a lower-indexed stage.

notation.meaning: Start and completion of route operation h
Number of route operations for job j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard operation-route definition allowing repeated or backward stage visits.
Authoritative scheduling source and exact locator are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite job routes containing repeated or backward visits in a nominally staged shop.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Recirculating routing assigns a job \(j\) a finite stage sequence \(R_j=(r_{j1},\ldots,r_{jk_j})\) that is not required to be strictly increasing. Route precedence imposes \(S_{j,h+1}\ge C_{jh}\) for \(h=1,\ldots,k_j-1\). The route is recirculating if either \(r_{jh}=r_{j\ell}\) for some \(h<\ell\), so a stage is revisited, or \(r_{j,h+1}<r_{jh}\) for some \(h\), so the job returns upstream. Distinct visits are distinct operations and may have different eligible machines and processing times even when their stage labels coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recirculating routing permits a job's operation sequence to revisit a stage or return to an earlier stage while retaining precedence between successive visits.
knowledge_statements.title: Recirculating Routing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied. A source with a specific locator is needed to verify that the local definition of recirculation includes both repeated stage labels and any backward transition, especially because terminology varies across reentrant and recirculating shop models.

children.title: Routing–Storage Interaction
children.top_down_role: Capacity and congestion effects created by bypass or recirculation under limited buffering.

assumptions_latex: A routed job occupies storage between completion of one route operation and start of the next.
Buffers have specified capacities and are associated with route transitions or physical locations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route assignment is storage-feasible exactly when every induced occupancy respects every buffer capacity.

notation.meaning: Buffer used after route operation h of job j
Occupancy of buffer b at time t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Direct capacity-feasibility predicate coupling chosen routes with induced buffer residence intervals.
A source specifying alternative blocking and transfer conventions is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility coupling between route selection and finite intermediate storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each consecutive pair of operations on job \(j\)'s selected route, let \(b(j,h)\) be the buffer used after completion \(C_{jh}\) and before the next start \(S_{j,h+1}\). The route and schedule satisfy routing-storage compatibility when \(S_{j,h+1}\ge C_{jh}\) and, for every buffer \(b\) and time \(t\), \(I_b(t)=\sum_{j,h:b(j,h)=b}\mathbf{1}_{[C_{jh},S_{j,h+1})}(t)\le B_b\). Consequently, bypass or recirculation decisions alter feasibility by changing both the selected buffer and its residence interval. For \(B_b=0\), the model must additionally specify whether immediate transfer, no-wait processing, or machine blocking applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Routes and storage are compatible when every selected transition has valid timing and the waiting intervals induced by all routes never exceed any buffer's capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Routing–Storage Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected content kind condition fits this feasibility leaf, but no source supports the exact route-to-buffer mapping, residence-interval convention, or zero-capacity alternatives. These conventions materially determine the formula, so a specifically located authoritative source is required.

children.title: Flexible Flow-Shop Structures
children.top_down_role: Flow-shop configurations permitting alternative machine choices at one or more stages.

assumptions_latex: All jobs traverse the same ordered set of stages.
At least one stage contains multiple eligible parallel machines.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting shop is a flexible flow shop with stagewise assignment decisions.

notation.meaning: Parallel machine set at stage s
Start and completion of job j at stage s
Machine selected for job j at stage s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard flexible-flow-shop structure with common stage order and parallel-machine assignment.
Terminology overlaps hybrid flow shop; an authoritative source fixing the local convention is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common stage route with assignment flexibility supplied by parallel machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flexible flow-shop structure consists of stages \(1,ldots,S\) visited by every job in that order, with a nonempty machine set \(M_s\) at each stage and \(\lvert M_s\rvert>1\) for at least one stage. Each job \(j\) is assigned to one machine \(a_{js}\in M_s\) at every stage. Technological precedence requires \(S_{j,s+1}\ge C_{js}\), and processing intervals assigned to the same machine must be pairwise nonoverlapping. Processing times may depend on \(j\), \(s\), and \(a_{js}\). The structural flexibility is the choice among machines within a prescribed common stage route, not a choice of operation order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every job visits the same stages in order but chooses one machine from a parallel set at each stage, subject to precedence and nonoverlap.
knowledge_statements.title: Flexible Flow-Shop Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement contains the malformed stage enumeration \(1,ldots,S\), where the intended LaTeX command is missing its backslash. More importantly, no citation establishes the local distinction between flexible and hybrid flow shops. Because that terminology determines whether this definition belongs in the exact leaf, an authoritative source with a specific locator is required before revision.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flexible flow shops with unlimited intermediate storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine environment, standard objective notation, and the proportionate-processing-time specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flexible flow shop has \(c\) stages in series, with \(m_l\) identical parallel machines at stage \(l\), and unlimited intermediate storage between successive stages. Each job \(j=1,\ldots,n\) must be processed at every stage on one machine at that stage, with processing times \(p_{1j},\ldots,p_{cj}\). Makespan and total-completion-time minimization are denoted by \(FFc\parallel C_{\max}\) and \(FFc\parallel\sum_j C_j\), respectively. In the proportionate specialization, \(p_{1j}=\cdots=p_{cj}=p_j\) for every job \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flexible flow shop consists of serial stages, each having identical parallel machines, with unlimited storage between stages. Every job visits every stage and may use any machine there. The standard makespan and total-completion-time problems are denoted FFc||Cmax and FFc||sum Cj. In the proportionate specialization, each job has the same processing time at every stage.
assumptions_latex: c,n\in\mathbb{N}
m_l\ge 1\quad(l=1,\ldots,c)
p_{lj}\ge 0\quad(l=1,\ldots,c;\ j=1,\ldots,n)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The machine environment is }FFc;\quad p_{1j}=\cdots=p_{cj}=p_j\text{ defines its proportionate specialization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characteristic-dependent setup times in a flexible flow shop
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A flexible flow shop with serial stages, parallel possibly heterogeneous machines, unlimited buffers, and machine-specific sequence-dependent setup times represented through job characteristics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a flexible flow shop whose stages are arranged in series, with parallel, possibly heterogeneous machines at each stage and unlimited intermediate buffers. Under the simplifying assumption that setup-relevant properties are represented by one parameter \(a_{ij}\) for job \(j\) on machine \(i\), if job \(k\) immediately follows job \(j\) on machine \(i\), then its setup time is \(s_{ijk}=h_i(a_{ij},a_{ik})\), where \(h_i\) may be machine dependent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic nonpreemptive job shop with fixed routes and unary machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A classical job-shop instance comprises jobs \(j\), each with an ordered operation sequence \((O_{j1},\ldots,O_{jk_j})\). Operation \(O_{jh}\) must execute nonpreemptively for \(p_{jh}>0\) time units on its prescribed unary machine \(m_{jh}\). A schedule assigns starts \(S_{jh}\ge0\) such that \(S_{j,h+1}\ge S_{jh}+p_{jh}\) for every consecutive pair in a job and, whenever \(m_{jh}=m_{i\ell}\), either \(S_{jh}+p_{jh}\le S_{i\ell}\) or \(S_{i\ell}+p_{i\ell}\le S_{jh}\). Thus routing is fixed and the combinatorial decision is principally the ordering of competing operations on each machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical job shop fixes each job's operation order and machine assignments; feasible schedules respect those precedences and prevent overlap on every machine.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Job Shops

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic nonpreemptive unary-machine formulation is standard and matches Classical Job Shops, but the record supplies neither a source nor a specific locator. Standard-field rationale alone does not satisfy the evidence requirement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LP-based sequencing heuristic for classical job shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A job-shop heuristic that converts optimal completion-time variables from a cutting-plane LP solution into a fixed operation order for each machine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Solve LP \((12.4)\) by the cutting-plane method using the separation algorithm of Theorem 12.2, obtaining optimal values \(C_{ij}^*\). For each machine \(r\), order the tasks \((i,j)\in M_r\) by nondecreasing \(C_{ij}^*\). Each machine processes its tasks in that order as soon as the corresponding jobs become available. The resulting schedule is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the job-shop LP with cutting planes, order each machine's tasks by increasing optimal LP completion time, and process them in that order as their jobs become available to obtain a feasible schedule.
assumptions_latex: C^*\text{ is an optimal solution of LP }(12.4)
M_r\text{ is the set of tasks assigned to machine }r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Processing each machine's tasks in nondecreasing }C_{ij}^*\text{ order as jobs become available yields a feasible schedule.}

A schedule chooses exactly one machine \(a_{jh}\in M_{jh}\), gives the operation duration \(p_{jh,a_{jh}}>0\), and assigns a start \(S_{jh}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Five-phase shifting-bottleneck decomposition for flexible job shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A decomposition-based adaptation of the shifting-bottleneck heuristic for flexible job shops, including workcenters comprising either one machine or a bank of parallel machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{1. Partition the flexible job shop into workcenters to be scheduled.}\\&\text{2. Represent the entire shop by a disjunctive graph.}\\&\text{3. Rank the unsequenced workcenters by a criticality measure and fix the sequence of the most critical one.}\\&\text{4. Use the disjunctive graph to capture interactions between sequenced and unsequenced workcenters.}\\&\text{5. Reschedule the sequenced workcenters using the updated information; stop if all workcenters are sequenced,}\text{ otherwise return to Step 3.}\end{aligned}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the flexible job shop into workcenters and represent the entire shop by a disjunctive graph. Rank the workcenters whose sequences remain undetermined by criticality and fix the sequence of the most critical one. Update the interactions between sequenced and unsequenced workcenters through the graph, then reschedule previously sequenced workcenters using the new information. Stop when all workcenters have been sequenced; otherwise repeat from the ranking step.
assumptions_latex: \text{The scheduling instance is a flexible job shop organized into workcenters.}
\text{Each workcenter consists of a single machine or a bank of parallel machines.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure iterates critical-workcenter sequencing, interaction updating, and rescheduling until every workcenter has been sequenced.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternative process plans that may change both visited resources and operation precedence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A job shop with routing alternatives gives each job \(j\) a nonempty finite set \(\mathcal{R}_j\) of admissible routes. Each route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_j\) is an ordered operation sequence \(O(j,r)\) with specified resource eligibility and processing requirements. A feasible solution selects exactly one route \(r_j\in\mathcal{R}_j\), schedules precisely its operations in the route order, and enforces nonoverlap on every selected unary resource. Operations belonging only to unselected routes are absent. This structure is more general than choosing a machine independently for each fixed operation because a route choice may add, remove, reorder, or revisit processing steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job chooses one admissible process route, then schedules that route's operations under precedence and resource-capacity constraints; different routes may change the operations themselves.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Standard continuous-time feasibility definition for a preemptive open shop.
Authoritative scheduling source and exact locator are required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preemptive open-shop feasibility with arbitrary operation order and no parallel processing of a job.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A preemptive open-shop schedule over \([0,T]\) is described by measurable indicators \(x_{jm}(t)\in\{0,1\}\). For every required job-machine pair, \(\int_0^T x_{jm}(t)\,dt=p_{jm}\). Unit machine capacity requires \(\sum_j x_{jm}(t)\le1\) for every machine \(m\) and almost every \(t\), while unit job capacity requires \(\sum_m x_{jm}(t)\le1\) for every job \(j\) and almost every \(t\). No precedence order is imposed among a job's machine operations. Preemption permits each set \(\{t:x_{jm}(t)=1\}\) to be disconnected, with processing resumed later without loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preemptive open shop may interrupt and resume operations in any order, while each machine and each job participates in at most one operation at a time.
knowledge_statements.title: Preemptive Open Shops

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The measurable-indicator formulation is a plausible definition of preemptive open-shop feasibility and the content kind fits the leaf, but no source or locator is supplied. An authoritative reference is required to verify the continuous-time and almost-everywhere conventions, including the no-parallel-processing condition for each job.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpreemptive Open Shops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite deterministic open-shop feasibility with nonpreemptive operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let jobs be indexed by \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and machines by \(M=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Each job \(j\) has one operation \((j,k)\) of processing time \(p_{jk}\ge 0\) on every machine \(k\), with no prescribed order among its operations. A nonpreemptive open-shop schedule assigns each operation a start time \(S_{jk}\ge 0\) such that its processing interval \([S_{jk},S_{jk}+p_{jk})\) is contiguous, intervals of operations belonging to the same job are pairwise disjoint, and intervals assigned to the same machine are pairwise disjoint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality result within the stochastic two-machine open-shop model, with comparisons over both preemptive and nonpreemptive dynamic policy classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence-Dependent Changeovers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine setup times determined by the immediately preceding operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each machine \(k\), let \(O_k\) be its assigned operations and let \(s^k_{uv}\ge 0\) be the changeover time when operation \(v\) immediately follows operation \(u\). If \(u\) precedes \(v\) consecutively on \(k\), feasibility requires \(S_v\ge S_u+p_u+s^k_{uv}\). Sequence dependence means that the matrix \((s^k_{uv})\) is part of the instance and need not satisfy \(s^k_{uv}=s^k_{u'v}\), symmetry, or a triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The setup before an operation depends on its immediate predecessor, and the successor cannot start until both processing and the corresponding changeover finish.
assumptions_latex: Each operation is assigned to a machine.
Changeovers and processing are nonpreemptive on the relevant machine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every consecutive machine pair \((u,v)\) satisfies \(S_v\ge S_u+p_u+s^k_{uv}\).

notation.meaning: changeover time from operation u to v on machine k

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation-Time Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit travel time between consecutive operations performed at different locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let operation \(u\) finish at location \(a(u)\), and let its successor \(v\) start at location \(a(v)\). Given transportation times \(\tau_{ab}\ge 0\), the temporal coupling is represented by \(S_v\ge C_u+\tau_{a(u),a(v)}\), where \(C_u=S_u+p_u\). If transport uses no capacity-constrained carrier, this inequality completely represents the transfer; if a carrier is capacity constrained, corresponding transport intervals must additionally satisfy resource-feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A successor operation starts only after its predecessor finishes and the item travels between their locations; limited transport capacity requires extra resource constraints.
assumptions_latex: The precedence arc \(u\to v\) requires physical transfer.
Travel times \(\tau_{ab}\) are specified and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The precedence lag on \(u\to v\) is at least \(\tau_{a(u),a(v)}\).

notation.meaning: location at which operation u is processed
travel time from location a to location b

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is coherent and locally appropriate, but the claim that the lag inequality completely represents transfer when no capacity-constrained carrier is present depends on modeling assumptions that are not fully stated or sourced.
