knowledge_statements.title: Interoperation-Lag Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum and maximum time lags on precedence-related operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a set of precedence arcs between operations. For every \((u,v)\in A\), prescribe a minimum lag \(\ell_{uv}\ge 0\) and optionally a maximum lag \(L_{uv}\in[\ell_{uv},+\infty]\). With completion time \(C_u=S_u+p_u\), an interoperation-lag schedule satisfies \(S_v-C_u\ge \ell_{uv}\) and, whenever \(L_{uv}<+\infty\), \(S_v-C_u\le L_{uv}\). Equality of both bounds imposes an exact lag.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each precedence arc can impose a minimum waiting time, a maximum waiting time, or an exact delay between predecessor completion and successor start.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a specified precedence relation.
\(0\le \ell_{uv}\le L_{uv}\le +\infty\) for every \((u,v)\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \((u,v)\in A\), the delay \(S_v-C_u\) lies in \([\ell_{uv},L_{uv}]\).

notation.meaning: minimum lag from u to v
maximum lag from u to v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-, maximum-, and exact-lag conditions are mathematically consistent and the content kind fits the leaf. However, no authoritative source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is cited.

children.title: Transfer-Resource Constraints
children.top_down_role: Capacity and availability restrictions on vehicles, handlers, conveyors, or transfer channels.

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer-Resource Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity feasibility for resources executing material transfers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each required transfer \(q\) occupy the interval \([T_q,T_q+d_q)\), consume \(b_{qr}\ge 0\) units of transfer resource \(r\), and have duration \(d_q\ge 0\). If resource \(r\) has capacity \(B_r\), transfer feasibility requires \(\sum_{q:T_q\le t<T_q+d_q} b_{qr}\le B_r\) for every time \(t\) and every \(r\). The transfer interval must also connect its adjacent operations: \(T_q\ge C_u\) and \(S_v\ge T_q+d_q\) when \(q\) transfers material from \(u\) to \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every transfer occupies carrier capacity during its travel interval and must occur after the predecessor finishes but before the successor begins.
assumptions_latex: Transfer capacities \(B_r\) are constant and nonnegative.
Each transfer has specified duration and resource demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All transfer intervals satisfy both cumulative resource capacity and operation-linking constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cumulative-resource model applied to transfers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cumulative-capacity and operation-linking constraints form a plausible transfer-resource condition, but no source supports this particular model or its boundary assumptions. An authoritative scheduling or resource-constrained scheduling citation with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Delay-Coupling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interactions among processing completion, transfer availability, and downstream readiness.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Coupling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by whether transfer delays are independent, shared, or endogenous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For precedence arcs \(A\), write \(S_v\ge C_u+d_{uv}(x)\) for each \((u,v)\in A\), where \(x\) denotes scheduling and transfer decisions. The regime is uncoupled when every \(d_{uv}\) is fixed independently of \(x\); pairwise coupled when a delay depends on the selected predecessor-successor or route; resource-coupled when simultaneous transfers affect feasibility or delay through shared capacity; and schedule-dependent when \(d_{uv}(x)\) otherwise depends on timing or assignment decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delay regimes distinguish fixed independent lags from delays coupled through routing choices, shared transfer capacity, or other scheduling decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a specified set of precedence arcs.
Every delay function \(d_{uv}(x)\) is nonnegative on feasible decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each arc satisfies \(S_v-C_u\ge d_{uv}(x)\), with the regime determined by the dependence structure of \(d_{uv}\).

notation.meaning: decision-dependent delay on arc from u to v

review_flags: taxonomy terminology may vary across scheduling sources

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed regime names and distinctions are not established by any cited source, and the categories are not demonstrably exclusive: pairwise or route-dependent delay is also schedule-dependent under the stated definitions. Source inspection is needed before the classification can be made reliable.

children.title: Machine-Availability Calendars
children.top_down_role: Fixed, periodic, stochastic, or job-dependent machine operating intervals.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Availability Calendars
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility against exogenously specified machine uptime intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each machine \(k\), let its availability calendar be \(A_k=\bigcup_{h=1}^{H_k}[a_{kh},b_{kh})\), where the component intervals are pairwise disjoint. If operation \(i\) is assigned to \(k\), has processing time \(p_{ik}\), and cannot be interrupted by downtime, calendar feasibility requires \([S_i,S_i+p_{ik})\subseteq A_k\). Equivalently, there exists an interval index \(h\) such that \(a_{kh}\le S_i\) and \(S_i+p_{ik}\le b_{kh}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpreemptive operation must fit wholly inside one of its assigned machine's predefined availability intervals.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_k\) is a finite union of disjoint half-open intervals.
Operations cannot execute or be suspended during unavailable periods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every operation interval is contained in one component of its machine's availability calendar.

notation.meaning: h-th availability interval of machine k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonpreemptive calendar condition is mathematically plausible and appropriate for the leaf, but no scheduling source with an inspectable locator is supplied. The treatment of downtime and the finite-calendar convention require source support.

children.title: Maintenance-Window Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Models coordinating production with preventive or corrective maintenance periods.

knowledge_statements.title: Maintenance-Window Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint placement of maintenance tasks and production operations within allowed windows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each maintenance task \(q\) on machine \(k(q)\), let duration \(d_q>0\) and admissible start window \([r_q,D_q-d_q]\) be given. A feasible start \(T_q\) satisfies \(r_q\le T_q\le D_q-d_q\). Its interval \([T_q,T_q+d_q)\) is disjoint from every production interval and every other maintenance interval assigned to \(k(q)\). If maintenance is mandatory, exactly one such interval is scheduled for each task \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every mandatory maintenance task is placed within its allowed window and cannot overlap production or another maintenance task on the same machine.
assumptions_latex: \(r_q+d_q\le D_q\) for each maintenance task \(q\).
Maintenance and production use their assigned machine exclusively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each maintenance interval lies in \([r_q,D_q)\) and satisfies machine nonoverlap.

notation.meaning: start time of maintenance task q
execution window for maintenance task q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maintenance-window and machine-nonoverlap conditions are coherent and fit the leaf, but the record has no cited source with a specific locator. The standard-field rationale alone is insufficient for this review.

children.title: Production–Maintenance Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions among output, machine condition, downtime, and maintenance timing.

knowledge_statements.title: Production–Maintenance Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biobjective scheduling tradeoff between production performance and maintenance burden.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the set of schedules satisfying production, machine, and maintenance constraints. Let \(P(x)\) measure production loss, such as makespan or total tardiness, and let \(M(x)\) measure maintenance cost, expected degradation, or maintenance-induced downtime. The production–maintenance tradeoff is represented by the attainable set \(Y=\{(P(x),M(x)):x\in X\}\). A schedule \(x^*\in X\) is Pareto efficient when no \(x\in X\) satisfies \(P(x)\le P(x^*)\) and \(M(x)\le M(x^*)\), with at least one strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible schedules trade production performance against maintenance burden; a schedule is efficient when neither criterion can improve without worsening the other.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
Both \(P\) and \(M\) are minimized and are finite on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The efficient tradeoff consists of the nondominated points of \(Y\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Pareto representation of a scheduling tradeoff

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto attainable-set representation is mathematically correct as a generic biobjective model and its content kind is suitable, but no source establishes that these production and maintenance criteria represent the intended scheduling leaf. A domain-specific source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Availability-Disruption Regimes
children.top_down_role: Planned outages, random failures, resumable interruptions, and nonresumable interruptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Availability-Disruption Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of machine unavailability by information and decision dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For machine \(k\), represent disruption by an unavailable-time set \(U_k(\omega,x)\), where \(\omega\) is exogenous information and \(x\) denotes scheduling or maintenance decisions. The regime is deterministic when \(U_k\) is known before scheduling; stochastic when \(U_k(\omega)\) is random with a specified probability law; robust when \(U_k\) ranges over a prescribed uncertainty set without probabilities; and endogenous when \(U_k\) depends on \(x\), for example through maintenance or accumulated usage. Processing is allowed only outside \(U_k(\omega,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machine disruptions may be known, probabilistic, uncertainty-set based, or caused by schedule and maintenance decisions; processing is forbidden during disrupted periods.
assumptions_latex: Every machine has a measurable unavailable-time set.
The selected information regime is fixed for the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An operation on machine \(k\) may execute only at times \(t\notin U_k(\omega,x)\).
review_flags: taxonomy terminology may vary across scheduling sources

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic, stochastic, robust, and endogenous labels mix information models with decision dependence and are not shown to be mutually exclusive. No cited source supports this exact classification, so its mathematical scope and terminology cannot be accepted reliably.

children.title: Secondary Resource Constraints
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary tools, operators, fixtures, space, or support assets required by scheduled work.

knowledge_statements.title: Secondary Resource Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous requirements for machines and auxiliary renewable resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let operation \(i\) be assigned to machine \(k(i)\), occupy \([S_i,S_i+p_i)\), and require \(b_{ir}\ge 0\) units of each secondary renewable resource \(r\). Besides machine nonoverlap, feasibility requires \(\sum_{i:S_i\le t<S_i+p_i} b_{ir}\le B_r\) for every time \(t\) and resource \(r\), where \(B_r\) is its capacity. Thus machine feasibility alone is insufficient whenever operations sharing a secondary resource overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operations must satisfy machine capacity and, simultaneously, the capacities of auxiliary resources such as workers, tools, or fixtures.
assumptions_latex: Secondary resources are renewable with constant capacities \(B_r\).
Resource demand is constant throughout each operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every time, aggregate demand for each secondary resource does not exceed its capacity.

notation.meaning: operation i's demand for secondary resource r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The renewable secondary-resource capacity condition is standard and fits the exact leaf, but no authoritative scheduling source or specific locator is supplied. Candidate rationale does not replace the required citation.

children.title: Discrete Resource Constraints
children.top_down_role: Indivisible resource units assigned exclusively or in integer quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Resource Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral allocation of distinguishable or unit-capacity auxiliary resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a finite set of discrete resource units. Each operation \(i\) requires an allocation \(y_{ir}\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\sum_{r\in E_i}y_{ir}=q_i\), where \(E_i\subseteq R\) is its eligibility set and \(q_i\) is its required number of units. For every \(r\in R\) and time \(t\), exclusivity requires \(\sum_{i:S_i\le t<S_i+p_i}y_{ir}\le 1\). Allocations remain fixed throughout an operation unless reassignment is explicitly permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each operation receives an integral number of eligible resource units, and no discrete unit can serve overlapping operations.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and every eligibility set \(E_i\) are finite.
Resource units are renewable and individually unit-capacitated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every operation receives \(q_i\) eligible units, with no unit allocated to two simultaneous operations.

notation.meaning: binary allocation of resource unit r to operation i
resource units eligible for operation i
number of discrete units required by operation i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-allocation model is plausible for discrete renewable resources, but no source with an inspectable locator is provided. Source-supported revision should also state that each required count q_i is a nonnegative integer and does not exceed the number of eligible units.

children.title: Cumulative Resource Constraints
children.top_down_role: Shared capacity consumed concurrently by multiple activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative Resource Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Renewable-resource feasibility for nonpreemptive activities in continuous time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite activity set and \(R\) a finite resource set. Activity \(j\in J\) has start time \(S_j\), processing time \(p_j>0\), and demand \(a_{jr}\ge 0\) for resource \(r\in R\), whose capacity is \(B_r\ge 0\). The schedule satisfies the cumulative resource constraints precisely when, for every \(r\in R\) and every time \(t\in\mathbb R\), \[\sum_{j\in J:\,S_j\le t<S_j+p_j}a_{jr}\le B_r.\] Thus each activity consumes its demand throughout the half-open interval \([S_j,S_j+p_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every time, the total demand of simultaneously active jobs may not exceed the capacity of any renewable resource.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(R\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j:S_j\le t<S_j+p_j}a_{jr}\le B_r\) for every \(r\in R\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: start time and processing time of activity j
demand of activity j for resource r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the cumulative-resource leaf and is mathematically coherent for finite, nonpreemptive activities with renewable capacities. However, source_refs is empty, and the local inventory contains no scheduling source supporting the formulation or its continuous-time scope.

children.title: Multi-Resource Coupling
children.top_down_role: Feasibility effects arising when jobs simultaneously require machines and auxiliary capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Resource Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint feasibility when one operation simultaneously consumes several resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set and \(R\) a finite set of renewable resources. For each job \(j\), let \(Q_j\subseteq R\) be its required resource bundle, and let \(a_{jr}>0\) for \(r\in Q_j\). A schedule exhibits multi-resource coupling when starting \(j\) at \(S_j\) requires every resource in \(Q_j\) simultaneously throughout \([S_j,S_j+p_j)\); feasibility is therefore the conjunction \[\sum_{j:\,r\in Q_j,\ S_j\le t<S_j+p_j}a_{jr}\le B_r\qquad(r\in R,\ t\in\mathbb R).\] A job cannot be processed using only a proper subset of its required bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each job requires a bundle of resources concurrently, so its processing interval is feasible only if every resource requirement is met simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(R\) are finite.
Each job is nonpreemptive and has \(p_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every active job receives all resources in \(Q_j\), and every resource-capacity inequality holds simultaneously.

notation.meaning: resource bundle required by job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is a plausible bundle-based interpretation of multi-resource coupling, but that title can cover broader coupling mechanisms than simultaneous renewable-resource consumption. No cited source establishes that this is the intended exact local sense or supports the formulation.

children.title: Multipurpose Machine Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Machines capable of serving multiple operation types, product families, or process modes.

knowledge_statements.title: Multipurpose Machine Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling with fixed heterogeneous machine capabilities and job eligibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set and \(M\) a finite machine set. Machine \(m\in M\) has a fixed capability set \(K_m\), while job \(j\in J\) requires capabilities \(H_j\). Define the eligible-machine set by \(E_j=\{m\in M:H_j\subseteq K_m\}\). A multipurpose-machine schedule assigns each job \(j\) to one machine \(m(j)\in E_j\) and a processing interval \([S_j,S_j+p_{j,m(j)})\), such that intervals assigned to the same machine are pairwise disjoint. Machine capabilities remain fixed during the scheduling horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs are assigned without overlap to machines whose fixed capability sets contain all capabilities required by the assigned job.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
\(p_{jm}>0\) whenever \(m\in E_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(j)\in E_j\) for every \(j\), and same-machine processing intervals are pairwise disjoint.

notation.meaning: fixed capability set of machine m
machines eligible to process job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this problem-family leaf, and the eligibility-set model is internally coherent. An authoritative scheduling citation is required because 'multipurpose machine scheduling' is used with varying capability, tooling, and assignment semantics, and no source supports the selected fixed-capability interpretation.

children.title: Reconfigurable Machine Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Machines whose capabilities or capacities change through configuration decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reconfigurable Machine Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine scheduling with endogenous capability configurations and reconfiguration transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each machine \(m\) possess a finite configuration set \(C_m\). Configuration \(c\in C_m\) enables job set \(J_{mc}\), and changing from \(c\) to \(c'\) requires transition time \(s^m_{cc'}\ge 0\). A reconfigurable-machine schedule chooses for every processed job \(j\) a machine \(m\), an enabling configuration \(c\) with \(j\in J_{mc}\), and a processing interval. If consecutive jobs on machine \(m\) use configurations \(c\) and \(c'\), their start times satisfy \[S_{j'}\ge S_j+p_{jmc}+s^m_{cc'}.\] Configuration changes are therefore explicit scheduling decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machines may change capability configurations; each job needs an enabling configuration, and consecutive jobs must allow the required reconfiguration time.
assumptions_latex: All job, machine, and configuration sets are finite.
Processing and transition times are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every job uses an enabling configuration, and every consecutive pair respects its configuration-transition time.

notation.meaning: jobs enabled on machine m in configuration c
time to change machine m from c to c-prime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the reconfigurable-machine problem-family leaf and consistently models configuration-dependent eligibility plus transition time. No source is cited for this particular model, including the treatment of configuration changes between consecutive jobs.

children.title: Configuration-Change Costs
children.top_down_role: Time, labor, tooling, and economic effects associated with machine reconfiguration.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Change Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-dependent costs induced by machine-configuration transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each machine \(m\), let \(c^m_0,c^m_1,\ldots,c^m_{q_m}\) be its initial configuration followed by the configurations used by its scheduled jobs. If changing from \(c\) to \(c'\) on machine \(m\) incurs cost \(\kappa^m_{cc'}\ge 0\), then the total configuration-change cost of the schedule is \[K=\sum_{m}\sum_{k=1}^{q_m}\kappa^m_{c^m_{k-1},c^m_k}.\] Repeated consecutive use of the same configuration contributes \(\kappa^m_{cc}\), conventionally zero. An optimization model may minimize \(K\) alone or include it as one term of its objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The schedule pays a sequence-dependent cost whenever a machine moves from one capability configuration to the next.
assumptions_latex: Each machine has an initial configuration.
Every transition cost \(\kappa^m_{cc'}\) is specified and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\sum_m\sum_{k=1}^{q_m}\kappa^m_{c^m_{k-1},c^m_k}\).

notation.meaning: configuration used at position k on machine m

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and sequence-dependent cost expression fit the leaf. A source is still required for the model and conventions, especially inclusion of the initial transition and the assertion that same-configuration transition cost is conventionally zero.

children.title: Capability-Flexibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Fixed capability sets, selectable modes, modular configurations, and capacity-scalable machines.

knowledge_statements.title: Capability-Flexibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-system representation of fixed machine eligibility and its flexibility extremes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be the machine set and let \(E_j\subseteq M\) be the machines capable of processing job \(j\). The family \(\mathcal E=(E_j)_{j\in J}\) represents a capability-flexibility regime. It is dedicated when \(|E_j|=1\) for every \(j\), fully flexible when \(E_j=M\) for every \(j\), and partially flexible otherwise. For two regimes \(\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal E'\), write \(\mathcal E\preceq\mathcal E'\) when \(E_j\subseteq E'_j\) for all \(j\). Under unchanged processing data and constraints, this inclusion implies \(\mathcal F(\mathcal E)\subseteq\mathcal F(\mathcal E')\) for their feasible schedule sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Job-to-machine eligibility sets encode dedicated, partial, and full flexibility; enlarging every eligibility set cannot remove feasible schedules.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
Only eligibility sets change when two regimes are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E\preceq\mathcal E'\) implies \(\mathcal F(\mathcal E)\subseteq\mathcal F(\mathcal E')\).

notation.meaning: machines capable of processing job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate content kind for an eligibility-set encoding, and feasible-set monotonicity is correct when all noneligibility data are unchanged. No source establishes that dedicated, partial, and full flexibility exhaust the intended local regimes or supports this exact representation.

children.title: Deteriorating Processing Times
children.top_down_role: Processing environments where later starts or accumulated use increase required processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Deteriorating Processing Times
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Start-time deterioration for nonpreemptive processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For job \(j\), let \(p_j(t)>0\) denote its realized processing time when it starts at time \(t\) in a domain \(T_j\subseteq\mathbb R_+\). The processing-time law is deteriorating when \[t_1\le t_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_j(t_1)\le p_j(t_2)\qquad(t_1,t_2\in T_j).\] In a schedule with start time \(S_j\in T_j\), completion is \(C_j=S_j+p_j(S_j)\). Strict deterioration replaces the final inequality by a strict one whenever \(t_1<t_2\). This condition concerns delay-induced processing growth, not merely later completion caused by a later start.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job deteriorates when delaying its start cannot decrease its required processing time; completion equals start time plus the resulting duration.
assumptions_latex: Each job is nonpreemptive.
\(p_j:T_j\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) is defined on allowable start times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t_1\le t_2\) implies \(p_j(t_1)\le p_j(t_2)\).

notation.meaning: processing time of job j when started at t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly describes start-time-dependent deterioration and fits the leaf, but deteriorating-job models also use position-dependent and other laws. A scheduling source with a specific locator is needed to support this selected variant and terminology.

children.title: Learning-Effect Processing
children.top_down_role: Processing environments where repetition, position, or experience reduces required processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Learning-Effect Processing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Position-based learning effect within a machine sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a machine sequence and let \(r_j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be the position at which job \(j\) is processed. A position-based learning effect assigns realized duration \(p_j(r_j)>0\) and requires \[r_1\le r_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_j(r_1)\ge p_j(r_2).\] A common power-law specification is \(p_j(r)=p_j^0r^{a}\), where \(p_j^0>0\) and \(a<0\). Thus later positions weakly reduce processing time. This definition does not assert that changing a job's position leaves the positions or durations of other jobs unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under position-based learning, processing a job later in a machine sequence weakly decreases its duration; a negative-exponent power law is a standard model.
assumptions_latex: Jobs are processed nonpreemptively in a finite sequence.
\(p_j(r)>0\) for each admissible position \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_1\le r_2\) implies \(p_j(r_1)\ge p_j(r_2)\).

notation.meaning: nominal processing time of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonic position-based condition and negative-exponent power-law example are coherent, and condition is a suitable kind. Learning-effect scheduling has multiple variants, so an authoritative source must support this exact position-based scope and specification.

children.title: Time-Dependent Processing
children.top_down_role: Processing durations varying with start time, completion time, calendar period, or machine state.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Processing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic processing duration as a function of temporal state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every eligible job-machine pair \((j,m)\), let \(T_{jm}\subseteq\mathbb R_+\) be the allowable start-time domain and let \(p_{jm}:T_{jm}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) be a specified function. A nonpreemptive schedule has time-dependent processing when assigning job \(j\) to machine \(m\) at start time \(S_j\in T_{jm}\) produces completion time \[C_j=S_j+p_{jm}(S_j).\] No monotonicity is required: deterioration and start-time improvement are special cases obtained when \(p_{jm}\) is respectively nondecreasing or nonincreasing. Feasibility must use the realized interval \([S_j,C_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job's duration is a specified function of its start time and assigned machine, with no general monotonicity requirement.
assumptions_latex: Processing is deterministic and nonpreemptive.
\(p_{jm}(t)>0\) on every allowable domain \(T_{jm}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_j=S_j+p_{jm}(S_j)\), and job \(j\) occupies machine \(m\) on \([S_j,C_j)\).

notation.meaning: duration of job j on machine m when started at t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits deterministic, nonpreemptive start-time-dependent processing and clearly distinguishes monotonic special cases. It has no cited source, and none of the inventoried sources concerns scheduling or supports this formulation.

children.title: Competing Temporal Effects
children.top_down_role: Regimes combining improvement, deterioration, aging, fatigue, or calendar-dependent productivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Competing Temporal Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Processing laws combining deterioration with sequence-position learning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let job \(j\) start at time \(t\ge 0\) in sequence position \(r\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A separable competing-effects model represents its realized processing time as \[p_j(t,r)=p_j^0d_j(t)\ell_j(r),\] where \(p_j^0>0\), \(d_j(t)>0\) is nondecreasing, and \(\ell_j(r)>0\) is nonincreasing. The first factor models deterioration from later starts and the second models learning from later positions. Because increasing \(r\) generally also changes \(t\), neither effect alone determines whether realized durations rise or fall along a schedule; the combined value \(p_j(t,r)\) must be evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processing time combines an increasing start-time deterioration factor with a decreasing sequence-position learning factor, so their net scheduling effect may be ambiguous.
assumptions_latex: \(d_j\) is positive and nondecreasing.
\(\ell_j\) is positive and nonincreasing.
Processing is deterministic and nonpreemptive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_j(t,r)=p_j^0d_j(t)\ell_j(r)\), with opposing monotonic effects in \(t\) and \(r\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate for a particular separable competing-effects model, but multiplicative separability is a substantive model choice rather than the general meaning of competing temporal effects. A specific source is required before this formula can represent the leaf.

children.title: Smith Ordering Families
children.top_down_role: Single-machine ordering landmarks based on processing-time and weight priorities.

knowledge_statements.title: Smith Ordering Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smith's ratio rule for single-machine total weighted completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite set of jobs available at time zero on one continuously available machine. Job \(j\) has processing time \(p_j>0\) and weight \(w_j>0\); processing is nonpreemptive, and there are no precedence constraints or sequence-dependent setup times. A schedule minimizes \(\sum_{j\in J}w_jC_j\) if its jobs are ordered by nondecreasing ratios \(p_j/w_j\), equivalently by nonincreasing ratios \(w_j/p_j\). Any ordering of jobs having equal ratios is optimal. Consequently, an adjacent pair \(i,j\) may occur in an optimal order with \(i\) before \(j\) whenever \(p_iw_j\le p_jw_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For single-machine weighted completion time, ordering jobs by increasing processing-time-to-weight ratio is optimal; ties may be resolved arbitrarily.
assumptions_latex: All jobs are available at time zero on one machine.
Processing is nonpreemptive, with \(p_j>0\) and \(w_j>0\).
There are no precedence constraints or sequence-dependent setup times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An order satisfying \(p_i/w_i\le p_j/w_j\) whenever \(i\) precedes \(j\) minimizes \(\sum_jw_jC_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits this landmark-ordering leaf, and the stated Smith ratio rule has the relevant positivity, release-time, machine, nonpreemption, precedence, and setup assumptions. Nevertheless, a theorem claim requires an authoritative scheduling citation with a specific locator; source_refs is empty.

children.title: Shortest-Processing-Time Families
children.top_down_role: Single-machine ordering landmarks prioritizing shorter processing requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Processing-Time Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SPT rule for unweighted single-machine total completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite set of jobs available at time zero on one continuously available machine. Each job \(j\) has processing time \(p_j>0\); processing is nonpreemptive, and there are no precedence constraints or sequence-dependent setup times. Every schedule ordering jobs by nondecreasing processing times minimizes total completion time \(\sum_{j\in J}C_j\), and hence also minimizes mean completion time \(|J|^{-1}\sum_{j\in J}C_j\). Jobs with equal processing times may be placed in any relative order. This is the equal-weight specialization of the processing-time-to-weight ratio rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On one machine with all jobs initially available, shortest-processing-time order minimizes total and average completion time; equal-length jobs may be tied arbitrarily.
assumptions_latex: All jobs are available at time zero on one machine.
Processing is nonpreemptive and \(p_j>0\).
There are no precedence constraints or sequence-dependent setup times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An order satisfying \(p_i\le p_j\) whenever \(i\) precedes \(j\) minimizes \(\sum_jC_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits the SPT landmark leaf, and the result is stated with sufficient standard single-machine assumptions. No authoritative citation or inspectable locator is supplied, so the theorem cannot pass source review.

children.title: Weighted Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Priority structures induced by heterogeneous job weights, costs, or importance.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Ordering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smith's ratio rule for the unconstrained single-machine weighted completion-time problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let there be finitely many jobs, all available at time zero, with processing times \(p_j>0\) and weights \(w_j>0\). Processing is nonpreemptive on one continuously available machine. A schedule minimizes \(\sum_j w_j C_j\) if its jobs are ordered by nondecreasing ratios \(p_j/w_j\), equivalently by nonincreasing ratios \(w_j/p_j\); ties may be resolved arbitrarily. Indeed, for two adjacent jobs \(i,j\), placing \(i\) before \(j\) is no worse precisely when \(w_jp_i\leq w_ip_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one machine with all jobs initially available, ordering jobs by decreasing weight-to-processing-time ratio minimizes total weighted completion time.
assumptions_latex: \(p_j>0\) and \(w_j>0\) for every job \(j\).
All jobs are available at time \(0\), and processing is nonpreemptive.
The objective is \(\sum_j w_jC_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An ordering with \(p_i/w_i\leq p_j/w_j\) whenever \(i\) precedes \(j\) is optimal.

notation.meaning: processing time and weight of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Smith's rule and its hypotheses are stated correctly, but no evidence is cited. The sentence beginning “Indeed” is proof-style text and should be removed when the sourced record is prepared.

children.title: Ordering-Landmark Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Release dates, setups, precedence restrictions, and alternative objectives that limit classical ordering structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Landmark Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of unconditional Smith and SPT ordering under additional feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A ratio or processing-time ordering theorem need not survive precedence constraints. Consider two jobs \(a,b\) with \((p_a,w_a)=(10,1)\) and \((p_b,w_b)=(1,100)\), subject to \(a\prec b\). Smith ordering would place \(b\) before \(a\), since \(p_b/w_b<p_a/w_a\), but that sequence is infeasible. The unique feasible sequence is \((a,b)\). Thus an interchange-based ordering landmark for \(1\|\sum_jw_jC_j\) cannot be applied unchanged after precedence constraints are introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precedence constraints can prohibit the Smith or SPT sequence, so their unconstrained optimality does not extend automatically to precedence-constrained instances.
assumptions_latex: Jobs are processed nonpreemptively on one machine.
The precedence relation requires \(a\prec b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unconstrained Smith order is infeasible, so its ordering theorem does not extend unconditionally to \(1\mid\mathrm{prec}\mid\sum_jw_jC_j\).

notation.meaning: job a must complete before job b starts
processing time and weight of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and failure-boundary classification are mathematically consistent, but the record provides neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Earliest-Due-Date Ordering
children.top_down_role: Due-date ordering for single-machine lateness criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Earliest-Due-Date Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: EDD optimality for maximum lateness without release dates or precedence constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let finitely many jobs be available at time zero on one machine, with processing times \(p_j>0\) and due dates \(d_j\in\mathbb{R}\). Processing is nonpreemptive, and define lateness by \(L_j=C_j-d_j\). Any schedule ordering jobs by nondecreasing due dates minimizes maximum lateness \(L_{\max}=\max_jL_j\). Jobs having equal due dates may be ordered arbitrarily, and an optimal schedule requires no inserted idle time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With all jobs available initially, earliest-due-date order minimizes maximum lateness on a single nonpreemptive machine.
assumptions_latex: All jobs are available at time \(0\).
Processing is nonpreemptive on one machine.
The objective is \(L_{\max}=\max_j(C_j-d_j)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every sequence satisfying \(d_i\leq d_j\) whenever \(i\) precedes \(j\) is optimal for \(1\|L_{\max}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical EDD optimality statement is precise and appropriately classified as a theorem, but it has no authoritative source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Jackson Ordering Rules
children.top_down_role: Jackson-family sequencing structures for due-date-sensitive schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Jackson Ordering Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preemptive Jackson rule for maximum lateness with release dates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given jobs with release dates \(r_j\), processing times \(p_j>0\), and due dates \(d_j\), initialize time at the smallest release date. At every time \(t\), process an available unfinished job having minimum due date. When a job with a smaller due date is released, preempt the running job and process the newly highest-priority job; break equal-due-date ties arbitrarily. Continue until all jobs finish and output the resulting preemptive schedule. This Jackson schedule minimizes \(L_{\max}=\max_j(C_j-d_j)\) for \(1\mid r_j,\mathrm{pmtn}\mid L_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Always process the available unfinished job with earliest due date, preempting when a more urgent job arrives; this minimizes preemptive maximum lateness.
assumptions_latex: A job may be processed only at times \(t\geq r_j\).
Preemption is allowed without cost, but a job cannot run on two processors simultaneously.
There is one continuously available machine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output schedule attains \(\min L_{\max}\) over all feasible preemptive schedules.

notation.meaning: release date, processing time, and due date of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preemptive earliest-due-date rule is plausibly the intended Jackson rule, but its exact theorem version requires authoritative support. The statement should also explicitly declare a finite job set.

children.title: Release-Date Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Ordering variants shaped by job availability dates.

knowledge_statements.title: Release-Date Ordering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Release dates invalidate a fixed, non-idling EDD sequence in the nonpreemptive model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider nonpreemptive jobs \(a,b\) on one machine with \((r_a,p_a,d_a)=(0,10,100)\) and \((r_b,p_b,d_b)=(1,1,2)\). A non-idling rule starts the only available job \(a\) at time zero, giving \(C_b=11\) and \(L_{\max}=9\). Idling until time one, processing \(b\), and then processing \(a\) gives completion times \(C_b=2\), \(C_a=12\), and \(L_{\max}=0\). Therefore release dates destroy the unconditional optimality of a static, non-idling EDD rule for nonpreemptive maximum lateness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With release dates, deliberate idling can beat non-idling EDD, so no unchanged static EDD theorem applies to nonpreemptive maximum lateness.
assumptions_latex: Processing is nonpreemptive on one machine.
A job cannot start before its release date.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The non-idling available-job rule has \(L_{\max}=9\), whereas a feasible idling schedule has \(L_{\max}=0\).

notation.meaning: release date, processing time, and due date of job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The numerical counterexample is internally correct and fits a failure-boundary leaf, but no citation or explicit standard-field rationale supports the recorded boundary claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Moore–Hodgson Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moore–Hodgson algorithm for minimizing the number of tardy jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For jobs with \(p_j>0\) and due dates \(d_j\), all available at time zero, first sort them by nondecreasing \(d_j\). Scan this list, appending each job to a provisional early-job sequence and maintaining its total processing time \(T\). Whenever \(T>d_j\) after inserting the current job, remove from the provisional sequence a job of maximum processing time and mark it tardy. After the scan, output the retained jobs in EDD order followed by all removed jobs in arbitrary order. The resulting schedule minimizes \(\sum_j U_j\), where \(U_j=1\) exactly when \(C_j>d_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan jobs in due-date order and remove the longest job whenever lateness appears; the retained early set maximizes the number of on-time jobs.
assumptions_latex: All jobs are available at time \(0\) on one machine.
Processing is nonpreemptive and \(p_j>0\).
Tardiness indicator is \(U_j=\mathbf{1}\{C_j>d_j\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output schedule minimizes \(\sum_jU_j\) for \(1\|\sum_jU_j\).

notation.meaning: total processing time of the provisional early-job sequence
indicator that job j is tardy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Moore–Hodgson algorithm and objective are stated in their standard form, but an authoritative algorithm source with a precise locator is absent. Finiteness of the job set should be explicit.

children.title: Lawler Backward Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Backward-selection structures associated with Lawler scheduling results.

knowledge_statements.title: Lawler Backward Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lawler's backward algorithm for precedence-constrained maximum lateness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the precedence constraints form an acyclic directed graph. Set \(S\) to all jobs and place positions from \(|S|\) down to one. At each position, consider the jobs in \(S\) having no successor in \(S\); choose among them a job with largest due date, place it in the current last unfilled position, and delete it from \(S\). Ties may be arbitrary. The resulting topological sequence is an optimal nonpreemptive schedule for \(1\mid\mathrm{prec}\mid L_{\max}\) when all jobs are available at time zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build the schedule backward, repeatedly placing a currently successor-free job with largest due date last; the result minimizes maximum lateness under precedence constraints.
assumptions_latex: The precedence graph is finite and acyclic.
All jobs are available at time \(0\) and have \(p_j>0\).
Processing is nonpreemptive on one machine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed sequence minimizes \(L_{\max}=\max_j(C_j-d_j)\) subject to the precedence constraints.

notation.meaning: set of jobs not yet placed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The backward sink-selection algorithm is consistent with Lawler's rule for precedence-constrained maximum lateness, but the exact theorem and tie conditions require an authoritative cited locator.

children.title: Sidney Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Sidney-family decompositions for precedence-constrained ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Sidney Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-density initial-set decomposition for precedence-constrained weighted completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a precedence poset on jobs, call \(A\) initial when \(j\in A\) and \(i\prec j\) imply \(i\in A\). Define \(p(A)=\sum_{j\in A}p_j\), \(w(A)=\sum_{j\in A}w_j\), and density \(\rho(A)=w(A)/p(A)\). For \(1\mid\mathrm{prec}\mid\sum_jw_jC_j\), there exists an optimal schedule whose first block is a nonempty initial set of maximum density. Applying the same assertion recursively within that block and to the remaining induced precedence instance yields a Sidney decomposition into consecutively scheduled density blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal precedence-feasible weighted-completion schedule can begin with a maximum-density initial set, enabling recursive decomposition into consecutive blocks.
assumptions_latex: The precedence relation is a finite partial order.
Every job has \(p_j>0\) and \(w_j>0\).
All jobs are initially available apart from precedence restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some optimal schedule has a maximum-density initial set as its first consecutive block and admits recursive decomposition.

notation.meaning: aggregate processing time and weight of A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-density initial-set claim is version-sensitive, especially its recursive block formulation, and needs an exact Sidney-decomposition source. Because it asserts existence of an optimal schedule, “theorem” may be more accurate than “principle.”

children.title: Precedence-Structured Ordering
children.top_down_role: Precedence classes supporting decomposition-based sequencing.

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-Structured Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility condition for a nonpreemptive single-machine order under precedence constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set and let \(\prec\) be an acyclic precedence relation on \(J\). A permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)\) is precedence-feasible exactly when, for every constraint \(i\prec j\), the position of \(i\) in \(\pi\) is smaller than the position of \(j\). Equivalently, every prefix \(\{\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k\}\) is an initial set: whenever it contains \(j\), it contains every predecessor of \(j\). Thus feasible single-machine orders are precisely the topological orderings of the precedence graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job permutation respects precedence exactly when every predecessor appears earlier, equivalently when every prefix is predecessor-closed.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
The precedence relation \(\prec\) is acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\) is precedence-feasible if and only if \(i\prec j\) implies \(\pi^{-1}(i)<\pi^{-1}(j)\).

notation.meaning: job i must precede job j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The topological-order feasibility equivalence is precise and the condition classification fits the leaf, but the record lacks either a cited definition with locator or explicit standard-field rationale.

knowledge_statements.title: Graham List-Scheduling Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case makespan guarantee for list scheduling on identical parallel machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\) independent jobs with processing times \(p_j>0\), a list schedule assigns each job, in any fixed list order, to a machine of currently smallest assigned load among \(m\geq1\) identical machines. If \(C_{\max}^{LS}\) is its makespan and \(C_{\max}^*\) is the minimum possible makespan, then \[C_{\max}^{LS}\leq\left(2-\frac{1}{m}\right)C_{\max}^*.\] With a priority queue for machine loads, the assignments require \(O(n\log m)\) time after the list has been supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any list order scheduled onto a least-loaded identical machine has makespan at most 2−1/m times optimum and can be implemented efficiently.
assumptions_latex: There are \(m\geq1\) identical parallel machines.
Jobs are independent, nonpreemptive, and available at time \(0\).
The supplied list order is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}^{LS}/C_{\max}^*\leq2-1/m\), with assignment time \(O(n\log m)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Graham's list-scheduling approximation factor and the stated implementation bound are mathematically standard, but neither claim has an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Longest-Processing-Time Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LPT approximation guarantee for identical parallel-machine makespan minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\geq2\) identical machines and independent jobs available at time zero, sort jobs by nonincreasing processing time and assign each successive job to a currently least-loaded machine. Let \(C_{\max}^{LPT}\) be the resulting makespan and \(C_{\max}^*\) the optimum. Then \[C_{\max}^{LPT}\leq\left(\frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{3m}\right)C_{\max}^*.\] Sorting and priority-queue assignment take \(O(n\log n+n\log m)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Longest-processing-time-first list scheduling on identical machines achieves approximation ratio 4/3−1/(3m).
assumptions_latex: There are \(m\geq2\) identical parallel machines.
Jobs are independent, nonpreemptive, and available at time \(0\).
Processing times satisfy \(p_j>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The LPT approximation ratio and assumptions are stated consistently, but the landmark bound and runtime claim require an authoritative source with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: McNaughton Preemptive-Scheduling Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McNaughton's wrap-around construction for preemptive identical-machine makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(m\geq1\) identical machines and jobs of lengths \(p_j>0\), set \(T=\max\{\max_jp_j,\sum_jp_j/m\}\). Arrange the jobs consecutively in any order along a strip partitioned into \(m\) rows of length \(T\). Whenever a job crosses a row boundary, split it there: process its first piece at the end of the current machine's interval and its remaining piece from time zero on the next machine. Output these row schedules. No job's pieces overlap, and the resulting feasible preemptive schedule has makespan \(T\), which is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wrap jobs across machine timelines of optimal length; boundary-crossing jobs are preempted, producing an optimal preemptive makespan schedule.
assumptions_latex: There are \(m\geq1\) identical continuously available machines.
Jobs are independent and available at time \(0\).
Preemption and migration are allowed, but parallel execution of one job is forbidden.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction attains \(C_{\max}^*=\max\{\max_jp_j,\sum_jp_j/m\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The McNaughton wrap-around construction and optimum makespan formula are standard, but no authoritative source is supplied. The statement should also explicitly specify a finite job set.

knowledge_statements.title: Johnson Flow-Shop Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Johnson’s rule for the two-machine permutation flow shop minimizing makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with processing times \(p_{i1},p_{i2}\ge 0\), each job visits machine \(1\) before machine \(2\), and each machine processes at most one job at a time. Partition \(J\) into \(U=\{i:p_{i1}\le p_{i2}\}\) and \(V=J\setminus U\). Order \(U\) by nondecreasing \(p_{i1}\), order \(V\) by nonincreasing \(p_{i2}\), and concatenate the orders. Scheduling both machines in this common job order, each operation starting as early as feasibility permits, minimizes \(C_{\max}=\max_i C_{i2}\) among all feasible two-machine flow-shop schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Johnson’s rule places jobs with shorter first-machine times first and jobs with shorter second-machine times last; the resulting common order minimizes two-machine flow-shop makespan.
assumptions_latex: \(p_{ik}\ge 0\) for every job \(i\) and machine \(k\in\{1,2\}\).
Operations are nonpreemptive, and all jobs are available at time \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Johnson order minimizes \(C_{\max}\) for the two-machine flow shop.

notation.meaning: processing time of job i on machine k
completion time of job i on the second machine

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and optimality claim fit the Johnson-family container and are mathematically standard, but the nontrivial global optimality claim has no cited source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Open-Shop Edge-Coloring Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-time open-shop schedules represented by edge colorings of a bipartite multigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a unit-time open shop with job set \(J\), machine set \(M\), and one required operation for each pair in \(E\subseteq J\times M\), form the bipartite multigraph \(G=(J\cup M,E)\). A slot-indexed feasible schedule is exactly a proper edge coloring \(c:E\to\{1,\ldots,T\}\): incident edges receive distinct colors because a job or machine cannot participate in two simultaneous operations. Consequently, the minimum number of slots equals \(\chi'(G)=\Delta(G)\), where the equality follows for bipartite multigraphs. Each color class is a matching and specifies the operations executed concurrently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-time open-shop schedule is a proper edge coloring of its job–machine bipartite graph; the optimal makespan is the graph’s maximum degree.
assumptions_latex: Every required operation has unit duration and starts at an integer time.
A job and a machine each process at most one operation per slot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal makespan is \(T^*=\chi'(G)=\Delta(G)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The edge-coloring representation and bipartite edge-chromatic equality fit the container, but neither is cited. A source should also clarify whether multiple operations per job–machine pair are intended, since E is written as a set while G is called a multigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Shifting-Bottleneck Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical shifting-bottleneck heuristic for minimizing makespan in a job shop.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a job shop, construct its disjunctive graph with fixed job-precedence arcs and one unresolved disjunctive edge for every pair of operations sharing a machine. Initialize all machine orders as unresolved. At each iteration, for every unresolved machine \(k\), solve the induced single-machine problem \(1\mid r_i,q_i\mid L_{\max}\), where release and tail values are longest-path quantities in the current graph. Select a machine attaining the largest optimized bottleneck value, orient its disjunctive edges according to its selected sequence, and reoptimize previously fixed machine sequences when allowed. Stop when every machine is ordered; output the earliest-start schedule induced by the resulting acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The heuristic repeatedly sequences the currently most restrictive machine, updates longest-path data, and returns the earliest-start schedule defined by all chosen machine orders.
assumptions_latex: Processing times are deterministic and operations are nonpreemptive.
Every accepted orientation preserves acyclicity of the disjunctive graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a feasible job-shop schedule whose makespan is the longest source-to-sink path length in the final graph.

notation.meaning: release value induced for operation i
tail value induced for operation i
maximum lateness in the machine subproblem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and topic fit, but the precise shifting-bottleneck variant, reoptimization rule, and notation \(1\mid r_i,q_i\mid L_{\max}\) require an authoritative source before the algorithmic statement can be trusted.

knowledge_statements.title: Hu Tree-Precedence Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hu’s highest-level-first rule for unit-time in-tree precedence scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(J,A)\) be an in-tree precedence digraph, so every job has at most one immediate successor, and let \(m\) identical parallel machines be available. Assign each job the level \(\ell(j)\), equal to the number of vertices on a longest directed path from \(j\) to a sink. At each integer time, among jobs whose predecessors have completed, schedule on the \(m\) machines up to \(m\) jobs of greatest level, breaking ties arbitrarily. Continue until all jobs complete. For unit processing times, the resulting nonpreemptive schedule minimizes the makespan among feasible schedules respecting the precedence constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For unit jobs with in-tree precedences, repeatedly scheduling available jobs of greatest distance from a sink gives a minimum-makespan schedule on identical machines.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is acyclic and every job has at most one immediate successor.
\(p_j=1\) for all \(j\in J\), with integer-time nonpreemptive scheduling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The highest-level-first schedule attains the minimum possible \(C_{\max}\) on \(m\) identical machines.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The highest-level-first algorithm and unit-time optimality claim fit the Hu-family container, but the in-tree orientation convention and theorem require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Coffman–Graham Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coffman–Graham precedence labeling and list scheduling, with the exact two-processor result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite acyclic precedence digraph \(G=(J,A)\) with unit-time jobs, construct a Coffman–Graham labeling by repeatedly assigning the next label to an unlabeled job whose successors are all labeled, choosing the job whose decreasing sequence of successor labels is lexicographically smallest. Then scan jobs in decreasing label order and place each job in the earliest unit-time level that follows all its predecessors and contains fewer than \(m\) jobs. The levels define a feasible schedule on \(m\) identical processors. When \(m=2\), this schedule has minimum makespan among all nonpreemptive schedules satisfying the precedences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coffman–Graham labels a precedence DAG from its sinks and packs jobs into precedence-feasible levels; for two processors and unit jobs, the schedule is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(J,A)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
Every job has processing time \(1\), and processors are identical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(m=2\), the constructed schedule minimizes \(C_{\max}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role and two-processor optimality claim fit the container, but the exact labeling direction, lexicographic convention, and optimality theorem lack an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Activity-on-Node Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic activity-on-node representation of project precedence constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An activity-on-node project network is a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,A)\) in which each vertex \(i\in V\) represents an activity of duration \(d_i\ge 0\), and each arc \((i,j)\in A\) imposes the finish-to-start constraint \(S_j\ge S_i+d_i\). Optional zero-duration source and sink vertices may be added so every activity lies on a source-to-sink path. A feasible project schedule is a vector \(S\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V}\) satisfying all arc constraints; without resource constraints, its earliest completion time is the length of a longest source-to-sink path under vertex durations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an activity-on-node network, vertices are activities and arcs impose finish-to-start precedence; feasible start times satisfy the corresponding difference inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and acyclic.
Activity durations satisfy \(d_i\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is characterized by \(S_j\ge S_i+d_i\) for every \((i,j)\in A\).

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

source_witnesses.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

knowledge_statements.title: Activity-on-Arc Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic activity-on-arc representation, including zero-duration dummy arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An activity-on-arc project network is a finite directed acyclic multigraph \(G=(V,A)\) in which vertices are events and each arc \(a=(u,v)\) represents an activity of duration \(d_a\ge0\). Event times \(T:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) are feasible when \(T_v\ge T_u+d_a\) for every arc \(a=(u,v)\). A zero-duration dummy arc may encode precedence without representing real work. With a unique source \(s\) fixed at \(T_s=0\), the earliest event time at \(v\) equals the maximum total duration of an \(s\)-to-\(v\) directed path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an activity-on-arc network, arcs are activities and vertices are events; longest-path event times give the earliest feasible project timing.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and acyclic.
Arc durations satisfy \(d_a\ge0\), including zero-duration dummy arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The earliest event time is \(T_v^E=\max_{P:s\leadsto v}\sum_{a\in P}d_a\).

children.title: Critical-Path Identification
children.top_down_role: Path-based identification of project duration drivers.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Path Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path criterion for an acyclic deterministic project network without resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be an activity-on-node network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and nonnegative activity durations. Compute earliest starts by \(ES_s=0\) and \(ES_j=\max_{(i,j)\in A}(ES_i+d_i)\); set \(C=ES_t+d_t\). Compute latest finishes backward from \(LF_t=C\) using \(LF_i=\min_{(i,j)\in A}(LF_j-d_j)\). An activity is critical exactly when its total float \(LF_i-d_i-ES_i\) is zero. A critical path is an \(s\)-to-\(t\) path of total duration \(C\); delaying any activity on it delays project completion unless another timing constraint changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Critical activities have zero total float, and critical paths are source-to-sink paths whose duration equals the earliest project completion time.
assumptions_latex: The project network is finite and acyclic with nonnegative deterministic durations.
Only precedence constraints are imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A critical path has length \(C\), and every activity on it has zero total float.

notation.meaning: latest finish preserving completion time C

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

source_witnesses.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

children.title: Total Float Analysis
children.top_down_role: Schedule flexibility measured against overall project timing.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Float Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total float of an activity in deterministic critical-path analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite acyclic activity-on-node network, fix the target project completion time \(C\) to its earliest feasible value. For activity \(i\) of duration \(d_i\), let \(ES_i\) and \(EF_i=ES_i+d_i\) be its earliest start and finish, and let \(LF_i\) and \(LS_i=LF_i-d_i\) be its latest finish and start compatible with completion by \(C\). Its total float is \[TF_i=LS_i-ES_i=LF_i-EF_i.\] Thus \(TF_i\) is the maximum amount by which activity \(i\) can be delayed from its earliest timing without increasing the prescribed project completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total float is latest start minus earliest start, equivalently latest finish minus earliest finish, and measures the delay allowed without postponing project completion.
assumptions_latex: The project network is finite and acyclic.
Latest times are computed relative to the earliest project completion time \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(TF_i=LS_i-ES_i=LF_i-EF_i\ge0\).

notation.meaning: earliest start and finish of activity i
latest start and finish preserving C

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

children.title: Free Float Analysis
children.top_down_role: Activity flexibility relative to immediate successor timing.

knowledge_statements.title: Free Float Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Free float under finish-to-start precedences in an activity-on-node network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let activity \(i\) have duration \(d_i\), earliest start \(ES_i\), earliest finish \(EF_i=ES_i+d_i\), and successor set \(Succ(i)=\{j:(i,j)\in A\}\). Its free float is \[FF_i=\min_{j\in Succ(i)}ES_j-EF_i.\] For a terminal activity, introduce a zero-duration sink with earliest start equal to the project completion time and use it as the successor. Because earliest times satisfy every precedence constraint, \(FF_i\ge0\). Delaying \(i\) by at most \(FF_i\), while leaving other activities at their earliest timings, does not delay the earliest start of any immediate successor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free float is the minimum earliest start among an activity’s immediate successors minus the activity’s earliest finish; using this amount of delay does not postpone any immediate successor.
assumptions_latex: The activity-on-node network is finite and acyclic.
All precedence arcs are finish-to-start constraints with zero lag.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(FF_i=\min_{j\in Succ(i)}ES_j-EF_i\ge0\).
