children.title: Benders Project Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Master–subproblem structures for project-scheduling decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Benders Project Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Benders decomposition with scheduling master variables and continuous recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x+d^{\mathsf T}y:x\in X,\ Wy\ge h-Tx,\ y\ge0\}\), use a master problem in \((x,\theta)\). Given \(x^q\), solve the linear subproblem \(Q(x^q)=\min\{d^{\mathsf T}y:Wy\ge h-Tx^q,\ y\ge0\}\). If its dual has an optimal extreme point \(\pi^q\), add \(\theta\ge(\pi^q)^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\); if it is unbounded along an extreme ray \(\rho^q\), add \((\rho^q)^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\le0\). Re-solve the master and repeat until its lower bound equals the best feasible objective within the chosen tolerance. With exact solves and finitely many relevant dual extreme points and rays, termination returns an optimal schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteratively solve a scheduling master and recourse subproblem, adding dual optimality or feasibility cuts until lower and upper bounds coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the discrete master-feasible set.
The recourse subproblem and its dual satisfy linear-programming strong duality whenever feasible and bounded.
Only finitely many relevant dual extreme points and rays exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\le\varepsilon\text{ at termination; for }\varepsilon=0\text{, the incumbent is globally optimal.}\)

notation.meaning: Master scheduling decisions and recourse variables.
Current global lower and incumbent upper bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits Benders decomposition, but no source is supplied and the assumptions do not exclude an unbounded primal recourse problem or state the dual feasibility conditions needed to justify the extreme-ray case and finite-termination guarantee.

children.title: Decomposition Coordination
children.top_down_role: Information exchange across decomposed project-scheduling components.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-based coordination of project master and component subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a master relaxation containing the coupling variables, set \(L=-\infty\), \(U=+\infty\), and choose tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\). At iteration \(q\), solve the master to obtain coupling decision \(x^q\) and master bound \(L_q\). Solve every induced component subproblem. From their solutions, generate valid prices, feasibility cuts, or optimality cuts and add them to the master; whenever the component decisions can be assembled into a feasible project schedule \(S^q\), update \(U\leftarrow\min\{U,C_{\max}(S^q)\}\). Set \(L\leftarrow\max\{L,L_q\}\) and stop when \(U-L\le\varepsilon\). The incumbent is then \(\varepsilon\)-optimal, provided every master bound and coordination message is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate decomposed subproblems through valid prices or cuts while maintaining global lower and upper bounds; stop when their gap meets tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Every reported master value \(L_q\) is a valid lower bound.
Every generated price or cut is valid for the undecomposed model.
Every incumbent schedule used to update \(U\) is globally feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le z^*\le U\text{ throughout, and termination implies }U-z^*\le\varepsilon.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound-coordination algorithm fits the leaf and its gap implication is valid under the listed invariants, but no source supports the generic claim that the stated prices or cuts preserve those invariants.

children.title: Precedence Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Project lower bounds derived from precedence-network timing.

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path certificate for nonpreemptive project makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite acyclic precedence graph, let each activity \(i\) have duration \(p_i\ge0\), and require \(S_i\ge0\) and \(S_j\ge S_i+p_i\) for every \((i,j)\in E\). For every directed path \(P\), precedence feasibility implies \(\sum_{i\in P}p_i\le C_{\max}\). Consequently, \[LB_{\mathrm{prec}}=\max_P\sum_{i\in P}p_i\le C^*_{\max}.\] A polynomially checkable certificate for \(LB_{\mathrm{prec}}\) consists of a path \(P^*\) and longest-path labels whose arc inequalities upper-bound every path weight and whose terminal value equals \(\sum_{i\in P^*}p_i\). Renewable-resource restrictions may increase the optimal makespan but cannot invalidate the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every precedence path must execute sequentially, so its duration is a makespan lower bound; a path together with valid longest-path labels certifies the critical-path value.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
Each activity is nonpreemptive with duration \(p_i\ge0\), and schedule start times satisfy \(S_i\ge0\).
Every arc \((i,j)\in E\) imposes \(S_j\ge S_i+p_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(LB_{\mathrm{prec}}=\max_P\sum_{i\in P}p_i\le C^*_{\max}.\)

children.title: Resource Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Project lower bounds derived from resource-capacity limitations.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Renewable-resource workload certificate for project makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For renewable resource \(k\) of capacity \(R_k>0\), activity \(i\) consumes \(r_{ik}\ge0\) units throughout its duration \(p_i\). Any feasible schedule of makespan \(C_{\max}\) provides at most \(R_kC_{\max}\) units of resource-time, whereas the activities require \(W_k=\sum_i r_{ik}p_i\). Hence \[LB_{\mathrm{res}}=\max_k\frac{W_k}{R_k}\le C^*_{\max}.\] For integral time, \(\max_k\lceil W_k/R_k\rceil\) is valid. The data \((W_k,R_k)\) constitute a directly checkable certificate; precedence constraints can only strengthen the optimal makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total demand for each renewable resource cannot exceed capacity times makespan, yielding the maximum workload-to-capacity ratio as a lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Activities execute within a common project interval of length \(C_{\max}\).
Resource \(k\) has constant renewable capacity \(R_k>0\).
Activity \(i\) consumes \(r_{ik}\) units for its entire duration \(p_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(LB_{\mathrm{res}}=\max_k\frac{\sum_i r_{ik}p_i}{R_k}\le C^*_{\max}.\)

notation.meaning: Total resource-time demand on resource k.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

children.title: Composite Project Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds combining precedence and resource information.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Project Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum aggregation of independently valid project lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(LB_1,\ldots,LB_m\) be certified lower bounds for the same project instance and objective, so that \(LB_j\le C^*_{\max}\) for every \(j\). Define \[LB_{\mathrm{comp}}=\max_{1\le j\le m}LB_j.\] Then \(LB_{\mathrm{comp}}\le C^*_{\max}\). In particular, combining the critical-path and renewable-resource workload bounds gives \(LB_{\mathrm{comp}}=\max\{LB_{\mathrm{prec}},LB_{\mathrm{res}}\}\). A certificate consists of the component certificates and the arithmetic comparison identifying their maximum. The aggregation is never weaker than a component bound, although it need not equal the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of valid lower bounds for the same project objective is itself valid and dominates every included component bound.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
\(LB_j\le C^*_{\max}\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
All component bounds use the same instance, time origin, and makespan convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(LB_j\le LB_{\mathrm{comp}}=\max_jLB_j\le C^*_{\max}\text{ for every }j.\)

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

children.title: Relaxation-Based Project Bounds
children.top_down_role: Project bounds obtained from tractable relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Based Project Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound certificate obtained by enlarging a minimization model's feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the exact project-scheduling formulation be \(z^*=\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\), and let \(\bar X\) be a relaxation satisfying \(X\subseteq\bar X\). If \(\bar z=\min\{f(x):x\in\bar X\}\) is attained at \(\bar x\), then \(\bar z=f(\bar x)\le z^*\). Thus an exactly solved relaxed solution and its objective value certify a project lower bound. For a linear-programming relaxation, a dual-feasible vector with dual value \(d\) additionally certifies \(d\le\bar z\le z^*\); equality of primal and dual relaxed values certifies the exact relaxation optimum without asserting integrality or scheduling feasibility of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging the feasible set of a minimization scheduling model lowers its optimum; a solved relaxation therefore supplies a valid project lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\) and \(X\subseteq\bar X\).
Both models minimize the same objective function \(f\).
The reported relaxed optimum is exact, or its dual value is independently feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\le\bar z\le z^*\text{ whenever }d\text{ is dual feasible for the relaxation.}\)

children.title: Cut-Based Project Bounds
children.top_down_role: Project bounds strengthened through valid cutting structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Based Project Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone strengthening of a project relaxation by valid inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the exact feasible set of a minimization project model and \(P_0\supseteq X\) an initial relaxation. If each inequality \(a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j\) is valid for every \(x\in X\), define \(P_q=P_0\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^q\{x:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j\}\) and \(L_q=\min\{f(x):x\in P_q\}\). Then \[L_0\le L_1\le\cdots\le L_q\le z^*,\qquad z^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x).\] A certificate comprises validity evidence for every added cut and an exact primal-dual certificate for \(L_q\). Invalid cuts can exclude feasible schedules and destroy the lower-bound guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding inequalities valid for all feasible schedules shrinks a minimization relaxation and monotonically strengthens its certified lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq P_0\).
Every added inequality is valid on all of \(X\).
Each relaxation value \(L_q\) is solved or certified exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{q-1}\le L_q\le z^*\text{ for every }q\ge1.\)

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the q-cut relaxation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonic lower-bound chain is mathematically valid when exact relaxation values are available, but no source is supplied. Moreover, an exact primal-dual certificate is not defined for the generic objective and relaxation stated; that certification claim requires a specified LP or another duality framework.

children.title: Hybrid Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates combining relaxation values with cut-based strengthening.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate combining independently checkable relaxation and cut lower bounds for a minimization project-scheduling instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^*\) be the optimal value of a minimization project-scheduling instance. Suppose a relaxation solution and its dual witness certify \(L_R\le z^*\), while a valid-cut system with a corresponding bound witness certifies \(L_C\le z^*\). Then the hybrid certificate consists of both witnesses and the aggregate bound \[L_H=\max\{L_R,L_C\}.\] Independent verification of the two component inequalities certifies \(L_H\le z^*\). If a feasible schedule of value \(U\) is also supplied, then \(L_H\le z^*\le U\), and \(U-L_H\) is a certified absolute optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two independently verifiable lower-bound witnesses certify their maximum; paired with a feasible incumbent, they also certify an optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: The project-scheduling objective is minimized.
Each component witness is valid for the same original instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_H=\max\{L_R,L_C\}\le z^*\le U\).

notation.meaning: relaxation, cut, and hybrid lower bounds
objective value of a feasible incumbent schedule

children.title: Interval-Capacity Tests
children.top_down_role: Capacity feasibility checks over selected project-time intervals.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval-Capacity Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary interval test for cumulative, nonpreemptive project scheduling with release times and deadlines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider activities \(i\in V\) with processing times \(p_i>0\), resource demands \(q_i\ge0\), release times \(r_i\), deadlines \(d_i\), and one renewable resource of capacity \(B\). For every interval \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), activities whose entire feasible execution window lies inside that interval must fit its capacity: \[\sum_{i:r_i\ge a,\ d_i\le b}q_i p_i\le B(b-a).\] Violation for any interval is a necessary-condition failure and proves that no schedule satisfying all time windows and resource capacity can exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every interval must accommodate the full resource energy of activities whose feasible windows are contained in it.
assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive and satisfy \(r_i\le s_i\) and \(s_i+p_i\le d_i\).
Resource consumption is constant during each activity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility implies \(\sum_{i:r_i\ge a,\ d_i\le b}q_i p_i\le B(b-a)\) for every \(a<b\).

notation.meaning: feasible execution window of activity i

review_flags: authoritative cumulative-scheduling source with an exact interval-test locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed interval-capacity inequality is a plausible necessary condition under the stated cumulative-resource assumptions, and condition fits the test container. No source is supplied, so the exact window convention and claimed infeasibility test lack inspectable support.

children.title: Energetic Feasibility Tests
children.top_down_role: Workload-based feasibility checks for constrained project intervals.

knowledge_statements.title: Energetic Feasibility Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energetic necessary condition using each activity's minimum unavoidable processing inside an interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For activity \(i\) and interval \([a,b]\), define its unavoidable processing in that interval by \[w_i(a,b)=\max\{0,\ p_i-\max(0,a-r_i)-\max(0,d_i-b)\}.\] With constant demand \(q_i\) and renewable-resource capacity \(B\), every feasible nonpreemptive schedule satisfies \[\sum_{i\in V}q_iw_i(a,b)\le B(b-a)\] for every \(a<b\). Thus an interval for which the displayed energetic demand exceeds available energy certifies infeasibility. Candidate intervals may be restricted algorithmically, but such restrictions require a separate completeness argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum resource energy unavoidably executed in any interval cannot exceed that interval's available capacity energy.
assumptions_latex: Each activity executes for \(p_i\) time units within \([r_i,d_i]\).
A single renewable resource has constant capacity \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility implies \(\sum_i q_iw_i(a,b)\le B(b-a)\) for all \(a<b\).

notation.meaning: minimum processing of activity i forced into the interval
constant capacity demand of activity i
resource energy available in the interval

review_flags: exact energetic-reasoning formula requires a scheduling-specific source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical role and energetic inequality are plausible, but the exact unavoidable-processing formula depends on the release-time, deadline, and execution-window conventions. An authoritative cumulative-scheduling source with a specific locator is required before accepting this version.

children.title: Overload Certificates
children.top_down_role: Interval-based evidence of infeasible resource demand.

knowledge_statements.title: Overload Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite witness of renewable-resource infeasibility over a specified time interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An overload certificate is an interval \([a,b]\), instance data \((r_i,d_i,p_i,q_i)_{i\in V}\), capacity \(B\), and certified lower bounds \(e_i(a,b)\) on processing that activity \(i\) must execute inside \([a,b]\), satisfying \[0\le e_i(a,b)\le p_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in V}q_i e_i(a,b)>B(b-a).\] The witness is verifiable by checking every lower bound from the activity's time window and then checking the strict inequality. Since available resource energy is insufficient, the instance is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval and unavoidable activity energies form an overload certificate when their sum strictly exceeds available capacity energy.
assumptions_latex: Every \(e_i(a,b)\) is a valid lower bound for all schedules respecting activity \(i\)'s time window.
The resource has capacity \(B\) throughout \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i q_i e_i(a,b)>B(b-a)\) certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: certified unavoidable processing inside the interval

review_flags: scheduling-specific source for overload certificates required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct content kind, and the overload implication is coherent provided every stated lower bound is valid. No cited source supports the intended certificate definition or the required verification of the activity-level lower bounds.

children.title: Project-Schedule Dominance
children.top_down_role: Comparative criteria for retaining stronger partial or complete schedules.

assumptions_latex: Both schedules are feasible for the same project instance.
All components of \(f\) are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(S\) dominates \(T\), then \(T\) is not Pareto efficient.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of Pareto dominance for feasible complete schedules under a minimization objective vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the feasible schedules of one project instance and let \(f:F\to\mathbb R^k\) be a vector of criteria to be minimized. A schedule \(S\in F\) dominates \(T\in F\) when \[f_j(S)\le f_j(T)\quad(j=1,\ldots,k),\qquad f(S)\ne f(T).\] Then \(T\) is not Pareto efficient and may be removed when the required output is the Pareto frontier. For a scalar objective, the same conclusion holds with strict improvement in its value. This definition alone does not justify pruning partial schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible schedule dominates another when it is no worse in every minimized criterion and strictly better in at least one.
knowledge_statements.title: Project-Schedule Dominance

children.title: Schedule-Set Reduction
children.top_down_role: Removal of redundant project schedules from candidate sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Set Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of a finite schedule set by deletion of Pareto-dominated complete schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite set \(X\subseteq F\) of feasible schedules and a minimized criterion map \(f:F\to\mathbb R^k\). Initialize \(Y=X\). For each \(T\in X\), delete \(T\) from \(Y\) if some \(S\in X\) satisfies \(f_j(S)\le f_j(T)\) for every \(j\) and \(f(S)\ne f(T)\). Output \(Y\). The output contains exactly the nondominated objective vectors represented in \(X\); if schedules with equal vectors are interchangeable, one representative of each equality class may additionally be retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare feasible schedules pairwise, discard every dominated one, and optionally keep one representative for each identical objective vector.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and every member is feasible.
Dominance is evaluated using the same minimized criteria for all schedules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y=\{T\in X:\nexists S\in X\text{ with }f(S)\le f(T)\text{ and }f(S)\ne f(T)\}\).
review_flags: source for the intended project-schedule reduction convention required

children.title: Dominance Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Project regimes where proposed dominance relations cease to preserve relevant candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for safe dominance pruning of partial project schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let partial schedules \(P\) and \(Q\) have completion sets \(E(P)\) and \(E(Q)\), and let \(g\) be the final minimized objective. A dominance rule based only on current values is unsafe unless every feasible completion \(Q\oplus R\) has a corresponding feasible completion \(P\oplus R'\) with \(g(P\oplus R')\le g(Q\oplus R)\). This implication can fail when partial schedules differ in residual renewable profiles, nonrenewable consumption, eligible future modes, or state-dependent costs. In that case, deleting \(Q\) from a smaller current objective value of \(P\) can delete the unique optimal completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial-schedule dominance is safe only when every completion of the discarded state can be matched no worse from the retained state.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are partial schedules for the same instance.
The proposed rule prunes \(Q\) in favor of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Safe pruning requires \(\forall R\in\mathcal C(Q)\,\exists R'\in\mathcal C(P):g(P\oplus R')\le g(Q\oplus R)\).

notation.meaning: feasible completions of partial schedule P
complete schedule obtained by extending P

review_flags: exact project-scheduling dominance boundary requires a specialized source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The safety boundary is plausible and failure_boundary is the correct content kind, but the statement introduces completion sets as \(E(P)\) and \(E(Q)\) while the conclusion and notation use \(\mathcal C(P)\) and \(\mathcal C(Q)\). More importantly, no specialized source supports the quantified completion-matching condition or the listed project-scheduling failure mechanisms.

children.title: Project Instance Libraries
children.top_down_role: Curated collections of project-scheduling instances.

children.title: Project Instance Formats
children.top_down_role: Representational conventions for exchanging benchmark instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Project Instance Formats
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical data representation for precedence- and resource-constrained project-scheduling instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical project-instance format represents an instance as \[I=(V,A,(p_i)_{i\in V},(q_{ik})_{i\in V,k\in R},(B_k)_{k\in R},\theta),\] where \((V,A)\) is an acyclic precedence graph, \(p_i\) are processing times, \(q_{ik}\) are renewable-resource demands, \(B_k\) are capacities, and \(\theta\) contains explicitly typed optional fields such as release times, deadlines, modes, or nonrenewable resources. A conforming parser must reject missing mandatory fields, cyclic precedence data, invalid indices, negative durations or demands, and dimensionally inconsistent resource arrays.

All mandatory numeric domains and indexing conventions are declared.

children.title: Benchmark Evaluation Protocols
children.top_down_role: Comparability conventions for project-scheduling computational studies.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Evaluation Protocols
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducible protocol for comparing project-scheduling algorithms on a fixed instance library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a versioned library \(\mathcal L\), algorithms \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\), a hardware-software environment \(H\), resource limit \(T\), replicate count \(r\), and prespecified metrics. Validate all instances, fix seeds and solver parameters, and run every designated pair \((A_j,I)\) under identical limits in \(H\). Record feasibility, objective value, certified bound, termination status, elapsed time, and resource use for every replicate. Aggregate only by declared statistics, treating timeouts and failures by a prespecified rule, and output raw records together with the library, environment, and configuration identifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate a fixed library, run every algorithm under identical declared conditions, retain raw outcomes, and aggregate by prespecified rules.
assumptions_latex: All algorithms are evaluated against the same instance semantics.
Limits, metrics, seeds, and failure handling are fixed before aggregation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a reproducible table indexed by \((A_j,I,\ell)\) for \(I\in\mathcal L\) and \(1\le\ell\le r\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is a reasonable role for this executable evaluation protocol, and the record is internally coherent. children.title: Chain Precedences
children.top_down_role: Precedence structures organized as linear dependency sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Chain Precedences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precedence class whose transitive reduction is a directed path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\) be activities and let \(A\subseteq V\times V\) define an acyclic precedence relation. The instance has chain precedences when the transitive reduction of \((V,A)\) has exactly the arcs \[(v_1,v_2),(v_2,v_3),\ldots,(v_{n-1},v_n)\] for some ordering of \(V\). Equivalently, the reachability order is total: for every two distinct activities \(u,v\), either \(u\) precedes \(v\) or \(v\) precedes \(u\). Under finish-to-start semantics, each arc imposes \(s_{v_{j+1}}\ge s_{v_j}+p_{v_j}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chain precedences totally order the activities; their transitive reduction is one directed path.
assumptions_latex: \((V,A)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
Arcs use finish-to-start precedence semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reachability relation on \(V\) is a total order.

notation.meaning: start time and processing time of activity i

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

children.title: Tree Precedences
children.top_down_role: Connected branching precedence structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree Precedences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Out-tree convention: every nonroot activity has exactly one immediate predecessor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((V,A)\) be a finite acyclic precedence graph. It has out-tree precedences when its transitive reduction contains a distinguished root \(r\), every vertex \(v\ne r\) has exactly one incoming arc, and the underlying undirected graph is connected. Hence the reduction has \(|V|-1\) arcs and a unique directed path from \(r\) to each activity. Under finish-to-start semantics, every reduced arc \((i,j)\) imposes \(s_j\ge s_i+p_i\). Reversing every arc gives the distinct in-tree convention, in which every nonroot vertex has one immediate successor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the out-tree convention, one root precedes all activities and each nonroot activity has exactly one immediate predecessor.
assumptions_latex: \((V,A)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
The term tree uses the out-tree orientation convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transitive reduction is a rooted arborescence with \(|V|-1\) arcs.

notation.meaning: start time and processing time of activity i

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

children.title: Forest Precedences
children.top_down_role: Collections of disjoint tree-structured precedence components.

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Precedences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the transitive-reduction convention for precedence graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(J,\prec)\) be a finite strict partial order, and let \(H(P)=(J,A)\) be its Hasse diagram, where \((i,j)\in A\) exactly when \(i\prec j\) and no \(k\in J\) satisfies \(i\prec k\prec j\). The precedence relation is a forest precedence if the undirected graph obtained from \(H(P)\) by forgetting arc orientations is a forest. Equivalently, every connected component of that undirected cover graph is a tree or an isolated vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A precedence order is a forest precedence when the undirected cover graph of its Hasse diagram contains no cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(\prec\) is irreflexive and transitive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is forest precedence}\iff \operatorname{und}(H(P))\text{ is a forest}.\)

notation.meaning: Hasse diagram, or transitive reduction, of the precedence order

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-poset definition using the undirected cover graph
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically precise and fits the Forest Precedences container, but no inspectable citation supports the adopted cover-graph convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Series–Parallel Precedence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite series–parallel precedence orders recursively by series and parallel composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(\mathcal{SP}\) of finite series–parallel precedence orders is the smallest class satisfying: every one-element order belongs to \(\mathcal{SP}\); if disjoint orders \(P_1,P_2\in\mathcal{SP}\), then their parallel composition \(P_1\parallel P_2\), having no cross-comparabilities, belongs to \(\mathcal{SP}\); and their series composition \(P_1\oplus P_2\), in which every element of \(P_1\) precedes every element of \(P_2\), belongs to \(\mathcal{SP}\). A precedence order is series–parallel exactly when it lies in this recursively generated class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Series–parallel precedences are built from singleton jobs by repeatedly placing two disjoint orders either entirely in sequence or entirely in parallel.
assumptions_latex: All component orders are finite and have disjoint ground sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is series--parallel}\iff P\in\mathcal{SP}.\)

notation.meaning: series composition placing every element of the first order before every element of the second

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard recursive definition of finite series-parallel posets
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive definition and definition content kind fit the series–parallel precedence container, but an authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Interval Orders
children.top_down_role: Precedence classes represented through interval-order structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses closed real intervals and strict left-to-right separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite strict partial order \(P=(J,\prec)\) is an interval order if there exist real numbers \(a_j\le b_j\) for every \(j\in J\) such that, with \(I_j=[a_j,b_j]\), one has \[i\prec j\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b_i<a_j\] for all distinct \(i,j\in J\). Thus two jobs are incomparable precisely when their representing intervals overlap or touch under this strict-separation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval order represents each job by a real interval; one job precedes another exactly when its interval lies strictly to the left.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
\(\prec\) is a strict partial order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is an interval order}\iff \exists\{[a_j,b_j]\}_{j\in J}\ \forall i\ne j:\ i\prec j\iff b_i<a_j.\)

notation.meaning: interval representing job or element j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard interval-representation definition of a finite interval order
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval-representation definition is standard, precise, and locally appropriate, but the record supplies no inspectable citation.

children.title: Quasi-Interval Orders
children.top_down_role: Relaxed interval-like precedence classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Interval Orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The label is noncanonical; a source-specific definition is required before fixing the represented class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The phrase “quasi-interval order” does not, without an adopted convention, determine a unique predicate on a finite order \(P=(J,\prec)\). In particular, the interval-order condition \(i\prec j\iff b_i<a_j\), a one-way implication \(b_i<a_j\Rightarrow i\prec j\), and restricted interval representations define different classes. Therefore membership, forbidden-suborder characterizations, and recognition claims for this node must remain unspecified until an authoritative scheduling source fixes the intended representation and endpoint convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasi-interval order is not sufficiently canonical here to choose a reliable definition; its representation and endpoint convention require an authoritative source.
assumptions_latex: \(P=(J,\prec)\) is a finite strict partial order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{label alone}\not\Rightarrow\text{a uniquely determined order class}.\)
review_flags: REQUEST_SOURCES: authoritative scheduling or order-theory definition needed

children.title: Interval-Order Recognition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings governing identification of interval-based precedence classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval-Order Recognition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the finite-poset positive certificate and the classical forbidden-suborder obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite strict partial order \(P=(J,\prec)\), an interval representation \(\{[a_j,b_j]brace_{j\in J}\) satisfying \(i\prec j\iff b_i<a_j\) is a positive certificate of interval-order membership. A negative certificate consists of four distinct elements \(a,b,c,d\) whose induced order has exactly \(a\prec b\) and \(c\prec d\) among cross-pair comparisons; this is an induced \(2+2\). The classical characterization states that \(P\) is an interval order if and only if it has no induced \(2+2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognition may certify an interval representation or reject membership by exhibiting four elements inducing two disjoint two-element chains.
assumptions_latex: \(P=(J,\prec)\) is a finite strict partial order.
The input relation is interpreted transitively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is an interval order}\iff P\text{ contains no induced }2+2.\)

notation.meaning: the disjoint union of two two-element chains as an induced suborder
certificate interval assigned to element j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical induced-2+2 characterization requires an authoritative citation. The positive-certificate expression uses a mismatched \{...\rbrace pair, and the phrase describing the negative certificate should explicitly say that the only comparabilities among the four induced elements are a≺b and c≺d.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Acyclic Precedence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents unrestricted finite precedence constraints by a directed acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(J,A)\) be a finite directed acyclic graph. Define \(i\prec_G j\) when a directed path of positive length leads from \(i\) to \(j\). Then \(\prec_G\) is a strict partial order and is the precedence relation represented by \(G\). Conversely, every finite strict partial order is represented by an acyclic digraph, for example its Hasse diagram. No forest, series–parallel, or interval-order restriction is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any finite DAG represents precedence by reachability, and every finite strict partial order has such a DAG representation.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(J,A)\) is finite and acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i\prec_G j\iff \text{a directed path from }i\text{ to }j\text{ exists in }G.\)

notation.meaning: strict order induced by directed reachability

source_refs.locator: Section 4. Acyclic Networks p. 68

source_witnesses.locator: Section 4. Acyclic Networks p. 68

children.title: Minimum Time Lags
children.top_down_role: Lower temporal separations between related activities or events.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Time Lags
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses finish-to-start lags; negative lag values permit controlled overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For jobs \(i,j\) with start times \(s_i,s_j\), processing time \(p_i\ge0\), and prescribed minimum finish-to-start lag \(\ell_{ij}^{\min}\in\mathbb{R}\), the temporal relation is \[s_j-(s_i+p_i)\ge \ell_{ij}^{\min}.\] Equivalently, \(s_j\ge s_i+p_i+\ell_{ij}^{\min}\). A schedule satisfies a family of minimum-lag relations exactly when this inequality holds for every designated ordered pair \((i,j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Job j must start at least the prescribed lag after job i finishes; negative lags allow overlap.

children.title: Mixed-Lag Temporal Networks

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Lag Temporal Networks

children.title: No-Wait Relations

knowledge_statements.title: No-Wait Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immediate-successor no-wait constraint for nonpreemptive operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let operations \(i\) and \(j\) have start times \(S_i,S_j\) and processing time \(p_i\), with \(j\) required immediately after \(i\). Their no-wait relation is the equality \[S_j=S_i+p_i.\] Thus \(i\) finishes exactly when \(j\) starts; neither an intervening delay nor an overlap is feasible. For a chain \((i_1,\ldots,i_k)\), the condition applies to every adjacent pair: \(S_{i_{r+1}}=S_{i_r}+p_{i_r}\) for \(r=1,\ldots,k-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A successor operation must start exactly when its predecessor finishes, so adjacent operations in a no-wait chain have neither idle time nor overlap.

Operations are nonpreemptive.

children.title: Blocking Relations

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocking-after-service relation in a consecutive-machine route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose operation \(i\) is processed on resource \(m\) from \(S_i\) for duration \(p_i\), and its route successor \(j\) requires another resource. Let \(D_i\) be the time at which the job leaves \(m\). A blocking relation requires \[D_i=\max\{S_i+p_i,S_j\},\] and resource \(m\) remains occupied by the job throughout \([S_i,D_i)\). In the usual zero-transfer blocking model, route feasibility also gives \(S_j=D_i\), so the completed job holds \(m\) until \(j\) can start.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After processing finishes, a job keeps occupying its current resource until its next operation can start on the successor resource.
assumptions_latex: Operations are nonpreemptive.
There is no intermediate buffer between the two route stages.
Transfer time is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_i=\max\{S_i+p_i,S_j\}\), with resource occupancy on \([S_i,D_i)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Permitted-Overlap Relations

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For predecessor operation \(i\), successor operation \(j\), and overlap parameter \(\alpha_{ij}\in[0,1]\), a permitted-overlap relation is \[S_j\ge S_i+\alpha_{ij}p_i.\] The successor may therefore begin after the prescribed fraction of \(i\)'s processing has elapsed. The cases \(\alpha_{ij}=1\) and \(\alpha_{ij}=0\) respectively recover ordinary finish-to-start precedence and unrestricted simultaneous starts subject to other constraints. If at most \(o_{ij}\) units of overlap are allowed, the equivalent lower bound is \(S_j\ge S_i+p_i-o_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The successor may start before its predecessor finishes, but only after a specified processing fraction or, equivalently, with bounded overlap.
assumptions_latex: Processing rates are constant when fractional completion is used.
Operations are otherwise governed by their resource constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Conflict Disjunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise disjunctive representation of unary-machine capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let distinct nonpreemptive operations \(i\) and \(j\) require the same unary machine, with start times \(S_i,S_j\) and durations \(p_i,p_j\). Machine capacity is represented by the disjunction \[(S_i+p_i\le S_j)\ \lor\ (S_j+p_j\le S_i).\] Equivalently, a binary orientation variable \(y_{ij}\) selects exactly one ordering. With a valid constant \(M\), the inequalities \(S_i+p_i\le S_j+M(1-y_{ij})\) and \(S_j+p_j\le S_i+My_{ij}\) encode the disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every pair of operations assigned to one unary machine must be ordered so that one finishes before the other starts.
assumptions_latex: The machine processes at most one operation at a time.
Operations are nonpreemptive.
\(M\) is a valid upper bound for the relevant time differences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S_i+p_i\le S_j)\lor(S_j+p_j\le S_i)\).

children.title: Critical Blocks

knowledge_statements.title: Critical Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path blocks in a feasible disjunctive schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a feasible nonpreemptive schedule represented by an acyclic oriented disjunctive graph, a critical path is a source-to-sink path whose total operation weight equals the makespan. A critical block is a maximal subsequence \(B=(i_1,\ldots,i_q)\), with \(q\ge2\), of consecutive operations on a critical path that are processed consecutively on the same machine. Maximality means that neither adjacent critical-path operation, when present, is processed on that machine as part of the same consecutive machine sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical block is a maximal run of at least two consecutive critical-path operations processed consecutively on one machine.
assumptions_latex: The oriented disjunctive graph is acyclic and represents a feasible schedule.
Vertex weights equal nonnegative operation durations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B=(i_1,\ldots,i_q)\) is maximal, \(q\ge2\), and all its operations are consecutive on one critical path and one machine.

children.title: Bottleneck Structures

knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Workload-based bottleneck set for a fixed resource assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O_m\) be the operations assigned to resource \(m\), and define its workload by \(L_m=\sum_{i\in O_m}p_i\). The workload bottleneck structure is the nonempty set \[\mathcal B=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{m\in\mathcal M}L_m.\] Every feasible schedule on unary resources has makespan \(C_{\max}\ge\max_{m\in\mathcal M}L_m\). Thus resources in \(\mathcal B\) attain the resource-workload lower bound; this definition concerns structural load and does not assert that every such resource lies on every critical path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workload bottlenecks are resources having maximum assigned processing load, whose load supplies a lower bound on the makespan.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a finite nonempty set of unary resources.
Each operation is assigned to exactly one resource.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{m\in\mathcal M}\sum_{i\in O_m}p_i\) and \(C_{\max}\ge\max_m L_m\).

children.title: Block–Bottleneck Interaction

knowledge_statements.title: Block–Bottleneck Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence representation linking critical blocks to workload bottlenecks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be the critical blocks of a feasible schedule, let \(m(B)\) be the unique machine processing block \(B\in\mathcal C\), and let \(\mathcal B\) be the set of workload-bottleneck machines. The block–bottleneck interaction incidence is \[I_{Bm}=\mathbf 1\{m=m(B)\}\mathbf 1\{m\in\mathcal B\}.\] Hence \(I_{Bm}=1\) exactly when critical block \(B\) occurs on bottleneck machine \(m\). The interacting critical blocks are \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal B}=\{B\in\mathcal C:m(B)\in\mathcal B\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical block interacts with the bottleneck structure exactly when its machine belongs to the selected bottleneck set.
assumptions_latex: Every critical block is processed on one unique machine.
The bottleneck set uses the workload-based definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal B}=\{B\in\mathcal C:m(B)\in\mathcal B\}\).

children.title: Setup-Time Sequences
children.top_down_role: Sequence-dependent temporal penalties between consecutive activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Setup-Time Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-dependent setup time along each resource order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a resource \(m\), let \((i_1,\ldots,i_k)\) be its ordered operations and let \(s^m_{ij}\ge0\) be the setup time incurred when \(j\) immediately follows \(i\). With dummy initial operation \(0\), temporal feasibility requires \[S_{i_1}\ge s^m_{0i_1},\qquad S_{i_{r+1}}\ge S_{i_r}+p_{i_r}+s^m_{i_ri_{r+1}}\quad(r=1,\ldots,k-1).\] The total setup time generated by the sequence is \(s^m_{0i_1}+\sum_{r=1}^{k-1}s^m_{i_ri_{r+1}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each adjacent pair in a machine sequence incurs a predecessor-dependent setup duration that separates their processing intervals.
assumptions_latex: Operations are nonpreemptive.
Setup times are nonnegative and depend on the ordered pair.
The dummy operation \(0\) represents the initial resource state.

knowledge_statements.title: Setup-Cost Sequences

assumptions_latex: A finite job set \(J\) is sequenced on one resource.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria representation for sequence-dependent setup time and setup cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every feasible permutation \(\pi=(\pi_0,\ldots,\pi_{n+1})\), define \[S(\pi)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}s_{\pi_r,\pi_{r+1}},\qquad C(\pi)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}c_{\pi_r,\pi_{r+1}}.\] A feasible sequence \(\pi\) is Pareto efficient if no feasible \(\sigma\) satisfies \(S(\sigma)\le S(\pi)\) and \(C(\sigma)\le C(\pi)\), with at least one strict inequality. knowledge_statements.title: Batch Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-batch representation with simultaneous processing inside each batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A batch sequence is an ordered tuple \((B_1,\ldots,B_m)\) of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets satisfying \(\bigcup_{r=1}^{m}B_r=J\), where each \(B_r\) is a feasible batch. All jobs in \(B_r\) start at the batch start \(S_r\) and complete at \(C_r=S_r+P(B_r)\). Consecutive batches obey \(S_{r+1}\ge C_r+s(B_r,B_{r+1})\), where \(s(B_r,B_{r+1})\ge0\) is the required transition time. The tuple therefore specifies both the partition into batches and their processing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs are partitioned into feasible batches, the batches are ordered, and jobs within each batch share its start and completion times.
assumptions_latex: A finite job set \(J\) is assigned to one batch-processing resource.
Every feasible batch satisfies the model's compatibility and capacity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A batch sequence is an ordered feasible partition of the jobs, inducing common batch start and completion times.

children.title: Campaign Sequences
children.top_down_role: Extended production runs organized into campaign structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Campaign Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Campaigns as maximal same-label runs in a production sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a job permutation \(\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n)\), a campaign is a maximal position interval \(K_r=\{a_r,\ldots,b_r\}\) such that \(f(\pi_k)=g_r\) for every \(k\in K_r\). Maximality requires \(a_r=1\) or \(f(\pi_{a_r-1})
e g_r\), and \(b_r=n\) or \(f(\pi_{b_r+1})
e g_r\). The campaign sequence \((K_1,\ldots,K_m)\) is ordered by position and satisfies \(g_r
e g_{r+1}\). Any minimum or maximum campaign-length rules are imposed as bounds on \(|K_r|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A campaign is a maximal consecutive run of jobs sharing one production label; campaigns inherit their order from the job sequence.
assumptions_latex: Each job has a production family or mode label.
A sequence is processed on one resource without interleaving positions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence decomposes uniquely into maximal campaigns, and campaign transitions occur exactly at label changes.

assumptions_latex: A finite set \(J\) of jobs must be visited exactly once.
Every permitted immediate succession \((i,j)\) is an arc of a directed graph \(G=(V,A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible job orders correspond to directed Hamiltonian paths, with transition objectives represented by arc sums.

notation.meaning: Binary indicator that j immediately follows i
Cost or duration of transition from i to j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian-path representation of sequence-dependent scheduling transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Add dummy start and end vertices \(0\) and \(n+1\). A routing-like sequencing model uses \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes one incoming and one outgoing selected arc for each \(j\in J\), one outgoing arc from \(0\), one incoming arc to \(n+1\), and no selected subtour on \(J\). These constraints make the selected arcs a directed Hamiltonian path from \(0\) through all jobs to \(n+1\). Sequence-dependent transition cost is then \(\sum_{(i,j)\in A}d_{ij}x_{ij}\); timing constraints may enforce \(S_j\ge C_i+d_{ij}\) whenever \(x_{ij}=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job order is represented as a Hamiltonian path whose arcs encode allowed immediate successors and their sequence-dependent transition values.
knowledge_statements.title: Routing-Like Sequencing Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hamiltonian-path representation is mathematically coherent and the representation kind fits the topic, but no scheduling-specific source supports the formulation or timing interpretation.

assumptions_latex: A finite set of operation types is repeated indefinitely.
Each operation occurrence has fixed processing time and renewable-resource requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cyclic schedule repeats its operation pattern every \(T\) time units while satisfying all precedence and resource constraints.

notation.meaning: Start time of occurrence k of operation type i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly periodic form of deterministic cyclic shop scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cyclic shop schedule with period \(T>0\) assigns starts \(S_i(k)=s_i+kT\) for every operation type \(i\) and repetition \(k\in\mathbb Z\). For each precedence relation from occurrence \((i,k)\) to \((j,k+h_{ij})\), feasibility requires \(S_j(k+h_{ij})\ge S_i(k)+p_i\), where \(p_i\ge0\). Occurrences requiring the same unary machine must occupy pairwise disjoint intervals \([S_i(k),S_i(k)+p_i)\). The optimization criterion commonly minimizes \(T\), equivalently maximizing the long-run cycle frequency \(1/T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cyclic shop schedule repeats fixed operation offsets every period while preserving cross-cycle precedence and preventing machine overlap.
knowledge_statements.title: Cyclic Shop Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement consistently describes a strictly periodic deterministic cyclic-shop variant, but cyclic-shop resource and precedence conventions vary and no source identifies this exact variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Event Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic event-scheduling constraints expressed with integer period offsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A periodic event relation \((i,j)\) is satisfied when there exists \(z_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\) such that \[\ell_{ij}\le \pi_j-\pi_i+Tz_{ij}\le u_{ij}.\] Equivalently, the directed time from event \(i\) to event \(j\), interpreted modulo \(T\), belongs to the prescribed interval whenever that interval selects the intended winding. A periodic event system is feasible precisely when phases \(\pi_i\in[0,T)\) and integer offsets \(z_{ij}\) satisfying every relation exist simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic event relations bound phase differences modulo a common period, with an integer variable recording how many periods separate related events.
assumptions_latex: Events repeat with a common period \(T>0\).
Each directed relation has lower and upper separation bounds \(\ell_{ij}\le u_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to satisfying bounded modular-difference constraints for all event relations.

notation.meaning: Phase of event i in one period

children.title: Steady-State Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Long-run recurring behavior of cyclic schedules.

assumptions_latex: The same finite production pattern is executed for repetitions \(k=0,1,\ldots\).
Start or completion vectors \(x(k)\) are finite for all sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In steady state, event times advance by a fixed vector after each fixed number of repetitions.

notation.meaning: Vector of event times at repetition k
Steady-state repetition span and temporal shift

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eventually periodic-affine event-time definition of scheduling steady state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A repetitive schedule reaches a periodic-affine steady state if there exist integers \(K\ge0\) and \(p\ge1\), and a scalar \(\Delta>0\), such that \[x(k+p)=x(k)+\Delta\mathbf 1\qquad\text{for every }k\ge K.\] The finite prefix \(x(0),\ldots,x(K+p-1)\) is the transient. When \(p=1\), each repetition has the same asymptotic temporal increment \(\Delta\); for \(p>1\), the schedule repeats its relative event pattern every \(p\) production repetitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Steady state begins when event-time vectors repeat after a fixed number of production repetitions, shifted uniformly forward in time.
knowledge_statements.title: Steady-State Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The periodic-affine definition is precise and fits steady-state scheduling, but its uniform scalar shift is model-specific and no cyclic- or max-plus-scheduling source is cited.

children.title: Repetition-Rate Models
children.top_down_role: Throughput-oriented timing of repeated schedule cycles.

assumptions_latex: Completed production cycles are counted by a nondecreasing function \(N(t)\).
The long-run limit exists and is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repetition rate is the asymptotic number of completed cycles per unit time.

notation.meaning: Number of completed repetitions by time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic throughput definition for repetitive schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The repetition rate of a feasible infinite schedule is \[\rho=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{N(t)}{t}.\] If completion times \(C(k)\) satisfy \(C(k)/k\to\lambda\) with \(0<\lambda<\infty\), then \(\rho=1/\lambda\). For an eventually periodic-affine schedule satisfying \(x(k+p)=x(k)+\Delta\mathbf 1\), the rate is \(\rho=p/\Delta\). Maximizing repetition rate is therefore equivalent, within this regime, to minimizing the average temporal increment \(\Delta/p\) per repetition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repetition rate is long-run throughput: completed production repetitions per unit time, equal to the reciprocal of average cycle time.
knowledge_statements.title: Repetition-Rate Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The throughput definition and periodic-affine specialization are mathematically coherent, but no repetitive-scheduling source supports the limit relations or modeling interpretation.

children.title: Transient-to-Steady-State Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Schedule behavior during transition into recurring operation.

knowledge_statements.title: Transient-to-Steady-State Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Earliest index separating a finite transient from periodic-affine behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed steady-state parameters \((p,\Delta)\), define \[K^*=\min\bigl\{K\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:x(k+p)=x(k)+\Delta\mathbf 1\ \text{for all }k\ge K\bigr\}.\] When this set is nonempty, repetitions \(0,\ldots,K^*-1\) form the transient and \(K^*\) is the transient-to-steady-state boundary. Minimality implies that, if \(K^*>0\), the identity fails at \(k=K^*-1\). If the set is empty, no finite boundary exists for those parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transient boundary is the smallest repetition index from which the chosen periodic time-shift pattern holds at every later repetition.
assumptions_latex: An event-time sequence \(x(k)\) is eventually periodic-affine.
Candidate parameters satisfy \(p\ge1\) and \(\Delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transient boundary is the earliest repetition after which the periodic-affine identity holds forever.

notation.meaning: Period in repetitions and associated time shift

children.title: Timetabling
children.top_down_role: Educational and sports event allocation; transport-specific periodic timetabling is retained as a cross-link to the transportation chapter.

assumptions_latex: Each examination \(e\in E\) must be assigned one period in \(P\).
Conflicting examinations are edges of an undirected graph \(G=(E,H)\).
Room and period capacities are ignored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible uncapacitated examination timetables are exactly proper colorings of the conflict graph by periods.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict-graph formulation without room or aggregate capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An uncapacitated examination timetable is a map \(\tau:E\to P\) satisfying \[\tau(e)\ne\tau(f)\qquad\text{for every }\{e,f\}\in H.\] Hence feasibility with at most \(q=|P|\) periods is equivalent to a proper \(q\)-coloring of \(G\). If a spacing requirement \(d_{ef}\ge1\) is specified for a conflicting or pedagogically linked pair, the strengthened condition is \(|\tau(e)-\tau(f)|\ge d_{ef}\) after periods are given an integer order. Enrollment sizes do not affect feasibility in the uncapacitated model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ignoring room capacities, examination timetabling is graph coloring: exams sharing students must receive different periods, possibly with stronger spacing requirements.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncapacitated Examination Timetabling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conflict-graph representation correctly fits the uncapacitated leaf, but no examination-timetabling citation supports the base model or its optional ordered-period spacing extension.

assumptions_latex: Each examination \(e\in E\) has demand \(a_e\ge0\) and is assigned one period.
Each period \(p\in P\) has available capacity \(b_p\ge0\).
Conflict edges \(H\) prohibit simultaneous examinations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible timetable is a conflict-free assignment whose total examination demand in every period does not exceed capacity.

notation.meaning: Binary assignment of examination e to period p
Demand of examination e and capacity of period p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate period-capacity version of capacitated examination timetabling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A capacitated examination timetable consists of variables \(x_{ep}\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \[\sum_{p\in P}x_{ep}=1\quad(e\in E),\qquad x_{ep}+x_{fp}\le1\quad(\{e,f\}\in H, p\in P),\] and \[\sum_{e\in E}a_ex_{ep}\le b_p\quad(p\in P).\] The first constraints assign every examination once, the second prevent conflicting examinations from sharing a period, and the third enforce aggregate seating or room capacity. A room-indexed variant replaces the last inequalities with explicit exam-to-room assignments and room-specific capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacitated examination timetabling assigns every exam once, separates conflicts, and keeps total demand within each period's available capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Examination Timetabling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aggregate period-capacity formulation is internally consistent and explicitly distinguishes room-indexed variants, but it is only one meaning of capacitated examination timetabling and lacks a supporting domain citation.

children.title: Exam Spacing Requirements
children.top_down_role: Temporal separation preferences or restrictions between examinations.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite and \(P=\{1,\ldots,H\}\) for some \(H\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
For every unordered pair \(\{e,f\}\subseteq E\), the data satisfy \(w_{ef}\ge 0\) and \(d_{ef}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\).
The timetable assigns exactly one indexed period to every examination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\) is hard-spacing feasible exactly when every positive-weight pair satisfies its prescribed separation; under the stated soft convention, \(V(t)=0\) exactly when all such requirements hold.

notation.meaning: number or weight of students common to exams e and f
required period-index separation for the exam pair

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pairwise minimum-separation constraints and weighted shortfall penalties are standard examination-timetabling formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard and soft minimum separations between examinations sharing students.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite set of examinations, let \(P=\{1,\ldots,H\}\) be a finite set of indexed periods, and let \(t:E\to P\) be a timetable. For each unordered pair \(\{e,f\}\subseteq E\), let \(w_{ef}\ge 0\) be its common-student weight and let \(d_{ef}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) be its required separation. The timetable satisfies the hard spacing requirements precisely when \[w_{ef}>0\Longrightarrow |t(e)-t(f)|\ge d_{ef}\qquad\text{for every }\{e,f\}\subseteq E.\] Under the stated soft convention, the total weighted spacing shortfall is \[V(t)=\sum_{\{e,f\}\subseteq E}w_{ef}\max\{0,d_{ef}-|t(e)-t(f)|\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflicting exams must be assigned at least their prescribed number of indexed periods apart; under the stated soft convention, violations are weighted by common enrollment and separation shortfall.
knowledge_statements.title: Exam Spacing Requirements

children.title: Student-Conflict Regimes
children.top_down_role: Examination settings classified by patterns of shared student enrollment.

knowledge_statements.title: Student-Conflict Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict regimes induced by individual students’ examination enrollments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be the examination set, \(S\) the student set, and \(E_s\subseteq E\) the exams taken by student \(s\). The student-conflict graph is \(G=(E,C)\), where \[C=\bigl\{\{e,f\}:e\ne f,\ \exists s\in S\text{ with }\{e,f\}\subseteq E_s\bigr\}.\] A conflict regime specifies whether each edge is hard, requiring \(t(e)\ne t(f)\), or soft, assigning a nonnegative penalty to simultaneous or insufficiently separated placement. An instance is pairwise-conflict-based when feasibility and conflict cost depend on enrollment only through \(G\) and its edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Student enrollments induce an exam-conflict graph. A regime declares its edges hard, soft, or weighted and determines whether pairwise conflicts fully describe the instance.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(S\) are finite.
Each enrollment set satisfies \(E_s\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{e,f\}\in C\) exactly when at least one student is enrolled in both examinations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conflict graphs are the standard pairwise representation of shared examination enrollment
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the student-conflict leaf, and the variables and graph construction are coherent. No source reference or specific locator is supplied, so the domain-specific hard/soft regime characterization cannot pass source review.

children.title: Conflict-Density Regimes
children.top_down_role: Timetabling structures associated with sparse through dense student-conflict graphs.

assumptions_latex: Each \(G_n=(E_n,C_n)\) is a finite simple graph with \(|E_n|=n\).
The asymptotic statements concern a sequence with \(n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every finite instance, \(0\le \rho(G)\le 1\). For a graph sequence, bounded average degree is equivalent to \(|C_n|=O(n)\), while density bounded below by a positive constant for all sufficiently large \(n\) is equivalent to \(|C_n|=\Theta(n^2)\).

notation.meaning: edge density of the conflict graph
number of examinations in the indexed graph

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simple-graph edge density and asymptotic sparse/dense regimes are standard graph-theoretic definitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative sparsity regimes for examination conflict graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a simple examination-conflict graph \(G=(E,C)\) with \(n=|E|\ge 2\), its edge density is \[\rho(G)=\frac{2|C|}{n(n-1)}.\] For a sequence \((G_n)\) with \(|E_n|=n\), the sparse regime is defined by \(|C_n|=O(n)\), equivalently bounded average degree. The dense regime is defined by \(|C_n|=\Theta(n^2)\), equivalently the existence of \(c>0\) such that \(\rho(G_n)\ge c\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). A sequence satisfying both \(|C_n|=\omega(n)\) and \(|C_n|=o(n^2)\) is in an intermediate regime. These asymptotic definitions do not prescribe application-specific thresholds for a single finite instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflict density is the fraction of possible examination pairs that conflict. A graph sequence is sparse when it has linearly many edges, dense when it has quadratically many edges, and intermediate when its edge count grows strictly between those rates.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Density Regimes
Curriculum-Based Course Timetabling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Course timetabling whose conflicts are prescribed by curricula rather than individual enrollments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A curriculum-based course-timetabling instance consists of finite courses \(C\), periods \(P\), rooms \(R\), curricula \(Q\subseteq 2^C\), course teachers, room capacities, and availability data. A timetable assigns every required lecture of each course to a period-room pair. It is feasible when no room hosts two lectures simultaneously, no teacher or curriculum contains simultaneous lectures, unavailable placements are avoided, and assigned rooms satisfy all designated hard requirements. Curriculum-based objectives may penalize capacity overflow, isolated curriculum lectures, noncompact curricula, or undesirable course-period patterns without changing this feasibility definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lectures receive room-period assignments, while curricula prescribe groups of courses that may not meet simultaneously; rooms, teachers, and availability impose additional constraints.
assumptions_latex: All course, period, room, and curriculum sets are finite.
Each required lecture receives exactly one placement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible timetable is a total lecture-to-room-period assignment satisfying room, teacher, curriculum, availability, and designated room constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: curriculum conflicts and lecture-to-room-period assignments define the standard curriculum-based timetabling model
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the curriculum-based course-timetabling topic, but the exact division between hard room requirements and soft benchmark objectives varies by formulation. No domain-specific source with a section, definition, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-Enrollment Course Timetabling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Course timetabling after individual course registrations are known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A post-enrollment course-timetabling instance consists of events \(L\), periods \(P\), rooms \(R\), students \(S\), enrollment sets \(L_s\subseteq L\), room features and capacities, and event availability data. A timetable assigns each event \(\ell\in L\) a period-room pair. It is feasible when no student has two enrolled events in one period, no room hosts two events simultaneously, every selected room has the required features and capacity, and all availability constraints hold. Soft objectives may additionally penalize consecutive, isolated, or late events for individual students.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Known student enrollments induce event conflicts. Each event receives a feasible room and period without student clashes, room collisions, or resource violations.
assumptions_latex: Enrollment is fixed before timetable construction.
All event, period, room, and student sets are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires a total event placement satisfying student, room-occupancy, room-suitability, and availability constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed individual enrollments distinguish post-enrollment from curriculum-based course timetabling
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits post-enrollment course timetabling and consistently uses fixed individual enrollments. Its detailed feasibility and soft-objective conventions require a domain-specific benchmark or survey citation, which is absent.

children.title: Student Section Formation
children.top_down_role: Covers the organization of enrolled students into course sections.

knowledge_statements.title: Student Section Formation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitioning course demand into capacitated instructional sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite student set and \(K\) a finite course set. For each course \(k\), section formation chooses a finite section set \(J_k\) and binary memberships \(x_{sj}\in\{0,1\}\). Given demand indicators \(d_{sk}\in\{0,1\}\) and section bounds \(\ell_j\le u_j\), a complete formation satisfies \[\sum_{j\in J_k}x_{sj}=d_{sk}\quad(s\in S,k\in K),\qquad \ell_j\le\sum_{s\in S}x_{sj}\le u_j\quad(j\in J_k).\] Additional eligibility or incompatibility rules restrict which memberships may equal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every demanded course, each student is placed in exactly one section, and every formed section respects its enrollment bounds and eligibility rules.
assumptions_latex: Each section belongs to exactly one course.
Demand indicators and section bounds are given.
\(0\le\ell_j\le u_j\) for every section.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The membership variables form capacitated course sections that cover each declared student-course demand exactly once.

notation.meaning: student demand indicator for course k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact demand coverage with lower and upper section bounds is a standard capacitated partition formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits student section formation, and the displayed constraints express exact demand coverage and section bounds. No inspectable source supports this particular formulation or the inclusion of lower bounds.

children.title: Student Choice Representation
children.top_down_role: Covers course, section, time, or instructor preferences expressed by students.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(A\) are finite.
For each \(s\in S\), the rank function is defined only on \(A_s\).
Whenever dissatisfaction costs are used to preserve the ordinal ranking, they are nondecreasing in rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The acceptable sets and request indicators encode acceptability, while rank functions or suitably rank-monotone costs additionally encode ordinal preference information and ties.

notation.meaning: ordinal rank assigned by student s to an acceptable alternative
dissatisfaction cost of assigning alternative a to student s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: acceptable sets, ordinal ranks, and rank-derived costs are standard finite preference representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-based and ranked encodings of student course or section preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite student set and \(A\) a finite set of alternatives. For each \(s\in S\), let \(A_s\subseteq A\) be the acceptable alternatives and let \(r_s:A_s\to\{1,\ldots,|A_s|\}\) be a rank function, with smaller values representing more-preferred alternatives and equal values representing ties. Acceptability can be encoded by \[d_{sa}=1\Longleftrightarrow a\in A_s.\] Given binary allocation variables \(x_{sa}\), an additive dissatisfaction score is \[D(x)=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A_s}c_{sa}x_{sa},\] where \(c_{sa}\le c_{sb}\) whenever \(r_s(a)<r_s(b)\). Unacceptable alternatives are excluded from the variable domain or explicitly forbidden. Strictly increasing costs preserve strict rank comparisons, whereas merely nondecreasing costs may also introduce cost ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceptable alternatives are encoded by sets or binary indicators. Rank functions encode ordinal preferences and ties, while rank-monotone assignment costs provide a numerical dissatisfaction representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Student Choice Representation

children.title: Choice-Aware Section Allocation
children.top_down_role: Covers placement decisions that account for expressed student choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Choice-Aware Section Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated section assignment respecting student acceptability and expressed preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be students, \(J_k\) the sections of course \(k\), and \(A_{sk}\subseteq J_k\) the sections acceptable to student \(s\). Binary variables \(x_{sj}\) define a choice-aware allocation when \[\sum_{j\in A_{sk}}x_{sj}=d_{sk}\quad(s\in S,k\in K),\qquad \sum_{s\in S}x_{sj}\le u_j\quad(j\in J_k),\] and \(x_{sj}=0\) whenever \(j\notin A_{sk}\). Among feasible allocations, choice awareness is expressed by minimizing \(\sum_{s,j}c_{sj}x_{sj}\), maximizing satisfied requests, or applying a stated lexicographic preference rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Students are assigned only to acceptable sections, every requested course is covered once, capacities hold, and the objective reflects expressed preferences.
assumptions_latex: Section sets and capacities are fixed.
Preference costs or an alternative preference rule are specified.
Each \(d_{sk}\) is binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any feasible solution covers every requested course with one acceptable, capacity-feasible section; optimization selects among such solutions using student choices.

notation.meaning: sections of course k acceptable to student s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: acceptable-edge assignment with exact demand coverage, capacities, and preference costs is a standard allocation formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits choice-aware section allocation and its feasibility constraints are coherent. The alternative preference objectives are application-dependent, and no source with a specific locator supports the selected formulation.

children.title: Section Capacity Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Covers choice conflicts arising from limited seats or incompatible selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Section Capacity Conflicts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand-based certificates that a section allocation cannot satisfy all requests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct the bipartite acceptability graph between students \(S\) requiring one placement and sections \(J\), with edge \((s,j)\) when section \(j\) is acceptable to student \(s\). Give section \(j\) capacity \(u_j\). For \(U\subseteq S\), let \(N(U)\subseteq J\) be its neighboring sections. If \[|U|>\sum_{j\in N(U)}u_j,\] then no allocation can assign every student in \(U\) to an acceptable section. Thus \(U\), together with its neighborhood and capacities, is a directly checkable section-capacity conflict certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A student subset is impossible to place when its acceptable neighboring sections have less total capacity than the subset’s demand.
assumptions_latex: Each student in \(S\) requires one section.
Assignments are permitted only along acceptability edges.
Section \(j\) accepts at most \(u_j\) students.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed strict inequality certifies infeasibility of complete acceptable assignment for all students in \(U\).

notation.meaning: subset of students whose demand is tested
sections acceptable to at least one student in U

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the capacitated Hall inequality is a standard verifiable obstruction to bipartite assignment
