children.title: Room Assignment
children.top_down_role: Covers allocation of events to rooms with capacity or facility restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Room Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment of scheduled teaching events to compatible rooms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be teaching events, \(R\) rooms, and \(t:L\to P\) a fixed period assignment. For each event \(\ell\), let \(R_\ell\subseteq R\) be its compatible rooms. A room assignment is a map \(r:L\to R\) satisfying \(r(\ell)\in R_\ell\) and \[t(\ell)=t(m)\ \Longrightarrow\ r(\ell)\ne r(m)\qquad(\ell\ne m).\] Compatibility may encode capacity, equipment, location, or accessibility requirements. If room splitting is forbidden, every event receives exactly one room; otherwise the variable domain must explicitly permit room subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given event periods, each event receives one compatible room, and simultaneous events cannot use the same room.
assumptions_latex: Event and room sets are finite.
The period assignment is fixed.
Each compatibility set \(R_\ell\) is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible room assignment is a compatible map that is injective among events occurring in every common period.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compatible-room assignment with per-period room exclusivity is the standard fixed-period subproblem

children.title: Period Assignment
children.top_down_role: Covers allocation of events to admissible teaching periods.

knowledge_statements.title: Period Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment of teaching events to permissible periods before or alongside room selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a finite event set and \(P\) a finite period set. For each event \(\ell\), let \(P_\ell\subseteq P\) contain its permissible periods, and let \(C\subseteq\binom{L}{2}\) contain pairs that may not overlap. A period assignment is a map \(t:L\to P\) satisfying \[t(\ell)\in P_\ell\quad(\ell\in L),\qquad \{\ell,m\}\in C\ \Longrightarrow\ t(\ell)\ne t(m).\] Further temporal restrictions, such as precedence, spacing, or daily limits, are additional predicates on \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every event receives an allowed period, and each declared conflicting pair receives different periods; other temporal rules may add further restrictions.
assumptions_latex: Events and periods are finite.
Permissible-period sets and conflict pairs are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible period assignment is a list-respecting proper coloring of the event-conflict graph, possibly subject to additional temporal predicates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: event-period feasibility is naturally a list-coloring constraint system
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Room–Period Coupling
children.top_down_role: Covers dependencies between temporal placement and room availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Room–Period Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint feasibility constraints linking each event’s period and room decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let binary \(x_{\ell pr}\) equal one when event \(\ell\) uses room \(r\) in period \(p\), and let \(F_\ell\subseteq P\times R\) contain its feasible room-period pairs. Joint room-period feasibility requires \[\sum_{(p,r)\in F_\ell}x_{\ell pr}=1\quad(\ell\in L),\qquad \sum_{\ell:(p,r)\in F_\ell}x_{\ell pr}\le 1\quad(p\in P,r\in R),\] with \(x_{\ell pr}=0\) outside \(F_\ell\). For every conflicting pair \(\{\ell,m\}\), it additionally requires \(\sum_r x_{\ell pr}+\sum_r x_{mpr}\le 1\) for each period \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each event selects one feasible room-period pair; rooms and conflict resources cannot be shared simultaneously, so room and period decisions are jointly constrained.
assumptions_latex: Each event requires exactly one room and one period.
Feasible pair sets encode event-specific room and period compatibility.
Conflict pairs are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary variables define a joint assignment with event coverage, room-time exclusivity, pair compatibility, and conflict nonoverlap.

notation.meaning: indicator that event l uses room r in period p
feasible room-period pairs for event l

children.title: Joint Assignment Infeasibility
children.top_down_role: Covers conflicts caused by incompatible room-period combinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Assignment Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall certificate for assigning events jointly to compatible room–period pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite event set, let \(Q=R\times P\) be the set of room–period pairs, and let \(A_e\subseteq Q\) contain the pairs compatible with event \(e\). A joint assignment is an injection \(f:E\to Q\) satisfying \(f(e)\in A_e\). It is infeasible if and only if there exists \(S\subseteq E\) such that
\[\left|\bigcup_{e\in S}A_e\right|<|S|.\]
Such a set \(S\), together with its compatible-pair union, is a verifiable certificate of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint room–period assignment is impossible exactly when some event subset has fewer collectively compatible room–period pairs than events.
assumptions_latex: \(E\), \(R\), and \(P\) are finite.
Each room–period pair can host at most one event.
All relevant compatibility restrictions are represented by \(A_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S\subseteq E:\left|\bigcup_{e\in S}A_e\right|<|S|\) certifies joint assignment infeasibility.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Hall's marriage theorem applied to event-to-room-period matching

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hall-type infeasibility certificate is mathematically precise and the certificate content kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Class–Teacher Timetabling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite school timetable with simultaneous class and teacher noncollision constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be a finite set of lessons. Each lesson \(\ell\in L\) has a class \(c(\ell)\in C\), a teacher \(u(\ell)\in U\), and an allowed-period set \(A_\ell\subseteq P\). A class–teacher timetable is a map \(\tau:L\to P\) such that \(\tau(\ell)\in A_\ell\) for every lesson and, whenever \(\ell\ne m\),
\[c(\ell)=c(m)\ \text{or}\ u(\ell)=u(m)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tau(\ell)\ne\tau(m).\]
Thus neither a class nor a teacher participates in two simultaneous lessons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lessons receive allowed periods so that no class and no teacher is assigned to two lessons at the same time.
assumptions_latex: \(L\), \(C\), \(U\), and \(P\) are finite.
Every lesson has exactly one designated class and teacher.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau\) is feasible precisely when it satisfies availability and both class and teacher noncollision constraints.

notation.meaning: class and teacher of lesson ℓ

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical finite constraint model for class–teacher timetabling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite class–teacher noncollision model is coherent and definition is the correct content kind, but the record lacks a domain source with a specific locator.

children.title: Lesson Compactness
children.top_down_role: Covers concentration of lessons within desirable portions of the school day or week.

knowledge_statements.title: Lesson Compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap-free daily occupancy condition for each class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Order the periods of each day consecutively. For class \(c\) and day \(d\), let \(T_{cd}\) be the set of within-day period indices occupied by its lessons. The timetable has lesson compactness when every nonempty \(T_{cd}\) is an integer interval. Equivalently,
\[\max T_{cd}-\min T_{cd}+1=|T_{cd}|\]
for all \((c,d)\) with \(T_{cd}\ne\varnothing\). A soft compactness penalty may instead count internal gaps as \(\max T_{cd}-\min T_{cd}+1-|T_{cd}|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class has compact lessons on a day when its occupied periods form one uninterrupted block; the interval deficit counts internal gaps.
assumptions_latex: Within-day periods have consecutive integer indices.
Simultaneous lessons of the same class are prohibited.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{cd}\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow \max T_{cd}-\min T_{cd}+1=|T_{cd}|\).

notation.meaning: period indices occupied by class c on day d

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interval characterization of gap-free daily occupancy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval condition correctly characterizes the stated gap-free convention, and condition fits the leaf. A source is needed because educational-timetabling compactness conventions and penalties vary.

children.title: Lesson Splitting
children.top_down_role: Covers division of instructional requirements across multiple meetings.

knowledge_statements.title: Lesson Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of required teaching duration as scheduled session lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each lesson requirement \(i\), let \(h_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) be its required number of periods. A split pattern is an ordered tuple \(\lambda_i=(\lambda_{i1},\ldots,\lambda_{ik_i})\) satisfying
\[\lambda_{ij}\in D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_{>0},\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{k_i}\lambda_{ij}=h_i.\]
A timetable realizes the pattern when it assigns each session \((i,j)\) to \(\lambda_{ij}\) consecutive periods and the resulting session intervals are pairwise disjoint for every shared class or teacher. Bounds on \(k_i\) or restrictions on \(D_i\) specify the permitted splitting policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lesson’s required duration is partitioned into permitted session lengths, each scheduled consecutively without class or teacher conflicts.
assumptions_latex: \(h_i\) is a positive integral number of periods.
Each permitted session length belongs to \(D_i\subseteq\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j=1}^{k_i}\lambda_{ij}=h_i\) and every session occupies \(\lambda_{ij}\) consecutive feasible periods.

notation.meaning: total required duration of lesson requirement i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integer-composition model of lesson splitting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duration-composition representation is internally consistent and fits the lesson-splitting leaf, but permitted splitting and session-contiguity conventions require an inspectable domain citation.

children.title: Lesson Synchronization
children.top_down_role: Covers coordinated timing among linked classes, teachers, or activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Lesson Synchronization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality constraint for designated lesson start times or occupied period sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be a finite set of lessons and let \(G\subseteq L\) be a designated synchronization group. For each \(\ell\in L\), let \(s_\ell\) and \(q_\ell\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) denote its start period and duration. Start synchronization requires
\[s_\ell=s_m\qquad\text{for all }\ell,m\in G.\]
Full synchronization additionally requires \(q_\ell=q_m\) for all \(\ell,m\in G\), so lessons in \(G\) have coincident occupied-period intervals. Feasibility also requires that synchronized lessons share no unit-capacity class, teacher, room, or other resource unless simultaneous sharing is explicitly permitted by the instructional model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Designated lessons are synchronized by equal start periods; equal durations additionally make their complete occupied intervals coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is finite.
Every lesson in \(G\) has a defined start period and positive integral duration.
Unit-capacity resource conflicts remain enforced unless simultaneous sharing is explicitly permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell,m\in G\Rightarrow s_\ell=s_m\), with \(q_\ell=q_m\) for full synchronization.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality constraints are the canonical synchronization model

children.title: Compactness–Synchronization Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Covers tensions between locally compact schedules and cross-class timing requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness–Synchronization Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal instance where synchronization destroys otherwise attainable daily compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one day with periods \(P=\{1,2,3,4\}\), two classes \(a,b\), fixed one-period lessons for \(a\) at period \(1\) and for \(b\) at period \(4\), and one additional one-period lesson for each class. Require the two additional lessons to be synchronized at a common period \(t\). Compactness for \(a\) forces \(t=2\), whereas compactness for \(b\) forces \(t=3\). Hence no timetable satisfies both synchronization and gap-free compactness, although either requirement is feasible when imposed alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed lessons at opposite ends of four periods, synchronized added lessons cannot make both classes’ two-lesson schedules gap-free.
assumptions_latex: All four lessons have unit duration.
A class cannot attend two lessons in one period.
Compactness means that each class's occupied periods form an interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t=2\) is required for class \(a\), while \(t=3\) is required for class \(b\); therefore joint feasibility fails.

notation.meaning: common period of the synchronized lessons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite counterexample is correct, matches both mathematical representations, and counterexample is the appropriate kind for this tradeoff leaf. It nevertheless has no inspectable cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Round-Robin Tournament Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single round robin for an even number of teams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a set of \(n\ge 2\) teams, where \(n\) is even, and let \(R=\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\). A single round-robin schedule is a map \(\rho:\binom{T}{2}\to R\) such that, for every round \(r\), the pairs in \(\rho^{-1}(r)\) form a perfect matching of \(T\). Consequently every unordered pair of teams meets exactly once, every team plays exactly once per round, and each round contains \(n/2\) matches. A home–away orientation may independently designate one endpoint of each pair as home.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an even-team single round robin, every pair meets once and every round is a perfect matching of all teams.
assumptions_latex: \(|T|=n\) is even and \(n\ge2\).
Each match occupies one round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho^{-1}(r)\) is a perfect matching for every \(r\in R\), and each pair in \(\binom{T}{2}\) is scheduled once.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: one-factorization formulation of an even-team round robin

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-factorization formulation correctly defines an even-team single round robin, and definition fits the topic, but no sports-scheduling source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Phased Tournament Structures
children.top_down_role: Covers tournaments partitioned into temporally distinct competition phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Phased Tournament Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Double round robin divided into phases with one meeting per pair in each phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) contain an even number \(n\) of teams, and partition the rounds into consecutive phases \(R_1\) and \(R_2\), each of size \(n-1\). A phased double round-robin schedule assigns two matches to every pair \(\{i,j\}\), with opposite home–away orientations, such that exactly one of those matches lies in \(R_1\) and exactly one lies in \(R_2\). In every round, the scheduled matches form a perfect matching of \(T\). No requirement is imposed that the opponent orders in the phases coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A phased double round robin places one meeting of every team pair in each phase, with roundwise perfect matchings and reversed venues.
assumptions_latex: \(|T|=n\) is even.
Each phase contains \(n-1\) rounds.
Every pair plays twice with opposite home–away orientations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|M_{ij}\cap R_1|=|M_{ij}\cap R_2|=1\) for every distinct \(i,j\in T\).

notation.meaning: first and second phase round sets
rounds containing meetings of teams i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently describes a phased double round robin, but the phased convention requires a specific sports-scheduling citation.

children.title: Mirrored Tournament Structures
children.top_down_role: Covers schedules whose later portions reproduce earlier pairings with reversed venues.

knowledge_statements.title: Mirrored Tournament Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second phase repeats first-phase pairings at a fixed offset with reversed venues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T\) be a finite team set, and let a double round-robin tournament on \(T\) have \(2q\) rounds divided into two blocks of \(q\) rounds. For each first-block match in which team \(i\in T\) hosts team \(j\in T\) in round \(r\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), the mirror condition requires \(j\) to host \(i\) in round \(r+q\). Equivalently, if \(H_r\subseteq T\times T\) is the set of ordered home–away pairs in round \(r\), then
\[H_{r+q}=\{(j,i):(i,j)\in H_r\}\qquad(1\le r\le q).\]
Thus the opponent sequence repeats with a constant offset and every venue is reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second block repeats every first-block pairing at the same relative round, reversing the home and away teams.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite team set.
The tournament has two blocks of equal length \(q\).
An ordered pair \((i,j)\) means that team \(i\) hosts team \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_{r+q}=\{(j,i):(i,j)\in H_r\}\) for every \(r\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\).

notation.meaning: ordered home–away matches in round r
number of rounds in each block

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-offset reversed-fixture definition of mirroring

children.title: Phased Mirror Integration
children.top_down_role: Covers tournament formats combining phase separation with mirrored fixtures.

knowledge_statements.title: Phased Mirror Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A full mirror of a single round robin automatically yields a phased double round robin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) have even cardinality \(n\), and suppose rounds \(1,\ldots,n-1\) form a single round robin. Construct rounds \(n,\ldots,2n-2\) by repeating the matches of each round \(r\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) in round \(r+n-1\), with every home–away orientation reversed. The resulting schedule is both mirrored and phased: every pair meets once in each block, its second meeting has the opposite venue, and every round remains a perfect matching. Thus full mirroring integrates the phase constraint without additional pair-allocation decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirroring a complete first phase produces a double round robin that is automatically both phased and venue-reversed.
assumptions_latex: \(|T|=n\) is even.
Rounds \(1,\ldots,n-1\) form a single round robin.
The second block is the venue-reversed mirror of the first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(2(n-1)\)-round schedule is simultaneously phased and mirrored.

notation.meaning: round index in the first block

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct combination of phased and mirrored definitions

children.title: Partial-Mirror Variants
children.top_down_role: Covers formats that relax complete mirroring across phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Mirror Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mirroring imposed on a selected subset of first-block matches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a double round robin have two blocks of \(q\) rounds, and let \(S\) be a selected subset of ordered matches from the first block. The schedule is partially mirrored with respect to \(S\) when every \((i,j)\in S\) played in round \(r\) is accompanied by \((j,i)\) in round \(r+q\). Matches outside \(S\) need only satisfy the underlying double-round-robin and resource constraints. Full mirroring is recovered when \(S\) contains every first-block match; \(S=\varnothing\) imposes no mirror equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial mirror fixes the offset and reversed venue only for selected first-block matches; all other return matches may move.
assumptions_latex: The tournament has two equal-length round blocks.
Every unordered team pair has two oppositely oriented meetings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((i,j)\in S\cap H_r\Rightarrow(j,i)\in H_{r+q}\), while matches outside \(S\) are not mirror-fixed.

notation.meaning: selected first-block ordered matches to mirror

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relaxation of full mirror equalities on a selected match subset

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected-subset relaxation is internally coherent and definition fits the variant leaf, but partial-mirror terminology and conventions vary and no specific source is cited.

children.title: Home–Away Pattern Construction
children.top_down_role: Covers venue-status sequences assigned to teams across rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Home–Away Pattern Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary team-round patterns coupled by scheduled opponent pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For teams \(T\) and rounds \(R\), a home–away pattern is a binary vector \(h_i=(h_{ir})_{r\in R}\) for each team \(i\), where \(h_{ir}=1\) denotes home and \(h_{ir}=0\) denotes away. Given roundwise match variables \(x_{ijr}\in\{0,1\}\) for unordered pairs, pattern feasibility requires
\[x_{ijr}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h_{ir}+h_{jr}=1.\]
Pattern construction selects the vectors subject to prescribed counts, forbidden runs, or break limits; assigning opponents then requires a roundwise matching compatible with complementary pattern entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each team receives a binary home–away sequence, and teams paired in any round must have complementary entries in that round.
assumptions_latex: Each team plays at most once per round.
Every played match has exactly one home team and one away team.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{ijr}=1\Rightarrow h_{ir}+h_{jr}=1\) for all distinct \(i,j\in T\) and \(r\in R\).

notation.meaning: home indicator for team i in round r
indicator that teams i and j meet in round r

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical binary representation of home–away patterns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary pattern representation and complementary-entry coupling are precise, and representation is appropriate for the construction leaf, but the record lacks an inspectable sports-scheduling citation.

children.title: Home–Away Break Structure
children.top_down_role: Covers repeated home or away status across consecutive rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Home–Away Break Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines breaks in a binary home–away pattern over consecutive rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a team with ordered rounds \(R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(h_r\in\{0,1\}\), where \(1\) denotes home and \(0\) denotes away. A break occurs after round \(r\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\) exactly when \(h_r=h_{r+1}\). Its indicator is \(b_r=\mathbf 1\{h_r=h_{r+1}\}\), and the number of breaks is \(B(h)=\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}b_r\). A maximal home or away run of length \(q\) therefore contains exactly \(q-1\) breaks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A break is a pair of consecutive home games or consecutive away games; a run of length q contributes q minus one breaks.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 2\) rounds are linearly ordered.
Each round has exactly one home–away status for the team.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard binary definition of a home–away break

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, and the LaTeX and plain statements agree. No inspectable sports-timetabling citation is supplied, so the conventional break definition remains unsupported.

children.title: Break Minimization Criteria
children.top_down_role: Covers evaluation criteria for reducing undesirable venue-status repetitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Break Minimization Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes weighted and minimax criteria for comparing feasible home–away schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be the team set and \(\mathcal F\) the feasible schedules. For \(x\in\mathcal F\), let \(B_i(x)\) be team \(i\)'s break count and let \(w_i\ge0\). A weighted-break optimum satisfies \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i\in T}w_iB_i(x)\). A minimax-break optimum instead satisfies \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal F}\max_{i\in T}B_i(x)\). Lexicographic minimization first minimizes the maximum count and then, among ties, the total count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Breaks may be minimized by weighted total, worst team count, or lexicographically by worst count followed by total count.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\).
Every \(B_i(x)\) is a nonnegative integer.
At least one weight \(w_i\) is positive for the weighted criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality is membership in the stated weighted, minimax, or lexicographic argmin set.

notation.meaning: Break count of team i in schedule x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard scalar and minimax objective criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted, minimax, and lexicographic criteria are mathematically coherent and fit this criteria leaf. An authoritative sports-timetabling source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Pattern Feasibility Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Covers conflicts between preferred patterns and tournament feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Pattern Feasibility Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes feasibility loss and Pareto tradeoffs induced by competing pattern restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty finite set of candidate home–away patterns, let \(k\in\mathbb N\), and let \(C_j\subseteq\mathcal P\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) encode operational restrictions. Joint pattern feasibility holds exactly when \(\mathcal F=\bigcap_{j=1}^{k}C_j\ne\varnothing\). Let \(q\in\mathbb N\) and let \(f_\ell:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R\) be a penalty function for every \(\ell\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). A pattern \(p\in\mathcal F\) is Pareto efficient when there is no \(p'\in\mathcal F\) such that \(f_\ell(p')\le f_\ell(p)\) for every \(\ell\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with strict inequality for at least one such \(\ell\). Thus infeasibility is represented by an empty intersection, while feasible multicriteria tradeoffs are represented by nondominated penalty vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Competing restrictions are jointly feasible exactly when their pattern sets have a nonempty intersection; among feasible patterns, tradeoffs are represented by nondominated penalty vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a nonempty finite pattern set.
\(k,q\in\mathbb N\).
Each restriction is represented by a subset \(C_j\subseteq\mathcal P\), and each penalty function has domain \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\) characterizes joint feasibility, and Pareto-efficient patterns characterize multicriteria compromises.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: set-intersection feasibility and Pareto dominance

children.title: Travel Constraints
children.top_down_role: Covers distance, itinerary, rest-location, or trip-duration restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Travel Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models travel budgets and limits on consecutive away travel for each team.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a finite team set, let the rounds be \(R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(V\) be a venue set. For each \(i\in T\), let \(v_{i,r}\in V\) be team \(i\)'s location after round \(r\), with \(v_{i,0}=v_{i,m+1}=H_i\), and let \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb R_+\) be a travel-cost function. A schedule satisfies team \(i\)'s travel budget \(D_i\ge0\) exactly when \(\sum_{r=0}^{m}d(v_{i,r},v_{i,r+1})\le D_i\). If \(L_i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is the maximum permitted number of consecutive away games, then every interval of \(L_i+1\) consecutive rounds contained in \(R\) must include a home game for team \(i\). The schedule is travel-feasible when these applicable conditions hold for every \(i\in T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Travel feasibility can require every team's route length to respect its budget and every window longer than its permitted away run to contain a home game.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and \(R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) are finite, and the rounds are ordered.
Each scheduled game determines every participating team's round location.
\(d\) is a nonnegative travel-cost function.
For every \(i\in T\), \(D_i\ge0\) and \(L_i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule is travel-feasible when the stated route-budget and consecutive-away conditions hold for every \(i\in T\).

notation.meaning: Location of team i after round r.
Maximum permitted consecutive away games for team i.

children.title: Venue Constraints
children.top_down_role: Covers availability, sharing, capacity, or event-hosting restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Venue Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States availability, capacity, and nonoverlap conditions for assigning games to venues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the games, \(R\) the time slots, and \(V\) the venues. Binary variables \(x_{gvr}\) form a venue-feasible assignment when \(x_{gvr}\le a_{gvr}\) for every \((g,v,r)\), \(\sum_{v\in V,\,r\in R}x_{gvr}=1\) for every \(g\in G\), and \(\sum_{g\in G}x_{gvr}\le c_{vr}\) for every \((v,r)\). Here \(a_{gvr}=1\) means venue \(v\) is eligible and available for game \(g\) in slot \(r\), while \(c_{vr}\) is its simultaneous-game capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every game must receive one eligible venue-slot assignment, and no venue-slot may exceed its available simultaneous-game capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(G\), \(R\), and \(V\) are finite.
\(c_{vr}\) is a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three displayed constraint families characterize venue feasibility under the stated data.

notation.meaning: Indicator that game g uses venue v in slot r.

children.title: Broadcast Constraints
children.top_down_role: Covers media windows, audience priorities, or production requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Broadcast Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models broadcast eligibility, channel capacity, and coverage quotas across time slots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\), \(C\), and \(R\) be finite sets of games, channels, and time slots. Let \(x_{gcr}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that game \(g\in G\) is assigned to channel \(c\in C\) in slot \(r\in R\). Given eligibility values \(e_{gcr}\in\{0,1\}\), capacities \(u_{cr}\in\mathbb Z_+\), and a collection \(\mathcal Q\subseteq 2^{G\times C\times R}\) of coverage sets with bounds \(0\le L_Q\le U_Q\) for every \(Q\in\mathcal Q\), broadcast feasibility requires \(x_{gcr}\le e_{gcr}\) for all \((g,c,r)\in G\times C\times R\), \(\sum_{g\in G}x_{gcr}\le u_{cr}\) for all \((c,r)\in C\times R\), and \(L_Q\le\sum_{(g,c,r)\in Q}x_{gcr}\le U_Q\) for every \(Q\in\mathcal Q\). Each game \(g\) declared to require exactly one broadcast additionally satisfies \(\sum_{c\in C,\,r\in R}x_{gcr}=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A broadcast plan must respect game-channel eligibility, channel-slot capacities, declared coverage quotas, and exact-one requirements for games to which those requirements apply.
assumptions_latex: \(G\), \(C\), and \(R\) are finite.
\(x_{gcr},e_{gcr}\in\{0,1\}\) and \(u_{cr}\in\mathbb Z_+\).
For every \(Q\in\mathcal Q\), \(0\le L_Q\le U_Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A binary assignment is broadcast-feasible exactly when every applicable eligibility, capacity, quota, and exact-one constraint holds.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper coverage quotas for coverage set Q.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: eligibility, capacity, and quota formulation

children.title: Operational Constraint Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Covers incompatible requirements spanning travel, venue use, or broadcast placement.

knowledge_statements.title: Operational Constraint Conflicts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a finite, directly checkable certificate of joint operational infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the set of candidate schedules and let each operational constraint \(j\in J\) define a feasible subset \(F_j\subseteq X\). A set \(K\subseteq J\) is a conflict certificate when \(\bigcap_{j\in K}F_j=\varnothing\). It is irreducible when \(\bigcap_{j\in K\setminus\{k\}}F_j\ne\varnothing\) for every \(k\in K\). For finite \(X\), the certificate is verifiable by confirming that every \(x\in X\) violates at least one constraint in \(K\), together with a feasible witness for every proper deletion in the irreducible case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint conflict is certified by an infeasible subset; it is irreducible when deleting any one member restores feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(J\) are finite.
Constraint satisfaction is decidable for each candidate schedule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) certifies infeasibility precisely when \(\bigcap_{j\in K}F_j=\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: irreducible infeasible subsystem specialized to finite schedules

children.title: Competitive Fairness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Covers balance criteria relating to opponents, venues, timing, or rest.

knowledge_statements.title: Competitive Fairness Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines checkable balance criteria for opponents, venues, rest, and schedule strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a finite team set, let \(K\) be a finite set of declared fairness dimensions, and let \(z_{ik}(x)\in\mathbb R\) denote the exposure of team \(i\in T\) under dimension \(k\in K\) in schedule \(x\). Partition \(K\) into dimensions \(K_{\mathrm{tar}}\) assessed against targets and dimensions \(K_{\mathrm{pair}}\) assessed pairwise. Given targets \(\tau_{ik}\in\mathbb R\), tolerances \(\delta_k\ge0\), and pairwise tolerances \(\Delta_k\ge0\), schedule \(x\) satisfies the declared fairness criteria when \(|z_{ik}(x)-\tau_{ik}|\le\delta_k\) for every \(i\in T\) and \(k\in K_{\mathrm{tar}}\), and \(|z_{ik}(x)-z_{jk}(x)|\le\Delta_k\) for every \(i,j\in T\) and \(k\in K_{\mathrm{pair}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Competitive fairness is evaluated using declared exposure dimensions, each assessed either against team targets or through bounded pairwise differences.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and \(K\) are finite.
The exposure measures, assessment type, and targets are fixed before schedules are compared.
For every applicable \(k\in K\), \(\delta_k\ge0\) and \(\Delta_k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fairness relative to the declared model holds exactly when every selected target-balance and pairwise-balance inequality is satisfied.

notation.meaning: Exposure of team i under fairness dimension k.

review_flags: sports-fairness source required to validate selected dimensions

children.title: Carryover Effect Structure
children.top_down_role: Covers schedule-dependent influence of one opponent on a team's subsequent fixture.

knowledge_statements.title: Carryover Effect Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directed carryover matrix induced by consecutive opponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a finite team set, let the rounds be \(R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(o_i(r)\in T\setminus\{i\}\) be team \(i\)'s opponent in round \(r\). For distinct \(a,b\in T\), define the directed carryover count by \(c_{ab}=\bigl|\{(i,r)\in T\times\{1,\ldots,m-1\}:o_i(r)=a,\ o_i(r+1)=b\}\bigr|\). Thus \(c_{ab}\) counts occasions on which a team plays \(b\) immediately after playing \(a\). The directed carryover matrix is \(C=(c_{ab})_{a,b\in T}\), with \(c_{aa}=0\) by the convention that only transitions between distinct opponents are recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For distinct teams a and b, entry (a,b) counts occasions on which a team faces b immediately after facing a; diagonal transitions are omitted by convention.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is finite and \(R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is linearly ordered.
For every \(i\in T\) and counted round \(r\in R\), the opponent \(o_i(r)\in T\setminus\{i\}\) is defined.
The carryover matrix records only transitions between distinct opponents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=(c_{ab})_{a,b\in T}\) records all directed consecutive-opponent transitions between distinct opponents.

notation.meaning: Opponent of team i in round r.
Directed carryover count from a to b for distinct opponents.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: consecutive-opponent carryover matrix with explicit off-diagonal convention

children.title: Carryover Balance
children.top_down_role: Covers distribution of carryover exposure across teams.

knowledge_statements.title: Carryover Balance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses exact and tolerance-based balance of directed carryover counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(c_{ab})\) be a carryover matrix and let \(P=\{(a,b)\in T^2:a\ne b\}\). Exact carryover balance holds when there is an integer \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \(c_{ab}=\lambda\) for every \((a,b)\in P\). When exact equality is arithmetically impossible or operationally relaxed, \(C\) is \(\Delta\)-balanced when \(\max_{(a,b)\in P}c_{ab}-\min_{(a,b)\in P}c_{ab}\le\Delta\). A quadratic imbalance score is \(Q(C)=\sum_{(a,b)\in P}(c_{ab}-\bar c)^2\), where \(\bar c=|P|^{-1}\sum_{(a,b)\in P}c_{ab}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Carryovers are exactly balanced when all directed counts agree, or approximately balanced when their range or squared deviation is small.
assumptions_latex: All carryover counts are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact balance is equivalent to constant off-diagonal carryover counts; approximate balance is quantified by \(\Delta\) or \(Q(C)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality, range, and variance-based balance criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact, range-based, and quadratic balance notions are internally coherent and fit the leaf. A carryover-balance source with a specific locator is required to establish that these are accepted domain criteria.

children.title: Fairness–Carryover Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Covers schedules where one balance criterion worsens another.

knowledge_statements.title: Fairness–Carryover Conflicts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes incompatibility and Pareto compromise between fairness and carryover objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be the feasible schedules, \(f:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) a competitive-unfairness score, and \(c:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R\) a carryover-imbalance score, both minimized. The two criteria have a strict optimality conflict exactly when \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal F}f(x)\cap\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal F}c(x)=\varnothing\). A schedule \(x\in\mathcal F\) is a valid compromise when no \(y\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(f(y)\le f(x)\) and \(c(y)\le c(x)\), with at least one strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fairness and carryover conflict when no schedule optimizes both; legitimate compromises are schedules not dominated on both scores.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is finite and nonempty.
Both scores are fixed and real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disjoint argmin sets characterize strict conflict, while nondominance characterizes Pareto compromises.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: argmin incompatibility and Pareto dominance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For finite nonempty feasibility sets, disjoint argmin sets correctly express failure of simultaneous optimality, and the nondominance condition correctly expresses Pareto compromise. No domain-specific fairness–carryover source is supplied.

children.title: Conflict-Graph Representations
children.top_down_role: Covers graph structures encoding mutually incompatible timetable events.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Graph Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents pairwise same-slot exclusions as graph adjacency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be timetable events and form the conflict graph \(G=(E,A)\), where \(\{e,f\}\in A\) exactly when distinct events \(e\) and \(f\) may not occupy the same time slot. For a slot set \(S\), an assignment \(t:E\to S\) satisfies every represented pairwise conflict exactly when \(t(e)\ne t(f)\) for all \(\{e,f\}\in A\); equivalently, \(t\) is a proper \(|S|\)-coloring of \(G\). This equivalence covers only pairwise noncoincidence restrictions; capacities, preferences, and temporal-spacing rules require additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Events are vertices and same-slot conflicts are edges; feasible slot assignments are precisely proper colorings for the represented pairwise restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(S\) are finite.
Every represented restriction is a pairwise prohibition against sharing a slot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairwise conflict-feasible assignments \(t:E\to S\) are exactly the proper colorings of \(G\) using colors from \(S\).

notation.meaning: Available time slots, interpreted as colors.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical graph-coloring representation of pairwise timetabling conflicts
provided graph-theory locators do not establish the timetabling correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, the coloring correspondence is precise, and its limitation to pairwise noncoincidence constraints is stated correctly. The available generic graph-theory locators do not support the timetabling correspondence, and the record cites none of them directly.

children.title: Graph-Coloring Representations
children.top_down_role: Covers color-based encodings of admissible event placements.

assumptions_latex: The timetable has a finite event set \(E\), period set \(P\), and an undirected conflict graph \(G=(E,F)\).
Every event occupies exactly one period, and the only feasibility restrictions are simultaneous-period conflicts represented by \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible timetables are exactly the proper \(|P|\)-colorings of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Conflict graph whose vertices are events

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation for pure event-conflict timetabling with unit-duration events and interchangeable periods.

source_refs.locator: 0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph-coloring representation associates each event \(e\in E\) with a color \(c(e)\in P\). It is proper precisely when \[\forall\{e,f\}\in F,\qquad c(e)\ne c(f).\] Under the stated assumptions, the map sending a timetable to its period assignment \(c:E\to P\) is a bijection between feasible timetables and proper colorings of \(G\) using colors from \(P\). Consequently, a feasible timetable exists if and only if \(\chi(G)\le |P|\), where \(\chi(G)\) is the chromatic number.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign periods as colors to event vertices. A timetable is feasible exactly when adjacent conflicting events receive different colors; existence is equivalent to the chromatic number not exceeding the number of periods.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Coloring Representations

children.title: Conflict-to-Color Translation
children.top_down_role: Covers mappings from timetable conflicts to coloring decisions.

assumptions_latex: The finite event set is \(E\), the available periods are \(P\), and \(F\subseteq\{\{e,f\}:e,f\in E,\ e\ne f\}\) lists all and only pairwise simultaneous-period prohibitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conflict predicates translate exactly into proper-coloring inequalities \(c(e)\ne c(f)\).

notation.meaning: Binary conflict indicator for distinct events
Period or color assigned to event e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of binary simultaneous-period conflicts, excluding capacities, preferences, and higher-arity restrictions.

source_refs.locator: 0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(q_{ef}=1\) exactly when distinct events \(e,f\in E\) may not occupy the same period, and set \(F=\{\{e,f\}:q_{ef}=1\}\). For a period assignment \(c:E\to P\), each timetable predicate \[q_{ef}=1\ \Longrightarrow\ c(e)\ne c(f)\] is identical to the proper-coloring constraint on edge \(\{e,f\}\in F\). Conversely, every edge inequality yields the corresponding binary conflict prohibition. Thus the translation preserves and reflects feasibility when all restrictions have this pairwise form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Create one edge for each pair forbidden from meeting simultaneously, then interpret periods as colors. The resulting edge inequalities are equivalent to the original binary conflict restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-to-Color Translation

children.title: Graph Representation Limits
children.top_down_role: Covers timetable restrictions not captured cleanly by basic graph structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Representation Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of simple conflict graphs without auxiliary vertices, hyperedges, labels, or side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) contain at least two periods and impose on events \(a,b,c\) only the restriction that they may not all share one period: \[\neg\bigl(s(a)=s(b)=s(c)\bigr).\] Every pair among \(a,b,c\) is nevertheless allowed to share a period. No simple conflict graph on these three event vertices represents exactly this feasible set: an edge would incorrectly forbid an allowed pairwise coincidence, while the edgeless graph would allow all three events to coincide. Thus timetable restrictions that are not expressible as conjunctions of binary same-period prohibitions require additional modeling structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rule forbidding three events from all coinciding, while allowing every pair to coincide, cannot be represented exactly by ordinary conflict edges alone; non-pairwise restrictions require additional modeling structure.
assumptions_latex: A simple graph representation uses one vertex per event and permits only binary same-period prohibitions expressed by edge inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Simple graph coloring cannot represent every higher-arity timetable restriction without auxiliary modeling structure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a simple graph encodes only binary edge predicates

assumptions_latex: The sets of events \(E\), periods \(P\), and rooms \(R\) are finite.
Each event requires exactly one compatible period-room pair, and each room hosts at most one event per period.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integral solutions of the displayed constraints are exactly feasible event-period-room assignments under the encoded compatibility and conflict rules.

notation.meaning: One iff event e is assigned to period p and room r

review_flags: locator_supports_assignment reduction but not the full timetabling formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary assignment model for unit-duration events, rooms, periods, compatibility, and pairwise conflicts.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.4 Reduction to an Assignment Problem p. 154
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((e,p,r)\in A\), let \(x_{epr}\in\{0,1\}\). A basic assignment model is \[\sum_{(p,r):(e,p,r)\in A}x_{epr}=1\quad(e\in E),\qquad \sum_{e:(e,p,r)\in A}x_{epr}\le 1\quad(p\in P,r\in R),\] together with \[\sum_{r:(e,p,r)\in A}x_{epr}+\sum_{r:(f,p,r)\in A}x_{fpr}\le 1\quad(\{e,f\}\in F,p\in P).\] The first constraints assign every event, the second prevent room collisions, and the third prevent conflicting events from sharing a period.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables select one compatible period-room pair per event; room-capacity and conflict inequalities exclude simultaneous use of a room or period by incompatible events.

children.title: Timetable Pattern Representations
children.top_down_role: Covers columns representing complete or partial feasible scheduling patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Timetable Pattern Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-oriented representation of complete locally feasible placements and their event-resource incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A timetable pattern \(p\in\mathcal P\) is a complete locally feasible placement of a prescribed event or event block. It is represented by incidence coefficients \(a_{ep}\in\{0,1\}\) for \(e\in E\), resource usages \(b_{up}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) for \(u\in U\), and optionally a cost \(c_p\in\mathbb R\). Local restrictions used to generate \(p\) are satisfied inside the pattern; compatibility between selected patterns is enforced by master constraints on the aggregate quantities \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}a_{ep}y_p\) and \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b_{up}y_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timetable pattern is a complete locally feasible placement represented by the events it covers, the resources it consumes, and, when applicable, its cost.
assumptions_latex: The event set \(E\), resource set \(U\), and admissible pattern family \(\mathcal P\) are finite.
Each pattern specifies a complete locally feasible placement for a designated event or event block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A timetable pattern is represented by its event and resource incidence data together with an optional local cost.

notation.meaning: Finite family of admissible timetable patterns
One iff pattern p covers event e
Amount of resource u consumed by pattern p

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: column patterns encode complete local schedules by incidence vectors

children.title: Set-Partitioning Representations
children.top_down_role: Covers exact-selection structures for covering timetable entities once.

assumptions_latex: The finite family \(\mathcal P\) contains admissible timetable patterns and every event \(e\in E\) must be covered exactly once.
Pattern costs \(c_p\in\mathbb R\) and incidence coefficients \(a_{ep}\in\{0,1\}\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer program selects a minimum-cost exact partition of the events by admissible patterns.

notation.meaning: One iff pattern p is selected

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-cover master formulation over a finite family of admissible timetable patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set-partitioning representation is \[\min\ \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}c_p y_p\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}a_{ep}y_p=1\quad(e\in E),\qquad y_p\in\{0,1\}\quad(p\in\mathcal P).\] Additional resource rows may impose \(\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b_{up}y_p\le B_u\) for each resource-period index \(u\). The equality rows require selected patterns to cover each event exactly once; hence their event sets form a partition whenever every selected pattern is internally feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select binary timetable patterns so that every event is covered exactly once, while optional resource rows limit aggregate usage; minimizing pattern costs yields an exact-cover master problem.

children.title: Pattern–Partitioning Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Pattern–Partitioning Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear projection connecting selected timetable columns to compact event-period-room variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pattern-partitioning interface is the linear map \[x_{epr}=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal P}d_{epr,\rho}y_{\rho}\qquad(e\in E,\ p\in P,\ r\in R),\] where \(d_{epr,\rho}=1\) exactly when pattern \(\rho\) assigns event \(e\) to period \(p\) and room \(r\). A binary pattern selection satisfying exact event coverage induces a binary compact assignment whenever selected patterns are mutually compatible. Conversely, a compact assignment belongs to the represented pattern model precisely when it can be decomposed into admissible patterns whose incidence vectors sum to that assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact assignment variables are obtained by summing the assignment incidences of selected patterns. Exact equivalence holds when every represented assignment decomposes into mutually compatible admissible patterns.
assumptions_latex: The event set \(E\), period set \(P\), room set \(R\), and admissible pattern family \(\mathcal P\) are finite.
Each pattern \(\rho\in\mathcal P\) specifies binary assignment incidences \(d_{epr,\rho}\) and is locally feasible.
Selected patterns satisfy exact event coverage and all required shared-resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregating selected pattern incidences produces an event-period-room assignment, and every assignment represented by the pattern model admits such a pattern selection.

notation.meaning: Assignment incidence for event e, period p, and room r within pattern rho

children.title: Set-Covering Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Covers relaxed selection structures permitting excess coverage.

assumptions_latex: The set-partitioning model has nonnegative pattern variables and equality rows \(Ay=\mathbf 1\).
The objective is minimization with the same cost vector in the original and relaxed models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-covering relaxation obtained by weakening exact event coverage while retaining other master constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) contain the nonnegativity, integrality if retained, and shared-resource restrictions of a set-partitioning model. Define \[z_{\mathrm{SP}}=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}y:Ay=\mathbf 1,\ y\in Y\},\qquad z_{\mathrm{SC}}=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}y:Ay\ge\mathbf 1,\ y\in Y\}.\] Since every vector feasible for the first problem is feasible for the second, \(z_{\mathrm{SC}}\le z_{\mathrm{SP}}\) whenever both optima are well defined. Covering solutions may select overlapping patterns and therefore need not decode to feasible exact timetables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakening exact event coverage to at-least-once coverage enlarges the feasible set and gives a minimization lower bound, but overlapping selected patterns may not form a timetable.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A timetabling constraint network is a triple \((X,D,C)\), where each variable \(x\in X\) has a finite domain \(D_x\), and each constraint \(c\in C\) consists of an ordered scope \(S_c=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) and a relation \(R_c\subseteq D_{x_1}\times\cdots\times D_{x_k}\). A complete assignment \(s\in\prod_{x\in X}D_x\) is a solution exactly when \[(s(x_1),\ldots,s(x_k))\in R_c\qquad\text{for every }c\in C.\] Variables may encode periods, rooms, resources, or other timetable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timetabling constraint network consists of finite-domain decision variables and scoped relations; its solutions are precisely the complete assignments belonging to every constraint relation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relational semantics of global constraints spanning a nonfixed number of timetable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A global timetabling constraint \(G\) on scope \(S=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) denotes a relation \[R_G\subseteq D_{x_1}\times\cdots\times D_{x_k},\] where the arity \(k\) is part of the instance rather than fixed by the constraint type. An assignment \(s\) satisfies \(G\) exactly when \(s|_S\in R_G\). Examples of admissible semantics include requiring all scoped events to occupy distinct periods or bounding, for every period, the total resource consumption of events assigned there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global timetabling constraint is one relation over an instance-sized scope, such as distinct-period or aggregate resource-capacity requirements across many events.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Timetabling Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relational semantics and instance-sized scope correctly characterize a global constraint, and the definition kind fits. An authoritative constraint-programming citation with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Network-Level Propagation
children.top_down_role: Covers information transfer across linked timetable constraints.

assumptions_latex: The constraint network is finite-domain, and each propagator is contracting, monotone, and sound on the lattice of domain tuples.
Propagators are scheduled fairly until none changes any domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Propagation terminates at a common fixed point preserving all solutions of the initial network.

notation.meaning: Sound contracting propagator for constraint c

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fair iteration of monotone contracting propagators on finite domains reaches a solution-preserving fixed point
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fair fixed-point propagation over finite timetable domains, independent of a particular queue policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a network \((X,D,C)\) and propagators \((\pi_c)_{c\in C}\). Initialize the current domains to \(D^{(0)}=D\) and place every constraint in a work queue. Repeatedly remove \(c\), set \(D^{(t+1)}=\pi_c(D^{(t)})\), and requeue constraints whose scopes meet any reduced domain. Stop with failure if some domain is empty; otherwise stop when the queue is empty and output \(D^*\). Finiteness and contraction imply termination, soundness preserves every initial solution, and fair scheduling gives \[\pi_c(D^*)=D^*\qquad(c\in C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly apply sound constraint propagators and reschedule affected constraints until domains stop shrinking. Finite domains guarantee termination, and the fixed point preserves every original solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Network-Level Propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The work-queue algorithm and its finite fixed-point conclusion are coherent under the stated monotonicity, contraction, soundness, and fairness assumptions. The nontrivial termination and common-fixed-point claims require an inspectable constraint-propagation source.

children.top_down_role: Covers replacement of aggregate constraints by smaller linked structures.

eq\varnothing\).
A proposed decomposition uses auxiliary variables \(Z\) with finite domains and component relations \((R_i)_{i\in I}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition is exact precisely when projecting the conjunction of component relations onto \(X\) yields \(R_G\).

Relation of the undecomposed global constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relational decomposition; propagation equivalence is not implied by solution-set equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The component constraints form an exact decomposition of \(R_G\) when, for every assignment \(s_X\in\prod_{x\in X}D_x\), \[s_X\in R_G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists s_Z\in\prod_{z\in Z}D_z\ \ \forall i\in I,\ (s_X,s_Z)|_{S_i}\in R_i.\] Equivalently, \(R_G\) is the projection onto \(X\) of the natural join of the component relations. This equality preserves complete solutions, but enforcing a chosen local consistency separately on the components may remove fewer unsupported values than propagating the undecomposed global constraint.

children.title: Hard Preference Models
children.top_down_role: Covers preferences treated as mandatory timetable requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard Preference Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models preferences whose violation makes a timetable inadmissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the set of candidate timetables and let \(H=\{h_1,\ldots,h_m\}\) be Boolean preference predicates \(h_i:X\to\{0,1\}\), where value \(1\) denotes satisfaction. The associated hard-preference feasible set is \[F_H=\{x\in X:h_i(x)=1\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,m\}.\] A hard-preference model declares exactly the members of \(F_H\) admissible; no objective improvement can compensate for violation of any \(h_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timetable is admissible exactly when it satisfies every hard preference; violations cannot be offset by improvements elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a specified set of candidate timetables.
Each \(h_i\) is a Boolean satisfaction predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is admissible}\iff x\in F_H\iff \bigwedge_{i=1}^m h_i(x)=1\).
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports hard-preference timetabling semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the hard-preference leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator supports the asserted timetabling semantics.

children.title: Soft Preference Models
children.top_down_role: Covers preferences evaluated through graded satisfaction or penalty.

knowledge_statements.title: Soft Preference Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models compensable preference violations through a finite penalty objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the set of timetables satisfying all hard constraints. For soft preferences indexed by \(J\), let \(v_j:F\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) measure violation and let \(w_j\ge 0\) be its weight. A weighted soft-preference model ranks timetables by \[P(x)=\sum_{j\in J}w_jv_j(x),\] and seeks an element of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}P(x)\). A positive violation affects quality but does not by itself remove \(x\) from \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft preferences assign weighted penalties to violations and rank hard-feasible timetables by total penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the hard-feasible timetable set.
\(J\) is finite and \(v_j(x),w_j\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\sum_{j\in J}w_jv_j(x)\).

notation.meaning: violation measure for soft preference j

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports weighted soft-preference timetabling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-penalty definition is mathematically coherent and fits the soft-preference leaf, but no cited source supports this particular timetabling formulation.

children.title: Hierarchical Preference Models
children.top_down_role: Covers preferences organized into ordered priority levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Preference Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses lexicographic priority levels rather than compensatory weights across levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the hard-feasible timetable set and let \(P_1,\ldots,P_L:F\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be penalty functions ordered from highest to lowest priority. A hierarchical preference model minimizes the vector \((P_1(x),\ldots,P_L(x))\) lexicographically: \(x^*\in F\) is optimal precisely when no \(y\in F\) and index \(k\) satisfy \(P_i(y)=P_i(x^*)\) for every \(i<k\) and \(P_k(y)<P_k(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hierarchical model minimizes penalties lexicographically, so lower-priority gains never compensate for a higher-priority loss.
assumptions_latex: \(F\ne\varnothing\).
The priority levels \(1,,,L\) are totally ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}^{\mathrm{lex}}(P_1(x),\ldots,P_L(x))\).
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports lexicographic timetabling preferences.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lexicographic definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the assumption stating the levels as \(1,,,L\) is malformed, and no source supports the selected hierarchical model. Source confirmation is needed before choosing the corrected mathematical version.

children.title: Preference Priority Transitions
children.top_down_role: Covers movement between mandatory, weighted, or lexicographic treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Preference Priority Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes promotion or demotion between hard, lexicographic, and weighted preference levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent preference \(j\) by a level \(\ell_j\in\{0,1,\ldots,L\}\), where \(0\) denotes hard status and positive values denote lexicographic penalty levels. A priority transition is a map \(T\) producing \(\ell'_j=T(j,\ell_j)\). The revised model has feasible set \[F'=\{x\in X:v_j(x)=0\text{ for every }j\text{ with }\ell'_j=0\}\] and, on \(F'\), lexicographically minimizes \(P'_k(x)=\sum_{j:\ell'_j=k}w_jv_j(x)\) for \(k=1,\ldots,L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transition reassigns preferences among hard and ordered soft levels, thereby changing feasibility and the lexicographic objective.
assumptions_latex: \(v_j:X\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) and \(w_j\ge0\).
Every revised level \(\ell'_j\) lies in \(\{0,1,\ldots,L\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) determines both \(F'\) and the ordered penalty vector \((P'_1,\ldots,P'_L)\).

notation.meaning: current priority level of preference j

review_flags: This precise transition formalism requires a domain-specific source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits a priority-transition leaf, but the map-based transition system is a bespoke formalism rather than an established definition supported by evidence. A domain-specific source is required to validate its levels, feasibility update, and aggregation rule.

children.title: Coloring-Based Timetabling Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Covers timetable construction guided by graph-coloring structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring-Based Timetabling Heuristics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy assignment on a conflict graph with timetable periods represented as colors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a conflict graph \(G=(V,E)\), an ordered period set \(C=(c_1,\ldots,c_q)\), and an event ordering \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Initialize all vertices uncolored. For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), assign \(v_i\) the first period \(c\in C\) not used by any colored neighbor; if none exists, report failure. If every vertex is assigned, output \(\phi:V\to C\). Then \(\phi(u)\ne\phi(v)\) for every conflict \(uv\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order events and greedily assign each the first period unused by its already scheduled conflicting neighbors.
assumptions_latex: Edges encode pairs of events that cannot share a period.
\(C\) is a finite ordered set of available periods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\) is a proper \(C\)-coloring whenever the algorithm returns an assignment.
review_flags: No supplied locator covers greedy graph-coloring timetabling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is correct and the returned assignment is properly characterized, but no specific source locator supports the greedy coloring heuristic or its interpretation as a timetabling method.

children.title: Saturation-Based Timetabling Heuristics
children.top_down_role: Covers event selection guided by the diversity of unavailable placements.

knowledge_statements.title: Saturation-Based Timetabling Heuristics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DSATUR-style event selection adapted to a fixed set of timetable periods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(G=(V,E)\) and ordered periods \(C\). Initialize all vertices uncolored. While an uncolored vertex remains, select one maximizing \(s(v)=|\{\phi(u):u\in N(v),\ u\text{ colored}\}|\), breaking ties by uncolored degree and then a fixed vertex order. Assign it the first period in \(C\) absent from its colored neighbors; report failure if none exists. Output \(\phi\) after all vertices are colored.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly schedule the event seeing the most distinct neighboring periods, then give it the first available period.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple conflict graph.
\(C\) is a finite ordered period set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the procedure terminates without failure, \(\phi(u)\ne\phi(v)\) for every \(uv\in E\).
review_flags: No supplied locator covers DSATUR or its timetabling adaptation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf and the procedure is internally coherent, but neither the DSATUR rule nor its fixed-period timetabling adaptation has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Saturation-Guided Coloring
children.top_down_role: Covers coloring heuristics whose selection priorities use saturation information.

knowledge_statements.title: Saturation-Guided Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The selection rule underlying saturation-driven constructive coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partial proper coloring \(\phi:U\to C\) with \(U\subsetneq V\), define the saturation degree of each uncolored vertex by \[s_\phi(v)=|\{\phi(u):u\in N(v)\cap U\}|.\] Saturation-guided coloring selects a vertex from \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in V\setminus U}s_\phi(v)\), commonly resolving ties by degree, and assigns an admissible color. Thus selection prioritizes the event whose colored neighborhood currently excludes the largest number of distinct periods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose next an uncolored event adjacent to the greatest number of distinct periods already in use.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
\(\phi:U\to C\) is a partial proper coloring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in V\setminus U}s_\phi(v)\).

notation.meaning: saturation degree under the partial coloring

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the saturation-degree selection principle.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind correctly captures the saturation-guided selection rule, but the rule and customary tie-breaking claim lack a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Coloring Heuristic Limits
children.top_down_role: Covers timetable features poorly represented by coloring priorities.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Heuristic Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that order-dependent greedy coloring can use arbitrarily more periods than necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), let \(G_n\) have vertices \(a_1,,,a_n,b_1,,,b_n\) and edges \(a_ib_j\) exactly when \(i\ne j\). The graph is bipartite, hence \(\chi(G_n)=2\). Under the greedy order \(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots,a_n,b_n\), first-fit coloring assigns both \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) color \(i\). It therefore uses \(n\) colors, demonstrating an unbounded approximation ratio for unrestricted event ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crown graphs need only two periods, yet a bad greedy event order uses arbitrarily many periods.
assumptions_latex: First-fit chooses the least positive color absent from colored neighbors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G_n)=2\) while first-fit uses \(n\) colors in the displayed order.

notation.meaning: chromatic number of the conflict graph

review_flags: The concrete crown-graph construction requires a graph-coloring source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind is correct and the crown-graph claim is mathematically plausible, but the vertex list contains malformed notation \(a_1,,,a_n,b_1,,,b_n\), and no source supports the construction. Source confirmation is needed before issuing a corrected replacement.

children.title: Integer-Programming Timetabling
children.top_down_role: Covers discrete optimization formulations for timetable decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Programming Timetabling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A binary assignment formulation for events, periods, and pairwise conflicts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For events \(V\), periods \(C\), and conflicts \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v\}\), introduce \(x_{vc}\in\{0,1\}\). A basic timetabling formulation is \[\sum_{c\in C}x_{vc}=1\quad(v\in V),\qquad x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le1\quad(\{u,v\}\in E, c\in C).\] With assignment costs \(p_{vc}\), minimize \(\sum_{v\in V}\sum_{c\in C}p_{vc}x_{vc}\). Feasible binary solutions correspond exactly to conflict-free assignments of every event to one period.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables assign every event to one period, while conflict inequalities forbid incompatible events from sharing periods.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(C\) are finite.
\(E\) contains all modeled pairwise conflicts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible}\iff x\text{ encodes a conflict-free complete timetable}\).

notation.meaning: one iff event v uses period c
cost of assigning v to c

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Integer Programming p. 103

review_flags: The locator supports integer programming generally; the timetabling specialization needs confirmation.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Integer Programming p. 103
