children.title: Restricted-Master Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination of generated schedule columns within exact enumeration.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Master Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination invariant between restricted-master optimization and exact scheduling pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a restricted pattern set \(R\subseteq\mathcal P\). At iteration \(t\), solve the restricted master to primal-dual optimality, obtaining \((\lambda^t,\pi^t)\). Pass \(\pi^t\) to the pricing oracle and obtain a minimum-reduced-cost pattern \(p^t\). If \(c_{p^t}-a_{p^t}^{\mathsf T}\pi^t<0\), set \(R\leftarrow R\cup\{p^t\}\) and reoptimize; otherwise stop. The master must not claim full-relaxation optimality before receiving the nonnegative exact-pricing certificate, and pricing must use dual values from the current optimized restricted master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted-master coordination alternates optimal master solves with pricing from current duals and stops only after exact pricing finds no negative reduced-cost pattern.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master remains feasible.
Each restricted master is solved to primal-dual optimality.
Pricing returns a global reduced-cost minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stopping with \(c_{p^t}-a_{p^t}^{\mathsf T}\pi^t\ge0\) certifies full-master LP optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Degeneracy Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily many equivalent priced columns can produce no objective-bound improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take any master column with coefficient vector \(a\) and cost \(c\), and replace it by \(M\) distinct pattern labels having identical pair \((a,c)\). At a dual vector \(\pi\) satisfying \(c-a^{\mathsf T}\pi=0\), all \(M\) columns have zero reduced cost. Adding any number of them leaves the restricted-master feasible region projected onto aggregate column weight unchanged and cannot improve its optimal objective value. Since \(M\) is arbitrary, the number of generated or retained columns cannot be bounded by observed bound improvement alone; duplicate control or stabilization may be required for computational progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily many duplicate schedule patterns can all have zero reduced cost, increasing the column pool without changing the master bound.
assumptions_latex: The master permits distinct pattern labels with identical coefficients and costs.
\(c-a^{\mathsf T}\pi=0\) at the current dual vector.
Duplicate variables have identical sign restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Up to \(M\) columns may be added with zero master-objective improvement, for arbitrary \(M\).

children.title: Scheduling Dynamic Programming

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dynamic programming on a finite acyclic scheduling state-transition graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal S,E)\) be a finite acyclic state-transition graph with initial state \(s_0\), terminal states \(T\), feasible actions \(A(s)\), transition \(f(s,a)\), and incremental cost \(g(s,a)\). Process states in reverse topological order using \(V(t)=0\) for \(t\in T\) and \[V(s)=\min_{a\in A(s)}\{g(s,a)+V(f(s,a))\}.\] Store a minimizing action at every reachable nonterminal state. Starting from \(s_0\), follow stored actions until a terminal state is reached. If states retain all information affecting future feasibility and cost, the resulting schedule has minimum total cost among all represented schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact scheduling dynamic program applies Bellman recursion on an acyclic sufficient state graph and reconstructs an optimal schedule from stored minimizing actions.
assumptions_latex: The state-transition graph is finite and acyclic.
Each state contains all information determining future feasibility and incremental costs.
Every represented complete schedule corresponds to an initial-to-terminal path and conversely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstructed path has cost \(V(s_0)\), equal to the minimum represented schedule cost.

notation.meaning: optimal remaining cost from state s

children.title: Scheduling State-Space Relaxation

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling State-Space Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a cost-preserving state aggregation that yields a valid lower bound for minimization scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an exact scheduling dynamic program be an acyclic state graph \(G=(V,A)\) with initial state \(s\), terminal set \(T\), and arc costs \(c:A\to\mathbb{R}\). A state-space relaxation is a surjection \(\phi:V\to\bar V\) preserving stages, with every arc \((u,v)\in A\) inducing \((\phi(u),\phi(v))\in\bar A\). Assign each relaxed arc the minimum cost of its inducing arcs and set \(\bar T\supseteq\phi(T)\). Every exact schedule path then maps to a relaxed path, so for minimization \(\bar z\le z^*\), where \(\bar z\) and \(z^*\) are the relaxed and exact shortest-path values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merging same-stage dynamic-programming states while retaining all induced transitions creates a relaxed scheduling problem whose minimization value is a lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and acyclic.
Every feasible schedule corresponds to an \(s\)-to-\(T\) path.
The objective is additive over path arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar z\le z^*\).

children.title: Scheduling State Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling State Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes a sufficient Markov state for finite deterministic scheduling dynamic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partial schedule history \(h\), let \(\sigma(h)\in\Sigma\) record the information retained by the dynamic program. The representation is sufficient when \(\sigma(h)=\sigma(h')\) implies that the feasible next-decision sets coincide and, for every common decision \(a\), both the incremental cost and successor state coincide: \(A(h)=A(h')\), \(g(h,a)=g(h',a)\), and \(\sigma(ha)=\sigma(h'a)\). Consequently, the optimal residual value depends only on the state: \(J(h)=V(\sigma(h))\). Typical coordinates include the scheduled-job set, resource availability times, and other constraint-relevant summaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduling state is sufficient when histories sharing it have identical feasible decisions, transition costs, and successor states; optimal continuation value then depends only on that state.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling instance has a finite decision horizon.
Costs decompose into decision-stage increments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(h)=\sigma(h')\Longrightarrow J(h)=J(h')\).

children.title: Scheduling Dominance Structures
children.top_down_role: State comparison structures supporting exact or relaxed pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Dominance Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a safe same-stage dominance predicate for pruning scheduling dynamic-programming states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) and \(v\) be states at the same decision stage, with accumulated costs \(C(u)\) and \(C(v)\). Let \(\mathcal{Y}(x)\) be the feasible completions from state \(x\), and let \(R(x,y)\) be the residual cost of completion \(y\). State \(u\) dominates \(v\) if for every \(y\in\mathcal{Y}(v)\) there exists \(y'\in\mathcal{Y}(u)\) satisfying \(C(u)+R(u,y')\le C(v)+R(v,y)\). Under minimization, deleting \(v\) cannot remove every optimal schedule; dominance is transitive whenever this completion-based predicate is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One same-stage state dominates another when every completion of the latter has a no-worse counterpart from the former, making the dominated state safely removable.
assumptions_latex: Both states belong to the same minimization instance and decision stage.
All compared completions produce feasible complete schedules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\succeq v\Longrightarrow v\) may be pruned without increasing the optimal value.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the dominance leaf, but the pruning and transitivity claims lack an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: State Explosion Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: State Explosion Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies the exponential size of subset-indexed scheduling dynamic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a subset dynamic program for \(n\) distinct jobs whose state includes the completed-job set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If every subset is reachable, the representation contains \(2^n\) subset states. If each state tests every unscheduled job as a possible next decision, the total number of tested extensions is \(\sum_{S}(n-|S|)=n2^{n-1}\). Thus direct tabulation requires \(\Theta(2^n)\) state storage and \(\Theta(n2^n)\) transition evaluations, before accounting for any additional resource-time coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reachable subset state for every job subset forces exponential storage; testing every possible next job also requires exponentially many transition evaluations.
assumptions_latex: States distinguish completed-job subsets.
All \(2^n\) subsets are reachable.
A transition evaluation has unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{space}=\Theta(2^n)\) and \(\text{transition evaluations}=\Theta(n2^n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Schedule Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A deterministic priority-based serial schedule-generation scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite job set \(J\), scheduling constraints, and a deterministic priority score \(p(j,S)\) for each currently eligible job. Initialize the partial schedule \(S_0=\varnothing\). At iteration \(k\), form the eligible set \(E_k\) of unscheduled jobs that can be appended or inserted feasibly by the prescribed decoder. Choose \(j_k\in\arg\min_{j\in E_k}p(j,S_k)\), breaking ties deterministically, and place \(j_k\) at its earliest decoder-feasible position to obtain \(S_{k+1}\). Stop after \(|J|\) placements and output \(S_{|J|}\); report failure if \(E_k=\varnothing\) before completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly select the highest-priority eligible job, place it at the decoder’s earliest feasible position, and stop when every job is scheduled or construction fails.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
The decoder can test and perform a feasible placement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a complete feasible schedule when every iteration has \(E_k\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonpreemptive scheduling in preemptive completion order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-machine scheduling with release dates, using an optimal preemptive SRPT schedule to determine the nonpreemptive job order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute an optimal preemptive schedule using SRPT and index the jobs so that \(C_1^P\leq C_2^P\leq\cdots\leq C_n^P\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find an optimal preemptive SRPT schedule, order jobs by their completion times in that schedule, and then run them nonpreemptively in that order. Each job starts as soon as both its release date and completion of the preceding job permit.

Preemption is permitted only in the reference schedule
\(C_1^P\leq\cdots\leq C_n^P\) is the reference schedule's completion order
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_1^N=r_1+p_1,\qquad C_j^N=\max\{C_{j-1}^N,r_j\}+p_j\quad(j=2,\ldots,n)

directory_assessment.rationale: Greedy Schedule Generation is a broader but legitimate existing home for this constructive sequencing rule; the statement records the precise scheduling specialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Beam Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Width-limited breadth-first search over partial schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a root partial schedule \(s_0\), beam width \(B\ge1\), a finite successor operator \(\Gamma\), and an evaluation function \(f\). Set \(L_0=\{s_0\}\). At depth \(k\), generate \(C_{k+1}=\bigcup_{s\in L_k}\Gamma(s)\), discard infeasible duplicates, and retain in \(L_{k+1}\) the at most \(B\) candidates having smallest \(f\)-values, using a fixed tie rule. Stop when a prescribed depth or resource limit is reached, or when no candidates remain. Output the best complete schedule encountered; if none exists, report failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Beam search expands all retained partial schedules at each depth but keeps only the best fixed number according to an evaluation function.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling construction tree has finite depth and finite branching.
\(B\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|L_k|\le B\) at every depth \(k\).

notation.meaning: retained partial schedules at depth k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits beam search and the width invariant is correct by construction, but the candidate supplies no authoritative citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Filtered Beam Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Levelwise filtered beam search for constructive scheduling trees, including filter and beam widths and the loss of exact-search guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each level \(k\) of a constructive scheduling tree, filtered beam search applies a crude evaluation to the generated nodes, selects up to the filter width \(F\) for more thorough evaluation, and then selects up to the beam width \(B\le F\) for further branching; rejected nodes are discarded permanently. A thorough evaluation may construct a feasible completion using a dispatching rule. For a minimization problem, its objective value is an upper bound on the minimum objective attainable by completions descending from that node. Because potentially good nodes may be discarded, the procedure does not in general certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each level of a constructive scheduling tree, filtered beam search cheaply evaluates the generated nodes, selects no more than the filter width for thorough evaluation, and branches from no more than the beam width, which cannot exceed the filter width. Rejected nodes are permanently discarded. Thorough evaluation may use a dispatching rule to construct a feasible completion; in a minimization problem, its value is an upper bound on the best completion descending from that node. Since potentially good nodes can be discarded, filtered beam search does not generally certify global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \text{The search proceeds levelwise over partial schedules.}
F,B\in\mathbb{N},\qquad B\le F.
\text{For the upper-bound interpretation, the objective is minimized and the thorough evaluation produces a feasible completion.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At each level, at most }F\text{ nodes receive thorough evaluation and at most }B\text{ are expanded; discarded nodes are not reconsidered, and global optimality is not guaranteed in general.}

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Multistart Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent repeated randomized construction with incumbent retention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a scheduling instance, restart count \(R\ge1\), and a randomized constructor \(C(\xi)\) driven by seed \(\xi\). Initialize the incumbent value to \(+\infty\). For \(r=1,\ldots,R\), draw an independent seed \(\xi_r\), construct a candidate \(S_r=C(\xi_r)\), discard it if infeasible, and otherwise replace the incumbent whenever \(F(S_r)\) is smaller. Output the best feasible candidate found, or report failure if none was produced. If a single run produces a schedule of value at most \(q\) with probability \(p_q\), independence gives success probability \(1-(1-p_q)^R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a randomized schedule constructor independently several times and retain the best feasible result; independent restarts amplify the probability of reaching a target quality.
assumptions_latex: Restart seeds are independent.
Each constructor run terminates.
The objective \(F\) is minimized.

notation.meaning: single-run probability of attaining value at most q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the probability equality requires identically distributed independent runs and a definition covering infeasible outcomes; independence of seeds alone is insufficient. No source is supplied to resolve the intended formulation.

children.title: Sequence Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Moves altering job or operation order within schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines local moves that alter processing order while holding assignment fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a schedule as \(x=(a,\pi,t)\), where \(a:J\to M\) assigns jobs to resources, \(\pi=(\pi_m)_{m\in M}\) gives each resource’s job sequence, and \(t\) contains induced timing variables. For a move family \(\mathcal{Q}\), the sequence neighborhood is \(N_{\mathrm{seq}}(x)=\{(a,\pi',t'): \pi'=q(\pi)\text{ for some }q\in\mathcal{Q},\ t'\text{ is recomputed by the decoder}\}\). Common families include adjacent swaps, arbitrary swaps, insertions, and subsequence reversals. Assignment \(a\) remains unchanged, while feasibility may be imposed either during generation or by filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence neighborhood changes job order on resources through swaps, insertions, or reversals while keeping every job’s resource assignment fixed.
assumptions_latex: Each job has exactly one assigned resource.
A decoder maps modified sequences to timing variables or declares infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in N_{\mathrm{seq}}(x)\Longrightarrow a_y=a_x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits sequence neighborhoods, but no scheduling-neighborhood source supports the move families or the convention for decoder-declared infeasibility.

children.title: Assignment Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Moves reallocating jobs, tasks, or operations across resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines local moves that reassign jobs while minimally repairing resource sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a schedule \(x=(a,\pi,t)\), an assignment move selects a nonempty job set \(K\subseteq J\), replaces \(a(j)\) by an eligible resource \(a'(j)\) for each \(j\in K\), and leaves \(a'(j)=a(j)\) otherwise. A specified repair operator removes moved jobs from their old sequences, inserts them into destination sequences, and recomputes timing. The assignment neighborhood \(N_{\mathrm{asg}}(x)\) contains every repaired schedule obtained from an allowed reassignment, optionally restricted to feasible outputs. Single-job relocation and two-job resource exchange are canonical move families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assignment neighborhood changes the resources of selected jobs, repairs affected sequences, and recomputes timing; relocation and resource exchange are standard examples.
assumptions_latex: Every reassigned job is eligible for its destination resource.
A fixed sequence-repair and timing decoder is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in N_{\mathrm{asg}}(x)\Longrightarrow a_y(j)=a_x(j)\) for every unmoved job \(j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits assignment neighborhoods and the variables are adequately introduced, but the repair convention and claimed canonical move families lack a cited source and locator.

children.title: Coupled Sequence–Assignment Moves
children.top_down_role: Moves jointly changing resource allocation plus processing order.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Sequence–Assignment Moves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines atomic moves that jointly modify resource assignment and processing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(a,\pi,t)\) be a schedule. A coupled sequence–assignment move chooses jobs \(K\subseteq J\), new eligible assignments \(a'|_K\), and insertion positions in the affected destination sequences; it simultaneously removes \(K\) from their old sequences, installs their new assignments, inserts them at the selected positions, and decodes timing \(t'\). Its neighborhood \(N_{\mathrm{cpl}}(x)\) contains the resulting schedules satisfying the chosen feasibility policy. Unlike a pure assignment move followed by a fixed repair, the insertion positions are decision components of the same atomic move.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled move simultaneously chooses new resources and sequence positions for selected jobs, allowing assignment and ordering changes to coordinate within one neighborhood step.
assumptions_latex: Selected destination resources are job-eligible.
The timing decoder is defined for every proposed assignment-sequence pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in N_{\mathrm{cpl}}(x)\) may satisfy both \(a_y\ne a_x\) and \(\pi_y\ne\pi_x\).

notation.meaning: jobs modified by the coupled move

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits coupled sequence-assignment moves, but the asserted distinction from fixed-repair assignment moves is uncited and no inspectable source locator is provided.

children.title: Feasibility-Preserving Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Neighborhoods restricted to precedence-, capacity-, plus timing-feasible schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Preserving Neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure criterion for neighborhoods restricted to feasible schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the set of feasible schedules and let \(N:X\rightrightarrows\mathcal{S}\) be a neighborhood mapping into an ambient schedule space \(\mathcal{S}\). The neighborhood is feasibility-preserving precisely when \(N(x)\subseteq X\) for every \(x\in X\). Equivalently, every permitted move operator \(m\) satisfies \(m(x)\in X\) whenever it is applicable to \(x\in X\). Under this closure property, a local-search sequence initialized at \(x_0\in X\) remains feasible at every iteration without a penalty function or post-move repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neighborhood preserves feasibility when every allowed move from every feasible schedule yields another feasible schedule, so feasible initialization guarantees feasible local-search iterates.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathcal{S}\) is the feasible schedule set.
Each iteration selects its successor from the current neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_0\in X\) and \(x_{k+1}\in N(x_k)\Longrightarrow x_k\in X\) for all \(k\ge0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the leaf and neighborhood closure implies feasible iterates. The operator formulation is equivalent only when the permitted operators generate exactly the stated neighborhood, and no source is cited.

children.title: Neighborhood Connectivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on reachability between feasible schedules under selected move families.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighborhood Connectivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies invariants that disconnect feasible-schedule neighborhood graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feasible set \(X\) and neighborhood \(N\), form the undirected graph \(G_N=(X,E_N)\), where \(\{x,y\}\in E_N\) when \(y\in N(x)\) or \(x\in N(y)\). If a nonconstant invariant \(I:X\to\mathcal{I}\) satisfies \(I(x)=I(y)\) on every edge, then vertices with different invariant values lie in distinct connected components. In particular, pure sequence moves preserve resource assignment, and pure assignment moves that retain a fixed relative-order invariant cannot connect schedules violating that invariant. Global reachability therefore requires move families capable of changing every nonconstant preserved attribute.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any attribute preserved by every neighborhood move partitions the feasible-schedule graph; schedules with different attribute values cannot be mutually reached.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the feasible schedule set.
Neighborhood adjacency is symmetrized in \(G_N\).
\(I\) is preserved by every neighborhood edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)\ne I(y)\Longrightarrow x\) and \(y\) are disconnected in \(G_N\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the connectivity leaf and the invariant argument is mathematically coherent, but neither the general claim nor its scheduling examples have an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Critical-Path Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Schedule moves focused on activities lying on critical paths.

assumptions_latex: A feasible schedule \(s\) induces an acyclic precedence-resource graph \(G_s=(V,A_s)\) with processing-time vertex weights \(p_v\ge 0\).
The objective is the makespan \(C_{\max}(s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every schedule in \(N_{\mathrm{CP}}(s)\) differs from \(s\) only through a move incident to an operation on a critical path.

notation.meaning: set of longest source-to-sink paths in the schedule graph

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard disjunctive-graph scheduling neighborhood definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a move-filtered neighborhood using longest paths in a fixed schedule graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)\) be the set of source-to-sink paths in \(G_s\) whose total weight equals \(C_{\max}(s)\). For a feasible move family \(\mathcal M(s)\), define the critical-path neighborhood by
\[
N_{\mathrm{CP}}(s)=\{m(s):m\in\mathcal M(s),\ m(s)\text{ is feasible},\ \operatorname{supp}(m)\cap V(P)\ne\varnothing\text{ for some }P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)\}.
\]
Thus only moves touching at least one operation on a current critical path are admitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical-path neighborhood contains feasible moves that alter at least one operation lying on a longest path of the current schedule graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Path Neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Critical-Path Neighborhoods leaf and is internally coherent, but no inspectable citation supports this particular support-filtered neighborhood convention. Critical-path neighborhood definitions vary with the underlying move family and with whether touching, moving, or reversing an arc adjacent to a critical operation is required.

children.title: Critical-Block Neighborhoods
children.top_down_role: Moves focused on contiguous critical operations sharing a resource.

assumptions_latex: A feasible schedule \(s\) has an acyclic disjunctive graph and makespan objective.
Each machine induces a total order on its assigned operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The neighborhood contains exactly feasible moves supported within a current critical block.

notation.meaning: set of maximal critical blocks in schedule s
operations whose relative machine order is changed by move m

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard job-shop critical-block neighborhood abstraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses maximal same-machine segments of critical paths; the permitted internal move family remains parameterized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A critical block is a maximal sequence \(B=(v_1,\ldots,v_k)\), with \(k\ge2\), of consecutive operations on some critical path such that all \(v_i\) use the same machine and occur consecutively in its order. Given feasible moves \(\mathcal M(s)\), define
\[
N_{\mathrm{CB}}(s)=\{m(s):m\in\mathcal M(s),\ m(s)\text{ is feasible},\ \varnothing\ne\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq B\text{ for some }B\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{crit}}(s)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical-block neighborhood applies feasible order-changing moves wholly within a maximal same-machine segment of a current critical path.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Block Neighborhoods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical role is correctly a definition and the local container is appropriate, but the notation entry for the block set contains a broken line break inside the TeX command. More importantly, the restriction that every changed order relation be supported wholly within one critical block is a particular neighborhood convention for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Criticality Detection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Static or dynamic identification of critical schedule structures.

assumptions_latex: The schedule graph \(G_s=(V,A_s)\) is a finite acyclic directed graph with dummy source \(0\), dummy sink \(t\), operation set \(V^{\circ}=V\setminus\{0,t\}\), vertex weights \(p_v\ge 0\), and \(p_0=p_t=0\).
Every operation vertex lies on a directed path from \(0\) to \(t\), and the makespan is the weight of a longest \(0\)-to-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact regime returns precisely the operations lying on at least one longest \(0\)-to-\(t\) path; the tolerance regime returns the explicitly defined superset whose longest-path slack is at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: longest-path weight from the source through operation v
maximum additional path weight strictly after operation v

review_flags: locator supports project-scheduling critical paths; recurrence notation is local
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact criticality from an explicitly parameterized tolerance regime for deterministic acyclic schedule graphs under a makespan objective.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Process the vertices in topological order, set \(E(0)=0\), and, for each \(v\ne 0\), compute
\[
E(v)=p_v+\max_{(u,v)\in A_s}E(u).
\]
Process the vertices in reverse topological order, set \(R(t)=0\), and, for each \(v\ne t\), compute
\[
R(v)=\max_{(v,w)\in A_s}\bigl(p_w+R(w)\bigr).
\]
Then \(C_{\max}(s)=E(t)\). The exact criticality regime outputs
\[
K_0(s)=\{v\in V^{\circ}:E(v)+R(v)=C_{\max}(s)\}.
\]
For a declared tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), the tolerance regime instead outputs
\[
K_\varepsilon(s)=\{v\in V^{\circ}:E(v)+R(v)\ge C_{\max}(s)-\varepsilon\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and backward longest-path labels identify operations on a longest schedule-graph path; a separately parameterized tolerance regime also includes operations whose longest-path slack is at most epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Criticality Detection Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

children.title: Path–Block Coupled Moves
children.top_down_role: Moves coordinating changes across critical paths plus resource blocks.

assumptions_latex: A feasible schedule \(s\) has identified critical paths and their maximal critical blocks.
A coupled move is accepted only if its resulting schedule is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A path-block coupled move changes machine order inside a critical block and simultaneously changes at least one additional relation incident to the same critical path.

notation.meaning: arcs reversed, inserted, or deleted by move m
critical path and one of its critical blocks

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formal synthesis of path-focused and block-focused moves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes composite moves rather than prescribing a particular swap, insertion, or reassignment operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a critical path \(P\) and a critical block \(B\subseteq P\), a feasible move \(m\) is path-block coupled when
\[
\Delta A(m)\cap(B\times B)\ne\varnothing
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Delta A(m)\cap\bigl((P\times V)\cup(V\times P)\bigr)\setminus(B\times B)\ne\varnothing.
\]
The coupled neighborhood is
\[
N_{\mathrm{PB}}(s)=\{m(s):m\text{ is feasible and satisfies these conditions for some }(P,B)\}.
\]
The second change may represent another block move, a reassignment, or a precedence adjustment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled move modifies order within a critical block and another relation incident to the same critical path.
knowledge_statements.title: Path–Block Coupled Moves

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is a plausible role for this leaf, but the proposed path-block coupling condition appears to be a local synthesis rather than a documented standard neighborhood. The meaning of inserted or deleted arcs also depends on the schedule-graph representation, and no source establishes the terminology or the claimed examples.

children.title: Critical-Neighborhood Blind Spots
children.top_down_role: Improving regions inaccessible when search is confined to currently critical structures.

assumptions_latex: The neighborhood \(N(s)\) contains only moves whose support intersects the current critical-operation set \(K(s)\).
All objective comparisons use the same scheduling objective \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Critical-only neighborhoods can declare local optimality even when a strictly improving feasible noncritical move exists.

notation.meaning: operations on at least one current critical path

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate limitation of support-filtered neighborhoods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the exclusion mechanism, not a universal claim that every critical neighborhood fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M(s)\) be an ambient feasible move family and
\[
N(s)=\{m(s):m\in\mathcal M(s),\ \operatorname{supp}(m)\cap K(s)\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
If there exists \(m^\star\in\mathcal M(s)\) such that
\[
\operatorname{supp}(m^\star)\cap K(s)=\varnothing,
\qquad f(m^\star(s))<f(s),
\]
while \(f(s')\ge f(s)\) for every \(s'\in N(s)\), then \(s\) is locally optimal for \(N\) but not for \(\mathcal M\). Such improvements are invisible to the critical filter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Filtering moves by current critical operations may hide improving moves supported entirely on currently noncritical operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Neighborhood Blind Spots

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the Blind Spots container, and the conditional implication is logically valid. However, it merely assumes the existence of the excluded improving move; without a scheduling instance or source demonstrating that this condition can occur, it does not substantiate a scheduling-specific failure phenomenon.

children.title: Variable-Neighborhood Search
children.top_down_role: Systematic traversal of multiple scheduling neighborhood families.

assumptions_latex: The feasible schedule set \(S\) is finite and nonempty.
Neighborhood structures \(N_1,\ldots,N_k:S\rightrightarrows S\) and objective \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a schedule locally optimal for \(N_1\) after the prescribed termination condition is reached.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic variable-neighborhood search with shaking, local improvement, and neighborhood-index reset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(s\in S\). Set \(i=1\). While the stopping rule is false, sample a shaken schedule \(y\in N_i(s)\), compute \(z=L_i(y)\) with \(f(z)\le f(y)\), and update
\[
(s,i)\leftarrow
\begin{cases}
(z,1),&f(z)<f(s),\\
(s,i+1),&f(z)\ge f(s)\text{ and }i<k,\\
(s,1),&f(z)\ge f(s)\text{ and }i=k.
\end{cases}
\]
Stop after a declared time, iteration, or no-improvement limit, and output the best schedule encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable-neighborhood search shakes and locally improves a schedule across ordered neighborhoods, resetting to the first after improvement.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Neighborhood Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and reset mechanism fit Variable-Neighborhood Search, but termination by an arbitrary time, iteration, or no-improvement limit does not imply local optimality for \(N_1\). The statement itself only promises the best schedule encountered, while the conclusion field makes the stronger unsupported claim. An authoritative VNS source and a corrected guarantee are required.

children.title: Large-Neighborhood Search
children.top_down_role: Search over broad schedule regions through partial reconstruction.

assumptions_latex: The feasible schedule set is \(S\), and \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) is minimized.
A destroy operator and a repair mapping are available for each selected neighborhood configuration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration explores a neighborhood implicitly defined by partial destruction followed by feasible repair.

notation.meaning: destroy operator producing a partial schedule

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic scheduling LNS; acceptance may be improving-only or controlled by a stated metaheuristic rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a destruction scale \(q\), define the implicit neighborhood
\[
N_q(s)=\bigcup_{u\in D_q(s)}R_q(u)\subseteq S.
\]
Initialize \(s\in S\). At each iteration select \(q\), generate \(u\in D_q(s)\), choose \(s'\in R_q(u)\), and replace \(s\) by \(s'\) when a declared acceptance predicate \(A(s,s')\) holds. Record the best schedule seen. Stop at the stated computational budget and output that best schedule; every accepted candidate must be a complete feasible schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large-neighborhood search destroys part of a schedule, repairs it feasibly, and accepts candidates under an explicit rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Large-Neighborhood Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is correct for Large-Neighborhood Search, and the destroy-repair abstraction is mathematically coherent. No citation supports this exact set-valued formulation, acceptance abstraction, or its use as the terminal scheduling definition, so authoritative LNS sourcing is required.

children.title: Scheduling Destroy Operators
children.top_down_role: Removal structures based on jobs, resources, time windows, or criticality.

assumptions_latex: A complete schedule assigns and orders a finite operation set \(V\).
Removing assignments or order decisions is permitted without asserting feasibility of the resulting partial schedule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A destroy operator returns partial schedules retaining exactly the decisions outside its removal set.

notation.meaning: set of removed operations or scheduling decisions

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard partial-solution destroy operator abstraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers operation removal and decision relaxation; it does not prescribe random, related, or critical removal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A scheduling destroy operator of scale \(q\) is a mapping \(D_q:S\rightrightarrows\bar S\), where \(S\) is the set of complete schedules and \(\bar S\) the set of partial schedules. For every \(u\in D_q(s)\), there is a removal set \(U\subseteq V\) or a decision set \(U\) such that
\[
1\le |U|\le q,
\]
and \(u\) agrees with \(s\) on every assignment, sequencing, and timing decision not removed or relaxed by \(U\). The operator records enough residual decisions for a repair procedure to construct completions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A destroy operator removes or relaxes at most a specified number of schedule decisions while preserving all untouched decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Destroy Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition fits the destroy-operator leaf, but the same symbol \(U\) alternates between operations and unspecified scheduling decisions, so \(|U|\le q\) has no uniform meaning. The claim that every untouched timing decision is preserved is also stronger than some standard relaxation-based destroy operators. A sourced scheduling-specific convention is needed.

children.title: Scheduling Repair Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Reconstruction frameworks for partial schedules.

assumptions_latex: A partial schedule \(u\) specifies retained decisions over a finite scheduling instance.
The complete feasible schedule set is \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid repair framework returns only feasible schedules that extend every retained decision of the partial schedule.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates validity of repair from greedy, randomized, optimization-based, or backtracking implementation choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in\bar S\), let
\[
\operatorname{Ext}(u)=\{s\in S:s\text{ preserves every assignment, order, and fixed-time decision retained in }u\}.
\]
A scheduling repair framework is a mapping \(R:\bar S\rightrightarrows S\) satisfying
\[
R(u)\subseteq\operatorname{Ext}(u).
\]
It is complete on a domain \(\mathcal U\subseteq\bar S\) when \(\operatorname{Ext}(u)\ne\varnothing\) implies \(R(u)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(u\in\mathcal U\). A selected candidate may minimize a surrogate score over \(R(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repair framework completes a partial schedule while preserving retained decisions and satisfying all scheduling constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Repair Frameworks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind matches the repair-framework leaf, and the extension-set formulation is internally precise. Nevertheless, no source supports the requirement that every repair preserve all retained assignment, order, and fixed-time decisions or the stated completeness terminology; repair frameworks use non-equivalent conventions.

children.title: Adaptive Neighborhood Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection regimes responding to search history or instance state.

assumptions_latex: There are \(k\) neighborhood operators with positive initial weights.
Each application yields an observed bounded reward \(r_t\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selection probabilities remain positive and shift toward operators with larger smoothed observed rewards.

notation.meaning: weight of neighborhood i at iteration t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit reward-weighted regime; it is not asserted to represent every adaptive selection method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(0<\rho\le1\), \(0<\epsilon<1\), and initialize \(w_i(0)>0\). At iteration \(t\), select \(I_t=i\) with
\[
p_i(t)=(1-\epsilon)\frac{w_i(t)}{\sum_{j=1}^k w_j(t)}+\frac{\epsilon}{k}.
\]
Apply neighborhood \(i\), observe reward \(r_t\in[0,1]\), and update
\[
w_i(t+1)=
\begin{cases}
(1-\rho)w_i(t)+\rho r_t,&i=I_t,\\
w_i(t),&i\ne I_t.
\end{cases}
\]
Stop at the declared budget and output the best schedule encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive selection samples neighborhoods from reward-weighted probabilities while retaining a positive exploration probability for every operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Neighborhood Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An algorithm is an appropriate role for one adaptive selection regime, but the update is not always well-defined under the stated assumptions. With \(\rho=1\) and zero rewards, operator weights can become zero and eventually make \(\sum_j w_j(t)=0\). The leaf is broader than this one rule, and no source identifies the rule or its intended scope.

children.title: Genetic Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Population-based scheduling search using inherited schedule representations.

assumptions_latex: Schedules are represented by chromosomes in a finite encoding space \(X\).
A decoder \(d:X\to S\) maps every chromosome to a feasible schedule.
Population size \(M\), selection, crossover, mutation, replacement, and stopping rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the best decoded feasible schedule encountered across all generations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decoder-based genetic scheduling with feasibility guaranteed by representation or restoration inside the decoder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize a multiset \(P_0\subseteq X\) with \(|P_0|=M\). At generation \(t\), evaluate each \(x\in P_t\) by \(F(x)=f(d(x))\); select parent pairs according to the declared selection rule; apply crossover and mutation to form offspring \(Q_t\subseteq X\); and set
\[
P_{t+1}=\operatorname{Replace}_M(P_t,Q_t;F).
\]
Maintain \(x^\star\in\bigcup_{	au\le t}P_\tau\) minimizing \(F\). On meeting the generation, time, or stagnation limit, output \(d(x^\star)\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Genetic scheduling evolves encoded schedules by selection, crossover, mutation, and replacement, returning the best decoded feasible schedule.
knowledge_statements.title: Genetic Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and decoder-based template fit Genetic Scheduling, and feasibility is explicitly guaranteed by the decoder. A source is still required for the scheduling-specific template and for the relationship among encoding, genetic operators, decoding, and replacement; standard-field rationale alone is insufficient here.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Genetic algorithms for scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population-based scheduling interpretation, common representations and operators, and the source's qualified comparison with single-schedule search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling genetic algorithm represents each individual, or chromosome, by a sequence or schedule and evaluates its fitness from the associated objective-function value. Each generation contains survivors from the preceding population and offspring produced from parents through reproduction, mutation, or crossover; population size is usually kept constant. In a multi-machine setting, a chromosome may contain one sub-chromosome for each machine, and mutation may correspond to an adjacent pairwise interchange. Because multiple schedules are carried between generations and crossover can combine parts of different schedules, the neighborhood is population-based. In this limited population-size sense, simulated annealing and tabu search may be viewed as population-size-one special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In scheduling, a genetic algorithm treats sequences or schedules as population members whose fitness is measured from their objective values. Generations combine survivors with offspring created through reproduction, mutation, or crossover, usually at constant population size. Multi-machine chromosomes may have one sub-chromosome per machine, and mutation may be an adjacent interchange. The source compares simulated annealing and tabu search to population-size-one genetic algorithms only in the qualified sense that they carry a single schedule between iterations.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each population member encodes a scheduling sequence or schedule.}
\text{Fitness is measured from the associated objective-function value.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The search maintains and transforms a population of schedules, usually with constant population size; the population-size-one comparison is only a qualified analogy.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-parent, two-replacement genetic scheduling algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-size scheduling population updated by replacing two worst schedules with offspring of two best schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(k=1\) and use a heuristic to select an initial population \(P_1=\{\mathcal S_{1,1},\ldots,\mathcal S_{1,\ell}\}\). At iteration \(k\), select two best schedules \(\mathcal S_k^+,\mathcal S_k^{++}\) and two worst schedules \(\mathcal S_k^-,\mathcal S_k^{--}\). Generate two offspring \(\mathcal S^*,\mathcal S^{**}\) from the two best schedules. Form the next population by replacing the two worst schedules with these offspring and retaining all other schedules. Increment \(k\). Stop when \(k=N\); otherwise repeat the selection and replacement step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize a heuristic population of l schedules with k equal to 1. At each replacement round, choose the two best schedules as parents, generate two offspring, replace the two worst schedules with the offspring, and retain all other schedules. Increment k and stop when it reaches N; otherwise repeat.
assumptions_latex: N\in\mathbb N,\quad N\ge 2
\ell\in\mathbb N,\quad \ell\ge 2
\text{Two best and two worst schedules can be selected from the current population.}
\text{Two offspring can be generated from the selected parents.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{k+1}=\bigl(P_k\setminus\{\mathcal S_k^-,\mathcal S_k^{--}\}\bigr)\cup\{\mathcal S^*,\mathcal S^{**}\},\qquad |P_{k+1}|=|P_k|,\qquad \text{with termination after }N-1\text{ replacement rounds.}

children.title: Memetic Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Population search augmented by schedule-focused local improvement.

assumptions_latex: A genetic scheduling scheme produces feasible decoded schedules.
For every feasible schedule, the local improvement routine terminates after finitely many strict improvements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every locally improved offspring is no worse than its decoded precursor and is locally optimal for the chosen neighborhood.

notation.meaning: decoder from chromosomes to feasible schedules

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memetic scheduling defined as population evolution augmented by finite descent on selected decoded individuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Generate offspring chromosomes by the genetic selection, crossover, and mutation rules. For each offspring \(x\) selected for intensification, initialize \(s_0=d(x)\) and repeatedly choose
\[
s_{j+1}\in\{s'\in N(s_j):f(s')<f(s_j)\}
\]
until this set is empty; define \(L_N(d(x))=s_j\). Insert the locally improved schedules, or chromosomes re-encoding them, through the declared replacement rule. At termination output the best schedule seen. By construction,
\[
f(L_N(d(x)))\le f(d(x)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memetic scheduling augments genetic evolution with terminating neighborhood descent on selected offspring before population replacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Memetic Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Memetic Scheduling, and finite strict descent supports the stated non-worsening and local-optimality properties for each intensified offspring. However, the option to insert chromosomes re-encoding improved schedules requires an encoder or a representability assumption that is not introduced. No authoritative source supports this particular memetic scheduling variant.

children.title: Ant-Colony Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Constructive population search guided by collective scheduling traces.

knowledge_statements.title: Ant-Colony Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic ant-colony construction for a finite scheduling problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite set of feasible construction moves and positive pheromones \(\tau_e\), initialize \(\tau_e=\tau_0>0\). At iteration \(t\), each ant constructs a schedule by selecting an admissible move \(e\) with probability \[p_t(e)=\frac{\tau_e(t)^\alpha\eta_e^\beta}{\sum_{f\in A_t}\tau_f(t)^\alpha\eta_f^\beta},\] where \(A_t\) is the current admissible set and \(\eta_e>0\) is heuristic information. Evaluate completed schedules, optionally repair infeasible ones, and update \[\tau_e(t+1)=(1-\rho)\tau_e(t)+\Delta_e(t),\qquad 0<\rho\leq1.\] Stop at a prescribed iteration limit and return the best feasible schedule encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ants probabilistically construct schedules from admissible moves; pheromone evaporation and reinforcement bias later constructions toward moves occurring in good feasible schedules.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling instance has finitely many construction states and moves.
At every nonterminal construction state, the admissible set \(A_t\) is nonempty.
Parameters satisfy \(\alpha,\beta\geq0\), \(\tau_0>0\), and \(0<\rho\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the best feasible schedule generated before the stopping rule is met.

notation.meaning: pheromone associated with construction move e
positive heuristic desirability of move e
moves admissible at the current construction state

review_flags: Scheduling-specific ant-colony source and precise canonical variant are missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role and local scheduling context fit, but no scheduling-specific source identifies the intended ant-colony variant or constrains the reinforcement term. In particular, the stated update does not ensure that pheromones remain positive when evaporation is complete and reinforcement is zero.

children.title: Population Schedule Encodings
children.top_down_role: Permutation, priority, assignment, random-key, plus indirect schedule encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Population Schedule Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Genotype–phenotype representation for population-based scheduling methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite genotype space and \(S\) the set of schedules, with feasible subset \(F\subseteq S\). A population schedule encoding is a decoding map \(D:G\to S\), together with variation operators on \(G\). It is feasibility-preserving when \(D(G)\subseteq F\), and complete when every feasible schedule is representable: \(F\subseteq D(G)\). If neither property holds, evaluation must assign values to infeasible decoded schedules or compose decoding with a repair map \(R:S\to F\). A population \(P=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in G^m\) represents the schedule multiset \((D(g_1),\ldots,D(g_m))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding maps population genotypes to schedules; feasibility preservation and completeness respectively ensure that all decoded schedules are feasible and all feasible schedules are representable.
assumptions_latex: The genotype space \(G\) and schedule space \(S\) are finite.
The feasible schedules form a specified subset \(F\subseteq S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation is feasibility-preserving iff \(D(G)\subseteq F\), and complete iff \(F\subseteq D(G)\).
review_flags: A scheduling-metaheuristics source supporting these encoding criteria is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role, decoding map, feasibility-preservation condition, and completeness condition are mathematically coherent, but no source supports this particular scheduling-encoding formulation.

children.title: Feasibility Restoration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Repair or decoding regimes for population-generated scheduling candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Restoration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repair of infeasible schedules produced by population variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite schedule space, let \(\varnothing\neq F\subseteq S\) be its feasible subset, let \(\bot\notin F\) denote repair failure, and let \(d:S\times S\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\) be a repair-distance function. A feasibility-restoration procedure is a map \(\mathcal{R}:S\to F\cup\{\bot\}\). Exact minimum-change repair returns \[\mathcal{R}(s)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in F}d(s,u).\] A bounded heuristic repair repeatedly selects a constraint violation and applies a permitted modification according to a prescribed rule, returning a member of \(F\) if feasibility is reached and returning \(\bot\) if its repair budget is exhausted. An unrepaired schedule is never reported as feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration procedure either returns a feasible schedule, using exact minimum-change optimization or bounded heuristic repair, or explicitly reports repair failure.
assumptions_latex: The schedule space \(S\) is finite and the feasible set \(F\subseteq S\) is nonempty.
The repair distance or heuristic modification rule is specified.
A heuristic repair has a finite stopping budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(s\in S\), declared repair success yields \(\mathcal{R}(s)\in F\), whereas exhausted unsuccessful repair yields \(\mathcal{R}(s)=\bot\).

notation.meaning: repair procedure returning a feasible schedule or failure
distance measuring changes introduced by repair

review_flags: A scheduling-specific source for exact and heuristic repair regimes is still required.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Matheuristics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid scheduling methods combining mathematical programming with heuristic search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scheduling optimization problem \(\min\{c(s):s\in F\}\), a scheduling matheuristic is an algorithm that interleaves heuristic search with one or more exact mathematical-programming subproblems. At an incumbent schedule \(s^t\), it constructs a restricted feasible region \(F_t\subseteq F\), solves or bounds \(\min\{c(s):s\in F_t\}\) by an integer-programming method, and uses the resulting feasible schedule, bound, or infeasibility certificate to guide subsequent search. Unless the restricted regions collectively exhaust \(F\) or a valid global bound closes the optimality gap, termination certifies only feasibility and incumbent quality, not global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduling matheuristic embeds exact mathematical-programming subproblems inside heuristic search; global optimality requires an exhaustive mechanism or a valid closing bound.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem has feasible set \(F\) and objective \(c:F\to\mathbb{R}\).
Each exact subproblem is a valid restriction or relaxation of the original formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method returns an incumbent in \(F\), while global optimality is certified only when a valid global lower bound equals its objective value.

notation.meaning: restricted region searched at iteration t

review_flags: The supplied integer-programming references do not support the scheduling-matheuristic definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the topic, but the record alternates between restricted subproblems and relaxations without distinguishing their different bound directions. No matheuristics source supports the proposed definition or optimality qualifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint–Integer-Programming Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling hybrids coupling constraint propagation and integer programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint–integer-programming scheduling hybrid represents the same scheduling decisions by a constraint model \(C\) and an integer-programming model \(P\), with a consistency map between their shared variables. During search, deductions from constraint propagation fix variables or tighten domains in \(P\), while valid integer-programming bounds, cuts, and infeasibility conclusions prune states of \(C\). The coupling is sound when every transferred restriction is valid for the common feasible schedule set \(F\). If the integrated search is exhaustive and each pruning step is sound, an incumbent accompanied by a matching global bound certifies optimality; otherwise the hybrid is heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hybrid exchanges sound domain deductions, bounds, cuts, and infeasibility information between constraint and integer-programming models of one scheduling problem.
assumptions_latex: Both component models describe a common feasible schedule set \(F\).
Every exchanged deduction is valid under the shared-variable mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sound exhaustive search preserves all optimal schedules and certifies optimality when its incumbent and global bound coincide.
review_flags: A source specifically treating constraint–integer-programming scheduling hybrids is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is plausible and fits the hybrid-method container, but no cited source establishes the shared-variable coupling, permitted information transfers, or exhaustive-search guarantee for scheduling hybrids.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomially Solvable Islands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted scheduling classes admitting polynomial-time exact algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{I}\) be a fixed class of finitely encoded scheduling instances, and let \(L(I)\) denote the binary encoding length of \(I\in\mathcal{I}\). The class is a polynomially solvable island when there exist an exact algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every \(I\in\mathcal{I}\), algorithm \(A\) returns an optimal feasible schedule or correctly reports infeasibility using at most \(p(L(I))\) elementary bit operations. The restrictions defining \(\mathcal{I}\), together with its encoding convention, are part of the regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomially solvable scheduling island is a fixed, precisely encoded instance class that has an exact algorithm polynomial in binary input length.
assumptions_latex: The instance class \(\mathcal{I}\) and its finite binary encoding are fixed.
Running time is measured in elementary bit operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist an exact algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that every \(I\in\mathcal{I}\) is solved within \(p(L(I))\) bit operations.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of instance I

children.title: Pseudopolynomial Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling families admitting runtime bounds polynomial in numeric magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudopolynomial Scheduling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling algorithms polynomial in numeric values but not necessarily their bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a scheduling instance containing nonnegative integer data \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\), and let \(L(I)\) be its binary encoding length. An exact scheduling algorithm is pseudopolynomial when its running time is bounded by \(p(L(I),A(I))\) for some polynomial \(p\), where \(A(I)=\max_j a_j\) or another explicitly specified aggregate numeric value, while no polynomial bound in \(L(I)\) alone is asserted. Under unary encoding of the numeric data, \(A(I)\) is at most linear in the encoded input size, so the same bound becomes polynomial in that unary size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudopolynomial scheduling algorithm is polynomial in input length and specified numeric magnitudes, becoming polynomial when those numbers are unary encoded.
assumptions_latex: All magnitude-dependent instance data are nonnegative integers.
The numeric parameter \(A(I)\) used in the running-time bound is explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is polynomial in \(L(I)\) and \(A(I)\), and hence polynomial in the corresponding unary encoding length.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of instance I

children.title: Weakly NP-Hard Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling families whose hardness depends on numerically encoded instance data.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly NP-Hard Scheduling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling classes whose hardness depends on binary-encoded numeric magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finitely encoded scheduling decision problem \(\Pi\) is weakly NP-hard when \(\Pi\) is NP-hard under binary encoding of its integer data, but admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm: for some explicitly identified numeric magnitude \(A(I)\), instances \(I\) are decided in time polynomial in \(L(I)\) and \(A(I)\). Equivalently for the stated algorithmic bound, the problem becomes polynomially solvable when the magnitude-bearing integers are unary encoded. Weak NP-hardness does not itself assert strong NP-hardness, nor does the existence of a pseudopolynomial algorithm alone establish NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly NP-hard scheduling regime combines binary-encoding NP-hardness with a pseudopolynomial algorithm dependent on numeric magnitudes.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem is stated as a finite decision problem.
Its integer data and binary encoding are fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is NP-hard in binary encoding and decidable in time polynomial in \(L(I)\) and the specified magnitude \(A(I)\).

children.title: Numeric-Encoding Boundary
children.top_down_role: The role of unary versus binary encoding in separating the two regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Encoding Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between bit-length polynomiality and magnitude-dependent running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a scheduling instance contain an integer \(a\geq0\). Under the convention that zero occupies one bit, its binary representation has length \[\ell_2(a)=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2(a+1)\rceil\},\] whereas a unary representation may be taken to have length \(\ell_1(a)=a+1\). Consequently, a running time polynomial in \(a\) is polynomial in unary length but may be exponential in binary length; for fixed \(k\geq1\), the bound \(O(a^k)\) is contained in \(O(2^{k\ell_2(a)})\). Thus a magnitude-dependent bound does not establish polynomial time in binary input length unless the magnitudes are polynomially bounded in that length or a separate bound polynomial solely in binary input length is proved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on a numeric value is polynomial under unary encoding but can be exponential in the value's binary encoding length.
assumptions_latex: Numeric scheduling data are nonnegative integers.
Binary zero is represented using one bit.
Running time uses the standard bit-complexity convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound polynomial in numeric magnitude does not by itself imply polynomial time in binary input length.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of a, with zero occupying one bit

source_refs.locator: Encoding p. 23; Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Hardness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling classes remaining NP-hard when numeric magnitudes are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling decision problem \(\Pi\) with integer-valued data is strongly NP-hard when there exists a polynomial \(q\) such that the restriction to instances \(I\) whose numeric values are at most \(q(L(I))\) remains NP-hard, where \(L(I)\) is binary input length. Equivalently under the standard integer-encoding formulation, NP-hardness persists when the numeric data are represented in unary. If such a problem admitted a pseudopolynomial algorithm, that algorithm would run in polynomial time on the bounded-number hard restriction; hence, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no pseudopolynomial exact algorithm exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strongly NP-hard scheduling remains NP-hard with polynomially bounded or unary-encoded numbers, excluding pseudopolynomial exact algorithms unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem is a finite decision problem with integer-valued data.
Strong hardness is measured under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), a strongly NP-hard scheduling problem has no pseudopolynomial exact decision algorithm.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of instance I

children.title: Fixed-Parameter Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling complexity organized by explicit instance parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Parameter Scheduling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scheduling tractability with respect to an explicit parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a parameterized scheduling problem whose instances are pairs \((I,k)\), where \(I\) has encoding length \(L(I)\) and \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) is the designated parameter. The regime is fixed-parameter tractable when an exact algorithm decides feasibility or returns an optimal schedule in time \[f(k)L(I)^c,\] where \(f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) is computable and the constant exponent \(c\) is independent of both \(I\) and \(k\). A bound \(L(I)^{g(k)}\) with parameter-dependent exponent establishes membership in \(\mathrm{XP}\), not fixed-parameter tractability unless that exponent can be made constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduling regime is fixed-parameter tractable when exact running time is arbitrary in the parameter but polynomial with a parameter-independent input exponent.
assumptions_latex: The parameter \(k\) is explicitly defined and computable from the instance.
Input size is the finite encoding length \(L(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is fixed-parameter tractable iff it admits an exact bound \(f(k)L(I)^c\) with constant \(c\) independent of \(k\).
review_flags: No supplied source covers parameterized complexity or fixed-parameter scheduling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and distinction between FPT and XP are mathematically standard and precise, but no parameterized-complexity or scheduling source is supplied.

children.title: Bounded-Structure Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Tractability arising from bounded precedence, resource, graph, or machine structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Structure Scheduling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling restrictions defined by uniformly bounded structural parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sigma(I)\in\mathbb{N}\) measure a structural feature of scheduling instance \(I\), such as machine count, precedence width, interaction-graph treewidth, or the number of job types. For a fixed constant \(b\), the bounded-structure regime is \[\mathcal{I}_b=\{I:\sigma(I)\leq b\}.\] The restriction is structural only when \(b\) is independent of input length and numeric magnitudes are not implicitly bounded unless stated separately. Bounded structure alone makes no tractability claim: polynomial-time solvability follows only from an algorithm with running time polynomial on \(\mathcal{I}_b\), while a bound \(f(\sigma(I))L(I)^c\) establishes uniform fixed-parameter tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-structure regime fixes an explicit structural parameter by a constant; tractability still requires a corresponding algorithmic bound.
assumptions_latex: The structural measure \(\sigma\) is explicitly defined on all considered instances.
The bound \(b\) is constant and independent of input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An instance belongs to the regime exactly when \(\sigma(I)\leq b\); this membership condition alone does not imply polynomial-time solvability.

notation.meaning: structural parameter of scheduling instance I

review_flags: No supplied source supports the parameterized bounded-structure formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role correctly matches a bounded-structure regime and appropriately avoids claiming tractability from boundedness alone, but the formulation has no supporting source.

children.title: Parameterized Hardness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of parameter choices that fail to yield fixed-parameter tractability.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Hardness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness transfer under parameterized many-one reductions between scheduling decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Pi,\kappa)\) and \((\Sigma,\lambda)\) be parameterized decision problems. Suppose an algorithm maps every instance \(x\) to \(R(x)\) in time \(f(\kappa(x))|x|^{O(1)}\), with \(x\in\Pi\) if and only if \(R(x)\in\Sigma\), and satisfies \(\lambda(R(x))\le g(\kappa(x))\) for computable functions \(f\) and \(g\). If \((\Pi,\kappa)\) is \(\mathrm{W[1]}\)-hard, then \((\Sigma,\lambda)\) is \(\mathrm{W[1]}\)-hard. Consequently, an fixed-parameter algorithm for \((\Sigma,\lambda)\) would imply \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W[1]}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPT reduction from a W[1]-hard problem establishes a parameterized hardness boundary for the target scheduling problem.
assumptions_latex: \((\Pi,\kappa)\) is \(\mathrm{W[1]}\)-hard.
\(R\) is an FPT many-one reduction with output parameter bounded solely by \(\kappa(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\Sigma,\lambda)\) is \(\mathrm{W[1]}\)-hard.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hardness-transfer theorem is mathematically standard and the theorem content kind fits the hardness-boundary leaf, but no inspectable source is cited. The phrase "an fixed-parameter algorithm" should be corrected, and the plain statement omits the explicit target-hardness conclusion and FPT=W[1] consequence. An authoritative parameterized-complexity theorem or section is required before the record can pass review.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Environment Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decision reduction between scheduling problems having different machine environments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scheduling decision problems \(A\) and \(B\) with machine environments \(E_A\) and \(E_B\), a machine-environment reduction is a polynomial-time map \(R\) from encoded instances \((I,K)\) of \(A\) to encoded instances \((I',K')\) of \(B\) such that \(I\) admits an \(E_A\)-feasible schedule of objective value at most \(K\) if and only if \(I'\) admits an \(E_B\)-feasible schedule of objective value at most \(K'\). The encoding length of \((I',K')\) must be polynomially bounded in that of \((I,K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A machine-environment reduction polynomially changes the machine model while preserving exactly whether a threshold-feasible schedule exists.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) use finite binary encodings.
\(R\) is computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I,K)\in A\iff R(I,K)\in B\).

children.title: Objective-Function Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transfers among makespan, completion-time, lateness, tardiness, and related criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Function Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimizer-preserving transformation between scheduling objectives on corresponding feasible schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let scheduling problems \(A\) and \(B\) have feasible sets \(S_A(I)\), \(S_B(R(I))\) and minimization objectives \(F_A\), \(F_B\). An exact objective-function reduction consists of polynomial-time maps \(R\) and \(\phi_I:S_A(I)\to S_B(R(I))\), together with a strictly increasing function \(h_I\), such that \(\phi_I\) is a bijection and \(F_B(\phi_I(s))=h_I(F_A(s))\) for every \(s\in S_A(I)\). Hence \(s\) minimizes \(F_A\) if and only if \(\phi_I(s)\) minimizes \(F_B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduction changes the objective by a strictly increasing transformation while bijectively preserving feasible schedules and exact optimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(S_A(I)\) and \(S_B(R(I))\) are nonempty.
\(h_I\) is strictly increasing on attainable objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in S_A(I)}F_A(u)\iff \phi_I(s)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in S_B(R(I))}F_B(v)\).

children.title: Constraint-System Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transfers involving release dates, deadlines, precedence, eligibility, or resource restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-System Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving transformation between scheduling constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_A(I,s)\) and \(C_B(R(I),t)\) be predicates defining feasible schedules for two scheduling formulations. A constraint-system reduction consists of a polynomial-time instance map \(R\) and polynomial-time mutually inverse schedule maps \(\phi_I\) and \(\psi_I\) such that, for every encoded schedule \(s\), \(C_A(I,s)\) holds if and only if \(C_B(R(I),\phi_I(s))\) holds. If objectives are present, the reduction is objective preserving when \(F_B(\phi_I(s))=F_A(s)\) for every feasible \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-system reduction gives a polynomially computable bijection between feasible schedules, optionally preserving their objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(R\), \(\phi_I\), and \(\psi_I\) are polynomial-time computable.
\(\psi_I\circ\phi_I\) and \(\phi_I\circ\psi_I\) are identities on feasible schedules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(I,s)\iff C_B(R(I),\phi_I(s))\).

children.title: Objective-Constraint Tradeoff Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations that encode an objective feature as a constraint feature or conversely.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Constraint Tradeoff Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph reduction exchanging a scheduling objective threshold for an explicit feasibility constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the minimization problem \(z^*(I)=\min\{F_I(s):s\in S(I)\}\). For any rational threshold \(K\), define the threshold-feasibility instance \(D(I,K)\) by adjoining the constraint \(F_I(s)\le K\) to the feasibility system defining \(S(I)\). Then \(D(I,K)\) is feasible if and only if \(z^*(I)\le K\). Conversely, when objective values are integral and polynomially bounded, binary search over \(K\) using a decision procedure for \(D\) recovers \(z^*(I)\) with polynomially many calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective threshold can become a constraint; feasibility at that threshold exactly decides whether the optimum is no larger.
assumptions_latex: \(S(I)\) is a finite encoded scheduling-feasibility set.
\(F_I(s)\) is polynomial-time evaluable.
For optimization recovery, attainable objective values are integral and polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(I,K)\text{ is feasible}\iff z^*(I)\le K\).

children.title: Shop-Scheduling Reductions
