knowledge_statements.title: Shop-Scheduling Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-preserving reductions whose target or source is a shop-scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shop-scheduling reduction maps an encoded decision instance \((I,K)\) in polynomial time to a shop instance \((J,K')\), or maps a shop instance to another decision problem, while preserving the answer. In a shop instance, each job comprises operations with processing times, admissible or prescribed machines, technological precedence relations, and nonoverlap constraints for operations assigned to the same unary machine. The reduction is exact when \(I\) has a schedule of value at most \(K\) if and only if \(J\) has a shop schedule of value at most \(K'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shop reduction polynomially encodes precedence and machine nonoverlap so that the source and target threshold questions are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: Instances and thresholds have finite binary encodings.
The transformation has polynomial running time and output size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I,K)\text{ is yes}\iff (J,K')\text{ is yes}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A project-scheduling reduction polynomially encodes activities, precedences, and resources while preserving the threshold decision answer.

The transformation has polynomial running time and output size.

children.title: Shop-to-Project Transfers
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences transferring complexity between shop and project settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Shop-to-Project Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of job-shop makespan scheduling as resource-constrained project scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a job-shop instance, create one project activity \(a_o\) for every operation \(o\), with duration equal to the processing time of \(o\). Add a precedence arc \(a_o\to a_{o'}\) for each consecutive pair of operations of the same job. For every machine \(m\), create a renewable resource of capacity \(1\); activity \(a_o\) demands one unit of the resource corresponding to its prescribed machine throughout execution. Then project schedules are exactly job-shop schedules, and their project makespan equals the shop makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operations become project activities, job orders become precedence arcs, and each unary machine becomes a capacity-one renewable resource.
assumptions_latex: Every operation has one prescribed machine and is nonpreemptive.
Machines process at most one operation at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}^{\mathrm{project}}=C_{\max}^{\mathrm{shop}}\), with feasibility preserved in both directions.

children.title: Coloring-Based Reductions
children.top_down_role: Scheduling reductions built from graph-coloring compatibility or conflict structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring-Based Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical encoding of graph coloring as unit-time conflict scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\ge1\), create one unit-time activity \(j_v\) for every vertex \(v\), and permit start times in \(\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\). For every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\), impose the conflict constraint \(S_{j_u}\ne S_{j_v}\). A map \(c(v)=S_{j_v}+1\) is then a proper \(k\)-coloring exactly when the corresponding activities satisfy every conflict constraint within the \(k\)-slot horizon. The construction has size polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices become unit activities, colors become time slots, and graph edges prohibit simultaneous placement of their endpoint activities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph.
Activities may occupy any of the \(k\) discrete slots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is }k\text{-colorable}\iff\text{the constructed conflict schedule is feasible}\).

children.title: Partitioning-Based Reductions
children.top_down_role: Scheduling reductions built from balanced partitioning or numerical allocation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioning-Based Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical reduction from PARTITION to two-machine makespan scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) with total \(A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\), create one nonpreemptive job \(j_i\) of processing time \(p_i=a_i\) and two identical parallel machines. Set the makespan threshold to \(K=A/2\). A schedule with \(C_{\max}\le K\) exists if and only if the jobs assigned to either machine have total processing time \(A/2\), equivalently if and only if the integers admit a partition into two subsets of equal sum. The construction is polynomial in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition numbers become processing times on two identical machines; meeting half the total-load threshold is equivalent to an equal partition.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) for every \(i\).
Jobs are nonpreemptive and available at time \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:\sum_{i\in S}a_i=A/2\iff C_{\max}^*\le A/2\).

children.title: Routing-Based Reductions
children.top_down_role: Scheduling reductions built from paths, tours, vehicle movement, or route selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Routing-Based Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding prescribed temporal routes as job-shop operation chains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider demands \(q\), each prescribed an ordered route \((r_{q1},\ldots,r_{q\ell_q})\) through unit-capacity resources, with traversal durations \(d_{qi}>0\). Create a job for each demand and an operation \(o_{qi}\) of duration \(d_{qi}\) on machine \(r_{qi}\). Impose \(o_{qi}\prec o_{q,i+1}\) along every route. Requiring traversals sharing a resource not to overlap is then identical to the job-shop machine constraint. Thus a temporal routing plan of horizon \(K\) exists if and only if the constructed job-shop instance has makespan at most \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each prescribed route becomes a job, each traversal becomes an operation, and unit-capacity route conflicts become machine nonoverlap constraints.
assumptions_latex: Every demand follows a fixed ordered route.
Each resource has unit capacity and traversal is nonpreemptive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{routing horizon}\le K\iff C_{\max}^{\mathrm{shop}}\le K\).

notation.meaning: Resource used at route position i by demand q.

children.title: Tractability-Boundary Transfers
children.top_down_role: Reductions used to locate transitions between tractable and intractable scheduling classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Tractability-Boundary Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of polynomial solvability and hardness across exact polynomial reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\le_p B\) denote a polynomial-time many-one reduction between scheduling decision problems. If \(B\) is decidable in polynomial time, then \(A\) is decidable in polynomial time by computing the reduction and invoking the algorithm for \(B\). If \(A\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard, then \(B\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard. Therefore, reductions directed toward an easier problem transfer tractability backward, whereas reductions directed from a hard problem transfer hardness forward. If both \(A\le_p B\) and \(B\le_p A\), the problems share the same polynomial-time tractability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial reductions transfer algorithms backward and hardness forward; mutual reductions place two scheduling problems on the same tractability boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are finitely encoded decision problems.
The reductions preserve yes-instances and no-instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\in\mathrm{P}\Rightarrow A\in\mathrm{P}\), and \(A\text{ NP-hard}\Rightarrow B\text{ NP-hard}\).

children.title: Approximation-Boundary Transfers
children.top_down_role: Reductions that preserve or transfer approximation thresholds across problem families.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Boundary Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation preservation under polynomial scheduling reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let scheduling minimization problems \(P\) and \(Q\) have nonnegative objectives. Suppose polynomial-time maps \(f\) and \(g\) send every instance \(I\) of \(P\) to \(f(I)\) of \(Q\), and every feasible solution \(y\) for \(f(I)\) to \(g(I,y)\) for \(I\). If constants \(\alpha,\beta>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{OPT}_Q(f(I))\leq \alpha\operatorname{OPT}_P(I)\) and \(c_P(g(I,y))-\operatorname{OPT}_P(I)\leq\beta(c_Q(y)-\operatorname{OPT}_Q(f(I)))\), then a \(\rho\)-approximation for \(Q\) yields a solution of value at most \((1+\alpha\beta(\rho-1))\operatorname{OPT}_P(I)\). Thus approximation or inapproximability boundaries transfer with the induced factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial reduction transfers approximation guarantees when it controls both optimum scaling and the decoded solution’s excess cost.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are minimization problems with positive finite optima on the considered instances.
\(f\) and \(g\) are computable in polynomial time.
The displayed optimum and excess-cost inequalities hold for every relevant instance and decoded feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_P(g(I,y))\leq (1+\alpha\beta(\rho-1))\operatorname{OPT}_P(I)\) whenever \(c_Q(y)\leq\rho\operatorname{OPT}_Q(f(I))\).

notation.meaning: Objective-value functions for the two scheduling problems.
Approximation ratio achieved for the target problem.

children.title: List-Scheduling Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation guarantees obtained from ordered job lists and availability-based placement.

knowledge_statements.title: List-Scheduling Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graham’s bound for identical-machine makespan scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(n\) independent, nonpreemptive jobs with processing times \(p_j\geq0\) on \(m\geq1\) identical parallel machines. Process the jobs in any fixed list order, assigning each job to a machine of currently minimum load. If \(C_{\mathrm{LS}}\) is the resulting makespan and \(C^*\) is the optimal makespan, then \[C_{\mathrm{LS}}\leq\left(2-\frac1m\right)C^*.\] Indeed, if job \(j\) finishes last and begins at \(s_j\), minimum-load assignment gives \(s_j\leq(\sum_{i\ne j}p_i)/m\), while \(C^*\geq\max\{\sum_i p_i/m,p_j\}\); these inequalities imply the stated guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning each next job to a least-loaded identical machine gives a makespan at most 2 minus 1 over the machine count times optimal.
assumptions_latex: Jobs are independent and available at time zero.
Machines are identical, and processing is nonpreemptive.
The list order is fixed independently of assignment ties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{LS}}/C^*\leq2-1/m\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and Graham bound match the list-scheduling leaf, but no source reference is provided. The sentences beginning with “Indeed” constitute proof text and must be removed before acceptance after an authoritative theorem-level citation is supplied.

children.title: Priority-Rule Approximation
children.top_down_role: Guarantees associated with priority indices or ordering criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Rule Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Priority-list scheduling on identical parallel machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input processing times \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\geq0\), \(m\geq1\) identical machines, and priority keys \(q_j\). Order jobs by nonincreasing \(q_j\), using a fixed tie rule. Initialize machine loads \(L_i=0\). In priority order, assign job \(j\) to an index \(i\in\arg\min_k L_k\), then update \(L_i\leftarrow L_i+p_j\). Output the assignments and \(C=\max_iL_i\). Every priority rule of this form is a list schedule and therefore satisfies \(C\leq(2-1/m)C^*\). For the longest-processing-time rule \(q_j=p_j\), the sharper bound \(C\leq(4/3-1/(3m))C^*\) holds when \(m\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort jobs by a priority key and repeatedly use a least-loaded machine; arbitrary priorities inherit the list bound, while longest-first has a sharper bound.
assumptions_latex: Jobs are independent, nonpreemptive, and available at time zero.
The \(m\) machines are identical.
Priority ordering and all tie rules are deterministic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the priority-rule leaf, and the stated arbitrary-list and LPT bounds are standard for identical-machine makespan scheduling. Both guarantees nevertheless lack authoritative citations with theorem or page locators.

children.title: List-Priority Guarantee Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instance conditions separating strong guarantees from adverse performance.

knowledge_statements.title: List-Priority Guarantee Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tight family for arbitrary-order list scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(m\geq2\), consider \(m\) identical machines and a list containing first \(m(m-1)\) unit-length jobs and then one job of length \(m\). List scheduling distributes the unit jobs evenly, leaving every machine at load \(m-1\); the last job therefore finishes at \(2m-1\). An optimal schedule runs the length-\(m\) job alone on one machine and partitions the unit jobs among the remaining \(m-1\) machines, each receiving \(m\) jobs, so \(C^*=m\). Hence \(C_{\mathrm{LS}}/C^*=2-1/m\), and no smaller universal ratio is valid for arbitrary list orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family with many unit jobs followed by one long job attains the list-scheduling ratio 2 minus 1 over the machine count.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq2\) identical machines are available.
Jobs are independent, nonpreemptive, and released at time zero.
The long job appears after all unit jobs in the list.

notation.meaning: Makespan of the specified list schedule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role exactly fits the guarantee-boundary leaf, and the construction and ratio calculation are internally correct. No inspectable source is cited for the tight family or its universal lower-bound interpretation.

children.title: Dual Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation frameworks organized around target-value feasibility decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-or-rejection framework for makespan minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\rho\geq1\). A \(\rho\)-dual approximation algorithm for makespan scheduling takes an instance \(I\) and threshold \(T>0\), runs in polynomial time, and returns either a feasible schedule of makespan at most \(\rho T\) or the declaration \(T<C^*(I)\). The declaration must be sound, but when \(C^*(I)\leq T\) the algorithm must return a schedule. Given bounds \(0<L\leq C^*(I)\leq U\), querying thresholds and retaining the smallest accepted one yields a \(\rho\)-approximation; with multiplicative threshold precision \(1+\varepsilon\), the returned makespan is at most \(\rho(1+\varepsilon)C^*(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At threshold T, either construct a schedule within rho times T or soundly certify that the optimum exceeds T.
assumptions_latex: The objective is makespan minimization and feasible schedules can be checked in polynomial time.
The dual procedure is complete whenever \(C^*(I)\leq T\).
Positive lower and upper bounds on \(C^*(I)\) are available for threshold search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multiplicative threshold search produces a schedule with makespan at most \(\rho(1+\varepsilon)C^*(I)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the dual-approximation leaf. The threshold behavior and resulting multiplicative-search guarantee are plausible, but the exact soundness/completeness convention and the rho-times-one-plus-epsilon conclusion need an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Parametric Search
children.top_down_role: Search over candidate objective thresholds within scheduling approximation frameworks.

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone threshold search for approximate scheduling feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D(T)\in\{\mathrm{reject},\mathrm{accept}\}\) be monotone: acceptance at \(T\) implies acceptance at every \(T'\geq T\). Given \(0<L\\leq U\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and a witness-producing decision procedure, repeatedly choose a threshold \(T\) between the current bounds, query \(D(T)\), replace the upper bound by \(T\) and store its witness upon acceptance, and replace the lower bound by \(T\) upon rejection. Stop when \(U\leq(1+\varepsilon)L\), and output the stored witness at \(U\). Geometric bisection in logarithmic coordinates uses \(O(\log(\log(U/L)/\log(1+\varepsilon)))\) decision calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary search in logarithmic threshold space locates the smallest accepted scale and returns its feasibility witness.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is monotone and each accepted query supplies a witness.
The initial lower threshold is rejected and the initial upper threshold is accepted.
Thresholds and arithmetic operations have an appropriate finite encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output threshold satisfies \(U\leq(1+\varepsilon)T^*\), where \(T^*=\inf\{T:D(T)=\mathrm{accept}\}\).

notation.meaning: Current rejected and accepted threshold bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the parametric-search leaf, but the input condition contains malformed TeX (`0<L\\leq U`), and the decision-call bound depends on a precise logarithmic-bisection and encoding model. No source is supplied to validate this variant or its complexity.

children.title: Feasibility-Threshold Coupling
children.top_down_role: How approximate feasibility information supports objective-value localization.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Threshold Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converting relaxed threshold feasibility into an approximation ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C^*\) be the minimum makespan and let an oracle at threshold \(T\) reject only when \(T<C^*\), while every accepted query returns a schedule of makespan at most \(\rho T\). If threshold search returns an accepted \(\widehat T\) satisfying \(\widehat T\leq(1+\varepsilon)C^*\), then its witness has makespan \(C\leq\rho(1+\varepsilon)C^*\). Conversely, any false rejection at some \(T\geq C^*\) destroys this implication because search may move its lower bound above the optimum. Thus approximation follows from the coupling of rejection soundness, acceptance completeness, witness dilation, and threshold accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound monotone threshold oracle plus a rho-dilated witness and accurate search yields a rho times one-plus-epsilon approximation.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling objective is makespan minimization.
Rejection is sound and acceptance returns a witness of makespan at most \(\rho T\).
The selected accepted threshold is within factor \(1+\varepsilon\) of the optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C/C^*\leq\rho(1+\varepsilon)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits the coupling leaf, and the displayed approximation implication follows from the stated accepted-threshold bound. An authoritative source is still required, and the record should distinguish rejection soundness from the completeness or monotonicity conditions needed to ensure that search actually finds such an accepted threshold.

children.title: LP-Rounding Scheduling Methods
children.top_down_role: Scheduling approximations derived from rounding fractional linear-program solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: LP-Rounding Scheduling Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic relaxation-and-rounding template for scheduling minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a scheduling instance \(I\), formulate a linear relaxation \(P(I)=\{x:Ax\geq b,\ x\geq0\}\) whose integral points encode feasible schedules, and minimize a linear surrogate \(c^{\mathsf T}x\). Compute an optimal fractional solution \(x^*\), then apply a polynomial-time rounding map \(R(I,x^*)\) producing an integral schedule \(S\). If the relaxation is valid and the rounding analysis establishes \(C(S)\leq\alpha c^{\mathsf T}x^*\), then \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*\leq C^*(I)\) implies \(C(S)\leq\alpha C^*(I)\). The algorithm outputs \(S\); failure to preserve feasibility or the displayed cost inequality invalidates the guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a valid scheduling LP, round its fractional optimum to a feasible schedule, and bound rounded cost by a multiple of the LP value.
assumptions_latex: Every integral feasible schedule has a corresponding point in \(P(I)\) with surrogate value no greater than its objective.
The LP and rounding map are computable in polynomial time.
Rounding always returns a feasible schedule satisfying the stated \(\alpha\)-bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(R(I,x^*))\leq\alpha C^*(I)\).

notation.meaning: Rounding map from fractional points to schedules.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role is suitable for the LP-rounding-methods leaf, and the conditional relaxation argument is coherent. It remains only a generic template rather than a specified scheduling method, and no scheduling or approximation source supports the stated interface.

children.title: Configuration-Based Scheduling Methods
children.top_down_role: Approaches organized around feasible machine, resource, or time configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Based Scheduling Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Configuration LP for assignment-style makespan feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a makespan threshold \(T\). For each machine \(i\), let \(\mathcal C_i(T)\) be the subsets \(C\) of jobs eligible on \(i\) with \(\sum_{j\in C}p_{ij}\leq T\). Introduce \(x_{iC}\geq0\), interpreted as fractional selection of configuration \(C\) on machine \(i\). The configuration relaxation is \[\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_i(T)}x_{iC}\leq1\quad(i),\qquad \sum_i\sum_{C\in\mathcal C_i(T):j\in C}x_{iC}\geq1\quad(j).\] An integral solution selecting at most one configuration per machine and covering every job encodes a schedule of makespan at most \(T\); a fractional solution is a relaxation of such a schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A configuration LP fractionally chooses one feasible job bundle per machine while requiring every job to be covered.
assumptions_latex: Jobs are assigned nonpreemptively to eligible machines.
\(p_{ij}\geq0\) is the processing time of job \(j\) on machine \(i\).
Configurations contain only eligible jobs and have total load at most \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every integral feasible point induces a schedule with makespan at most \(T\), and every such schedule induces an integral feasible point.

notation.meaning: Threshold-feasible job configurations for machine i.
Fractional weight placed on configuration C of machine i.
Processing time of job j on machine i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the configuration-based-methods leaf. The covering formulation can encode a schedule after choosing one selected occurrence for each multiply covered job, but that decoding step is not stated, and no source verifies the covering-versus-equality convention or formulation.

children.title: Configuration-Rounding Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Rounding structures specific to configuration-based relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Rounding Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient interface from fractional configurations to bounded-load assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) satisfy the threshold-\(T\) configuration relaxation. A configuration-rounding interface with factor \(\alpha\geq1\) consists of a polynomial-time map producing assignment variables \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) such that \[\sum_i y_{ij}=1\quad(j),\qquad y_{ij}=0\ \text{if job }j\text{ is ineligible on }i,\qquad \sum_jp_{ij}y_{ij}\leq\alpha T\quad(i).\] These three predicates respectively preserve job coverage, eligibility, and bounded machine load. Whenever they hold, the rounded assignment is a feasible nonpreemptive schedule of makespan at most \(\alpha T\); marginal preservation alone does not imply the load bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid configuration-rounding interface must assign every job once, respect eligibility, and limit every rounded machine load to alpha times the threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for the threshold-\(T\) configuration relaxation.
Each job is nonpreemptively assigned to exactly one eligible machine.
The rounding map runs in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\) encodes a feasible schedule with makespan at most \(\alpha T\).

notation.meaning: Indicator that job j is assigned to machine i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the configuration-rounding-interface leaf, and the three displayed predicates are sufficient for the stated makespan conclusion. No authoritative citation is supplied for this interface or for its connection to configuration-LP rounding.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Large–Small-Job PTAS Construction for Two-Machine Nonpreemptive Makespan
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the extracted two-machine construction without adding a performance theorem not stated in the algorithm body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(0<\epsilon<1\) and set \(\mathcal L=\max\{p_{\max},\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\}\). Classify job \(j\) as big if \(p_j>\epsilon\mathcal L\) and small otherwise, and let \(P^s\) be the total small-job processing time. Form a modified instance containing every big job and \(\left\lfloor P^s/(\epsilon\mathcal L)\right\rfloor\) artificial small jobs of length \(\epsilon\mathcal L\). Enumerate an optimal two-machine schedule of the modified instance, and let \(P_i^{s'}\) be the artificial small-job load assigned to machine \(i\). Preserve the big-job assignments, then place original small jobs successively on machine 1 within reserved space \(P_1^{s'}+2\epsilon\mathcal L\); when the next small job does not fit, place it and all remaining small jobs on machine 2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split jobs into big and small jobs using the threshold epsilon times L, replace the small-job workload by equal artificial pieces, optimally enumerate the resulting two-machine instance, preserve its big-job assignments, and unpack the original small jobs into reserved space on machine 1 before sending the remainder to machine 2.
assumptions_latex: p_j\text{ is the processing time of job }j
0<\epsilon<1
\text{jobs are scheduled nonpreemptively on two machines}
\mathcal L=\max\{p_{\max},\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure constructs a schedule of the original jobs by transferring the enumerated big-job assignment and repacking the small jobs.}

source_evidence.locator: Appendices / D. Complexity Theory / Algorithm D.5.3

source_refs.locator: Appendices / D. Complexity Theory / Algorithm D.5.3

knowledge_statements.title: Large–Small-Job PTAS Construction for Two-Machine Nonpreemptive Makespan

source_witnesses.locator: Appendices / D. Complexity Theory / Algorithm D.5.3

children.title: Rounding-Based Approximation Schemes
children.top_down_role: Schemes based on discretizing processing times, loads, costs, or schedule states.

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding-Based Approximation Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PTAS template based on geometric processing-time rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a makespan instance and \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choose a scale \(B>0\), classify jobs below a prescribed \(\varepsilon B\) threshold as small, and round every remaining processing time upward to a value in a geometric grid with ratio \(1+\varepsilon\). Enumerate or optimize over the polynomially many rounded job types and machine patterns, reconstruct assignments using original processing times, and insert small jobs by a load-balancing rule. Accept the first threshold whose reconstruction succeeds. If rounding and insertion increase every machine load by at most \(O(\varepsilon)B\), and the accepted \(B\leq(1+O(\varepsilon))C^*\), the output has makespan \((1+O(\varepsilon))C^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round large processing times to few geometric types, optimize the compressed instance, then insert small jobs while controlling additive load.
assumptions_latex: For fixed \(\varepsilon\), the number of rounded types and enumerated patterns is polynomial in the input size.
Reconstruction preserves eligibility and assignment feasibility.
Rounding and small-job insertion add at most \(O(\varepsilon)B\) load per machine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstructed schedule satisfies \(C\leq(1+O(\varepsilon))C^*\) and is computed in polynomial time for fixed \(\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the rounding-based-schemes leaf, but the statement does not identify a scheduling problem class for which the enumeration, reconstruction, and insertion assumptions hold. The hidden constants in the O(epsilon) terms also prevent an exact PTAS guarantee from being checked without a problem-specific source.

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Approximation Schemes
children.top_down_role: Schemes based on compressed state spaces or bounded numeric ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Programming Approximation Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PTAS template using rounded finite-state dynamic programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given accuracy \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), round job sizes or resource consumptions so that only \(K(\varepsilon)\) distinct values remain. Define a dynamic-programming state recording the counts of scheduled rounded types and a rounded load or capacity profile; initialize the empty state, and for each job type transition by assigning one job to an admissible machine or pattern. Discard dominated states with componentwise no smaller resource use. At termination choose the feasible state of minimum rounded objective and reconstruct its schedule. If every original schedule maps to a state of value at most \((1+\varepsilon)C^*\), and reconstruction does not increase that value, the algorithm is a PTAS whenever the state count is polynomial for fixed \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round data to finitely many types, optimize a compressed state space by dynamic programming, discard dominated states, and reconstruct a near-optimal schedule.
assumptions_latex: For fixed \(\varepsilon\), rounding leaves \(K(\varepsilon)\) types and polynomially many nondominated states.
Transitions exactly represent feasible assignments in the rounded instance.
Rounding and reconstruction together lose at most a factor \(1+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstructed schedule has objective at most \((1+\varepsilon)C^*\) in time polynomial in the input size for each fixed \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Optimal objective value of the original instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the dynamic-programming-schemes leaf, but the record is a conditional template rather than a fully specified scheduling algorithm. The state dimension, dominance relation, transition system, polynomial state bound, and approximation loss require specialization and an authoritative source.

children.title: Rounded-State Approximation Schemes
children.top_down_role: Scheme architectures coupling discretization with dynamic state enumeration.

assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem is a minimization problem with optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)>0\).
For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a finite rounded state set \(S_\varepsilon(I)\) and exact transition dynamic program are available.
Rounding any reachable exact state to its dominating rounded state increases the represented objective by at most \(\varepsilon\mathrm{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned schedule satisfies \(F(A_\varepsilon(I))\leq(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}(I)\); the construction is a PTAS whenever \(|S_\varepsilon(I)|\) and the transition work are polynomial in \(|I|\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Finite set of rounded dynamic-programming states
Schedule returned after rounded-state optimization and reconstruction

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard rounded-state dynamic-programming scheme under an explicit bounded-rounding-loss hypothesis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic minimization scheme; the state representation and rounding map remain problem-specific.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(I\) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), construct \(S_\varepsilon(I)\) by rounding every state coordinate according to the prescribed grid. Initialize the rounded image of the empty schedule. For each job, enumerate every feasible transition from each retained state, round the successor to its dominating representative, and retain for each representative a predecessor of minimum represented objective. After the final job, select the minimum-objective terminal state and reconstruct its schedule \(A_\varepsilon(I)\). The domination and loss assumptions imply \(F(A_\varepsilon(I))\leq\mathrm{OPT}(I)+\varepsilon\mathrm{OPT}(I)=(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round dynamic-programming states, optimize exactly over the finite rounded state graph, and reconstruct a schedule whose objective is within a factor one plus epsilon of optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounded-State Approximation Schemes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No scheduling-specific source is cited. The per-rounding loss assumption does not control accumulated loss across multiple transitions, so the stated PTAS guarantee is not established reliably.

assumptions_latex: For every instance \(I\), \(F^*(I)>0\) denotes the optimum of a polynomially encoded minimization problem.
Algorithms are polynomial-time in the ordinary deterministic computational model unless stated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A threshold \(\alpha\) is an inapproximability boundary when ratios below \(\alpha\) are complexity-theoretically impossible while ratios arbitrarily above \(\alpha\) are achievable in polynomial time.

notation.meaning: Optimal objective value on instance I
Objective value returned by algorithm A

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard threshold formulation for approximation hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract minimization boundary; concrete scheduling classes require separate reductions and complexity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A value \(\alpha\geq1\) is a sharp polynomial-time inapproximability boundary if both conditions hold. First, for every \(\delta>0\), some polynomial-time algorithm \(A_\delta\) satisfies \(F_{A_\delta}(I)\leq(\alpha+\delta)F^*(I)\) on every instance \(I\). Second, under the stated complexity assumption, no polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) satisfies \(F_A(I)\leq(\alpha-\u0000delta)F^*(I)\) on every instance for any fixed \(\delta>0\). If only the second condition is known, \(\alpha\) is a lower inapproximability threshold rather than a sharp boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inapproximability boundary separates approximation ratios achievable in polynomial time from strictly better ratios ruled out by an explicit complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.title: Inapproximability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hardness claim has no supporting source or explicit complexity hypothesis. The expression containing a NUL-corrupted delta command is invalid LaTeX and prevents reliable interpretation.

children.title: Online Arrival Regimes
children.top_down_role: Models distinguished by when jobs, requests, or availability information is revealed.

assumptions_latex: Jobs are indexed by \(j=1,2,\ldots\) and have nondecreasing release times \(r_j\).
The information revealed with job \(j\) is denoted by \(x_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is online precisely when every decision made by time \(t\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_t\), so it cannot depend on unrevealed jobs.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard filtration-based definition of online arrivals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers adversarial arrival sequences; stochastic assumptions may be added by specifying a probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online arrival regime is specified by a sequence \((r_j,x_j)_{j\geq1}\) and the information filtration \(\mathcal F_t=\sigma(x_j:r_j\leq t)\). Before time \(r_j\), neither the existence of job \(j\) nor any component of \(x_j\) is available to the scheduler. At time \(r_j\), the regime reveals exactly the declared components of \(x_j\), such as processing requirements, eligibility sets, deadlines, or weights. A scheduling policy is admissible only if every assignment, ordering, or speed decision taken at time \(t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs and declared attributes become known only at release; every online decision may use the revealed history but not future arrivals.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Arrival Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No online-scheduling source is supplied. The filtration notation presupposes random variables and an underlying measurable probability space, whereas the scope simultaneously describes adversarial arrivals without defining such a space.

children.title: Online Dispatching Policies
children.top_down_role: Immediate assignment or sequencing choices made under partial information.

assumptions_latex: At release \(r_j\), job \(j\), its feasible action set \(D_j\), and the current state \(s_{j-1}\) are known.
Dispatch decisions are irrevocable once issued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an online dispatch sequence \((d_j)\) with \(d_j\in D_j(s_{j-1})\), determined solely by information available at each release.

notation.meaning: Feasible dispatch actions for job j in the current state
System state immediately before dispatching job j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generic score-based formalization of an online dispatch policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic immediate-dispatch template; the feasible actions and score encode the scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On arrival of job \(j\), observe its revealed data and current state \(s_{j-1}\). Form the currently feasible set \(D_j(s_{j-1})\). If this set is empty, return the model's declared rejection or infeasibility outcome. Otherwise choose \(d_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in D_j(s_{j-1})}\phi_j(d;s_{j-1})\), resolve ties by a fixed history-independent rule, irrevocably issue \(d_j\), and update the state to \(s_j=T_j(s_{j-1},d_j)\). The policy stops after the final arrival and outputs the resulting assignment and schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each release, score the currently feasible dispatch actions, choose a minimum-score action using fixed tie-breaking, commit it, and update the schedule state.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Dispatching Policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives one score-minimizing immediate-dispatch template, not a characterization of online dispatching policies generally. A source is needed to justify this particular policy class and model conventions.

children.title: Arrival-Dispatch Timing Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Performance effects of decision timing relative to information revelation.

assumptions_latex: Job \(j\) is revealed at time \(r_j\).
A feasible dispatch time \(d_j\) must satisfy \(d_j\geq r_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Immediate dispatch is the boundary case \(d_j=r_j\); deferred dispatch permits \(d_j>r_j\) and therefore access to the larger information set \(\mathcal F_{d_j}\).

notation.meaning: Time at which job j receives its irrevocable dispatch decision

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: timing boundary defined by equality or strict delay between release and commitment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates immediate commitment from models allowing information-gathering delay before assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every job \(j\), let \(r_j\) be its release time and \(d_j\) the time of its irrevocable dispatch. The immediate-dispatch regime imposes \(d_j=r_j\), so the decision must be \(\mathcal F_{r_j}\)-measurable. A deferred-dispatch regime permits \(d_j>r_j\), subject to any deadline or buffer constraint, and the decision may be \(\mathcal F_{d_j}\)-measurable. Thus immediate dispatch is the zero-delay boundary of deferred dispatch. Any competitive comparison across this boundary must hold fixed all other permissions, including preemption, migration, rejection, and knowledge of processing times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Immediate dispatch commits at release; deferred dispatch may wait and exploit later arrivals. Comparisons must keep preemption, migration, rejection, and revealed data fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Arrival-Dispatch Timing Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The timing distinction is plausible, but no source supports the precise commitment model, filtration convention, or list of permissions that must be held fixed.

children.title: Online Machine Choice
children.top_down_role: Online assignment among identical, related, unrelated, or eligible machines.

assumptions_latex: Job \(j\) reveals processing time \(p_{ij}\in(0,\infty]\) on each machine \(i\in M\).
The assignment of each arriving job is immediate and irrevocable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy assigns job \(j\) to a machine minimizing its prospective completion load \(L_i+p_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: Processing requirement of job j on machine i
Load already assigned to machine i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard greedy online machine-selection rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy immediate assignment for unrelated machines; identical and related machines are special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(L_i=0\) for every \(i\in M\). When job \(j\) arrives, observe \((p_{ij})_{i\in M}\) and form \(E_j=\{i\in M:p_{ij}<\infty\}\). If \(E_j=\varnothing\), report that the job is ineligible on every machine. Otherwise choose \(i_j\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{i\in E_j}(L_i+p_{ij})\), using a fixed tie-breaking order, assign \(j\) irrevocably to \(i_j\), and update \(L_{i_j}\leftarrow L_{i_j}+p_{i_jj}\). After the final arrival, output the assignment and its induced per-machine job lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each arriving job irrevocably to an eligible machine with minimum load after assignment, then update that machine's load.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Machine Choice

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind is appropriate for the stated greedy algorithm, but the broad leaf title does not itself identify this minimum-prospective-load rule, and no online load-balancing source is cited.

children.title: Online Load Balancing
children.top_down_role: Competitive control of machine loads under sequential job revelation.

assumptions_latex: Jobs arrive sequentially and must be assigned irrevocably to eligible machines.
The objective is to minimize the final maximum assigned load.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An online algorithm is \(\rho\)-competitive with additive constant \(\beta\) exactly when \(C_A(\sigma)\leq\rho C^*(\sigma)+\beta\) for every finite arrival sequence \(\sigma\).

notation.meaning: Makespan produced online by algorithm A
Offline optimal makespan for the same sequence

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard makespan and competitive-ratio definition for online load balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Makespan formulation with optional additive constant; machine environment and eligibility must be fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an arrival sequence \(\sigma\), an irrevocable assignment \(a\) induces machine loads \(L_i(a,sigma)=\sum_{j:a(j)=i}p_{ij}\) and makespan \(C(a,sigma)=\max_{i\u0000in M}L_i(a,sigma)\). An online load-balancing algorithm \(A\) selects \(a(j)\) using only the prefix ending at job \(j\), and its cost is \(C_A(sigma)=C(a_A,sigma)\). The offline benchmark is \(C^*(sigma)=\min_a C(a,sigma)\), where the minimum ranges over feasible assignments knowing all of \(sigma\). The competitive guarantee \((\rho,beta)\) requires \(C_A(sigma)\leq\rho C^*(sigma)+beta\) for every finite \(sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online load balancing minimizes final maximum machine load; competitiveness compares its makespan with the offline optimum on every arrival sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Load Balancing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied. The statement contains corrupted or missing TeX commands, including the NUL-corrupted membership expression and undelimited textual forms of sigma and beta, so it does not faithfully encode the formulas in the conclusion.

children.title: Assignment-Balance Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: How local machine choices influence global load disparity and competitive performance.

assumptions_latex: Each feasible assignment \(a\) has total assignment cost \(K(a)\) and maximum load \(B(a)\).
At least one feasible assignment satisfies the chosen cost budget \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frontier \(B^*(C)\) is nonincreasing in \(C\), and an assignment is Pareto efficient precisely when no feasible assignment weakly improves both criteria and strictly improves one.

notation.meaning: Best balance attainable under cost budget C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria assignment model trading total placement cost against maximum machine load.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be the set of feasible assignments. The budgeted assignment-balance frontier is \[B^*(C)=\min\{B(a):a\in\mathcal A,\ K(a)\leq C\}.\] If \(C_1\leq C_2\), then the feasible set at \(C_1\) is contained in that at \(C_2\), hence \(B^*(C_2)\leq B^*(C_1)\). An assignment \(a\in\mathcal A\) is Pareto efficient when no \(a'\in\mathcal A\) satisfies \(K(a')\leq K(a)\) and \(B(a')\leq B(a)\), with at least one strict inequality. Supported frontier points minimize \(K(a)+\lambda B(a)\) for some \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff frontier gives the least possible maximum load under each assignment-cost budget; relaxing the budget cannot worsen optimal balance.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-Balance Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines a static offline bicriteria Pareto frontier. It contains no arrival order, online information restriction, irrevocable decision rule, or online performance comparison, so it does not match this leaf under Online Assignment-Balance Tradeoffs.

children.title: Resource-Augmented Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Online guarantees under additional machines, capacity, memory, or related resources.

assumptions_latex: Algorithm \(A\) receives augmentation parameter \(s\geq1\).
The offline benchmark uses the unaugmented machine environment and the same job instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A \(c\)-competitive resource-augmented guarantee is \(F_A^{(s)}(I)\leq cF_{operatorname{OPT}}^{(1)}(I)+beta\) for every instance \(I\), with augmentation excluded from the benchmark.

notation.meaning: Resource augmentation factor available only to the online algorithm
Objective achieved by A with augmentation s
Offline optimum in the baseline environment

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard asymmetric benchmark definition for resource augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmentation may mean faster processors, extra machines, memory, or capacity, but must be declared explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Resource-augmented scheduling compares an online algorithm operating in an enhanced environment with an offline optimum operating in the baseline environment. For augmentation factor \(s\geq1\), let \(F_A^{(s)}(I)\) be the objective attained by \(A\) and let \(F_{\operatorname{OPT}}^{(1)}(I)\) be the baseline optimum on the same instance \(I\). Algorithm \(A\) is \(c\)-competitive with augmentation \(s\) and additive constant \(\beta\geq0\) if \(F_A^{(s)}(I)\leq cF_{\operatorname{OPT}}^{(1)}(I)+\beta\) for every \(I\). The resource, augmentation map, feasibility rules, and objective must be fixed before this comparison is meaningful.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource-augmented guarantee compares an online scheduler given extra declared capacity with an offline optimum using only baseline resources.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Augmented Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymmetric benchmark is standard in spirit, but the inequality assumes a minimization objective without saying so. The conclusion also contains malformed operator-name and beta notation, and no resource-augmentation source is cited.

children.title: Speed-Scaling Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Scheduling with controllable processing speeds and performance or energy criteria.

assumptions_latex: Each job \(j\) has release time \(r_j\), work \(w_j>0\), and optional weight \(v_j>0\).
A processor may choose measurable speed \(s(t)\geq0\), incurring power \(P(s(t))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible speed-scaling schedule completes each job's work while optimizing an objective combining service performance with energy \(E=int_0^infty P(s(t))\,dt\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard continuous-speed energy-aware scheduling model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous single-processor formulation; multiprocessor, discrete-speed, and migration variants require additional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A speed-scaling schedule chooses a measurable speed \(s(t)\geq0\) and, whenever \(s(t)>0\), allocates that processing rate among jobs released by time \(t\). If \(x_j(t)\) is the rate assigned to job \(j\), feasibility requires \(x_j(t)geq0\), \(x_j(t)=0\) for \(t<r_j\), \(sum_jx_j(t)leq s(t)\), and \(int_{r_j}^{C_j}x_j(t)\,dt=w_j\). Energy is \(E=int_0^infty P(s(t))\,dt\). A speed-scaling objective specifies a performance term, such as weighted flow \(sum_jv_j(C_j-r_j)\), and its combination with \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A speed-scaling scheduler varies processor speed over time, completes every released job's work, and trades service performance against integrated power consumption.
knowledge_statements.title: Speed-Scaling Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical model cannot be accepted as written: integral, infinity, summation, inequality, and membership commands are missing backslashes, and the completion time C_j is used without definition. No speed-scaling source is supplied.

children.title: Augmentation-Speed Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons between extra capacity and faster processing as sources of online advantage.

assumptions_latex: For each augmentation level \(s\geq1\), algorithms are compared with the same unaugmented offline benchmark.
The objective and additive-constant convention are fixed across augmentation levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal competitive frontier \(\rho^*(s)\) is nonincreasing in \(s\), provided an algorithm may leave surplus augmented capacity unused.

notation.meaning: Competitive ratio of algorithm A at augmentation s
Best achievable ratio at augmentation s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: monotonicity follows from nested resource sets when surplus capacity may be ignored
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract competitive frontier for nested augmentation levels; quantitative rates are problem-specific.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(s\geq1\), define \(\rho_A(s)\) as the least \(\rho\) for which algorithm \(A\), using augmentation \(s\), satisfies the fixed competitive inequality against the baseline optimum. Define \(\rho^*(s)=\inf_A\rho_A(s)\). If every schedule feasible with augmentation \(s_1\) remains feasible with augmentation \(s_2\geq s_1\), and an algorithm at \(s_2\) may emulate one at \(s_1\) by ignoring surplus capacity, then \(\rho^*(s_2)\leq\rho^*(s_1)\). The function \(s\mapstoho^*(s)\) is therefore the augmentation-speed tradeoff frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When higher augmentation contains all lower-augmentation capabilities, the best achievable competitive ratio cannot worsen as augmentation increases.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation-Speed Tradeoffs

children.title: Prediction-Augmented Scheduling

knowledge_statements.title: Prediction-Augmented Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online scheduling with instance predictions available before irrevocable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an online scheduling problem with instance sequence \(I\), a prediction-augmented algorithm receives, in addition to each revealed request, a prediction \(\widehat I\) of designated unknown data. Its cost is \(A(I,\widehat I)\). Relative to an error measure \(\eta(I,\widehat I)\), the algorithm is \(\alpha\)-consistent and \(\beta\)-robust if \(A(I,I)\leq \alpha\,\mathrm{OPT}(I)\) and \(A(I,\widehat I)\leq \beta\,\mathrm{OPT}(I)\) for every admissible pair \((I,\widehat I)\), respectively. An error-dependent guarantee has the form \(A(I,\widehat I)\leq f(\eta(I,\widehat I))\mathrm{OPT}(I)+g(I,\widehat I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prediction-augmented scheduler uses forecasts of unrevealed data and is evaluated by its perfect-prediction consistency, worst-case robustness, and performance as prediction error grows.

\(\mathrm{OPT}(I)>0\), and smaller objective values are preferred.

Its population performance under distribution \(\mathcal P\) is \(R(A,L)=\mathbb E_{D,I\sim\mathcal P}[c_I(A(I;L(D)))]\). children.title: Information-Robustness Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Consistency and worst-case robustness across imperfect information regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Robustness Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto tradeoff between trusted-information performance and adversarial protection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization scheduling problem, associate with each information-augmented online algorithm \(A\) the pair \((\alpha(A),\beta(A))\), where \(\alpha(A)=\sup_I A(I,I)/\mathrm{OPT}(I)\) is its consistency ratio and \(\beta(A)=\sup_{I,\widehat I}A(I,\widehat I)/\mathrm{OPT}(I)\) is its robustness ratio. Algorithm \(A\) dominates \(B\) if \(\alpha(A)\leq\alpha(B)\) and \(\beta(A)\leq\beta(B)\), with at least one strict inequality. The information-robustness frontier is the set of nondominated attainable pairs; any claimed tradeoff must identify an attainable upper-bound curve and, separately, a matching impossibility region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consistency and robustness form a bicriteria performance pair; the tradeoff frontier contains precisely the attainable pairs not improved in both coordinates by another algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)>0\) for every instance considered.
Algorithms and adversarial predictions range over explicitly fixed admissible classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frontier equals the nondominated subset of \(\{(\alpha(A),\beta(A)):A\text{ is admissible}\}\).

children.title: Workload Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds derived from total or class-specific processing requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Workload Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total-work lower bound for identical parallel-machine makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider preemptive or nonpreemptive scheduling of a finite job set \(J\) on \(m\geq 1\) identical unit-speed machines. If job \(j\in J\) has processing time \(p_j\geq 0\), then every feasible schedule with makespan \(C_{\max}\) satisfies \[C_{\max}\geq \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j\in J}p_j.\] Consequently, with \(W=\sum_{j\in J}p_j\), the optimal makespan satisfies \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)\geq W/m\). This remains a valid lower bound when release dates, precedence constraints, or other restrictions are added without increasing machine capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On m identical unit-speed machines, every feasible makespan, and hence the optimal makespan, is at least the total processing work divided by m. Restrictions that do not increase capacity preserve the bound.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is a finite job set and \(m\geq1\).
The \(m\) machines are identical and unit-speed, and each machine processes at most one job at a time.
\(p_j\geq0\) for every \(j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}\geq W/m\) and \(\mathrm{OPT}(I)\geq W/m\), where \(W=\sum_{j\in J}p_j\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary aggregate-work lower bound for parallel-machine scheduling

children.title: Capacity Lower Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate renewable-resource capacity bound over a schedule horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let jobs \(J\) require processing time \(p_j\geq0\) and constant amount \(q_j\geq0\) of a renewable resource whenever processed. If the resource has capacity \(C>0\) and all processing lies in a horizon of length \(T\), every feasible schedule satisfies \[T\geq \frac{\sum_{j\in J}q_jp_j}{C}.\] More generally, for resources \(k\) with capacities \(C_k>0\) and job demands \(q_{jk}\), one has \(T\geq\max_k C_k^{-1}\sum_j q_{jk}p_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule horizon must accommodate total resource-time demand; dividing each resource’s demand by its capacity gives a lower bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Workload-Capacity Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined certificate obtained from multiple conserved workload resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each job \(j\) requires \(a_{jr}p_j\) units of resource-time from resource \(r\), whose aggregate rate is at most \(C_r>0\). Define \(B_r=C_r^{-1}\sum_j a_{jr}p_j\). For any feasible schedule of horizon \(T\), integration of the capacity constraint for each resource gives \(T\geq B_r\); hence \[T\geq B:=\max_r B_r.\] A resource \(r^\star\) attaining the maximum, together with the listed demands and capacity, is a checkable bottleneck certificate for the lower bound \(B\).

children.title: Critical-Path Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Path Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Longest-chain lower bound for precedence-constrained makespan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(J,E)\) be an acyclic precedence graph, with processing time \(p_j\geq0\) for each job. If \(P\) is any directed path in \(G\), jobs on \(P\) must execute sequentially in every precedence-feasible schedule, even when arbitrarily many machines are available. Therefore every makespan satisfies \[C_{\max}\geq L:=\max_{P\text{ directed path in }G}\sum_{j\in P}p_j.\] The value \(L\) is the weighted critical-path length and is a lower bound for both preemptive and nonpreemptive variants whenever precedence forbids overlapping comparable jobs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precedence forces all jobs on a directed path to occur sequentially, so makespan is at least the longest path’s total processing time.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(J,E)\) is a directed acyclic precedence graph.
A precedence arc requires the predecessor to complete before the successor starts or resumes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}\geq L=\max_P\sum_{j\in P}p_j\).

children.title: Precedence-Structure Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-Structure Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-interval lower bounds induced solely by precedence structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(J,E)\) be an acyclic precedence graph and let \(u\preceq v\) denote reachability, including equality. For comparable jobs \(u\preceq v\), define the order interval \([u,v]=\{j\in J:u\preceq j\preceq v\}\). In any schedule respecting completion-before-start precedence, the elapsed time from the start of \(u\) through the completion of \(v\) is at least the maximum weighted chain contained in \([u,v]\): \[C_v-S_u\geq\max_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{j\in P}p_j.\] Thus every such interval supplies a locally checkable precedence-structure lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For comparable jobs, the elapsed time between starting the first and completing the second is at least the heaviest precedence chain connecting them.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is acyclic and \(p_j\geq0\).
Each precedence relation requires completion of its predecessor before its successor starts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_v-S_u\geq\max_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{j\in P}p_j\) for every \(u\preceq v\).

knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-Capacity Interactions

Hence the joint lower bound is \[C_{\max}\geq\max\{W/m,L\}.\] Neither term generally dominates the other, so both workload and precedence structure are necessary in the certificate.

children.title: Subset Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eligibility-aware workload bound for arbitrary job subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider preemptive scheduling in which job \(j\) has work \(p_j\geq0\) and may run only on machines in \(M_j\). Machine \(i\) processes work at speed \(s_i>0\). For a job subset \(S\subseteq J\), let \(N(S)=\bigcup_{j\in S}M_j\). Since all work of \(S\) must be processed by \(N(S)\), every schedule of makespan \(T\) satisfies \[T\geq \frac{\sum_{j\in S}p_j}{\sum_{i\in N(S)}s_i}.\] Maximizing this ratio over nonempty subsets gives an eligibility-sensitive lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any job subset must fit on its eligible machines, so its total work divided by their total speed lower-bounds makespan.
assumptions_latex: Each job may be preempted but can execute only on an eligible machine.
A job cannot execute simultaneously on multiple machines.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\geq\max_{\varnothing\neq S\subseteq J}\left(\sum_{j\in S}p_j\right)/\left(\sum_{i\in N(S)}s_i\right)\).

children.title: Interval Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds derived from workload or feasibility within selected time intervals.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary window-density condition for jobs with release times and deadlines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider jobs on \(m\) identical unit-speed machines, where job \(j\) has release time \(r_j\), deadline \(d_j\), and processing time \(p_j\). For every interval \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\), define \(J[a,b]=\{j:r_j\geq a,\ d_j\leq b\}\). Every feasible schedule must satisfy \[\sum_{j\in J[a,b]}p_j\leq m(b-a).\] Indeed, every job whose entire availability window lies inside \([a,b]\) must receive all its processing there. Violation for any interval certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs whose release-to-deadline windows lie inside an interval must have total processing no greater than the machines’ capacity within that interval.
assumptions_latex: There are \(m\geq1\) identical unit-speed machines.
Each job must be processed entirely between \(r_j\) and \(d_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j:r_j\geq a,\ d_j\leq b}p_j\leq m(b-a)\) for every \(a<b\).

notation.meaning: jobs whose availability windows lie inside the interval

children.title: Energy Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Energy Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mandatory-energy feasibility condition for a cumulative renewable resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Job \(j\) has release time \(r_j\), deadline \(d_j\), processing time \(p_j\), and constant resource demand \(q_j\); the renewable resource has capacity \(C\). For interval \([a,b]\), the processing necessarily executed inside it is \(e_j(a,b)=\max\{0,p_j-\max(0,a-r_j)-\max(0,d_j-b)\}\). Every feasible preemptive schedule satisfies \[\sum_j q_j e_j(a,b)\leq C(b-a)\qquad\text{for every }a<b.\] An interval violating this inequality is an energy-overload certificate of infeasibility.

While executing, job \(j\) consumes \(q_j\geq0\) units of a resource of capacity \(C>0\).

children.title: LP-Dual Bounds
children.top_down_role: Scheduling bounds interpreted through dual solutions of linear relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: LP-Dual Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization-form LP lower bounds for an integer scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) and let \(S_{\mathrm{IP}}\subseteq P\) be the integer-feasible schedule set. The dual of \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\) is \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,\ y\ge0\}\). Every dual-feasible \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfies \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}\). Thus \(y\), together with verification of \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\) and \(y\ge0\), is a lower-bound certificate. If a primal-feasible \(x\in P\) also satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\), then \(x\) and \(y\) certify LP optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP-dual vector certifies a lower bound on both the LP relaxation and the integer scheduling optimum; equality with a feasible primal value certifies LP optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The LP feasible set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) is nonempty and has finite optimum \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\).
The nonempty integer-feasible schedule set satisfies \(S_{\mathrm{IP}}\subseteq P\), with \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\min_{x\in S_{\mathrm{IP}}}c^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(y\in\mathbb R_+^m\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\) certifies \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}\); equality with a primal-feasible objective certifies LP optimality.

children.top_down_role: Scheduling bounds obtained by pricing or relaxing complicating restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem is \(z^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\).
The multiplier satisfies \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bounds obtained by dualizing selected scheduling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Lagrangian function by \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)\) and the dual function by \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\). If \(x\) is feasible and \(\lambda\ge0\), then \(L(x,\lambda)\le f(x)\); hence \(q(\lambda)\le z^*\). Maximizing over admissible multipliers gives the Lagrangian bound \(z_{\mathrm{Lag}}=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)\le z^*\). Any computable value \(q(\lambda)\) therefore certifies a valid lower bound for the minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative penalties on relaxed constraints produce lower bounds; maximizing the resulting dual function gives the strongest Lagrangian bound.

children.title: Dual-Lagrangian Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Connections between dual multipliers, relaxed restrictions, and bound strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Lagrangian Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence for a feasible continuous minimization LP with finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\), write the relaxed inequalities as \(b-Ax\le0\) and define \(L(x,y)=c^{\mathsf T}x+y^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\) for \(y\in\mathbb R_+^m\). The dual function is \(q(y)=b^{\mathsf T}y\) when \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\), and \(q(y)=-\infty\) otherwise. Consequently, the Lagrangian dual is \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,\ y\ge0\}\), exactly the ordinary LP dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lagrangian relaxation of all covering inequalities of a feasible, finite minimization LP produces exactly its ordinary LP dual.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The primal LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) is feasible and has a finite optimum.
All inequalities \(Ax\ge b\) are Lagrangian-relaxed using multipliers \(y\in\mathbb R_+^m\), while \(x\ge0\) remains in the subproblem domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Lagrangian dual is exactly \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,\ y\ge0\}\), and its optimum is attained and equals the primal LP optimum.

children.title: Configuration Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds based on feasible machine, resource, or temporal configurations.

assumptions_latex: \(J\) is a finite set of jobs and \(\mathcal C\) is a finite family of feasible machine configurations.
Each configuration \(C\) has cost \(d_C\) and incidence \(a_{jC}\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The configuration-LP value \(z_{\mathrm{conf}}\) is a lower bound on every integral schedule represented by configurations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-covering configuration relaxation for minimization scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The configuration relaxation is \(z_{\mathrm{conf}}=\min\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}d_Cz_C:\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}a_{jC}z_C\ge1\text{ for every }j\in J,\ z_C\ge0\}\). An integral schedule represented by chosen configurations supplies a vector with \(z_C\in\mathbb Z_+\) satisfying the same covering constraints. Dropping integrality enlarges the feasible set, so for a minimization model \(z_{\mathrm{conf}}\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}\). The relaxation value is therefore a configuration-based lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing fractional use of feasible machine configurations yields a set-covering LP whose value lower-bounds any integral represented schedule.

children.title: Decomposition Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds obtained by separating a scheduling model into coordinated substructures.

assumptions_latex: The integer model is \(\min\{\sum_{k=1}^K c_k^{\mathsf T}x_k:\sum_{k=1}^K A_kx_k\ge b,\ x_k\in X_k\}\).
Each finite set is enumerated as \(X_k=\{x_k^p:p\in P_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convexified master optimum \(z_{\mathrm{DW}}\) satisfies \(z_{\mathrm{DW}}\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}\).

notation.meaning: convex weight on block alternative p

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dantzig-Wolfe convexification of a finite block-angular scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace each block by \(x_k=\sum_{p\in P_k}\lambda_{kp}x_k^p\), where \(\sum_{p\in P_k}\lambda_{kp}=1\) and \(\lambda_{kp}\ge0\). The resulting master minimizes \(\sum_{k,p}(c_k^{\mathsf T}x_k^p)\lambda_{kp}\) subject to \(\sum_{k,p}A_kx_k^p\lambda_{kp}\ge b\). Every integral solution selects one alternative per block and is master-feasible. Hence the master relaxes the integer model and its optimum \(z_{\mathrm{DW}}\) is a valid lower bound on \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying each scheduling block and retaining the coupling constraints produces a decomposition master whose optimum is a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite Dantzig-Wolfe convexification claim is standard but unsupported by an inspectable source. The leaf concerns bounds, so property is more fitting than representation.

children.title: Configuration-Decomposition Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Bound structures combining configuration representations with decomposed subproblems.

assumptions_latex: The full configuration master minimizes \(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}d_Cz_C\) subject to \(\sum_Ca_{jC}z_C\ge1\) and \(z_C\ge0\).
A restricted master uses \(\mathcal C'\subseteq\mathcal C\) and has optimal dual vector \(\pi\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(d_C-\sum_ja_{jC}\pi_j\ge0\) for every \(C\in\mathcal C\), then the restricted-master solution is optimal for the full configuration LP.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-generation interface between configurations and a decomposition master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each omitted configuration define its reduced cost by \(\bar d_C=d_C-\sum_{j\in J}a_{jC}\pi_j\). The pricing problem computes \(\min_{C\in\mathcal C}\bar d_C\). If this minimum is nonnegative, then \(\sum_ja_{jC}\pi_j\le d_C\) holds for every full-master column, so \(\pi\) is feasible for the full dual. The restricted primal value equals its dual value and is simultaneously feasible for the full primal; therefore primal-dual equality certifies full configuration-LP optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing connects configurations to decomposition: absence of a negative-reduced-cost configuration certifies that the restricted master solves the full relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Decomposition Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduced-cost optimality condition is mathematically plausible, but it lacks a column-generation source. For this interface leaf, condition or duality better describes the record than certificate.

assumptions_latex: A scheduling instance has a finite constraint index set \(R\) and predicates \(P_r(s)\) on encoded schedules \(s\).
Each predicate can be evaluated in time polynomial in the instance and schedule encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An encoded schedule \(s\) with \(P_r(s)=\mathrm{true}\) for every \(r\in R\) is a polynomially verifiable feasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic certificate for finite, explicitly encoded deterministic schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A schedule-feasibility certificate is an encoding \(s\) specifying every decision needed by the model, such as assigned resource and start time for each activity. The verifier checks \(P_r(s)=\mathrm{true}\) for all \(r\in R\). Acceptance is equivalent to \(s\in F\), where \(F=\{t:P_r(t)=\mathrm{true}\text{ for every }r\in R\}\). Under polynomial-time predicate evaluation and polynomial encoding length, this establishes membership of the instance in the feasible-scheduling language.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete encoded schedule certifies feasibility when every model constraint can be checked and all checks succeed in polynomial time.

children.title: Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Checkable evidence that no feasible schedule improves the reported objective value.

assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem minimizes \(f(s)\) over feasible schedules \(s\in F\).
The lower-bound witness is independently verifiable and proves \(L\le\inf_{s\in F}f(s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a feasible schedule \(s^*\) and a lower-bound witness satisfy \(f(s^*)=L\), then \(s^*\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching feasible upper and valid lower bounds for minimization scheduling.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimality certificate for a minimization scheduling instance consists of a feasible schedule \(s^*\in F\), its objective value \(U=f(s^*)\), and a verifiable lower-bound witness establishing \(L\le f(s)\) for every \(s\in F\). If \(U=L\), then every feasible schedule satisfies \(f(s)\ge L=U=f(s^*)\). Thus the feasibility checks, lower-bound checks, and equality of the two values certify global optimality without enumerating all schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible schedule is certified optimal when its objective equals an independently verified lower bound on every feasible schedule.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 104

children.title: Lower-Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Checkable evidence supporting a claimed lower bound on scheduling performance.

assumptions_latex: The scheduling model is a minimization problem with optimum \(z^*=\inf_{s\in F}f(s)\).
A witness \(w\) has a verifier whose acceptance implies a stated inequality \(L(w)\le f(s)\) for all \(s\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted witness \(w\) certifies \(L(w)\le z^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic lower-bound witness for a minimization scheduling objective.

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lower-bound certificate is a witness \(w\) together with a polynomially checkable validity condition implying \(L(w)\le f(s)\) for every feasible schedule \(s\in F\). Taking the infimum over \(F\) yields \(L(w)\le z^*\). Examples of admissible witnesses include a feasible dual vector, nonnegative Lagrangian multipliers with an exactly evaluated subproblem, or a valid combinatorial counting argument; acceptance requires checking the conditions specific to the chosen witness class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-bound certificate is a checkable witness proving that no feasible schedule can have objective below a stated value.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

The encoded candidate schedule \(\hat s\) satisfies every feasibility constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value \(U=f(\hat s)\) certifies \(z^*\le U\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent-based upper bound for minimization scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An upper-bound certificate consists of a fully encoded schedule \(\hat s\), successful verification that \(\hat s\in F\), and reproducible evaluation of \(U=f(\hat s)\). Since \(z^*=\inf_{s\in F}f(s)\), feasibility immediately gives \(z^*\le f(\hat s)=U\). The certificate verifier must check both every feasibility predicate and the objective computation; an objective value without its feasible schedule is not, by itself, an upper-bound certificate.
