children.title: Primal-Dual Certificate Gaps
children.top_down_role: Residual separation between attainable values and certified lower bounds.

assumptions_latex: A lower-bound certificate establishes \(L\le z^*\).
A feasible schedule establishes \(z^*\le U\), with \(U\) and \(L\) finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The absolute certificate gap \(G=U-L\) is nonnegative; \(G=0\) certifies optimality, while \(G\le\varepsilon\) certifies additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.

notation.meaning: certified lower and upper objective bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute gap convention for finite minimization objectives.

source_refs.locator: 5.2 The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 105

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given certified bounds \(L\le z^*\le U\), define the absolute certificate gap by \(G=U-L\). Then \(G\ge0\), and the incumbent's suboptimality satisfies \(0\le U-z^*\le G\). Consequently, \(G=0\) forces \(L=z^*=U\) and certifies exact optimality. More generally, for a prescribed tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the condition \(G\le\varepsilon\) certifies that the incumbent objective is within additive error \(\varepsilon\) of the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The difference between certified upper and lower bounds controls incumbent suboptimality; a zero gap certifies exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Certificate Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 105

children.title: Infeasibility Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Conflicting scheduling restrictions that jointly prevent feasibility.

assumptions_latex: The scheduling model has a finite constraint family \(\{C_i\}_{i\in I}\) over a common decision domain \(X\).
Each constraint denotes the admissible set \(F_i=\{x\in X:C_i(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subset \(K\subseteq I\) is an infeasibility conflict exactly when \(\bigcap_{i\in K}F_i=\varnothing\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-subsystem conflicts; minimality is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An infeasibility conflict is a subset \(K\subseteq I\) such that no decision satisfies all selected constraints, equivalently \(\bigcap_{i\in K}F_i=\varnothing\). A conflict certificate consists of \(K\) and an independently checkable derivation of this emptiness, such as contradictory bound propagation, a valid dual ray for a linear subsystem, or exhaustive reasoning over a polynomially bounded local domain. Because every solution of the full model would satisfy each constraint indexed by \(K\), a verified conflict certifies infeasibility of the full scheduling instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conflict is a subset of scheduling constraints with no common solution; a checkable contradiction for that subset certifies full-model infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Conflicts

children.title: Infeasibility Explanations

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Explanations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-type explanation for an infeasible linear scheduling formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the scheduling-feasibility system \(Ax\le b\), whose row index set is \(I\). An infeasibility explanation is a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{I}\) satisfying \(y\ge0\), \(y^{\mathsf T}A=0\), and \(y^{\mathsf T}b<0\). Indeed, multiplying every constraint by its corresponding component of \(y\) and summing would give \(0\le y^{\mathsf T}b<0\). The support \(E=\{i\in I:y_i>0\}\) identifies the capacity, precedence, assignment, or timing constraints participating in the contradiction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative linear combination of scheduling constraints that reduces to an impossible inequality certifies infeasibility and identifies the constraints responsible for it.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\).
All modeled feasibility constraints occur as rows of \(Ax\le b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\ge0,\ y^{\mathsf T}A=0,\ y^{\mathsf T}b<0\implies\{x:Ax\le b\}=\varnothing\).

children.title: Minimal Conflict Cores
children.top_down_role: Irreducible or compact subsets of restrictions responsible for infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Conflict Cores
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion-minimal infeasible subsystem of scheduling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{c_i:i\in I\}\) be a finite family of scheduling constraints over a common decision domain \(X\). A set \(K\subseteq I\) is a minimal conflict core if \(\{x\in X:x\text{ satisfies }c_i\text{ for every }i\in K\}=\varnothing\), while for every \(j\in K\), the reduced subsystem indexed by \(K\setminus\{j\}\) is feasible. Minimality is by set inclusion and does not imply that \(|K|\) is minimum among all infeasible subsystems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal conflict core is an infeasible subset of scheduling constraints that becomes feasible whenever any one of its constraints is removed.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
Every \(c_i\) is a predicate on the same domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is a minimal conflict core exactly when it is infeasible and every proper one-element deletion is feasible.

children.title: Fixed-Sequence Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies committing to a job or activity order before uncertainty is observed.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Sequence Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ex-ante machine ordering under stochastic processing information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set, \(M\) a machine set, and \(\Omega\) the scenario space. A fixed-sequence policy selects before observing \(\omega\in\Omega\), for each \(m\in M\), an ordered list \(\sigma_m\) of jobs assigned to that machine. Whenever two jobs \(i\) and \(j\) occur in this order in \(\sigma_m\), the policy may choose scenario-dependent feasible start times, but it may not start \(j\) on \(m\) before \(i\) has completed. Thus realized durations may alter timing and idle periods but not the committed within-machine order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-sequence policy commits to each machine’s job order before uncertainty is observed, although realized durations may change start times and idle periods.
assumptions_latex: Each job is processed nonpreemptively on its assigned machine.
The lists \((\sigma_m)_{m\in M}\) are selected before scenario information is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\omega\in\Omega\), realized processing respects the same within-machine orders \((\sigma_m)_{m\in M}\).

notation.meaning: fixed ordered list for machine m

children.title: Static Assignment Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies fixing machine, resource, or time assignments before execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Static Assignment Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ex-ante job-to-resource assignment under uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite set of jobs, \(M\) a finite set of machines, and \(\Omega\) a scenario space. A static assignment policy is a map \(a:J\to M\) chosen before any information about \(\omega\in\Omega\) is observed. For every realized scenario, job \(j\) must be processed on machine \(a(j)\); sequencing and start-time decisions may subsequently depend on admissible observations unless they are separately committed. For unrelated machines, feasibility additionally requires that \(a(j)\) belong to the eligibility set of \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static assignment policy fixes every job’s machine before uncertainty is observed, while later sequencing or timing may remain adaptable unless separately restricted.
assumptions_latex: Every job requires one machine assignment.
Machine eligibility, when present, is known before assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(j,\omega)=a(j,\omega')\) for all \(j\in J\) and all \(\omega,\omega'\in\Omega\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard two-stage stochastic scheduling commitment definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Static-Policy Commitment Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among decisions fixed initially and decisions deferred until execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Static-Policy Commitment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability boundary separating ex-ante commitments from later execution decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the information filtration and let \(D\) be a scheduling decision component. The static-commitment condition is that \(D\) be \(\mathcal F_0\)-measurable; equivalently, \(D(\omega)=D(\omega')\) whenever the scenarios \(\omega\) and \(\omega'\) are indistinguishable at time \(0\). Decisions not included in \(D\), such as dispatch times or inserted idle time, may be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable when taken at time \(t\). The commitment boundary is the declared partition between these two classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The static boundary requires committed decisions to depend only on initial information; execution decisions outside that boundary may use observations available when they are made.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) represents the scheduler's information over time.
The committed decision component \(D\) is specified before optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Static commitment holds exactly when \(D\) is \(\mathcal F_0\)-measurable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard filtration-based characterization of static decisions

children.title: Adaptive Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies whose decisions respond to information revealed during execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Scheduling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling decisions represented as functions of observed histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_t\) denote the observable scheduling history through time \(t\), including completed operations and revealed processing, release, or disruption data. An adaptive scheduling policy is a family \(\pi=(\pi_t)_{t\ge0}\) in which \(\pi_t(H_t)\) selects a feasible action at time \(t\), such as starting, delaying, assigning, or resuming an eligible job. Policies may prescribe different actions for scenarios having different observed histories; feasibility requires resource capacity, eligibility, and precedence constraints to hold along every scenario path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive policy chooses each scheduling action from the history observed so far and may react differently after different processing, arrival, or disruption outcomes.
assumptions_latex: Each history \(H_t\) contains only information observable by time \(t\).
The admissible-action set is defined for every reachable history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The realized schedule is generated recursively by actions \(\pi_t(H_t)\) that are feasible on every scenario path.

notation.meaning: decision rule used at time t

children.title: Nonanticipative Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies restricted to information available at each decision time.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipative Scheduling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-consistency condition for implementable adaptive schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the scheduler's information filtration and let \(D_t\) denote the action selected at time \(t\). A scheduling policy is nonanticipative if \(D_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable for every \(t\). Equivalently, if scenarios \(\omega\) and \(\omega'\) have identical observable histories through time \(t\), then \(D_t(\omega)=D_t(\omega')\). Hence a decision may depend on realized information but not on future processing times, arrivals, failures, or other unrevealed data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonanticipative policy makes identical decisions in scenarios that are observationally indistinguishable at the decision time and never uses unrevealed future information.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) models exactly the information available to the scheduler.
Each decision \(D_t\) is taken at its indexed time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable for every \(t\ge0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard nonanticipativity condition in stochastic optimization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Information-Adaptation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on responsiveness imposed by observation timing and information access.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Adaptation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between implementable adaptation and anticipative scenario-wise optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an information filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\). The admissible adaptation boundary permits a decision \(D_t\) only when it is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. If \(D_t\) instead depends on a random quantity not measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_t\), then two scenarios with the same observed history can receive different actions, so the rule is anticipative and not implementable under the stated information structure. At the opposite boundary, requiring every \(D_t\) to be \(\mathcal F_0\)-measurable reduces the policy to static commitment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptation is implementable only within the current information filtration; using unrevealed data is anticipative, while restricting every decision to initial information yields a static policy.
assumptions_latex: The filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) accurately represents observable information.
Decisions are indexed by the times at which they must be implemented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_t\notin L^0(\mathcal F_t)\) violates nonanticipativity, whereas \(D_t\in L^0(\mathcal F_0)\) for every \(t\) enforces static commitment.

notation.meaning: random variables measurable with respect to current information

knowledge_statements.title: Random Processing Times
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic processing-duration data for scheduling models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), the processing requirement of job \(j\in J\) on eligible machine \(m\in M_j\) is a nonnegative random variable \(P_{jm}:\Omega\to[0,\infty]\). The random vector \(P=(P_{jm})\), together with its joint distribution, specifies the random-processing-time regime. Dependence across jobs or machines is permitted unless independence is explicitly assumed. A realized schedule must allocate job \(j\) its realized duration \(P_{jm}(\omega)\) when it is processed on machine \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random processing times model job durations as jointly distributed nonnegative random variables whose realized values determine the required machine occupation.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and each eligibility set \(M_j\) are finite.
Every \(P_{jm}\) is measurable and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each scenario \(\omega\), processing job \(j\) on machine \(m\) occupies that machine for \(P_{jm}(\omega)\) time units.

notation.meaning: random processing time of job j on machine m
machines eligible to process job j

children.title: Random Release Processes
children.top_down_role: Uncertain times at which known jobs or activities become available.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Release Processes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic times at which known jobs become eligible for processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\). A random release process is the vector \(R=(R_j)_{j\in J}\) of nonnegative random release times. In scenario \(\omega\), job \(j\) is unavailable before \(R_j(\omega)\); consequently every feasible start time \(S_j(\omega)\) satisfies \(S_j(\omega)\ge R_j(\omega)\). The joint law of \(R\) may encode dependence among releases and with other stochastic scheduling data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random release process assigns each job a random eligibility time, and no feasible schedule may start that job earlier.
assumptions_latex: Every \(R_j\) is a measurable random variable taking values in \([0,\infty]\).
Jobs are indexed independently of their realized release times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_j(\omega)\ge R_j(\omega)\) for every job \(j\) and scenario \(\omega\).

notation.meaning: random release time of job j
scenario-dependent start time of job j

children.title: Random Arrival Processes
children.top_down_role: Stochastic streams through which new jobs or requests enter the system.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Arrival Processes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting-process model for jobs entering a scheduling system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random arrival process is a right-continuous, integer-valued, nondecreasing stochastic process \((N(t))_{t\ge0}\), where \(N(t)\) counts jobs that have entered the scheduling system by time \(t\). Its jump times are \(T_n=\inf\{t\ge0:N(t)\ge n\}\), so the \(n\)-th arriving job is unavailable before \(T_n\). Batch arrivals correspond to jumps larger than one. No Poisson, renewal, stationarity, or independence assumption is included unless separately imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random arrival process counts jobs entering the system over time; its jump times give arrival epochs, and larger jumps represent batches.
assumptions_latex: Every sample path of \(N\) is right-continuous, nondecreasing, and integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_n=\inf\{t\ge0:N(t)\ge n\}\) is the availability time of the \(n\)-th arriving job.

notation.meaning: number of arrivals by time t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard counting-process representation of arrivals
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting-process representation is standard and fits the leaf, but it lacks a source. The conclusion should address T_n=∞ when the nth arrival never occurs rather than unconditionally calling T_n an availability time.

children.title: Release-Arrival Dependence
children.top_down_role: Dependence structures linking job availability with workload arrival patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Release-Arrival Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-law characterization of dependence between release and arrival data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=(R_j)_{j\in J}\) be random release times and \((N(t))_{t\ge0}\) a random arrival process on the same probability space. Release and arrival data are independent exactly when, for every Borel set \(B\) and every event \(C\) in \(\sigma(N(t):t\ge0)\), one has \(\mathbb P(R\in B, C)=\mathbb P(R\in B)\mathbb P(C)\). Otherwise their joint law exhibits release-arrival dependence. Consequently, specifying only the marginal laws of \(R\) and \(N\) does not determine expected scheduling performance when such dependence is present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Release times and arrivals are dependent when their joint law does not factor; their separate marginal distributions then cannot determine expected schedule performance.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and \(N\) are defined on a common probability space.
The scheduling objective is integrable under the considered joint laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Independence is equivalent to \(\sigma(R)\) and \(\sigma(N(t):t\ge0)\) being independent sigma-fields.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard probabilistic independence criterion applied to scheduling data
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sigma-field independence criterion is standard, but no source is supplied. The claim that marginal laws cannot determine expected scheduling performance is too broad: some objectives or policies depend only on marginals, so the performance consequence needs qualification.

children.title: Random Machine Failures
children.top_down_role: Stochastic loss of machine or resource availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Machine Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic scheduling model with exogenous machine availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let machines be indexed by \(m\in M\). For each machine, let \(A_m(t)\in\{0,1\}\) be a stochastic availability process, where \(A_m(t)=1\) means that machine \(m\) is operational at time \(t\). A random-machine-failure scheduling model requires processing on \(m\) to occur only during \(\{t:A_m(t)=1\}\). Failure epochs, repair durations, and their joint law are specified independently of scheduling decisions unless dependence is explicitly modeled. A policy is nonanticipative when each dispatching, preemption, or reassignment decision at time \(t\) is measurable with respect to the observed history through \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machines alternate randomly between operational and failed states; feasible nonanticipative policies process work only while assigned machines are available.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite machine set.
Each \(A_m\) is an observable stochastic process.
Failure and repair laws are specified as model data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Processing assigned to \(m\) is feasible only when \(A_m(t)=1\), and admissible policies cannot use future availability information.

notation.meaning: availability indicator of machine m at time t

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Random Machine Failures leaf and is internally coherent, but no inspectable citation supports the availability-process formulation, the exogeneity convention, or the stated information structure.

children.title: Random Processing Interruptions
children.top_down_role: Stochastic suspension of jobs or activities during execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Processing Interruptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Job-level stochastic interruptions, distinct from machine-wide failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each job \(j\in J\), let \(I_j(t)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether its processing is permitted at time \(t\). A random-processing-interruption model has stochastic intervals on which \(I_j(t)=0\), so the accumulated service of job \(j\) by time \(t\) is \(S_j(t)=\int_0^t u_j(s)I_j(s)\,ds\), where \(u_j(s)\) is its assigned processing rate. Completion occurs at the first \(t\) with \(S_j(t)\ge P_j\). The model must specify whether interrupted work resumes from accumulated service or restarts, and admissible policies must be nonanticipative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job receives no effective service during random interruption intervals; the model specifies whether completed work is retained or lost.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(P_j>0\) is the required service.
The interruption processes are observable through the current time.
The resume-or-restart convention is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Job \(j\) completes when its convention-adjusted accumulated service reaches \(P_j\).

notation.meaning: indicator that job j can receive effective service

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf and definition role are appropriate, but the accumulated-service integral models preemptive resume only and does not define restart-after-interruption service, despite the statement and conclusion claiming to cover both conventions. An authoritative source is needed to determine and support the intended formulation.

children.title: Failure-Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Repair, restart, resume, and reassignment settings following random disruptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure-Recovery Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled stochastic failure, repair, and scheduling dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A failure-recovery scheduling regime is specified by a stochastic state process \(X(t)\) whose components record resource availability, interrupted jobs, and repair status; an admissible action set \(U(X(t))\); and a transition law for failures and recoveries under chosen actions. A scheduling policy \(\pi\) selects \(u(t)\in U(X(t))\) using only the observed history. Recovery may restore a resource, resume retained work, restart lost work, or trigger reassignment, as fixed by the transition law. Performance is evaluated by a declared criterion such as \(\mathbb E_\pi[C_{\max}]\), expected weighted completion cost, or long-run average cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A failure-recovery regime jointly specifies disruptions, repairs, work-retention rules, feasible responses, and a stochastic scheduling objective.
assumptions_latex: The state and admissible-action spaces are specified.
Failure and recovery transition laws are defined.
Policies are nonanticipative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime induces a controlled stochastic scheduling process and a well-defined performance criterion for every admissible policy.

notation.meaning: actions feasible in the current state

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The controlled-state description fits Failure-Recovery Regimes, but no source supports this particular synthesis. The claim that every admissible policy has a well-defined performance criterion also requires conditions appropriate to the selected criterion, such as integrability or existence of a long-run average.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary-Distribution Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-free structural class, not distributionally robust ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An arbitrary-distribution stochastic scheduling model permits each primitive random quantity \(Z_k\), such as a processing time, release time, or repair duration, to have any probability distribution \(F_k\) on its declared measurable domain, subject only to explicitly stated conditions such as nonnegativity, independence, or finite moments. No parametric family, memorylessness, stochastic ordering, or hazard-rate shape is assumed unless separately imposed. A policy must be measurable with respect to the available information filtration, and any expected-value objective is admitted only when its defining random cost is integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primitive durations may follow any distributions satisfying only the model’s explicit support, dependence, and integrability assumptions.
assumptions_latex: Each primitive \(Z_k\) is a measurable random variable.
All support and dependence restrictions are stated explicitly.
Expected objectives use integrable random costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The admissible distribution class contains every joint law satisfying the declared restrictions and no additional distributional structure.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the distributional-structure leaf and correctly distinguishes arbitrary distributions from ambiguity sets. However, the marginal notation \(F_k\) does not by itself specify the joint law when dependence is allowed, and no inspectable source supports the exact model class.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastically Ordered Distribution Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Usual first-order stochastic order for scheduling primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For real-valued random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), write \(X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y\) when \(\mathbb P(X>t)\le\mathbb P(Y>t)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). Equivalently, \(F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)\) for every \(t\). A family \(\{X_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\) is stochastically ordered by an order \(\preceq\) on \(\Theta\) when \(\theta_1\preceq\theta_2\) implies \(X_{\theta_1}\le_{\mathrm{st}}X_{\theta_2}\). Consequently, whenever expectations exist, every increasing measurable function \(\phi\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[\phi(X_{\theta_1})]\le\mathbb E[\phi(X_{\theta_2})]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger parameters produce distributions with uniformly larger upper-tail probabilities, equivalently larger expectations for every integrable increasing transform.
assumptions_latex: \(X_\theta\) are real-valued random variables.
\((\Theta,\preceq)\) is an ordered parameter set.
Relevant transformed expectations exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\theta_1\preceq\theta_2\), then \(X_{\theta_1}\le_{\mathrm{st}}X_{\theta_2}\) and increasing expected costs are ordered accordingly.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The usual stochastic order, its distribution-function characterization, and its increasing-transform implication are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but the record supplies no citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone coupling of stochastically ordered distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional stochastic ordering represented by an almost-surely ordered coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F_1 and F_2 be distribution functions on \mathbb R. If F_1(x)\geq F_2(x) for every x\in\mathbb R, then there exist jointly distributed real random variables (\xi_1,\xi_2) such that \xi_i has distribution function F_i for i=1,2 and \xi_1\leq\xi_2 almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If F1 is pointwise at least F2, the two distributions admit a coupling in which the first random variable is no greater than the second almost surely.
assumptions_latex: F_1,F_2\text{ are distribution functions on }\mathbb R
F_1(x)\geq F_2(x)\quad\forall x\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(\xi_1,\xi_2):\ \xi_i\sim F_i\ (i=1,2),\quad \mathbb P(\xi_1\leq\xi_2)=1

knowledge_statements.title: Memoryless Processing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential remaining-processing-time property in continuous time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a job processing requirement satisfy \(P\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)\) with \(\mu>0\). For all \(s,t\ge0\), \(\mathbb P(P>s+t\mid P>s)=\mathbb P(P>t)=e^{-\mu t}\). Hence, conditional on the job remaining unfinished after receiving \(s\) units of uninterrupted service, its residual processing requirement has distribution \(\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)\) and does not depend on \(s\). In a preemptive-resume scheduling model with independent exponential requirements, the unfinished jobs’ attained service need not be included in the Markov state; their identities and rates suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unfinished exponentially distributed job has the same residual processing distribution regardless of how much service it has already received.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is exponentially distributed with rate \(\mu>0\).
Service accumulation is measured in processing-time units.
Job requirements are independent when the multi-job conclusion is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual requirement conditional on survival past \(s\) is again \(\operatorname{Exp}(\mu)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is appropriate for the exponential memorylessness statement, and the single-job formula is precise. The scheduling-state consequence is a nontrivial modeling claim requiring an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completion rate and exponential memorylessness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completion-rate definition and its exponential specialization for stochastic processing times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X be a nonnegative continuously distributed processing time with density f and distribution function F. Whenever 1-F(t)>0, its completion rate is c(t)=f(t)/(1-F(t)), which is the hazard rate. If X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda) with \lambda>0, then c(t)=\lambda for every t\ge0 and, for all s,t\ge0, \mathbb{P}(X-t>s\mid X>t)=\mathbb{P}(X>s)=e^{-\lambda s}. Thus the remaining processing time conditional on noncompletion by t is again exponentially distributed with rate \lambda.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The completion rate is the density divided by the survival probability and equals the usual hazard rate. An exponential processing time has constant completion rate, and its conditional remaining processing time has the original exponential distribution.
assumptions_latex: X\ge0\ \text{has density }f\text{ and distribution function }F
\text{for the specialization, }X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda),\ \lambda>0
s,t\ge0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(t)=\frac{f(t)}{1-F(t)};\qquad X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\Rightarrow c(t)=\lambda\ \text{and}\ \mathbb{P}(X-t>s\mid X>t)=\mathbb{P}(X>s)=e^{-\lambda s}.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Single-Machine Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-capacity-resource stochastic scheduling environment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic single-machine model consists of a finite job set \(J\), one machine of unit capacity, random primitive data such as processing requirements \(P_j\) or release times \(R_j\), an information filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\), and a performance functional. At every time, at most one job may receive service. An admissible policy is \(\mathcal F_t\)-adapted and obeys the specified preemption convention. If job \(j\) receives unit-rate service, its completion time is the first \(t\) at which its cumulative allocated service reaches \(P_j\), subject to \(t\ge R_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random jobs share one unit-capacity machine, and scheduling decisions use only currently available information while respecting release and preemption rules.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
The machine has unit capacity.
Primitive random data and their observation times are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible policy produces completion times while allocating service to at most one released job at each time.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Parallel-Machine Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiple simultaneous-capacity resources with stochastic job data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic parallel-machine model consists of jobs \(J\), machines \(M\), random processing requirements \(P_{jm}\) for eligible job-machine pairs, an information filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\), and a performance functional. At any time, each machine processes at most one job and each job occupies at most one machine, unless parallel execution is explicitly allowed. An admissible policy is \(\mathcal F_t\)-adapted and respects eligibility, preemption, and migration conventions. Identical, uniform, and unrelated machines correspond respectively to common rates, multiplicative machine speeds, and arbitrary pair-dependent processing requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several machines process jobs concurrently under stochastic durations, with eligibility, machine type, preemption, and information rules explicitly specified.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(M\) are finite.
Eligible processing requirements \(P_{jm}\) are defined.
Policies are nonanticipative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An admissible schedule respects job-machine capacity and the declared eligibility, preemption, and migration conventions almost surely.

children.title: Stochastic Shop Models

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Shop Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic job-shop or flow-shop operation networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic shop model has jobs decomposed into operations \(O\). Each operation \(o\in O\) requires a designated machine \(m(o)\), has random processing requirement \(P_o\), and is constrained by a precedence relation \(\prec\). An operation may start only after all predecessors are complete; each machine processes at most one operation at a time. A policy selects eligible operations using only observed information and obeys the stated preemption convention. A flow shop uses a common machine order for all jobs, whereas a job shop permits job-specific routes. The objective is a declared expected or risk-sensitive function of completion times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Jobs traverse precedence-constrained machine operations with random durations; nonanticipative policies decide which eligible operation each machine processes.
assumptions_latex: \(O\) and the machine set are finite.
The precedence relation \(\prec\) is acyclic.
Processing requirements and observation rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible realization respects both machine capacity and operation precedence.

notation.meaning: random processing requirement of operation o

children.title: Stochastic Project Models

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Project Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precedence-constrained stochastic activity scheduling with renewable resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic project scheduling model is defined by a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), random activity durations \(D_i\), renewable resource requirements \(a_{ik}\), capacities \(b_k\), and an information filtration. An activity \(i\) may start only after every predecessor has completed, and at every time the total requirement of active activities satisfies \(\sum_{i\text{ active}}a_{ik}\le b_k\) for each resource \(k\). A nonanticipative policy chooses eligible starts from observed information. The project completion time is the completion time of a designated sink, or equivalently the maximum activity completion time after adding a zero-duration sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-duration project activities obey precedence and renewable-resource capacities; a nonanticipative policy chooses eligible starts and determines project completion time.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
Durations \(D_i\) are nonnegative random variables.
Resource capacities and information timing are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy generates precedence- and resource-feasible activity start times and a well-defined random project completion time.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Network Dependencies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-duration precedence network and induced completion recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed acyclic graph and let \(D_i\ge0\) be the random duration of node \(i\). With unlimited resources and immediate starts, define \(C_i=D_i+\max_{(j,i)\in E}C_j\), taking the maximum over an empty set as \(0\). Then \(C_i\) equals the maximum total duration along a directed path ending at \(i\): \(C_i=\max_{p\in\mathcal P_i}\sum_{j\in p}D_j\). For a designated sink \(s\), \(C_s\) is the stochastic network completion time. Dependence among the \(D_i\) is part of the model’s joint probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an unlimited-resource acyclic network, each completion time is the longest realized duration of any path ending at that node.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and acyclic.
Node durations \(D_i\) are nonnegative random variables.
Resources are unlimited and eligible nodes start immediately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\in V\), \(C_i=\max_{p\in\mathcal P_i}\sum_{j\in p}D_j\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gittins-Index Scheduling Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Index policies for independent, preemptible stochastic jobs with discounted completion rewards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let jobs evolve independently as Markov processes when served and remain frozen otherwise. For job \(j\) in state \(x\), with completion time \(T_j\), reward \(R_j\), and discount factor \(\beta\in(0,1)\), define
\[G_j(x)=\sup_{\tau\ge 1}\frac{\mathbb E_x[\beta^{T_j}R_j\mathbf 1_{\{T_j\le \tau\}}]}{\mathbb E_x[\sum_{t=0}^{\min(T_j,\tau)-1}\beta^t]}.\]
A Gittins-index scheduling policy assigns each available server at every decision epoch to an unfinished job having maximal current index, with a fixed rule for ties. The Gittins-index scheduling family consists of policies obtained from this construction under the applicable job-state, reward, and discount models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gittins-index policy repeatedly serves an unfinished stochastic job with the greatest current ratio of optimally stopped discounted reward to discounted service effort.
assumptions_latex: Job processes are mutually independent and frozen while passive.
Service is preemptible at decision epochs without penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(j_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{j\in A_t}G_j(X_j(t))\) at every decision epoch \(t\).

notation.meaning: Gittins index of job j in state x
completion time measured in active service periods
set of unfinished available jobs at epoch t

A topic-specific source is required to verify the discounted-reward formulation and the conditions under which maximal-index server assignment is valid.

children.title: Uncertainty-Set Robust Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Scheduling protected against realizations drawn from explicit uncertainty sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty-Set Robust Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static robust schedules protected against every parameter realization in a prescribed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a set of admissible schedules, let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty uncertainty set, and let \(F(s,u)\) and \(g(s,u)\) denote performance and constraint residuals. An uncertainty-set robust scheduling problem is
\[\min_{s\in S}\ \sup_{u\in U}F(s,u)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad g(s,u)\le 0\quad\text{for every }u\in U.\]
A schedule is robust feasible precisely when it satisfies all uncertain scheduling constraints for every realization in \(U\). Its robust objective value is its worst performance over \(U\); no probability distribution on \(U\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust schedule satisfies every uncertain constraint and minimizes worst-case performance over all parameter realizations in a specified uncertainty set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\neq\varnothing\) and \(U\neq\varnothing\).
\(F:S\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:S\times U\to\mathbb R^q\) are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) is robust feasible if and only if \(s\in S\) and \(g(s,u)\le0\) for all \(u\in U\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is a plausible generic robust-optimization definition, but no inspectable source supports its use as the scheduling-specific definition in this terminal container.

children.title: Distributionally Robust Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Scheduling protected across families of probability distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributionally Robust Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schedules optimized against the worst probability law in an ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a schedule set, let \(\xi\) be an uncertain scheduling parameter on a measurable space \(\Xi\), and let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty set of probability measures on \(\Xi\). A distributionally robust scheduling problem has the form
\[\min_{s\in S}\ \sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[F(s,\xi)]\]
possibly subject to distributionally robust constraints such as
\[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P\{g(s,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon.\]
Thus one schedule is selected before the distribution is known, and its expected performance or reliability is protected uniformly over every law in \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributionally robust scheduling chooses one schedule whose expected cost or reliability is protected against every probability distribution in a specified ambiguity set.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\neq\varnothing\).
\(F(s,\cdot)\) is measurable and has defined expectation for every relevant \(s\) and \(P\).
\(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) is distributionally robust chance-feasible when \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P\{g(s,\xi)\le0\}\ge1-\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic distributionally robust formulation is plausible, but the record provides no source for the scheduling specialization or the stated worst-case chance-constraint convention.

children.title: Set-to-Distribution Ambiguity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Transitions between realization-based uncertainty and distribution-based ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-to-Distribution Ambiguity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding a deterministic uncertainty set as a support-only distributional ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty measurable uncertainty set \(U\subseteq\Xi\), define its support-only ambiguity set by
\[\mathcal P(U)=\{P:\ P\text{ is a probability measure on }\Xi,\ P(U)=1\}.\]
If every Dirac measure \(\delta_u\), with \(u\in U\), belongs to the admissible class and \(f:U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is measurable with defined expectations, then
\[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(U)}\mathbb E_P[f(\xi)]=\sup_{u\in U}f(u).\]
Consequently, support information alone converts uncertainty-set robustness into a distributionally robust model without reducing worst-case conservatism; additional moment or distance restrictions generally produce a smaller ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All distributions supported on an uncertainty set reproduce its pointwise worst case because the ambiguity set includes a point mass at every realization.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is nonempty and measurable.
Every \(\delta_u\), for \(u\in U\), is admissible.
The displayed expectations of \(f\) are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(U)}\mathbb E_P[f(\xi)]=\sup_{u\in U}f(u)\).

notation.meaning: all probability laws supported on U
Dirac probability measure concentrated at u

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-only equality is plausible when all Dirac laws are admitted, but no source is cited. A source should also specify the measurable function on the ambient space and the admissible probability class so the expectations are well defined.

children.title: Time-Buffer Allocation
children.top_down_role: Placement of reserved time intended to absorb execution variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Buffer Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allocation of nonnegative temporal reserves within a baseline schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s_i\) be the planned start time of activity \(i\), let \(p_i\ge0\) be its nominal duration, and let \(A\) be the precedence-arc set. A time-buffer allocation is a vector \(b\in\mathbb R_+^{A}\) satisfying
\[s_j\ge s_i+p_i+b_{ij}\qquad ((i,j)\in A).\]
Here \(b_{ij}\) is reserved time between completion of \(i\) and planned start of \(j\). Under a total reserve budget \(B\ge0\), an allocation additionally satisfies \(\sum_{(i,j)\in A}b_{ij}\le B\). A positive buffer can absorb an upstream delay of at most its unused amount without shifting the downstream planned start.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time-buffer allocation inserts budgeted nonnegative gaps between linked activities so that bounded upstream delays can be absorbed before propagating downstream.
assumptions_latex: \(p_i\ge0\) for every activity \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\) is a feasible time-buffer allocation when \(b\ge0\), \(s_j-s_i-p_i\ge b_{ij}\) on every precedence arc, and \(\sum_{(i,j)\in A}b_{ij}\le B\).

notation.meaning: time reserved between activities i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No scheduling source supports this particular arc-buffer model. The claim that a buffer absorbs upstream delay also depends on execution, precedence, and unused-reserve conventions that are not established here.

children.title: Capacity-Buffer Allocation
children.top_down_role: Reservation of machines, labor, or other capacity against disruptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Buffer Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reservation of resource capacity above nominal scheduled demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_{rt}\ge0\) be available capacity of resource \(r\) in period \(t\), and let \(y_{irt}(s)\ge0\) be the capacity used by scheduled activity \(i\). A capacity-buffer allocation is a nonnegative array \(c=(c_{rt})\) for which
\[\sum_i y_{irt}(s)+c_{rt}\le K_{rt}\qquad\text{for every }r,t.\]
The amount \(c_{rt}\) is deliberately reserved rather than assigned to nominal work. If reserve has cost \(q_{rt}\ge0\) and budget \(C\ge0\), the allocation may also be required to satisfy \(\sum_{r,t}q_{rt}c_{rt}\le C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity-buffer allocation leaves budgeted resource capacity unused by nominal work, making it available to absorb disruptions or demand surges.
assumptions_latex: \(K_{rt},y_{irt}(s),q_{rt},C\ge0\).
Resource use is additive within each resource-period pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is feasible when \(c_{rt}\ge0\), \(\sum_i y_{irt}(s)+c_{rt}\le K_{rt}\) for all \(r,t\), and \(\sum_{r,t}q_{rt}c_{rt}\le C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inequalities define a coherent reserve-capacity model, but no inspectable source establishes it as the intended capacity-buffer allocation concept for scheduling.

children.title: Schedule-Slack Allocation
children.top_down_role: Distribution of temporal flexibility across jobs, activities, or constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Slack Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution of permissible timing flexibility among activities or precedence relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed project deadline \(D\), let \(e_i\) and \(\ell_i\) be the earliest and latest feasible start times of activity \(i\). Its total slack is \(h_i=\ell_i-e_i\ge0\). A schedule-slack allocation selects nonnegative protected amounts \(a_i\) satisfying
\[0\le a_i\le h_i\quad(i\in V),\qquad \sum_{i\in V}w_i a_i\le H,\]
where \(w_i>0\) are allocation weights and \(H\ge0\) is a reserve budget. The allocated amount \(a_i\) is timing flexibility assigned to activity \(i\); unlike an inserted time buffer, it need not appear as a single explicit idle interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule-slack allocation assigns portions of feasible start-time flexibility to activities, subject to their available slack and an optional weighted reserve budget.
assumptions_latex: The earliest and latest starts are computed under the same feasibility constraints and deadline \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) is a feasible slack allocation if \(0\le a_i\le\ell_i-e_i\) for all \(i\) and \(\sum_iw_i a_i\le H\).

notation.meaning: total start-time slack of activity i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Total slack is model dependent, and selecting protected amounts with a weighted aggregate budget is not a source-independent standard definition of slack allocation. A scheduling-specific citation is required.

children.title: Buffer-Placement Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons among concentrated, distributed, local, and global protection.

knowledge_statements.title: Buffer-Placement Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto tradeoff between reserve cost and disruption protection across candidate placements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\subseteq\mathbb R_+^m\) be the feasible set of buffer-placement vectors. Let \(C(b)\) be reserve cost and \(R(b)\) be a disruption-loss functional, with smaller values preferred. A placement \(b^*\in B\) is efficient when no \(b\in B\) satisfies
\[C(b)\le C(b^*),\qquad R(b)\le R(b^*),\]
with at least one strict inequality. For any \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), every minimizer of \(\lambda C(b)+(1-\lambda)R(b)\) over \(B\) is efficient. Conversely, if the attainable upper image is convex, every properly supported efficient placement minimizes such a weighted sum for some positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Efficient buffer placements balance reserve cost against disruption loss; positive weighted-sum optimization finds supported Pareto-efficient placements.
assumptions_latex: \(B\neq\varnothing\).
Both \(C\) and \(R\) are minimized.
For the converse, the attainable upper image is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{b\in B}\{\lambda C(b)+(1-\lambda)R(b)\}\) with \(0<\lambda<1\) implies that \(b^*\) is Pareto efficient.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record states weighted-sum Pareto results rather than only a general principle, so the selected content kind requires review. A source is also needed for the precise upper-image and proper-support conditions in the converse.

children.title: Schedule Stability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of planned assignments, sequences, or times to uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-based stability of realized or revised schedules relative to a baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s^0\in\mathbb R^n\) be a baseline vector of activity start times and let \(s(\xi)\in\mathbb R^n\) be the implemented or revised schedule under disruption \(\xi\). For weights \(w_i\\ge0\), define deviation
\[D_w(s(\xi),s^0)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\lvert s_i(\xi)-s_i^0\rvert.\]
Given a disruption set \(U\) and tolerance \(\Delta\ge0\), the baseline is \(\Delta\)-stable under the associated recovery rule when \(D_w(s(\xi),s^0)\le\Delta\) for every \(\xi\in U\). An expected-stability variant replaces this uniform bound by \(\mathbb E[D_w(s(\xi),s^0)]\le\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule stability bounds the weighted change between baseline and implemented start times, either uniformly over disruptions or in expectation.
assumptions_latex: \(w_i\ge0\) for every activity \(i\).
\(\Delta\ge0\) and \(U\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s^0\) is \(\Delta\)-stable exactly when \(\sup_{\xi\in U}D_w(s(\xi),s^0)\le\Delta\).

notation.meaning: implemented or revised schedule under disruption

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes this weighted start-time deviation as the intended stability definition. The displayed text contains malformed LaTeX in `w_i\\ge0`, and the uniform and expected variants are combined without separately specifying the probability model for the latter.

children.title: Quality Robustness
children.top_down_role: Preservation of objective performance across uncertain realizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Quality Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform control of realized schedule quality across a disruption set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a feasible baseline-schedule set, let \(U\) be a nonempty disruption set, and let \(Q(s,\xi)\in\mathbb R\) be a loss, with smaller values preferred, after applying the prescribed execution or recovery rule. For a benchmark \(q^{\mathrm{ref}}(\xi)\) and tolerance \(\Gamma\ge0\), schedule \(s\in S\) is \(\Gamma\)-quality-robust when
\[Q(s,\xi)-q^{\mathrm{ref}}(\xi)\le\Gamma\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in U.\]
Using \(q^{\mathrm{ref}}(\xi)=\inf_{z\in S(\xi)}Q(z,\xi)\) yields a uniform absolute-regret criterion; using a constant benchmark yields a uniform quality threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule is quality-robust when its realized loss remains within a fixed tolerance of a chosen benchmark for every modeled disruption.
assumptions_latex: \(U\neq\varnothing\) and \(\Gamma\ge0\).
The loss and benchmark are finite on the evaluated realizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) is \(\Gamma\)-quality-robust if and only if \(\sup_{\xi\in U}\{Q(s,\xi)-q^{\mathrm{ref}}(\xi)\}\le\Gamma\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Quality robustness admits multiple scheduling definitions. No citation supports this benchmark-regret convention, and the prescribed execution or recovery rule affecting Q is not mathematically introduced as a map.

children.title: Stability-Quality Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tension between limiting plan changes and maintaining operational performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability-Quality Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto efficiency between baseline deviation and disrupted operating quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the set of admissible baseline-and-recovery policies. Let \(D(x)\) measure schedule deviation from the baseline and let \(Q(x)\) measure disrupted operating loss, with both minimized. A policy \(x^*\in X\) is stability-quality efficient if no \(x\in X\) satisfies
\[D(x)\le D(x^*),\qquad Q(x)\le Q(x^*),\]
with at least one strict inequality. For each \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), every minimizer of \(\lambda D(x)+(1-\lambda)Q(x)\) is efficient. If the attainable upper image is convex, every properly supported efficient policy is obtainable using some strictly positive pair of weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Policies that balance schedule deviation and disrupted operating loss form a Pareto frontier; positive weighted sums recover its supported efficient points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
Both \(D\) and \(Q\) are loss criteria.
For the converse, the attainable upper image is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\{\lambda D(x)+(1-\lambda)Q(x)\}\), with \(0<\lambda<1\), implies stability-quality efficiency.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record presents formal Pareto and weighted-sum results, which fit a property or theorem more closely than a generic principle. A source is required to verify the scheduling interpretation and the exact converse conditions.

children.title: Event-Driven Rescheduling
children.top_down_role: Schedule revision triggered by disruptions, deviations, or threshold events.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Driven Rescheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reactive rescheduling initiated by detected state-changing events rather than fixed review times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a baseline schedule \(s^0\), an event stream, a state estimator, a feasibility model, and a rescheduling optimizer \(\mathcal R\). Initialize \(t=0\) and \(s=s^0\). Whenever an event \(e_k\) is detected at time \(t_k\), freeze completed operations and any operations inside the commitment horizon, update the state to \(x_k\), and compute
\[s^k\in\mathcal R(x_k,s^{k-1})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{z\in F(x_k)}\{Q(z,x_k)+\rho D(z,s^{k-1})\}.\]
Implement \(s^k\) until the next triggering event. Stop at the planning horizon and output the executed schedule together with the sequence of revisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Event-driven rescheduling detects a disruption, freezes committed work, updates system state, optimizes a feasible revision, and implements it until another event occurs.
assumptions_latex: Triggering events and their detection times are observable.
\(F(x_k)\neq\varnothing\) whenever rescheduling is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At each trigger \(t_k\), the implemented revision \(s^k\) belongs to \(F(x_k)\) and minimizes the stated quality-plus-deviation objective.

notation.meaning: feasible revised schedules in updated state

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits the leaf, but no source supports the chosen trigger, commitment-horizon, and revision-objective conventions. The optimizer is equated with an argmin set while s^k is treated as a selected schedule, so a selection rule or set-valued notation must be established.

children.title: Periodic Rescheduling
children.top_down_role: Schedule revision at predetermined review times.

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Rescheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-interval triggering for finite-horizon reactive scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a planning interval \([0,T]\), a period \(\Delta>0\), and trigger epochs \(t_k=\min\{k\Delta,T\}\). A policy is periodically rescheduled when it recomputes a feasible schedule only at the epochs \(t_k\), using information available at \(t_k\), and retains the most recently issued schedule between consecutive epochs. The optimization model, horizon, or committed decisions may change with \(k\), but no off-grid observation alone initiates recomputation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic rescheduling recomputes a schedule at fixed time intervals using current information and retains the latest schedule between successive trigger epochs.
assumptions_latex: A feasible scheduling model is available at every trigger epoch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trigger set is \(\{\min(k\Delta,T):k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\}\), independent of event arrival times.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the periodic-trigger leaf, and the TeX delimiters are valid. However, the record cites no source and the supplied inventory contains no relevant reactive-scheduling reference, so the fixed-interval characterization cannot be admitted as candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Hybrid Rescheduling Triggers
children.top_down_role: Trigger structures combining periodic reviews with exceptional event responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Rescheduling Triggers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trigger rule combining periodic reviews with asynchronous disruption events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{k\Delta:k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\}\cap[0,T]\) be periodic review times and let \(E\subseteq[0,T]\) be a locally finite set of qualifying event times. A hybrid trigger regime invokes rescheduling at every time in \(R=P\cup E\). Equivalently, after trigger \(\tau_k\), the next trigger is \(\tau_{k+1}=\min\bigl((P\cup E)\cap(\tau_k,T]\bigr)\), when this set is nonempty. Coincident periodic and event triggers produce one rescheduling invocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hybrid regime reschedules at either the next periodic review or the next qualifying event, whichever occurs first.
assumptions_latex: \(T>0\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(E\) is locally finite.
Each member of \(E\) satisfies a predetermined event-qualification rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rescheduling epochs are exactly the ordered distinct elements of \(P\cup E\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union of periodic and qualifying event times is a plausible definition of this trigger regime, and definition is the correct content kind. No relevant source or inspectable locator supports this exact formulation, including its treatment of coincident triggers.

children.title: Local Schedule Repair
children.top_down_role: Targeted modification of affected assignments, sequences, or start times.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Schedule Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood-based repair retaining most incumbent scheduling decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible incumbent schedule \(\bar x\), updated feasible set \(X'\), objective \(f\), and neighborhood map \(N\). Initialize \(x^0=\bar x\). At iteration \(r\), search \(N(x^r)\cap X'\) and select \(x^{r+1}\) with \(f(x^{r+1})<f(x^r)\); if no such schedule exists, stop. The output is the final feasible schedule \(x^r\). If \(\bar x\notin X'\), first select any feasible member of \(N(\bar x)\cap X'\), or report local repair failure when that set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local repair searches a prescribed neighborhood of the incumbent, accepting improving feasible schedules until no local improvement exists or the neighborhood cannot restore feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The schedule space is finite, or accepted moves decrease \(f\) by a positive minimum amount.
Neighborhood search can determine feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a locally optimal member of \(X'\) relative to \(N\), or reports that the initial neighborhood contains no feasible repair.

notation.meaning: allowed local neighborhood of schedule x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is an appropriate content kind, but the record selects a particular improving-neighborhood procedure without evidence. Its alternative termination assumption is also insufficient as stated: a positive minimum decrease does not ensure termination unless the objective is bounded below on the reachable feasible schedules. A scheduling-specific source is required before choosing and correcting the algorithmic variant.

children.title: Partial Schedule Reoptimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization restricted to selected jobs, resources, or time windows.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Schedule Reoptimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted reoptimization with selected incumbent decisions frozen.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in X'\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) encode an updated scheduling problem, let \(\bar x\) be the incumbent decision vector, and partition the indices as \(F\mathbin{\dot\cup}U=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Partial schedule reoptimization is represented by
\[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X'} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_i=\bar x_i\ \text{for every }i\in F.\]
Only coordinates indexed by \(U\) are reoptimized. Infeasibility of this restricted problem certifies that the chosen frozen set prevents repair under the updated constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial reoptimization freezes selected incumbent decisions and optimizes only the remaining decisions under the updated scheduling constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(X'\) is the updated feasible set and \(f\) is the chosen scheduling objective.
The incumbent values \(\bar x_i\) are defined for every \(i\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any solution \(x^*\) is optimal over \(\{x\in X':x_F=\bar x_F\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The frozen-coordinate formulation fits the leaf and representation is an appropriate content kind. Nevertheless, no cited source supports this particular formalization of partial schedule reoptimization, and the supplied inventory is unrelated.

children.title: Repair-Scope Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Criteria distinguishing local adjustments from broader schedule reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair-Scope Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicate delimiting which incumbent decisions a repair may alter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For decision indices \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), an incumbent \(\bar x\), and an allowed repair scope \(B\subseteq I\), a candidate schedule \(x\) respects the repair-scope boundary precisely when
\[x_i=\bar x_i\quad\text{for every }i\in I\setminus B.\]
If decisions are time-indexed and the mutable interval is \([a,b]\), this condition uses \(B=\{i:\text{decision }i\text{ is executed or announced within }[a,b]\}\). Feasibility constraints may couple indices inside and outside \(B\), but values outside \(B\) remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repair respects its scope when every decision outside the declared mutable index or time region equals its incumbent value.
assumptions_latex: The incumbent and candidate schedules share a common decision index set \(I\).
The mutable scope \(B\) is fixed before repair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The admissible repair set is \(X'\cap\{x:x_{I\setminus B}=\bar x_{I\setminus B}\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct mathematical role for a boundary predicate, and the fixed-outside-B equation matches the title. The proposed index and time-interval interpretation has no supporting scheduling source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Rolling-Horizon Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated finite-window optimization with shorter irrevocable commitment intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input decision epochs \(\tau_k\), look-ahead length \(H>0\), and commitment length \(h\in(0,H]\). At epoch \(\tau_k\), update all known data, optimize the scheduling model over \([\tau_k,\tau_k+H]\) while fixing previously committed decisions, and implement only decisions in \([\tau_k,\tau_k+h)\). Set \(\tau_{k+1}=\tau_k+h\), reveal or update data, and repeat until the terminal time is committed. The output is the concatenation of implemented segments; uncommitted tail decisions are provisional and may be revised later.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rolling-horizon scheduling repeatedly optimizes a look-ahead window, commits only its leading segment, advances time, and revises the provisional tail with new information.
assumptions_latex: \(0<h\le H\) and the overall planning horizon is finite.
Each window model preserves all decisions committed at earlier epochs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every implemented decision is selected once, while decisions beyond the current commitment interval remain eligible for later revision.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the rolling-horizon topic, but this is one specific fixed-step implementation rather than a uniquely determined definition. It lacks a relevant citation, and the treatment of the final truncated window and commitment segment is not specified when the terminal time is not aligned with h.

children.title: Disruption-Cost Criteria
children.top_down_role: Penalties associated with changing assignments, sequences, times, or resource commitments.

knowledge_statements.title: Disruption-Cost Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted deviation of a revised schedule from its incumbent announcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For jobs \(J\), let \((\bar s_j,\bar a_j)\) and \((s_j,a_j)\) denote incumbent and revised start times and resource assignments. A separable disruption-cost criterion is
\[D(s,a;\bar s,\bar a)=\sum_{j\in J}\left(w_j|s_j-\bar s_j|+q_j\mathbf{1}\{a_j\ne\bar a_j\}\right),\]
where \(w_j,q_j\ge0\). Additional cancellation or reassignment penalties may be represented by further nonnegative terms. The criterion is zero exactly when every positively weighted start time and assignment remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disruption cost measures weighted start-time shifts and assignment changes between an incumbent schedule and its revision.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite.
The incumbent and revised schedules specify comparable start times and assignments for every \(j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The criterion satisfies \(D\ge0\), and \(D=0\) when all positively weighted compared decisions coincide.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is an appropriate content kind, and the displayed criterion is internally coherent. The particular separable start-time and reassignment penalty is only one disruption-cost model and requires a scheduling-specific source with a precise locator.

children.title: Schedule Nervousness
children.top_down_role: Instability caused by frequent or cascading revisions to near-term plans.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Nervousness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instability of successive announced schedules before execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^0,x^1,\ldots,x^m\) be successive announced schedules for a common set of not-yet-executed decisions, and let \(d\) be a nonnegative schedule-deviation measure. Their cumulative nervousness is
\[N_m=\sum_{k=1}^{m} d(x^k,x^{k-1}).\]
A weighted time-sensitive version uses \(d_k\) whose weights increase as affected decisions approach execution. The sequence is stable under this measure exactly when \(N_m=0\); larger values record more frequent, larger, or more urgent revisions according to the selected deviation measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule nervousness is the cumulative measured change between successive announced schedules, optionally weighting changes more heavily near execution.
assumptions_latex: All compared schedules encode the same announced decisions or use an explicit common projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nervousness score is \(N_m=\sum_{k=1}^{m}d(x^k,x^{k-1})\ge0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cumulative-deviation definition plausibly fits schedule nervousness, but no relevant source supports this selected metric. Moreover, the claim that N_m=0 means the sequence is stable requires d(x,y)=0 only when the compared schedules coincide; the assumptions provide only nonnegativity and d(x,x)=0.

children.title: Revision-Frequency Effects
children.top_down_role: Operational consequences of how often schedules are recomputed or altered.

knowledge_statements.title: Revision-Frequency Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic relation between revision count and cumulative schedule deviation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a schedule is revised \(m\) times during an interval of length \(T>0\), with successive deviations \(D_k=d(x^k,x^{k-1})\). Define revision frequency \(\rho=m/T\) and cumulative nervousness \(N_m=\sum_{k=1}^{m}D_k\). If \(D_k\le D_{\max}\) for every revision, then
\[\frac{N_m}{T}\le \rho D_{\max}.\]
Thus increasing revision frequency increases the worst-case upper bound on nervousness per unit time unless the maximum deviation per revision decreases correspondingly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When each revision has bounded size, cumulative nervousness per unit time is at most revision frequency times the per-revision bound.
assumptions_latex: \(T>0\) and \(m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\).
\(0\le D_k\le D_{\max}\) for every \(k=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_m/T\le(m/T)D_{\max}=\rho D_{\max}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is the correct content kind, and the inequality follows from the stated per-revision bound. It nevertheless has no cited evidence or relevant locator establishing that this elementary bound is the intended knowledge statement for the scheduling-specific leaf.

children.title: Cost-Nervousness Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between explicit revision penalties and temporal plan instability.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Nervousness Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biobjective representation of operating performance and schedule stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the feasible revised schedules, \(C:X\to\mathbb{R}\) an operating-cost criterion, and \(N:X\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) a nervousness criterion relative to announced schedules. The tradeoff is the attainable set
\[Y=\{(C(x),N(x)):x\in X\}\]
and its nondominated subset. For \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), any minimizer of \(\lambda C(x)+(1-\lambda)N(x)\) is weakly Pareto efficient. Weighted sums recover supported efficient points; nonsupported points can require an alternative such as minimizing \(C(x)\) subject to \(N(x)\le\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost–nervousness tradeoffs are the nondominated feasible pairs of operating cost and schedule instability; scalarization finds supported compromises.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\), and the stated scalarized minimum is attained.
Both criteria are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive weighted-sum minimizer is weakly Pareto efficient in \(Y\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate for an attainable-set description of cost-nervousness tradeoffs, and the weighted-sum claim is mathematically conservative under positive weights and attainment. No relevant source supports the scheduling-specific criteria or scalarization discussion.

children.title: Uncertain Staffing Demand
children.top_down_role: Variability in required staffing levels across times, skills, or service categories.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertain Staffing Demand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-vector representation of time- and skill-specific coverage requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(D_{st})_{s\in S,t\in P}\) be a nonnegative random vector of required workers by skill \(s\) and period \(t\). For roster variables \(x_{ist}\in\{0,1\}\), a joint chance-constrained coverage requirement is
\[\mathbb{P}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ist}\ge D_{st}\ \text{for every }(s,t)\in S\times P\right)\ge1-\varepsilon.\]
The joint law of \(D\) may encode dependence across skills and periods. Scenario and robust formulations arise by replacing the probability constraint with coverage over selected scenarios or an uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncertain staffing demand is modeled as a random skill-by-period requirement, with rosters constrained to provide coverage at a chosen reliability level.
assumptions_latex: \(I\), \(S\), and \(P\) are finite.
\(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\), and the joint distribution or uncertainty description of \(D\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible rosters satisfy simultaneous staffing coverage with probability at least \(1-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: random staffing requirement for skill s in period t
assignment of worker i to skill s in period t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is suitable for uncertain staffing demand, but the joint chance constraint is one particular stochastic-programming model rather than an intrinsic definition of the leaf. No workforce-rostering or stochastic-programming source with a specific locator is cited.

children.title: Workforce Absenteeism
children.top_down_role: Uncertain loss of scheduled personnel due to absence or unavailability.

knowledge_statements.title: Workforce Absenteeism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random worker-availability representation for realized roster coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For worker \(i\) and period \(t\), let \(A_{it}\in\{0,1\}\) equal one when the worker is available and zero when absent. Given roster assignments \(x_{ist}\in\{0,1\}\), realized skill coverage is
\[C_{st}(A,x)=\sum_{i\in I}A_{it}x_{ist}.\]
An absenteeism-aware joint coverage constraint is \(\mathbb{P}(C_{st}(A,x)\ge d_{st}\text{ for every }(s,t))\ge1-\varepsilon\). No independence is implicit: the joint law of \(A\) may represent common shocks, serial dependence, or correlated absences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absenteeism is represented by random worker-availability indicators that reduce realized coverage and may be statistically dependent across workers and periods.
