assumptions_latex: \(I\), \(S\), and the period set are finite.
The joint distribution or uncertainty description of \(A\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Realized coverage equals \(C_{st}(A,x)=\sum_{i\in I}A_{it}x_{ist}\) and excludes every absent assigned worker.

notation.meaning: availability indicator for worker i in period t
rostered assignment of worker i to skill s in period t
realized coverage for skill s in period t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The availability-indicator representation fits the leaf, but no relevant source supports the selected chance-constrained extension. The period index set is not named, and d_{st} and epsilon are used in the probability constraint without being introduced or constrained, so the complete mathematical version also requires correction after sourcing.

children.title: Demand-Absenteeism Dependence
children.top_down_role: Joint uncertainty patterns linking coverage requirements with workforce availability.

assumptions_latex: Finite worker set \(W\), time-period set \(T\), and common probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\).
Demand \(D_t\) and worker-absence indicators \(A_{wt}\) are integrable random variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dependence is present exactly when the joint law does not factor into its demand and absenteeism marginals.

notation.meaning: indicator that worker w is absent in period t

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the joint-distribution definition; authoritative stochastic-rostering source required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-law definition for correlated staffing demand and absenteeism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(D_t)_{t\in T}\) and \(A=(A_{wt})_{(w,t)\in W	imes T}\). Demand and absenteeism are dependent when there exist measurable sets \(B\) and \(C\) such that \[\mathbb P(D\in B,A\in C)
e \mathbb P(D\in B)\mathbb P(A\in C).\] Equivalently, their joint probability law satisfies \(P_{D,A}
e P_D\otimes P_A\). A covariance condition such as \(\operatorname{Cov}(D_t,A_{ws})
e0\) is sufficient for dependence when the covariance exists, but zero covariance alone does not establish independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Demand-absenteeism dependence means their joint probability distribution does not factor into separate marginal distributions; nonzero cross-covariance is sufficient but not necessary.
knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Absenteeism Dependence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probability-law definition is mathematically standard and internally consistent, but no citation or inspectable locator supports its use in the demand–absenteeism rostering context.

children.title: Coverage Robustness
children.top_down_role: Protection of staffing coverage across demand or attendance realizations.

assumptions_latex: Finite periods \(T\), scheduled coverage \(x_t\), and uncertain net requirement \(R_t(\xi)\) for scenarios \(\xi\in U\).
Coverage is measured in a common nonnegative capacity unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The roster is robust precisely when its scheduled coverage satisfies every scenario-indexed coverage inequality.

notation.meaning: scheduled usable coverage in period t
net staffing requirement under scenario xi

review_flags: No supplied source addresses robust workforce coverage or its uncertainty-set formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static robust-feasibility condition without recourse or chance constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A roster has coverage robustness with respect to \(U\) when \[x_t\ge R_t(\xi)\qquad\text{for every }t\in T\text{ and }\xi\in U.\] Its additive robustness margin is \[\rho(x;U)=\min_{t\in T,\,\xi\in U}\bigl(x_t-R_t(\xi)\bigr).\] Thus robust coverage is equivalent to \(\rho(x;U)\ge0\). If \(U_1\subseteq U_2\), robustness for \(U_2\) implies robustness for \(U_1\), while the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A roster is coverage-robust when scheduled capacity meets net staffing requirements in every period under every scenario in its uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Robustness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this robust-coverage formulation. Moreover, the displayed minimum need not be attained for an arbitrary uncertainty set U; compactness/attainment assumptions or an infimum formulation are required.

children.title: On-Call Capacity
children.top_down_role: Reserve personnel or shifts available for contingent activation.

assumptions_latex: Finite worker set \(W\), periods \(T\), and binary on-call assignments \(y_{wt}\).
Worker \(w\) contributes nonnegative capacity \(q_{wt}\) if activated in period \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Available on-call capacity is the sum of assigned capacities and bounds every feasible activation response.

notation.meaning: activated on-call capacity in period t

review_flags: No supplied locator defines on-call capacity in a rostering model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodwise capacity definition for assigned and activated on-call workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The on-call capacity assigned to period \(t\) is \[Q_t(y)=\sum_{w\in W}q_{wt}y_{wt}.\] If \(u_{wt}(\xi)\in\{0,1\}\) denotes activation after scenario \(\xi\) is observed, feasibility requires \(u_{wt}(\xi)\le y_{wt}\). Consequently, the activated capacity \[z_t(\xi)=\sum_{w\in W}q_{wt}u_{wt}(\xi)\] satisfies \(0\le z_t(\xi)\le Q_t(y)\). Assignment therefore reserves an upper bound on recourse capacity but does not itself imply activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On-call capacity is the total capacity of workers assigned for possible activation; actual activated capacity cannot exceed that reserved amount.
knowledge_statements.title: On-Call Capacity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The capacity accounting is coherent, but no cited rostering source or locator supports this particular definition of assigned and activated on-call capacity.

children.title: Reserve-Activation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Timing, eligibility, and trigger structures governing use of on-call resources.

assumptions_latex: First-stage roster \(x\), on-call assignments \(y\), and realized scenario \(\xi\).
Activation variables obey assignment, eligibility, and period-capacity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An activation regime is specified by its information timing and its feasible scenario-to-activation mapping.

notation.meaning: feasible activation set after scenario xi

review_flags: Activation-regime taxonomy and information structure require a dedicated stochastic-rostering source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage representation distinguishing fixed, adaptive, and threshold activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reserve-activation regime is a policy \(\pi\) satisfying \[u(\xi)=\pi(I(\xi))\in\mathcal U(y,\xi),\] where \(I(\xi)\) is the information available at activation. A fixed regime has \(I(\xi)\) constant; an adaptive regime permits dependence on observed components of \(\xi\); and a threshold regime has \(u_k(\xi)=1\) exactly when a specified statistic \(h_k(I(\xi))\) exceeds a threshold \(\tau_k\), subject to \(u(\xi)\in\mathcal U(y,\xi)\). Coverage feasibility additionally requires activated capacity to dominate \(g(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reserve-activation regime maps available scenario information to feasible reserve calls; fixed, adaptive, and threshold regimes differ by permitted information dependence.
knowledge_statements.title: Reserve-Activation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A dedicated source is required for the proposed activation-regime taxonomy. The threshold rule also needs a precise index set and tie convention, while the meaning and ordering used for activated capacity to dominate g(x,xi) are unspecified.

children.title: Coverage-Reserve Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Balance between baseline roster protection and contingent staffing capacity.

assumptions_latex: Primary coverage decision \(x\) and reserve decision \(y\) belong to a feasible set \(F\).
Coverage risk \(R(x,y)\) and reserve cost \(C(x,y)\) are real-valued and minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Efficient coverage-reserve plans are exactly the nondominated attainable risk-cost pairs.
review_flags: No supplied source supports the bicriteria coverage-reserve formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto formulation of reserve cost versus coverage-shortfall risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible plan \((x,y)\in F\) is coverage-reserve efficient when no \((x',y')\in F\) satisfies \[R(x',y')\le R(x,y),\qquad C(x',y')\le C(x,y),\] with at least one strict inequality. The coverage-reserve tradeoff set is the nondominated frontier of \[\{(R(x,y),C(x,y)):(x,y)\in F\}.\] For every \(\lambda>0\), any minimizer of \(R(x,y)+\lambda C(x,y)\) is weakly efficient; unsupported efficient points may be missed when the attainable objective set is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage-reserve tradeoffs are the nondominated combinations of coverage-shortfall risk and reserve cost; weighted sums may miss efficient points in nonconvex models.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage-Reserve Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the bicriteria formulation or its application to coverage reserves. The record chiefly defines Pareto efficiency and its frontier, so content_kind 'property' does not accurately describe its mathematical role.

children.title: Scheduling Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural boundaries where natural rules, representations, bounds, or deployed schedules cease to behave reliably.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Complexity hierarchy, model discussions, robustness, and implementation

children.title: Release-Date Priority Distortions
children.top_down_role: Priority failures caused by job availability timing.

assumptions_latex: A nonpreemptive single machine and two jobs \(i,j\) with processing times \(p_i=2\), \(p_j=1\).
Release dates are \(r_i=0\) and \(r_j=1\), and shorter processing time has higher static priority.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Release feasibility can force execution of a lower-priority available job before a globally higher-priority unreleased job.
review_flags: Concrete release-date priority example lacks support from the supplied locators.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-machine distortion of static shortest-processing-time priority by release dates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Since \(p_j<p_i\), static shortest-processing-time priority ranks \(j\) above \(i\). At time \(0\), however, only \(i\) is released. Any non-idling list schedule starts \(i\) at \(S_i=0\), so nonpreemption gives \(S_j\ge2\). Hence the realized order is \(i,j\), the reverse of the static priority order. The reversal is caused solely by the feasibility constraints \(S_k\ge r_k\); removing the release-date difference makes the higher-priority job selectable first.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-priority short job released later can be executed after a lower-priority available job, reversing the static priority order.
knowledge_statements.title: Release-Date Priority Distortions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-job counterexample is valid for a non-idling, nonpreemptive list schedule and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but it has no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Precedence Priority Distortions
children.top_down_role: Priority failures caused by dependency restrictions.

assumptions_latex: A finite acyclic precedence graph \(G=(J,E)\).
A strict priority order ranks job \(j\) above job \(i\), while \((i,j)\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Precedence feasibility overrides the conflicting priority comparison and forces \(i\) before \(j\).
review_flags: The supplied project-scheduling locator is only indirect evidence for this priority-conflict boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct conflict between a static priority order and a precedence arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every feasible nonpreemptive schedule, the arc \((i,j)\in E\) imposes \[C_i\le C_j-p_j,\] and therefore \(i\) completes before \(j\) starts. If the priority order instead requires \(j\) before \(i\), no schedule can realize both orders. A priority rule restricted to currently precedence-eligible jobs remains feasible, but its realized sequence necessarily violates this pairwise priority comparison. Thus unrestricted priority dominance ends at any precedence arc oriented opposite to the priority order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a precedence arc points opposite to a static priority comparison, every feasible schedule must violate that priority comparison.
knowledge_statements.title: Precedence Priority Distortions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The precedence conflict is standard, but no source is cited. The equation C_i <= C_j-p_j additionally presumes the usual relation between start and completion times and no intervening setup convention, which should be stated explicitly.

children.title: Joint Feasibility Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Regimes where availability timing conflicts with dependency feasibility.

assumptions_latex: A finite job set \(J\), strict priority relation \(P\), and mandatory precedence relation \(E\).
A schedule realizes both relations only if its job order is a common linear extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joint feasibility holds exactly when the directed graph formed by the union of mandatory and priority arcs is acyclic.
review_flags: Standard order-extension claim is unambiguous, but no supplied locator directly supports the union-acyclicity formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclicity test for simultaneous precedence and priority-order feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mandatory constraints and all priority comparisons are jointly feasible if and only if \(H=(J,E\cup P)\) is acyclic. Indeed, the required schedule order must be a topological ordering of \(H\). A directed cycle \[j_1\to j_2\to\cdots\to j_m\to j_1\] is therefore a finite certificate of conflict: no linear order can satisfy every arc on that cycle. When \(H\) is acyclic, any topological ordering simultaneously respects every mandatory precedence and retained priority arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mandatory precedence and priority comparisons admit a common schedule order exactly when their union digraph is acyclic; a directed cycle certifies conflict.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Feasibility Conflicts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union-acyclicity characterization and directed-cycle certificate are mathematically correct for arc relations on a finite job set, but no citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Priority Dominance Reversals
children.top_down_role: Cases where locally preferred jobs become globally inferior choices.

assumptions_latex: Two jobs \(i,j\) satisfy strict static priority \(i\succ j\).
A feasibility system \(F\) restricts admissible schedules, and at least one admissible schedule orders \(j\) before \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Priority dominance is reversed whenever every feasible optimum places the nominally lower-priority job first.
review_flags: The intended priority metric and scheduling objective are unspecified; statement uses an objective-relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-relative definition of reversal under feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_{i\prec j}\) and \(F_{j\prec i}\) denote feasible schedules ordering \(i\) before \(j\) and \(j\) before \(i\), respectively. A priority dominance reversal occurs when \(i\succ j\) but \[\inf_{\sigma\in F_{j\prec i}}f(\sigma)<\inf_{\sigma\in F_{i\prec j}}f(\sigma),\] with the convention that the infimum of an empty set is \(+\infty\). Under this strict inequality, every optimal schedule orders \(j\) before \(i\), despite the opposite nominal priority. Release dates, precedence, or resource compatibility may create the reversal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dominance reversal occurs when every optimal feasible schedule places a nominally lower-priority job before the higher-priority job.
knowledge_statements.title: Priority Dominance Reversals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source fixes the intended objective-relative notion of reversal. The strict inequality between infima does not by itself imply that an optimal schedule exists or that every optimum orders j before i; attainment and an exhaustive partition of feasible schedules by the two orders are required.

assumptions_latex: A nonpreemptive single machine starts in state \(0\) and processes jobs \(a,b\) with \(p_a=p_b=1\).
Sequence-dependent setup times satisfy \(s_{0a}=s_{0b}=s_{ba}=0\) and \(s_{ab}=M\) for \(M>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed priority ordering can have an unbounded approximation ratio when it ignores sequence-dependent setup times.

notation.meaning: setup time from state or job i to job j

review_flags: No supplied source covers sequence-dependent setup counterexamples for priority rules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-job unbounded-ratio counterexample for a setup-blind fixed priority rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a fixed setup-blind priority rule orders \(a\) before \(b\). Its makespan is \[C_{\max}(a,b)=p_a+s_{ab}+p_b=M+2.\] The reverse sequence has makespan \[C_{\max}(b,a)=p_b+s_{ba}+p_a=2.\] Hence the rule's approximation ratio is \((M+2)/2\), which tends to infinity as \(M\to\infty\). Thus processing-time or job-weight priority alone cannot guarantee any constant makespan approximation factor over unrestricted sequence-dependent setup instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unrestricted sequence-dependent setups, a setup-blind fixed priority rule can be arbitrarily worse than the reverse sequence, even for two equal jobs.
knowledge_statements.title: Setup-Dependent Priority Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-job construction correctly gives an unbounded ratio for the specified setup-blind fixed ordering, but no source is cited. The broader claim about processing-time or job-weight priorities requires an explicit adversarial relabeling argument or narrower wording, especially since weights are not defined.

children.title: Nonregular Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling settings where earlier completion is not uniformly preferable.

assumptions_latex: A scheduling objective \(f(C_1,\ldots,C_n)\) is minimized over feasible completion-time vectors.
Coordinatewise comparison uses the usual order on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is nonregular exactly when delaying at least one completion time can strictly improve the objective while no completion time becomes earlier.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the standard regular-objective definition or its negation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completion-time definition of a nonregular minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(f\) is regular when \[C\le C'\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(C)\le f(C')\] for every pair of completion-time vectors in its domain. A nonregular objective regime is one for which this monotonicity fails: there exist \(C\le C'\) such that \(f(C)>f(C')\). Earliness-tardiness objectives can be nonregular because completing a job earlier than its due date may increase its earliness penalty. Consequently, transformations that only reduce completion times need not improve the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization objective is nonregular when making no job earlier, and at least one job later, can strictly improve its value.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonregular Objective Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of regularity and its negation are standard and the plain and LaTeX statements agree, but no authoritative scheduling reference with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Beneficial Idling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where intentional machine inactivity improves schedule quality.

assumptions_latex: One nonpreemptive job is available at time \(0\), has processing time \(p=1\), and due date \(d=2\).
The objective is absolute deviation \(f(C)=|C-d|\), and inserted idle time is allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Intentional idle time strictly improves the schedule, so immediate processing is not optimal.
review_flags: Concrete beneficial-idling example is standard but unsupported by the supplied source locators.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-job example showing beneficial idling under a nonregular due-date objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting immediately yields \(C=1\) and objective value \(f(1)=|1-2|=1\). Idling on \([0,1]\) and then processing the job yields \(C=2\) and \(f(2)=0\). Therefore deliberate idling strictly improves the objective even though the machine and job are both available. The mechanism disappears for objectives that are nondecreasing in completion times, because removing such idle time cannot increase any completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a job due at time two with unit processing time, waiting one unit eliminates earliness cost and strictly beats immediate processing.
knowledge_statements.title: Beneficial Idling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-job beneficial-idling counterexample is correct and fits the leaf, but it lacks a source. The final generalization about removing idle time needs additional feasibility assumptions and is broader than the demonstrated instance.

children.title: Idling-Optimality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits separating useful inactivity from avoidable delay.

assumptions_latex: Single-machine schedules are nonpreemptive.
A regular objective is coordinatewise nondecreasing in job completion times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without release dates an optimal non-idling schedule exists, whereas release dates can make voluntary idling strictly optimal.

notation.meaning: processing time, release date, weight, and completion time of job j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: left-shifting is valid without release dates; the displayed release-date instance is directly checkable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between removable idle time and voluntary idle time induced by future releases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If all jobs are available at time \(0\), left-shifting every operation until either time \(0\) or the preceding completion does not increase any \(C_j\); hence every regular objective has an optimal schedule with no idle interval before completion. This fails with release dates. For two jobs with \((r_1,p_1,w_1)=(0,10,1)\) and \((r_2,p_2,w_2)=(1,1,100)\), starting job \(1\) immediately gives \(F=1110\). Idling until time \(1\), then processing job \(2\) before job \(1\), gives \(F=212\), so voluntary idling is strictly optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-idling is sufficient when all jobs are initially available and the objective is regular, but future high-priority releases can make deliberate idling strictly better.
knowledge_statements.title: Idling-Optimality Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and the mathematical example fit the node, but no inspectable scheduling source is cited for the non-idling result or the release-date boundary. Standard-field rationale alone does not satisfy the citation requirement for this nontrivial claim.

children.title: Priority-Rule Reversal Effects
children.top_down_role: Consequences for dispatching preferences under nonregular objectives.

assumptions_latex: Two jobs are simultaneously eligible at each compared decision time.
The objective permits sequence-dependent or time-dependent pairwise preferences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A priority reversal occurs exactly when \(\Delta_{ij}(t)\Delta_{ij}(t')<0\) for some \(t<t'\).

notation.meaning: objective value when i is processed immediately before j starting at t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pairwise-interchange sign changes formalize time-dependent priority reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise priority reversal for time-dependent or nonregular scheduling objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For eligible jobs \(i\) and \(j\), define the pairwise interchange difference at start time \(t\) by \(\Delta_{ij}(t)=F_{ij}(t)-F_{ji}(t)\). The local preference is \(i\prec_t j\) when \(\Delta_{ij}(t)\le 0\). A strict priority-rule reversal occurs if there are \(t<t'\) such that \(\Delta_{ij}(t)<0<\Delta_{ij}(t')\), or equivalently with both inequalities reversed. Thus no static priority index can represent the pairwise preference over all decision times whenever \(\Delta_{ij}(t)\Delta_{ij}(t')<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reversal occurs when delaying the same pairwise scheduling decision changes which job order has the smaller objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Rule Reversal Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition precisely captures a strict time-dependent pairwise priority reversal and fits the terminal container. No source with a specific locator supports this scheduling interpretation or the claimed obstruction to a static priority index.

assumptions_latex: Time is discretized into \(H+1\) candidate start periods.
Each of \(n\) jobs has a binary start variable for every feasible period.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation has \(\Theta(nH)\) start variables and is pseudopolynomial when \(H\) is binary encoded.

notation.meaning: binary variable indicating that job j starts at time t
number of jobs and time horizon

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct counting of a standard time-indexed formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-size boundary for discrete-horizon time-indexed scheduling formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time-indexed formulation containing \(x_{jt}\) for each job \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and each feasible start time \(t\in\{0,\ldots,H-p_j\}\) has \(\sum_j(H-p_j+1)\) start variables, which is \(\Theta(nH)\) when all \(p_j=O(H)\) and a constant fraction of periods is feasible. Consequently, if \(H\) is specified in binary and may be exponential in its encoding length \(\log H\), the formulation is pseudopolynomial rather than polynomial in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time-indexed models use order nH start variables, so a numerically large binary-encoded horizon can make their explicit size pseudopolynomial.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Indexed Size Explosion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the representation-boundary node, and the variable count is appropriately qualified by horizon feasibility. An inspectable source is still required for the time-indexed formulation and its pseudopolynomial encoding-size characterization.

assumptions_latex: All \(n\) equal-length jobs require one nonpreemptive machine.
Pairwise precedence disjunctions use a valid constant \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For sufficiently large \(M\), the LP makespan can be \(p\) while the integer optimum is \(np\).

notation.meaning: start time and common processing time
binary ordering variable for jobs i and j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the fractional construction directly exhibits relaxation degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise big-M disjunctions for single-machine nonoverlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each pair \(i<j\), impose \(s_i+p\le s_j+M(1-y_{ij})\) and \(s_j+p\le s_i+My_{ij}\). In the LP relaxation, if \(M\ge 2p\), the assignment \(s_i=0\) and \(y_{ij}=1/2\) for every pair is feasible and gives \(C_{\max}=p\). Every integer solution must process all jobs sequentially and therefore has \(C_{\max}=np\). Hence this big-M relaxation has integer-to-LP objective ratio \(n\), even though the disjunction is valid for integer ordering variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional ordering variables can neutralize big-M nonoverlap constraints, allowing all jobs to overlap and producing a makespan bound weaker by a factor of n.
knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Relaxation Degradation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fractional construction supports the stated factor-n relaxation degradation when M is sufficiently large and valid for the bounded scheduling formulation. A source is required to establish the precise validity assumptions on M and support this formulation-specific boundary.

children.title: Scheduling Symmetry Sources
children.top_down_role: Interchangeable jobs, resources, periods, or assignments that create redundant representations.

assumptions_latex: A finite group acts on the feasible schedules.
The objective and all constraints are invariant under that action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identical resources, indistinguishable jobs, and interchangeable time labels generate scheduling symmetries.

notation.meaning: feasible schedule set and symmetry group
action of symmetry g on schedule S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: invariance under relabeling is the standard mathematical definition of formulation symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group-action description of common label symmetries in scheduling models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling symmetry is a permutation \(g\) of formulation labels such that \(gS\in\mathcal S\) and \(f(gS)=f(S)\) for every \(S\in\mathcal S\). Typical generators are permutations of identical machines, permutations of jobs having identical data and constraints, and permutations of interchangeable rooms, employees, or time slots. Products and compositions of these generators form a group \(G\) acting on \(\mathcal S\); each nonidentity element maps every schedule to a feasibility- and objective-equivalent relabeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scheduling symmetries arise when identical machines, jobs, rooms, staff, or time slots can be relabeled without changing feasibility or objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Symmetry Sources

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits a leaf about symmetry sources, and the group-action formulation is mathematically coherent. No scheduling or optimization-symmetry source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Equivalent-Schedule Classes
children.top_down_role: Families of distinct representations sharing the same scheduling outcome.

assumptions_latex: A finite symmetry group \(G\) acts on the feasible schedule set \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalence classes are precisely the orbits \(G S\), with size \(|G|/|G_S|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: orbit equivalence and orbit-stabilizer counting are standard finite group-action facts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit representation of schedules equivalent under label symmetries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S\sim S'\) if and only if \(S'=gS\) for some \(g\in G\). This is an equivalence relation on \(\mathcal S\), and the class containing \(S\) is exactly its orbit \([S]=GS\). For finite \(G\), the orbit-stabilizer identity gives \(|[S]|=|G|/|G_S|\). Because feasibility and objective value are invariant under \(G\), optimization may retain one representative from every orbit without changing the attainable objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedules related only by an allowed relabeling form one group orbit; one representative per orbit preserves every attainable objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Schedule Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind correctly describes equivalent schedules as group orbits and fits the node. The orbit-stabilizer statement and its scheduling application lack an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Search-Tree Duplication
children.top_down_role: Computational expansion caused by repeated exploration of equivalent schedules.

assumptions_latex: A branching algorithm distinguishes formulation labels.
No symmetry-breaking rule identifies nodes related by the group action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An orbit of size \(|G|/|G_S|\) can induce that many equivalent labeled leaves.

notation.meaning: symmetry group and a feasible terminal schedule

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: orbit cardinality counts distinct labeled copies when branching preserves labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duplication caused by label-sensitive branching over a symmetric formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose distinct labeled schedules correspond to distinct terminal nodes of a complete search tree. If \(S\) is feasible, then every schedule in its orbit \(GS\) is feasible with the same objective value. In the absence of symmetry pruning, the tree may therefore contain \(|GS|=|G|/|G_S|\) equivalent terminal nodes for that single unlabeled schedule. When the action is free at \(S\), \(G_S=\{e\}\), so the duplication factor is \(|G|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Label-sensitive search may explore an entire symmetry orbit, creating up to one equivalent leaf per group element when no schedule has a nontrivial stabilizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Duplication

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the search-duplication leaf, and the conclusion is properly conditional on labeled schedules corresponding to distinct terminal nodes. A branch-and-bound or symmetry-in-search source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Symmetry-Breaking Limits
children.top_down_role: Regimes where redundancy controls remain incomplete or counterproductive.

assumptions_latex: The full formulation symmetry group is \(G\).
Added constraints distinguish only symmetries in a subgroup \(H\le G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Breaking \(H\) alone cannot guarantee one representative per \(G\)-orbit when residual symmetries remain.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subgroup-breaking conditions do not remove equivalences generated outside the targeted subgroup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of partial symmetry breaking based on only one source of relabeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complete symmetry-breaking region \(R\) must satisfy \(|R\cap GS|=1\) for every feasible orbit \(GS\). Constraints that choose one representative only within each \(H\)-orbit guarantee at most \(|R\cap HS|=1\). If some \(g\in G\setminus H\) maps a retained schedule \(S\in R\) to another retained schedule \(gS\in R\), then \(|R\cap GS|\ge 2\). Thus ordering identical machines does not eliminate symmetries generated independently by identical jobs or interchangeable time slots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraints aimed at one symmetry subgroup do not remove equivalent schedules generated by other relabelings, so multiple representatives of a full orbit may remain.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Breaking Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the node, and the distinction between breaking H-orbits and selecting one representative from each G-orbit is precise. No inspectable source supports the scheduling symmetry-breaking limitation.

assumptions_latex: A master problem has one variable for every feasible pattern.
Columns are generated by solving an exact reduced-cost pricing problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: NP-hard pricing prevents polynomial-time exact pattern generation unless \(P=NP\), and even easy pricing does not bound the number of generated columns polynomially.

notation.meaning: pattern set, pattern cost, and master-column vector
current dual vector and reduced cost

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact column generation requires reduced-cost minimization over the implicit pattern family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational boundaries of implicit pattern formulations solved by column generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a restricted-master solution with dual vector \(\pi\), exact pricing computes \(p^*\in\arg\min_{p\in\mathcal P}\{c_p-\pi^\top a_p\}\) and terminates only when \(\bar c_{p^*}\ge0\). If this optimization contains an NP-hard scheduling problem, no polynomial-time exact pricing algorithm exists unless \(P=NP\). Moreover, polynomial-time pricing alone does not imply a polynomial column-generation algorithm: the number of distinct improving columns or degenerate master iterations may still be exponential in the encoded instance size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pattern methods bottleneck at reduced-cost pricing when pricing is NP-hard; even tractable pricing does not prevent exponentially many master iterations or generated columns.
knowledge_statements.title: Pattern-Generation Bottlenecks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the node, but the claims about NP-hard exact pricing and potentially exponential column-generation behavior require a column-generation source and explicit encoded-problem context. The available inventory contains no directly supporting citation.

assumptions_latex: Each instance has an integer formulation with finite optimum.
The LP relaxation uses the same minimization objective and has positive optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regime has unbounded integrality gap when its instance ratios are not bounded by any constant.

notation.meaning: integer and LP-relaxation optimal values for instance I

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: ratio and supremum are standard for positive minimization objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative integrality gaps for minimization formulations of scheduling problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance \(I\) with \(0<z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)<\infty\), define \(\gamma(I)=z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)/z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\). A class \(\mathcal I\) is a bounded-gap regime if \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\gamma(I)<\infty\). It is an unbounded-gap regime if, for every \(K>0\), some \(I\in\mathcal I\) satisfies \(\gamma(I)>K\). Additive gaps require a separate normalization and are not implied by this multiplicative definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimization relaxation has an unbounded integrality-gap regime when integer-to-LP optimum ratios exceed every fixed constant across a family of instances.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the regime node, and the positivity and finiteness hypotheses make the multiplicative minimization gap well defined. A specific authoritative locator for this integrality-gap convention is absent.

children.title: Weak Workload Bounds
children.top_down_role: Loss of bound strength from aggregate workload information.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) unit-time jobs and \(n\) identical machines.
The jobs form one precedence chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The aggregate workload lower bound is \(1\), while the true makespan is \(n\).

notation.meaning: processing time, machine count, and makespan

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the chain instance directly demonstrates that aggregate workload ignores precedence serialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of aggregate workload bounds when precedence forces serialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=n\), let \(p_j=1\) for every \(j\), and impose the chain \(1\prec2\prec\cdots\prec n\). The aggregate workload bound is \(L_W=\sum_jp_j/m=n/n=1\). Nevertheless, the precedence chain permits at most one job to execute at a time, so every feasible schedule has \(C_{\max}\ge n\), and executing the chain consecutively attains \(C_{\max}=n\). Hence \(C_{\max}/L_W=n\), showing arbitrarily weak workload-only bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With n machines and an n-job precedence chain, the average-workload bound is 1 although serialization forces makespan n.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Workload Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind exactly fits the weak-workload-bound leaf, and the chain instance consistently yields a factor-n gap. No scheduling lower-bound source with an inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Weak Capacity Bounds
children.top_down_role: Loss of bound strength from coarse resource-capacity information.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) unit-time jobs and a renewable resource of capacity \(n\).
Every pair of jobs has a mutual-exclusion constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resource-capacity bound is \(1\), while the true makespan is \(n\).

notation.meaning: resource demand of job j and total capacity

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed conflict-clique instance directly shows what an aggregate capacity bound omits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of aggregate renewable-resource bounds when separate conflicts dominate capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_j=q_j=1\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\), and let the renewable-resource capacity be \(B=n\). The energy-capacity bound is \(L_C=\sum_jp_jq_j/B=n/n=1\). Add mutual-exclusion constraints requiring every pair of jobs to occupy disjoint time intervals. These conflicts force all jobs to execute sequentially, so \(C_{\max}=n\). Therefore \(C_{\max}/L_C=n\), and a capacity-only bound can be arbitrarily weak when it ignores independent incompatibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource may have enough nominal capacity for all jobs, yet pairwise conflicts can force complete serialization and make the capacity bound arbitrarily weak.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Capacity Bounds

children.title: Coupled Bound Failures
children.top_down_role: Weakness arising when workload pressure interacts with capacity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Bound Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate workload and capacity bounds can overlook simultaneous-resource compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let one unit-duration job require resources \(A\) and \(B\) simultaneously, and let the available periods be \(T=\{1,2\}\). Resource \(A\) has capacity one only in period \(1\), while resource \(B\) has capacity one only in period \(2\). For each resource, required workload equals total available capacity, so the separate workload-capacity inequalities hold. Nevertheless, a feasible start would require a period in \(\{1\}\cap\{2\}=\varnothing\). Thus independently valid resource bounds do not imply feasibility when resource requirements are coupled temporally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each resource has enough total capacity, but the job cannot run because the resources are never available simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: The job requires \(A\) and \(B\) simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_A\le C_A\) and \(W_B\le C_B\), but no feasible schedule exists.

notation.meaning: total available capacity of resource r

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit finite scheduling counterexample establishes the claimed boundary
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite counterexample is mathematically coherent and fits the Coupled Bound Failures leaf, but it has no inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Regime-Specific Tightness Loss
children.top_down_role: Instance structures associated with especially loose lower or upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Regime-Specific Tightness Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate workload bounds lose tightness under concentrated machine eligibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(m\ge2\), consider \(m\) unit-processing-time jobs on \(m\) parallel machines, with every job eligible only for machine \(1\). The aggregate workload lower bound is \(L=W/m=1\), because \(W=m\). Every feasible schedule, however, processes all jobs sequentially on machine \(1\), giving optimal makespan \(C_{\max}^*=m\). Hence \(C_{\max}^*/L=m\), so the aggregate bound has an unbounded multiplicative loss as \(m\to\infty\) in the restricted-eligibility regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An aggregate workload bound becomes arbitrarily weak when all jobs are eligible for only one machine.
assumptions_latex: \(p_j=1\) for every job \(j\)
Every job is eligible only for machine \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}^*/L=m\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Interaction Blind Spots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility of every single-resource projection need not imply joint feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_r\) be the schedules satisfying all restrictions associated with resource \(r\). A resource-separable relaxation checks only \(\mathcal F_r\ne\varnothing\) for each \(r\), whereas joint feasibility requires \(\bigcap_r\mathcal F_r\ne\varnothing\). These conditions are not equivalent: for one job requiring resources \(A\) and \(B\) simultaneously, take \(\mathcal F_A=\{\text{start at period }1\}\) and \(\mathcal F_B=\{\text{start at period }2\}\). Both projections are feasible, but \(\mathcal F_A\cap\mathcal F_B=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every resource projection may be feasible even though their joint scheduling requirements have no common solution.

children.title: Overconstraint Sources
children.top_down_role: Modeling choices that remove intended feasible schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Overconstraint Sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A newly imposed requirement overconstrains a finite scheduling model exactly when it excludes every previously feasible schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a finite schedule set, let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), and define \(F=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,k\}\ne\varnothing\). For \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\), adding the requirement \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) produces \(F'=\{x\in F:a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\}\). The added requirement is an overconstraint source precisely when \(F'=\varnothing\), equivalently when \(\min_{x\in F}a^{\mathsf T}x>b\). Thus infeasibility can be attributed to that requirement relative to the original feasible model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An added constraint causes overconstraint exactly when its threshold lies below the minimum value of its left-hand side over all previously feasible schedules.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is finite.
\(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\).
\(F\ne\varnothing\).
\(a\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'=\varnothing\iff\min_{x\in F}a^{\mathsf T}x>b\).

notation.meaning: feasible set after adding the requirement
coefficient vector and threshold of the added requirement

children.title: Hidden Infeasibility Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Indirect conflicts that conceal the origin of infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Infeasibility Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall-deficient job subsets certify infeasibility hidden by individual availability and aggregate capacity checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent unit jobs and unit-capacity slots by a bipartite graph \(G=(J,T;E)\), where \((j,t)\in E\) means job \(j\) may occupy slot \(t\). A complete schedule exists exactly when \(|N(S)|\ge|S|\) for every \(S\subseteq J\). Consequently, any subset \(S\) satisfying \(|N(S)|<|S|\) is a verifiable infeasibility certificate. This mechanism may remain hidden even when every job has an admissible slot and \(|T|\ge|J|\), because those aggregate checks do not examine shared neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of jobs collectively having too few admissible slots certifies infeasibility despite adequate total capacity.
assumptions_latex: Jobs and slots have unit demand and unit capacity.
Feasibility is represented by a bipartite matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A complete schedule exists iff \(\lvert N(S)\rvert\ge\lvert S\rvert\) for every \(S\subseteq J\).

notation.meaning: slots adjacent to at least one job in S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matching formulation and Hall-deficiency certificate are correct and the certificate kind fits the leaf, but the invoked theorem requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Constraint-Interaction Failures
children.top_down_role: Infeasibility emerging only through combinations of individually plausible restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Interaction Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimal infeasible subsystem isolates infeasibility caused only by the simultaneous action of several constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ambient decision set \(X\) and constraint-feasible sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq X\), an index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is a minimal constraint-interaction failure when \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i=\varnothing\) but \(\bigcap_{i\in I\setminus\{j\}}C_i\ne\varnothing\) for every \(j\in I\). For example, in \(\mathbb R^2\), the constraints \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), and \(x+y\le-1\) are jointly infeasible, while every proper pair is feasible. No individual constraint alone explains the failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal interaction failure is an infeasible constraint family whose every one-constraint deletion is feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq X\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is minimal infeasible iff \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i=\varnothing\) and every one-constraint deletion has nonempty intersection.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard minimal-infeasible-subsystem definition with an explicit example

children.title: Infeasibility-Diagnosis Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on locating actionable causes within large scheduling models.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility-Diagnosis Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-based infeasibility certificates cannot diagnose purely integrality-induced infeasibility while the relaxation remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integer scheduling formulation \(P_I=\{x\in\mathbb Z:2x=1,0\le x\le1\}\). It is infeasible, but its linear relaxation \(P_L=\{x\in\mathbb R:2x=1,0\le x\le1\}\) contains \(x=1/2\). Therefore no certificate asserting infeasibility of \(P_L\), including a Farkas certificate for its linear constraints, exists. Any diagnosis procedure restricted to infeasibility of the current LP relaxation consequently fails to detect this integrality-only mechanism without branching, valid inequalities, or integer reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer model may be infeasible while its LP relaxation is feasible, beyond the reach of LP-infeasibility certificates.
assumptions_latex: Diagnosis uses only infeasibility of the displayed LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I=\varnothing\) while \(P_L=\{1/2\}\ne\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly separates integer infeasibility from LP infeasibility and fits the diagnosis-boundary leaf, but the claim about Farkas certificates and LP diagnosis needs a specific authoritative locator.

children.title: Objective Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between optimized criteria and intended scheduling outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimization of a misspecified objective can have arbitrarily large deployment regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(M>0\), let the feasible schedules be \(X=\{a,b\}\). Let the modeled costs satisfy \(f(a)=1\) and \(f(b)=0\), while the true deployment costs satisfy \(U(a)=0\) and \(U(b)=M\). Exact minimization of \(f\) uniquely selects \(b\), although \(a\) uniquely minimizes \(U\). The resulting true-cost regret is \(U(b)-\min_{x\in X}U(x)=M\), which is unbounded as \(M\to\infty\). Optimization accuracy therefore cannot compensate for objective misspecification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfectly solved modeled objective can select a schedule whose true cost is arbitrarily worse than optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min_{x\in X}f(x)=\{b\}\) and \(U(b)-\min_{x\in X}U(x)=M\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-schedule construction proves arbitrary regret
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-schedule construction correctly demonstrates unbounded regret from objective misspecification and the counterexample kind fits the leaf, but no source is cited.

children.title: Penalty Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Poor representation of soft-constraint severity or operational cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An undersized soft-constraint penalty can make an infeasible schedule optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the penalized objective be \(F_\lambda(x)=f(x)+\lambda v(x)\), where \(v(x)\ge0\) and feasibility means \(v(x)=0\). For schedules \(a,b\), set \(f(a)=0\), \(v(a)=0\), \(f(b)=-M\), and \(v(b)=1\), with \(M>0\). Then \(F_\lambda(b)=-M+\lambda<F_\lambda(a)=0\) whenever \(0\le\lambda<M\). Thus every penalty below the objective advantage \(M\) selects the violating schedule; a penalty is not exact merely because it is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive penalty can still favor an infeasible schedule when it is smaller than that schedule's objective advantage.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le\lambda<M\)
Feasibility is equivalent to \(v(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\lambda(b)<F_\lambda(a)\), although \(v(b)>0=v(a)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The penalty-threshold calculation is correct and fits a penalty-misspecification failure boundary, but it lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Objective-Penalty Misalignment
children.top_down_role: Conflicts between primary criteria and penalty incentives.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Penalty Misalignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alignment requires the modeled objective-plus-penalty ordering to preserve deployment-optimal choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite schedule set, let \(F_\lambda(x)=f(x)+\lambda v(x)\) be the modeled penalized cost, and let \(D(x)\) be deployment cost. Objective and penalty are selection-aligned when \(\arg\min_{x\in X}F_\lambda(x)\subseteq\arg\min_{x\in X}D(x)\). A sufficient witness of misalignment is a pair \(x,y\in X\) with \(F_\lambda(x)<F_\lambda(y)\) but \(D(x)>D(y)\), provided \(x\) is a modeled minimizer. Then modeled optimization selects a deployment-dominated schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misalignment occurs when a modeled optimum is not deployment-optimal; a reversed pairwise ranking provides a direct witness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite.
\(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Alignment holds iff \(\arg\min_X F_\lambda\subseteq\arg\min_X D\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selection-alignment condition and its pairwise witness are internally consistent and appropriate for this leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Schedule-Quality Distortions
children.top_down_role: Operationally undesirable schedules favored by a misspecified scoring structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Quality Distortions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalarized quality can conceal arbitrarily poor performance on a weakly weighted deployment metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(M>1\), let schedules \(a,b\) have metric vectors \(q(a)=(0,M)\) and \(q(b)=(1,0)\), where both components are minimized. Use the scalarized modeled cost \(F(x)=q_1(x)+\varepsilon q_2(x)\) with \(\varepsilon=1/(2M)\). Then \(F(a)=1/2<F(b)=1\), so the model selects \(a\). If deployment quality is measured by \(q_2\), its regret is \(q_2(a)-\min_xq_2(x)=M\), which can be arbitrarily large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak scalarization weight can select a schedule with arbitrarily bad performance on the corresponding quality metric.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon=1/(2M)\)
Both quality components are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(a)<F(b)\) while \(q_2(a)-\min_x q_2(x)=M\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit bicriteria construction establishes unbounded distortion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bicriteria construction correctly gives arbitrarily large distortion on the weakly weighted metric and fits the counterexample role, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Fairness Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling conflicts driven by equitable allocation or burden distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Fairness Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Changing the fairness weight produces distinct optimal regimes along an efficiency-fairness conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two feasible schedules have worker-burden vectors \(d(a)=(0,2)\) and \(d(b)=(2,2)\). Define efficiency cost \(E(d)=d_1+d_2\), disparity \(D(d)=|d_1-d_2|\), and scalarized cost \(F_\lambda(d)=E(d)+\lambda D(d)\) for \(\lambda\ge0\). Then \(F_\lambda(d(a))=2+2\lambda\) and \(F_\lambda(d(b))=4\). Schedule \(a\) is uniquely optimal for \(\lambda<1\), both tie at \(\lambda=1\), and \(b\) is uniquely optimal for \(\lambda>1\). Neither schedule dominates the other in both criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low fairness weight favors lower total burden; high fairness weight favors equal burdens, with a threshold at weight one.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda\ge0\)
Both efficiency cost and disparity are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) is optimal for \(\lambda<1\), \(a,b\) tie for \(\lambda=1\), and \(b\) is optimal for \(\lambda>1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-schedule Pareto tradeoff calculation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalarization calculations and threshold regimes are correct and fit the fairness-tradeoff leaf, but the property is unsupported by a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Robustness Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling conflicts driven by protection against uncertainty or disruption.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An epsilon-constraint boundary between nominal schedule quality and worst-case protection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty finite set of feasible schedules, \(c:X\to\mathbb R\) a nominal cost, and \(r:X\to\mathbb R_+\) a robustness loss. For a permitted robustness level \(\rho\), define \(v(\rho)=\min\{c(x):x\in X,\ r(x)\le\rho\}\), with \(v(\rho)=+\infty\) if the constrained set is empty. A strict robustness tradeoff regime occurs on \([\rho_1,\rho_2]\) when \(v(\rho)<+\infty\) throughout and \(v(\rho')>v(\rho)\) whenever \(\rho'<\rho\) in that interval. Thus every stricter robustness requirement there forces a strictly larger nominal cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robustness tradeoff regime is a range where every stricter bound on worst-case loss necessarily increases the best attainable nominal scheduling cost.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and nonempty.
\(c\) and \(r\) are real-valued on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho'<\rho\Longrightarrow v(\rho')>v(\rho)\) throughout a strict tradeoff regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: epsilon-constraint value functions are a standard formalization of multiobjective tradeoff regimes
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the terminal container, and the epsilon-constraint formulation is internally coherent. However, no inspectable citation supports treating this particular value-function regime as a scheduling robustness boundary; the standard-field rationale alone is insufficient for source review.

children.title: Efficiency Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling conflicts driven by utilization, throughput, or cost performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Efficiency Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A resource-budget boundary between computational efficiency and schedule quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a scheduling instance and let \(\mathcal A_B\) denote algorithms whose computation uses at most budget \(B\), measured in a fixed resource model. For minimization cost \(c_I\), define \(q_I(B)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_B}c_I(A(I))\), assigning \(+\infty\) to infeasible outputs. A strict efficiency tradeoff regime occurs on \([B_1,B_2]\) when \(q_I(B)\) is finite and \(q_I(B')>q_I(B)\) for every \(B'<B\) in the interval. Hence no algorithm using the smaller budget can attain the best quality achievable with the larger budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An efficiency tradeoff regime is a budget range where reducing computational resources strictly worsens the best schedule quality attainable under the fixed resource model.
assumptions_latex: The resource model and budget unit are fixed.
Every algorithm returns either a feasible schedule or an infeasibility-marked output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B'<B\Longrightarrow q_I(B')>q_I(B)\) in a strict efficiency tradeoff regime.

notation.meaning: best cost attainable under budget B

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: budget-indexed attainable quality is a standard efficiency-quality boundary
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits, but the interpretation requires explicit nesting of algorithm classes when B'<B. Moreover, q_I is defined by an infimum, while the conclusion speaks of an achievable best quality without an attainment assumption. No source is supplied to settle the intended computational resource model or formulation.

children.title: Three-Way Pareto Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Nondominated compromises spanning fairness, robustness, and efficiency criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Way Pareto Conflicts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local condition certifying conflict among fairness, robustness, and efficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the feasible schedules and let \(F,R,E:X\to\mathbb R\) be losses for unfairness, nonrobustness, and inefficiency, respectively. A schedule \(x\in X\) is Pareto efficient if no \(y\in X\) satisfies \(F(y)\le F(x)\), \(R(y)\le R(x)\), and \(E(y)\le E(x)\), with at least one strict inequality. A three-way Pareto conflict holds on \(S\subseteq X\) if every \(x\in S\) is Pareto efficient and, for every distinct \(x,y\in S\), neither objective vector weakly dominates the other. Consequently, improving any one loss from a point in \(S\) requires worsening at least one of the other two losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-way conflict is a mutually nondominated set of schedules where improving fairness, robustness, or efficiency necessarily harms at least one other criterion.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
All three criteria are expressed as losses to minimize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(x\in S\), no feasible schedule improves one component of \((F,R,E)\) without worsening another.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: componentwise nondominance is the standard mathematical definition of Pareto conflict
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is plausible, and global Pareto efficiency supports the stated no-improvement-without-worsening consequence. However, mutual nondominance does not by itself establish that all three named criteria participate in the conflict; the tradeoff could involve only two components. A source or a stronger three-way condition is needed.

children.title: Benchmark Overfitting Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Specialization to benchmark structures that inflates apparent scheduling performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Overfitting Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection-induced failure of benchmark performance to estimate deployment performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=(I_1,\ldots,I_n)\) be benchmark instances drawn from distribution \(P_B\), let \(L(A,I)\in[0,1]\) be the loss of solver \(A\), and let \(\mathcal A\) be a finite set of candidate solvers. Selecting \(\widehat A\in\arg\min_{A\in\mathcal A}\widehat L_B(A)\), where \(\widehat L_B(A)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nL(A,I_i)\), overfits the benchmark whenever \(L_{P_D}(\widehat A)-\widehat L_B(\widehat A)>\varepsilon\) for the deployment distribution \(P_D\). Repeated tuning, solver selection, or instance-specific parameter choice using the same \(B\) enlarges the effective candidate set and permits this optimism gap even when every reported benchmark value is computed correctly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benchmark overfitting occurs when repeated selection on one test set makes the chosen scheduler's measured loss substantially more optimistic than its deployment loss.
assumptions_latex: The same benchmark influences solver or parameter selection.
Deployment performance is evaluated under \(P_D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{P_D}(\widehat A)-\widehat L_B(\widehat A)>\varepsilon\) marks benchmark overfitting at tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adaptive selection on reused evaluation data is the standard benchmark-overfitting mechanism
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind matches the mechanism container, but L_{P_D}(A) and the domain of epsilon are not explicitly defined in the statement. More importantly, no source supports the claims about adaptive benchmark reuse and effective candidate-set enlargement in this scheduling context.

children.title: Model-Transfer Limits
children.top_down_role: Restrictions on reusing scheduling models across operational settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Transfer Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasibility and objective-consistency boundary for transferring a scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a source model use feasible set \(X_s\) and cost \(c_s\), while the target operation has feasible set \(X_t\) and cost \(c_t\), both defined over a common schedule universe \(U\). Direct transfer of a source optimizer \(x_s\in\arg\min_{x\in X_s}c_s(x)\) is valid at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) only if \(x_s\in X_t\) and \(c_t(x_s)\le\inf_{x\in X_t}c_t(x)+\varepsilon\). A model-transfer limit is reached whenever either condition fails. In particular, omitted target constraints cause feasibility failure, while changed costs or preferences can make a feasible transferred schedule arbitrarily suboptimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduling model transfers only when its selected schedule remains target-feasible and near-optimal under the target objective; constraint or preference mismatch breaks transfer.
assumptions_latex: \(X_s,X_t\subseteq U\) are nonempty.
Both optimization problems attain their minima when an optimizer is referenced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transfer fails if \(x_s\notin X_t\) or \(c_t(x_s)>\min_{x\in X_t}c_t(x)+\varepsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: feasibility preservation and target regret give a standard optimization transfer criterion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits. Feasibility preservation and target suboptimality form a coherent stipulated transfer criterion, but epsilon should be declared nonnegative and the cost-function domains should be explicit. No citation supports presenting this criterion as the model-transfer boundary for scheduling.

children.title: Distribution-Shift Failures
children.top_down_role: Performance degradation under changed demand, resource, or disruption patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Shift Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deployment failure caused by a change in the distribution of scheduling instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be benchmark and deployment distributions on scheduling instances, and let \(L(A,I)\in[0,1]\) be a fixed solver's loss. Define the shift-induced degradation by \(\Delta(A;P,Q)=\mathbb E_{I\sim Q}L(A,I)-\mathbb E_{I\sim P}L(A,I)\). Deployment fails at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) when \(\Delta(A;P,Q)>\varepsilon\). For bounded loss, \(|\Delta(A;P,Q)|\le d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\); therefore a total-variation neighborhood of radius at most \(\varepsilon\) excludes degradation beyond \(\varepsilon\), whereas shifts outside that neighborhood admit losses whose benchmark and deployment expectations differ by more than \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distribution-shift failure occurs when a scheduler's expected deployment loss exceeds its benchmark loss beyond tolerance; total variation bounds this degradation for bounded losses.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are probability distributions on the same measurable instance space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta(A;P,Q)>\varepsilon\) is failure, while \(|\Delta(A;P,Q)|\le d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the expectation bound by total-variation distance is standard for losses bounded in the unit interval
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is appropriate. The expectation bound is standard for [0,1]-valued measurable losses under the usual total-variation convention, but that convention, measurability, and the domain of epsilon are unstated. No inspectable source is supplied for the bound or its deployment interpretation.

children.title: External-Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on generalizing benchmark evidence to live scheduling environments.

knowledge_statements.title: External-Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantified boundary for generalizing an evaluated scheduler to target environments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Q\) be a declared class of target instance distributions, \(P_B\) the benchmark distribution, and \(L(A,I)\in[0,1]\) the loss of scheduler \(A\). The benchmark conclusion is externally valid over \(\mathcal Q\) at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) if \(\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}|L_Q(A)-L_{P_B}(A)|\le\varepsilon\), where \(L_Q(A)=\mathbb E_{I\sim Q}L(A,I)\). Its external-validity boundary is the largest specified class \(\mathcal Q\) for which this inequality is supported. Any target distribution outside that class carries no guarantee from the benchmark result alone, even if its instances share the same nominal problem label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: External validity extends only to the declared target distributions whose expected scheduler loss remains within tolerance of benchmark performance.
assumptions_latex: All distributions use a common measurable instance space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: External validity over \(\mathcal Q\) requires \(\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}|L_Q(A)-L_{P_B}(A)|\le\varepsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform performance deviation over a declared target class formalizes external validity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-deviation condition is coherent, but a largest admissible distribution class need not exist without specifying an ordered family of candidate classes. Because the exact terminal is a boundary under Scheduling Failure Boundaries, failure_boundary is more suitable than condition. A source is also required to support this formalization.

children.title: Timetabling Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Educational, examination, sports, transport, and event timetabling domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Timetabling Problem Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-domain formulation covering course, examination, and related timetabling families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A timetabling problem consists of events \(E\), periods \(T\), optional resources \(R\), permitted assignments \(D_e\subseteq T\times(R\cup\{\bot\})\), hard constraints \(H\), and soft-constraint penalties \(p_k\). A timetable is a map \(\tau:E\to T\times(R\cup\{\bot\})\) satisfying \(\tau(e)\in D_e\) and every constraint in \(H\). The optimization form minimizes \(\sum_k w_kp_k(\tau)\) over feasible \(\tau\). Problem families are distinguished by event semantics, resource types, conflict and capacity constraints, temporal patterns, and penalty structure; examination and course timetabling are obtained by specializing these components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Timetabling assigns events to allowed periods and resources, satisfies all hard constraints, and minimizes weighted soft violations; families differ by their specialized events and constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(E,T,R\) are finite.
Each penalty \(p_k\) is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{\tau}\{\sum_k w_kp_k(\tau):\tau(e)\in D_e\ \text{for all }e,\ \tau\text{ satisfies }H\}\) is the canonical optimization form.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-domain assignment with hard and soft constraints is the canonical timetabling formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct kind for this problem-family container. However, the weights w_k are not introduced or constrained, and the single optional-resource assignment does not clearly cover timetabling variants requiring multiple simultaneous resources. An authoritative timetabling source is needed before the formulation can be treated as canonical.

children.title: Rostering Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Personnel, crew, healthcare, service, and cyclic rostering domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Rostering Problem Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-horizon formulation covering personnel and workforce rostering families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rostering problem consists of workers \(W\), time slots \(T\), shift or duty types \(S\), qualifications, demands \(d_{t,s}\), and hard and soft labor rules. Binary variables \(x_{w,t,s}\) equal \(1\) when worker \(w\) receives duty \(s\) at time \(t\). A feasible roster satisfies worker availability and qualification, nonoverlap, coverage \(\sum_{w\in W}x_{w,t,s}\ge d_{t,s}\), and all hard temporal rules. Its optimization form minimizes weighted understaffing, preference, fairness, and rule-violation penalties. Families differ by horizon, duty structure, demand model, skill hierarchy, and whether duties or complete work patterns are assigned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rostering assigns qualified workers to duties over time, enforcing availability, coverage, and labor rules while minimizing staffing, preference, fairness, and pattern penalties.
assumptions_latex: \(W,T,S\) are finite.
Hard rules admit at least one roster when feasibility is asserted.
